To address this limitation, we developed a physics-enhanced Hydrological Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation (H-SWAP) to better characterize effective hydrological input. Independent validation showed that H-SWAP increased the mean correlation with runoff from 0.55 to 0.58 and the correlation with soil moisture from 0.168 to 0.171 relative to the Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation (SWAP). Based on H-SWAP, DFAA events in the Yangtze River Basin were characterized by increasing frequency and intensity, shortening duration, and earlier occurrence over the study period. Spatial analysis further indicates a divergence in risk centers, with high-intensity areas tending to shift upstream and high-frequency areas concentrating in downstream regions. Random Forest was used to capture nonlinear and interacting climatic controls, while SHAP and Structural Equation Modeling revealed dominant local moisture effects and indirect influences of Nino3.4 and NAO through local hydroclimatic pathways. Overall, this study provides an improved framework for identifying DFAA events and advances understanding of their multi-scale drivers, with implications for basin-scale risk assessment and water-resources management.

title: Role of moisture transport and land–atmosphere feedbacks in meteorological drought formation over Inner Mongolia
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Xiaolan Yu, Zhiming Han, Limin Duan, Chao Gao, Ziyi Yan, Wenrui Zhang, Jianan Wang, Zhi Li
abstract: Understanding moisture-source contributions and land–atmosphere feedbacks associated with meteorological drought is crucial for early prediction. This study extends meteorological drought analysis beyond precipitation deficits to atmospheric moisture supply and associated moisture-source processes. By integrating monthly analyses with assessments of six representative droughts during 1991–2022, we investigated drought development in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (IMAR) from perspectives of atmospheric moisture-source dynamics and large-scale climate modes. Approximately 92.7% of the multi-year mean precipitation moisture over IMAR originated from terrestrial sources, including 19.9% from locally recycling and 72.8% from external terrestrial regions, whereas oceanic sources contributed only 7.3%. Significant spatial associations between drought severity and locally recycled moisture deficits occurred in four representative events (Moran’s I = 0.42–0.61, p < 0.01). During two long-duration droughts, locally recycled moisture deficits contributed more than 120% of net total moisture deficit because increased moisture from other sources partially compensated for local deficit, whereas local and external terrestrial moisture jointly contributed more than 90% during four short-duration droughts. The contribution of locally recycled moisture increased from −24% during mild droughts to 57% under the most severe conditions, indicating a shift from compensation to drought amplification. Cross-wavelet analysis identified the strongest standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index covariability with arctic oscillation highlighting the importance of mid-to-high-latitude circulation for IMAR drought variability. These findings provide a scientific basis for drought risk assessment and early warning in IMAR, offering a moisture-source perspective on associations between meteorological drought and land–atmosphere feedback in arid and semi-arid regions.

title: A three-step hydrogeochemical approach for designing groundwater-based monitoring networks in seismically active regions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Lorenzo Chemeri, Marco Taussi, Jacopo Cabassi, Marino Domenico Barberio, Davide Fronzi, Alberto Renzulli, Orlando Vaselli
abstract: Hydrogeochemical monitoring of groundwater systems is increasingly recognized as a powerful tool for investigating crustal processes and for the potential identification of geochemical precursors associated with seismic activity. However, the lack of standardized procedures to select and validate suitable monitoring sites still limits the comparability and effectiveness of the existing networks. This study proposes a three-step hydrogeochemical approach aimed at identifying the most appropriate and suitable sampling sites to be included in water monitoring networks for seismic surveillance. The approach was tested in the Pesaro-Urbino (PU) Province (northern Apennines, Italy) that was selected as the pilot-site due to the moderate-to-high seismicity occurring in the area. The characterization phase enabled the definition of four main geochemical facies and the identification of sites potentially affected by deep fluid circulation. The (subsequent) assessment phase integrated chemical and isotopic parameters (δ13C–TDIC, δ34S–SO4, δ11B, 87Sr/86Sr), highlighting deep and structurally controlled flow systems related to the Triassic Anhydrite Burano Formation, located in the area at a depth of at least 620 m. The monitoring phase on selected sites evaluated temporal stability and geochemical resilience, identifying a subset of stable and structurally influenced sites as the most suitable for inclusion in a long-term hydrogeochemical surveillance network. This approach, combining multi-parametric datasets and reproducible criteria, provides a flexible and transferable framework that can be applied to a wide range of geological and geodynamic contexts to support the design of permanent groundwater monitoring systems for seismic research.

title: Exploring the mutual interactions among population, income and water resource availability using a coupled socio-hydrological model
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Elena Cristiano, Carlotta Atzori, Roberto Deidda, Günter Blöschl, Francesco Viola
abstract: Throughout human history, water availability and societal development have been tightly interconnected, mutually influencing one another. Population size and economic prosperity tend to increase when water is not a limiting factor. Conversely, as the population grows, the corresponding water demand rises. To support sustainable water resource management, a socio-hydrological model that includes the interactions among climate, population and wealth is here proposed to represent these complex dynamics. Differently from previous socio-hydrological models, we explicitly couple water availability with both demographic and economic dynamics through two key bidirectional feedback mechanisms. The aim of the model is to explore how water availability influences long-term economic and population dynamics with a particular focus on the consequences of investments in hydraulic infrastructure. Through the analysis of different initial conditions of population density, average income and mean annual rainfall, the evolution of the socio-economic variables and water availability is explored. Results reveal a strong interdependence between water availability and socio-economic dynamics, highlighting the importance of incorporating mutual feedback mechanisms in the model. Mean annual precipitation strongly structures long-term population, income and infrastructure investment, while initial socio-economic conditions modulate the resulting trajectories. Increasing mean annual precipitation from approximately 400 to 1,000 mm yr−1 increases median population density from approximately 50 to 220 inh km−2, while reducing median per-capita infrastructure investment by approximately 60%, largely as a consequence of the inverse relationship between per-capita capital and population density under full water-resource exploitation. The model also identifies combinations of rainfall, population density and income compatible with steady conditions, whose comparison with country-level observations provides a qualitative real-world consistency check.

title: Stratification and mixing alter the response of chlorophyll-a regime to physical constraints in a shallow ice-covered lake
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Wen Zhao, Ming Li, Wenfeng Huang, Georgiy Kirillin, Youpeng Wang, Zhijun Li
abstract: Under-ice phytoplankton biomass and community composition are critical to winter lake ecosystem and can mediate subsequent spring bloom, but their responses to physical constraints remain poorly understood, particularly in mid-latitude cold-arid regions. Using chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) as an indicator of algal biomass, field observations were conducted in a shallow ice-covered lake on the Mongolian Plateau to investigate stratification and aquatic habitats dynamics, and Chl-a’s response. Results indicated that local mixing is primarily governed by rapid changes in thermal structure, while salinity exerts a slower, stabilizing influence on the water column, jointly regulating the vertical position of the deep chlorophyll-a maximum (DCM). Two mixing modes were detected: 1) long-term mixing associated with a temperature dichotomy, which promoted a persistent DCM right beneath the ice; and 2) short-term mixing triggered by abrupt cooling, which produced temporary algal blooms followed by rapid dissolved oxygen (DO) drawdown. Compared to the open-water season, metabolic rate estimation shows that algae require substantially lower irradiance to experience photoinhibition during ice-covered period. Mixing relieves the photoinhibition under cold water just beneath the ice as well as reshapes Chl-a profiles via suspension and settling. Elevated pre-recovery respiration may delay net algal growth by offsetting photosynthetic gains. These findings reveal favorable conditions for under-ice temperature dichotomy, mixing, and algal growth in shallow lakes of temperate arid regions, and clarify the specific role of local mixing in shaping the winter algal dynamics.

title: Quantifying preferential-flow evolution in seasonally frozen irrigated soils under coupled freeze-thaw controls: evidence from the Ningxia Yellow River Irrigation District
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Chunying Wang, Juanjuan Wu, Wangcheng Li, Mingtang Chai, Juanjuan Yu, Yu Zhang
abstract: Preferential flow in seasonally frozen ground exerts a critical control over water and nutrient transport within irrigation districts and underlying groundwater systems. However, quantitative assessments of how interacting environmental drivers govern this process under freeze–thaw conditions remain scarce. To address this knowledge gap, soil profiles from the Ningxia Yellow River Irrigation District—a typical seasonally frozen region in China—were selected for investigation. A Box-Behnken design (BBD) coupled with dye-tracing techniques was employed to visualize preferential flow morphology features, and response surface methodology (RSM) was subsequently used to elucidate the interactive effects of initial water content (IWC), freeze–thaw cycles (FTC), and freezing temperature (FT) on preferential flow metrics. The five fitted response-surface models captured relationships between freeze–thaw factors and target variables, yet predictive performance varied across models. IWC exerted the dominant control over preferential flow development; specifically, low IWC significantly promoted the formation of deep preferential flow pathways. A nonlinear interaction was observed between FTC and FT. Model outputs showed that high FTC combined with less‑negative freezing temperatures generated larger infiltration extents and a higher preferential flow proportion (PFP). Finally, laboratory-based multi-objective optimization yielded the mathematically optimal freeze–thaw parameter combination for preferential flow formation within the parameter range of this experiment. This study offers theoretical insights into preferential flow behavior under multi-factor freeze–thaw coupling and provides tentative references for regional water-resource management and soil ecological improvement.

title: Multi-horizon early warning of harmful algal blooms in cascade reservoirs using mechanistic data augmentation and machine learning
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Sungjin Kim, Sewoong Chung
abstract: Hydrologic regulation and variability influence cyanobacterial blooms in cascade reservoirs, yet sparse monitoring and infrequent bloom events constrain early warning. We developed a hybrid framework coupling CE-QUAL-W2 simulations with machine-learning classifiers to predict bloom alerts across multiple horizons in a Korean cascade reservoir system. Mechanistic augmentation increased training data resolution from weekly to daily while preserving physically plausible hydrodynamic, thermal, and water-quality dynamics. Recall reached 0.89 and 0.76 at 1-day and 2-day horizons, respectively, exceeding persistence baselines of 0.68 and 0.58. At 3 days, recall approached persistence, indicating limited additional predictive skill. Because predictions used observed meteorological inputs, performance represents a retrospective upper bound on operational forecasting skill. External validation using held-out observations from two independent bloom years with contrasting hydrologic regimes yielded caution-level recall of 0.60–0.71 at 1 day and 0.50–0.71 at 2 days. These estimates, reported with 95% confidence intervals, provide preliminary evidence of transferability given the small numbers of observed alert events (10 and 7). Explainable artificial intelligence identified water temperature, residence time, and discharge as dominant predictors, linking warning skill to thermal and hydrologic controls. Mechanistic augmentation outperformed non-mechanistic interpolation, whereas synthetic oversampling degraded performance, potentially through physically implausible samples. The findings demonstrate the value of process-informed data augmentation for bloom early warning under sparse monitoring. Using routinely monitored variables, the framework could support intensified monitoring and assessment of coordinated upstream flow regulation within a 1–2-day warning window, with transfer to other cascade reservoirs requiring site-specific recalibration and evaluation using forecast meteorological inputs.

title: A multiscale equivalent porous media method for simulating flow and solute transport in fractured media
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Lei Tian, Litang Hu, Jianchong Sun, Junchao Zhang
abstract: Multiscale fracture networks are common in fractured porous media (FPM), yet their complex geometries and interactions with the rock matrix remain difficult to characterize. This complexity poses a major challenge for accurately simulating groundwater flow and solute transport in FPM systems. Here, we develop a multiscale equivalent porous media (MEPM) method for simulating flow and solute transport in coupled fracture–matrix systems. In the MEPM framework, small-scale fractures are implicitly incorporated into a synthetically enhanced matrix through permeability tensors, whereas medium- and large-scale fractures are explicitly mapped onto refined grids to represent their geometries and hydraulic controls. Numerical experiments show that, relative to a conventional equivalent porous media (CEPM) model, the MEPM model more accurately reproduces complex solute distribution patterns, particularly preferential flow caused by heterogeneous and anisotropic fracture hydraulics. Compared with the discrete fracture network (DFN) model, the MEPM approach reduced the computational time from 2,200 to 8 min. The corresponding root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) for flow and solute transport were 0.18 m and 0.05–0.08 mg/L, respectively, demonstrating a substantial improvement in computational efficiency without a significant loss of accuracy. The MEPM model also captured mass exchange between the fracture and matrix domains. Neglecting the enhancement of the matrix by small-scale fractures led to differences of 21.70–65.40 m in the predicted solute migration distance. In addition, simulations of solute transport involving different adsorption and attenuation processes successfully reproduced spatiotemporal concentration differences between the fracture and matrix domains. These results demonstrate that the MEPM method provides an efficient and accurate framework for simulating groundwater flow and solute transport in multiscale fractured porous media while maintaining a practical computational burden.

title: A physically based event model coupling litter interception, lateral drainage and dynamic surface-seal conductivity on afforested loess slopes
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Changkun Ma, Jiayi Lu, Quanjiu Wang, Xiaoxu Jia
abstract: The forest-floor litter layer has long been known to protect the soil surface from raindrop impact, yet litter-specific event models typically treat the layer as an interception or storage deduction that leaves the infiltration capacity of the soil beneath it unchanged. We show that, of the three litter processes examined here, omitting this protective function is the largest structural source of error in predicting storm infiltration and the outlet hydrograph on afforested loess slopes, and correct it with a Green–Ampt model extended by three interface processes: litter interception, lateral drainage within the saturated litter, and a surface conductivity that decays with the raindrop kinetic energy transmitted through the litter. The model was tested with a simulated-rainfall factorial (30–120 mm h−1 × 10–30° × bare versus litter-covered soil; 96 runs) and natural-rainfall runoff plots (2023–2024) in a Robinia pseudoacacia plantation on the Chinese Loess Plateau. Litter held event-end surface conductivity at 15.1–16.9 mm h−1, near the uncrusted 18.2 mm h−1, whereas bare surfaces sealed to 3.6–6.4 mm h−1, with diminishing returns above about 0.6 kg m−2 of litter within the tested range. Cover consequently raised infiltration by up to 78%, delayed runoff onset by 4.9–12.5 min and lowered peak discharge significantly at ≥ 60 mm h−1 but not at 30 mm h−1, while litter interflow carried 14–52% of outlet discharge, rising with slope. The coupled model reached a validation NSE of 0.87 (KGE 0.88), against 0.64 for an interception-deduction model and 0.38 for bare soil. Removing the seal-suppression term lowered NSE by 0.16 and caused a 17% underestimate of storm infiltration, whereas omitting lateral drainage overestimated infiltration and underestimated discharge on steeper slopes. On these surfaces the litter layer matters less for the water it stores than for the sealing it prevents. Within the bounds of plot scale, two rainfall seasons and one soil type, the model supports event-runoff and precipitation-resource assessment in loess plantations.

title: Changes in drought transition dynamics under future climate in Great Britain: A Markov chain analysis using SPI and SSI
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Nishant Gaur, Encarni Medina-Lopez, Lindsay Beevers
abstract: Drought in Great Britain (GB) has received increasing attention following recent events, including those of 2018–2019 and 2022. Previous studies based on UKCP18 climate projections and the enhanced Future Flows and Groundwater dataset (eFLaG) have reported increasing drought frequency, duration, and severity across much of GB. However, these conventional drought characteristics do not fully describe how drought states evolve over time. This study addresses that gap by quantifying projected changes in drought transition dynamics across 133 parent catchments in GB using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Standardized Streamflow Index (SSI). Drought frequency and severity were evaluated for baseline, near-future, and far-future periods. First-order Markov chain transition matrices were constructed for meteorological and hydrological drought states and compared between baseline and future periods using a non-parametric permutation test. The matrices were then decomposed into downward mobility, upward mobility, dry-to-dry persistence, and wet-to-wet persistence metrics. Results reveal a clear south-east to north-west contrast in future drought transition behaviour. Southern and south-eastern catchments show stronger increases in downward mobility and dry-state persistence, indicating a greater tendency towards drying and weaker recovery towards wetter states. In contrast, north-western catchments show more heterogeneous responses, including simultaneous increases in dry-to-dry and wet-to-wet persistence. Directional change and persistence do not peak in the same regions, indicating that future drought intensification may arise through different transition mechanisms across GB. These findings provide a process-based perspective on future drought evolution, with implications for drought-risk assessment and long-term water management.

title: A nonstationary index reveals intensifying global dry–wet abrupt alternation events and their climate drivers
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Pengcheng Xu, Shuchang Luo, Dong Wang, Yuankun Wang, Xiaolei Fu
abstract: As global water cycles become more erratic, the sudden flip from drought to flood is putting immense pressure on ecosystems and water security worldwide. However, how the trend-induced nonstationarity within the water balance series modulates the evolution of dry-wet abrupt alternation (DWAA) events remains poorly understood, especially as climate change fundamentally alters the atmospheric supply–demand balance. With the help of Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS), this study introduces a nonstationary standardized DWAA ( I NSDWA ) index to investigate how often and how intensely regions flip between extreme dry and wet conditions. By accounting for these shifting climatic trends, we can more accurately track global whiplash events and uncover the physical forces driving them. Contrasting stationary and nonstationary frameworks reveals that trend-caused nonstationarity driven by large-scale climatic factors, play a much larger role in triggering these extreme transitions than previously thought. Over the last six decades (1961–2024), the world has seen a sharp rise in both the frequency and intensity of sudden “whiplash” transitions between drought and flood. This escalation is not accidental and is fueled by increasingly erratic atmospheric moisture and shifting circulation patterns. Our data shows that ENSO appears to be consistently associated with these flips, with La Niña phases notably intensifying their impact. As the climate continues to warm, the danger from these rapid hydrological swings will only grow. These results highlights the need for enhanced monitoring systems to better anticipate such abrupt shifts.

title: A realistic spatiotemporally variable rainfall event generator for flood catastrophe modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Yuran Li, Jian He, Lun Dai, Yunhong Lv, Yuanen Pang, Limin Zhang
abstract: Catastrophe modeling, which simulates regional hazard scenarios and losses under extreme events, has become an important tool for flood risk management. Observations of extremes are inherently scarce because such events are rare, making it essential to augment the historical record with synthetic rainfall events that are realistic and spatiotemporally variable. Current probabilistic rainfall models primarily focus on either single-station analysis or the spatial dependence of rainfall metrics (e.g., cumulative rainfall). However, these approaches often fail to capture the dynamic spatiotemporal characteristics of short-duration extreme rainfall events, which are the primary drivers of urban flooding. In this study, we propose a novel spatiotemporal stochastic rainfall generator to simulate rainfall sequences at multiple stations while preserving spatial correlation, as well as realistic hourly temporal variability and correlation. The generator is applied to and calibrated in Hong Kong, a densely urbanized and flood-prone coastal city, using hourly in-situ observations from 141 stations during 1984–2017. Despite operating at hourly resolution, the generator reproduces rainfall statistics consistently across accumulation durations of 1–24 h. It reproduces the main statistical characteristics of historical rainfall, with Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency values of 0.836–0.986 for accumulation durations of 4–72 h. It also captures the spatial patterns of extremes, with a Pearson correlation of 0.806. Hydrodynamic simulations further demonstrate that the realistic temporal variability produced by the generator leads to average flood depth differences of 18.1% and 25.8% compared with the simplified exponential and constant hyetograph scenarios, respectively. These results highlight the importance of representing realistic short-term rainfall variability in stochastic rainfall models for reliable catastrophe modeling.

title: Freezing onset of soil pore water under non-stationary conditions: a heterogeneous nucleation framework
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Zunyi Wu, Zhaohe Wang, Jiaqi Tian, Dihan Zhao, Mengke Zhou, Shuangyang Li, Yuanming Lai, Chong Wang
abstract: The freezing onset of soil pore water is initiated by nucleation, and the nucleation temperature ( T s n ) marks the critical condition at which pore water exits the supercooled state and crystal growth begins. Based on classical nucleation theory (CNT), a heterogeneous nucleation model was developed using the cluster approach. Non-stationary effects were incorporated under non-isothermal conditions, and phase transition in finite time and pore volume was described using a stochastic nucleation model based on the Poisson process. Comparison with 45 datasets reported by different researchers showed that the model captures T s n variations with soil properties and cooling conditions and clarifies the microscopic mechanism of initial phase transition during soil freezing. Freezing onset occurs within a stochastic temperature interval rather than at a single fixed temperature. Solute concentration and pore radius ( r p ) affect T s n by changing the energetic state of pore water: T s n decreases with decreasing water activity ( a w ), whereas equilibrium freezing temperature ( T f ) and T s n increase with increasing r p as curvature effect weakens. When r p approaches 1 μm, the energetic state of pore water stabilizes; when r p approaches 10 μm, the statistical effect weakens, nucleation is promoted only in local water regions around impurities, and T s n becomes insensitive to further increases in r p . The contact angle ( θ i s ) serves as an equivalent material parameter for the ice nucleation ability of impurity interfaces, and lower θ i s markedly increases T s n . The cooling rate weakly affects bulk water but induces a pronounced temperature lag in systems with restricted molecular migration.

title: Changes in groundwater storage and driving factors in China’s major developed plains under over-exploitation control and strict management policies
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Minhua Ling, Weiting Zhu, Jiangbo Yu, Tao Li, Guangpeng Pu, Jiawei Yao
abstract: In response to severe groundwater over-exploitation, China government has implemented comprehensive governance and strict management policies. Analyzing changes in groundwater storage and their drivers in China’s major developed plains under these interventions offers critical insight into policy efficacy and supports the enhancement of groundwater recovery and conservation strategies. This study leveraged GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite data alongside in-situ groundwater monitoring records to estimate and validate Groundwater Storage Anomalies (GWSA) across China’s major developed plains from 2003 to 2023.The study period is divided into three phases according to the policy implementation process: a pre-intensification phase (2003–2010), an initial control phase (2011–2018), and an intensified governance phase (2019–2023). Results show that groundwater storage generally declined during 2003–2023, but the trajectories differed markedly among phases and regions. In some heavily exploited eastern plains, depletion intensified during Phase 2 and then shifted to stabilization or recovery in Phase 3; for example, the trend in the Haihe Plain changed from −2.24 mm/month in Phase 2 to +1.91 mm/month in Phase 3. By contrast, several arid northwestern plains remained under persistent depletion, with Phase 3 declines reaching −2.34 mm/month in the Ordos Plateau and −2.75 mm/month on the northern slopes of the Tianshan Mountains. Random forest regression further indicates a phased shift in dominant controls from precipitation during the earlier stage to groundwater extraction during the later stage in most regions. These results suggest that strengthened groundwater governance, together with inter-basin water transfer and extraction reduction, has promoted recovery in some eastern plains, whereas climatic aridity and rigid agricultural water demand still constrain groundwater restoration in northwestern China. The study provides a transferable framework for evaluating groundwater policy effectiveness in regions facing concurrent climate stress and intensive groundwater use.

title: Key roles of river network structure in the spatial distribution of dissolved and suspended particle-associated per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Liang Yu, Yueyang Dong, Xiaolei Xing, Wucheng Ma, Xiang Zhu, Zulin Hua, Wenqing Shi
abstract: River network structures can significantly influence the distribution of watershed dissolved and suspended particle-associated per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (D- and S-PFASs), yet current prioritization studies emphasize land use and environmental variables, neglecting their potential impacts. This study integrates field investigations, GIS-based information, and spatial stream network models (SSNMs) to clarify whether river network structures can provide additional information for explaining watershed PFAS distributions. The results showed that D-PFASs displayed a clear stream order-dependent distribution pattern, revealed by relatively consistent profiles and increasing concentrations along downstream gradients. River network structures exerted a higher explanatory capacity (17.4%) for D-PFAS distribution than land use (10.5%) and environmental variables (7.3%), with hydrological connectivity (HCI) identified as a key factor facilitating its downstream transport and spatial dependence. SSNMs supported the significance of distribution dependence for D-PFASs, attributing 39.4% of the variance to residual flow-connected spatial autocorrelation and 60.6% to fixed effects from HCI and turbidity. In contrast, S-PFASs showed regional-specific enrichments mostly influenced by environmental variables (30.8%), particularly particle-related processes as indicated by SPM and turbidity, followed by river network structures (12.2%) and land use (3.5%). Fixed covariates, including storage capacity, turbidity, and agricultural land, constituted a significant 95.9% of the variance in explaining S-PFAS distribution, as determined by SSNMs. The findings provide a new insight into hydrological controls on the transport and distribution of PFASs.

title: N-tuple collocation for reference-free uncertainty estimation from multi-source hydrological data: beyond triple collocation and three-cornered hat
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Hung T. Pham, Seokhyeon Kim
abstract: Reference-free uncertainty estimation is needed when multiple hydrological datasets are available but reliable ground truth is sparse, scale-mismatched, or absent. Existing approaches, including triple collocation (TC) and the three-cornered hat method (TCH), are limited by fixed triplet requirements, negative error-variance failures, or sensitivity to multiplicative scaling. We introduce N-tuple collocation (NC), a reference-free framework that estimates residual error covariance from three or more collocated datasets by decomposing the observation covariance into a rank-one signal component and a residual covariance term while constraining error variances to remain non-negative and enforcing residual covariance feasibility. In covariance experiments, the box-constrained NC stage produced no negative-variance failures across the tested error-correlation and scaling conditions, remained weakly sensitive to signal-to-noise ratio, became more stable as the number of datasets increased, and improved with longer records. Additional seasonal experiments supported feasibility of the final estimator, with condition-dependent accuracy. We demonstrated NC in a global soil moisture application using ASCAT, SMAP, LPRM, and ERA5-Land products for 2020–2024, with held-out 2023–2024 validation against International Soil Moisture Network observations. In the three-product ASCAT–SMAP–ERA5 experiment, NC increased the valid-pixel domain relative to TC and TCH, with small favorable differences in paired validation comparisons and uncertainty in others. In the four-product ASCAT–SMAP–LPRM–ERA5 experiment, NC remained applicable beyond the classical TC setting and provided broader feasible coverage than TCH. These results indicate that NC provides a scalable, variance-admissible framework for reference-free uncertainty estimation from multi-source hydrological data, with soil moisture merging serving as a global demonstration of its utility in reference-limited settings.

title: Urban river water quality heterogeneity across contrasting scenarios and within river reaches in relation to riparian anthropogenic activities and antecedent meteorological conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Anqi He, Junjiang Zhou, Bin Yang, Qinghe Qu, Fenfen Tian, Shiqing Zhou, Dongbo Wang, Bin Yang, Shenglian Luo
abstract: Characterizing spatial heterogeneity in urban river water quality is essential for identifying localized water quality contrasts, distinguishing broader differences among river contexts from within-reach variability, and designing representative monitoring. This study investigated eight water quality parameters (WQPs) across six city–river–sampling-date scenarios in four Chinese cities using field measurements, unmanned aerial vehicle multispectral imagery, and an instance-adaptive mixed-distance ensemble (IMDE) model. Field sampling identified eutrophic conditions based on Chla at 86.41% of sites and heavy-pollution classifications for COD (66.99%), NH3-N (48.54%), CODMn (40.78%), and TP (31.07%). IMDE adaptively weighted four base models at each prediction location to generate spatially continuous WQP information, achieving a mean R2 of 0.877 under a random 7:3 train–test split and retaining predictive capability under stricter spatial and grouped validation. All eight WQPs differed significantly among scenarios, while within-reach analysis identified localized high- and low-value clusters and spatial outliers. Riparian anthropogenic associations varied across buffer scales and scenarios, with maximum adjusted explained variation reaching 64.23–89.42% in four cities. Industrial and agricultural activities showed recurrent associations with several nutrient- and pollution-related WQPs, whereas residential and commercial patterns were less consistent. Contrasting antecedent meteorological backgrounds coincided with parameter- and scenario-specific differences in spatial dispersion and local extremes. Together, these findings show that scenario-level summaries can mask parameter-specific clusters and spatial outliers within individual reaches, highlighting the value of high-resolution mapping for targeted monitoring. Riparian associations require scale- and scenario-specific interpretation, while antecedent meteorological conditions warrant consideration when comparing sampling campaigns.

title: Anticipating climate-change effects on coastal water quality: development of ensemble machine-learning models
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mehvish Bilal, Zaher Mundher Yaseen, Syed Masiur Rahman, Haitham Elnakar, Mohammad Al-Suwaiyan, Shaikh Abdur Razzak
abstract: Growing concern surrounds the impacts of climate change on nearshore coastal water quality (CWQ), yet systematic and in-depth research remains scarce. This study integrates in-situ CWQ observations, satellite-derived variables, and climate variables to assess the effects of climate change on chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and Turbidity in Deep Bay, Hong Kong. Machine learning (ML) models were trained on historical in-situ and satellite observations and then driven with downscaled Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) scenarios to generate projections for 2025–2100. Under the moderate-emissions Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP2-4.5),MRI-ESM2-0-based Chl-a projections show relatively small changes in magnitude through 2100, although the Seasonal Mann-Kendall test identifies a statistically significant increasing trend for XGBoost. In contrast, the high-emission pathway SSP5-8.5 produces a modest decline in Chl-a after 2080, indicating potential late-century vulnerability. Turbidity projections remain within a narrow range (0.048–0.051 m−1), although the direction and statistical significance of trends vary across ML models. Shapley Additive Explanations, Sobol indices, and partial dependence plots identified sea-surface salinity, sea-surface temperature, and air temperature as influential predictors of Chl-a, with nonlinear and interaction effects under increased warming. The study provides a scenario-based, interpretable assessment of potential climate-related shifts in CWQ to support targeted monitoring and adaptive management.

title: From ESWB to CDI-ESWB: A novel daily drought warning and monitoring method based on Eigen small water bodies using sentinel-1&2 and machine learning
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Yunyuan Yang, Zhe Wang, Zhen Zhang, Hui Wang, Xi Wang, Linguang Miao, Yangyang Ma, Ping He, Linyi Li, Wen Zhang, Lingkui Meng
abstract: Eigen Small Water Bodies (ESWB) are micro-scale hydrological units that can provide sensitive and directly observable signals of drought conditions in advance, making them well suited for drought warning and monitoring. In this study, Chuxiong City in Yunnan Province, southwestern China, was selected as the study area. A total of 982 Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 images from February 15, 2017 to June 1, 2025, together with Dynamic World V1, DEM, daily precipitation, and daily soil moisture data were employed. Under spatiotemporal constraints with machine learning, water bodies identified by SDWI (Sentinel-1) and NDWI (Sentinel-2) provided positive training samples, whereas the maximum water extent derived from Dynamic World V1 was used to define negative samples for Random Forest–based ESWB extraction, achieving IoU of 0.967 (Sentinel-1) and 0.996 (Sentinel-2), with only a 0.05% ESWB area difference between same-day images, outperforming four UNet-based methods. Missing ESWB were filled with the nearest available observations, and the resulting ESWB area and number were then individually interpolated to daily scale to calculate drought Eigen Small Water Bodies Index (ESWBI). The mean ESWBI exhibited an annual “V”-shaped pattern, reaching its minimum around mid-July each year. Drought warning rules were established based on the ESWBI change rate and the difference between the mean ESWBI and the current ESWBI values. A total of 74.6% (53 cases) of drought warnings matched the results of official meteorological warnings, and the ESWBI-based approach provided earlier warnings by approximately 5 days. The CDI-ESWB integrates three complementary components: precipitation, which characterizes the atmospheric water supply; the ESWBI derived from the dynamics of ESWB area and number, which captures the integrated surface water response to drought; and soil moisture, which represents the land-surface water status in the vegetation root zone. The daily CDI-ESWB was then computed as the arithmetic mean of the Z-scores of the three components with equal weights. Based on the daily CDI-ESWB, five categories—Severe Wet, Mild Wet, Normal, Mild Drought, and Severe Drought—were defined using threshold values of 1.5, 0.5, −0.5, and −1.5, enabling daily quantification of drought dynamics. Severe drought events in 2019 and 2023 were successfully captured, consistent with historical records, demonstrating the effectiveness of CDI-ESWB for drought monitoring. This study introduces a novel framework for daily drought warning and daily drought monitoring based on ESWB, providing a new perspective for drought warning and drought monitoring applications using Remote Sensing.

title: Advancing CMIP6 daily precipitation projections through hybrid bias-correction and semi-supervised downscaling with uncertainty quantification
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mahnoosh Moghaddasi, Mansour Moradi, Mehdi Mohammadi Ghaleni, Mehdi Jamei, Kaveh Mohammadpour
abstract: Challenges such as the underestimation of extreme events limit the effectiveness of statistical downscaling models in accurately projecting daily precipitation. This study introduces a machine-learning-based downscaling framework that integrates a novel semi-supervised preprocessing approach, Intra-Extrapolation Representative Labeling (IERL), which forms the basis of the Hybrid Bias-Correction and Semi-Supervised Learning Downscaling (HBC-SSLD) method, to improve the representation of precipitation extremes. The proposed framework was evaluated under different climatic conditions in Iran and compared with conventional machine-learning and standalone downscaling approaches using multiple performance metrics. The best-performing models were subsequently identified based on their ability to reproduce Precipitation Extreme Indices (PEIs) and their predictive uncertainty across arid and humid climates. The selected models were then applied to project PEIs under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for two future periods, 2025–2054 and 2084–2114. The results showed that the proposed approach substantially improved performance, reducing the average relative error by 83% in arid climates and 75% in humid climates compared with the standalone models. Among the evaluated models, HBC-SSLD-XGB and HBC-SSLD-RVFL achieved the highest accuracy and lowest uncertainty in arid and humid climates, respectively, when applied to CanESM5 and IPSL-CM6A-LR. The selected models projected the largest reduction in annual mean precipitation under SSP5-8.5 during the long-term period, reaching 0.3 and 0.4 mm/day in arid and humid climates, respectively. Monthly precipitation generally decreased across all months in the humid climate, whereas the arid climate showed variable changes. No significant trends were detected for most PEIs under either scenario or future period, except for Consecutive Dry Days (CDD) and Consecutive Wet Days (CWD), which exhibited significant trends in both climatic conditions.

title: Attribution analysis of differentiated changes in hydrological variables in the Qinling mountain watershed based on an improved SWAT model
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Li Gong, Kang Liang
abstract: Hydrological attribution in mountainous zones is complicated by uncertainties in runoff generation, soil hydraulics, and vegetation dynamics. We improved the SWAT model for the two Qinling subregions: the southern mountainous region of the Wei River (SMWR) and the Yiluo River Basin (YLR) by incorporating experimentally derived SCS-CN initial abstraction ratios (λ), field-constrained saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks), and external leaf area index (LAI). Using the improved model, a two-level attribution framework was applied for 1993–2020. The first level quantified the effects of direct climate, land-use/cover change (LUCC), and LAI on runoff (Q) and evapotranspiration (ET); the second partitioned direct climate effects into precipitation (P) and other climatic factors and LAI-mediated effects into climate-, CO2-, and LUCC-driven pathways. Model improvements increased validation-period Kling–Gupta efficiency from 0.638 to 0.711 in the SMWR and from 0.506 to 0.718 in the YLR. Direct climate effects dominated Q and ET changes, contributing 90.93% and 88.53% to Q and 85.88% and 66.77% to ET in the SMWR and YLR, respectively, whereas LUCC and LAI had minor contributions. Direct climate effects were driven primarily by P, with weaker effects from other climatic factors. LAI-mediated effects were small because source-specific pathways offset each other. In the SMWR, CO2-driven LAI offset Q but enhanced ET, whereas climate-driven LAI enhanced Q but offset ET. In the YLR, LUCC-driven LAI enhanced Q whereas CO2-driven LAI offset Q; CO2-driven LAI enhanced ET, whereas LUCC-driven LAI generally offset ET. Separating overall drivers from internal pathways improves interpretation of climate–vegetation–hydrology interactions.

title: The hydrological effects of dispersed stormwater management at the catchment scale
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Congying Li, Matthew J. Burns, Christopher J. Walsh, Moss J. Imberger, Peter J. Poelsma, Robert James, Darren G. Bos, Tim D. Fletcher
abstract: Urban stormwater drainage alters stream flow regimes. Even small rainfall events produce greater quickflow volumes and peak flows from catchments drained using traditional stormwater management, degrading stream ecosystems. Stormwater Control Measures (SCMs) aim to mitigate such impacts. However, the cumulative effect on stream flow regimes of SCMs applied across a catchment, including widespread application of at-source SCMs, has been little studied. We assessed storm-event quickflow volume and peak-flow responses to dispersed SCMs retrofitted into existing urban catchments across five experimental catchments on two streams, including three upstream tributaries of one stream, over eight years, alongside observations from three reference and two control streams as part of a BACRI (Before-After-Control-Reference-Impact) experimental design. Results showed that the dispersed implementation of SCMs reduced quickflow volume and peak flow at the storm-event scale. The effect was greatest for frequent small storm events (2–8 mm). This is the first catchment-scale study to demonstrate such effects for the retrofit of SCMs, largely applied at-source, into urban catchments, and thus increases confidence that such investments will reduce flow-induced degradation of urban streams.

title: Spatial and temporal variability in model parameters governing groundwater flood-potential
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Beatrice Richieri, Pablo Merchán-Rivera, Gabriele Chiogna
abstract: Groundwater flooding poses a hazard in shallow aquifers, yet predicting its spatial occurrence is highly challenged by parameter uncertainty and the limited availability of observation points. Using a distributed MODFLOW-NWT model of a shallow alluvial aquifer in Garching (Germany), we performed Morriś global screening and ranking sensitivity analyses on 20 uncertain parameters, including zonally parameterized hydraulic conductivity and specific yield, across three hydrologic periods. We compared how four monitoring configurations influence parameter-sensitivity patterns using a head-based objective function and mapped spatially distributed sensitivities of cell-wise shallow-groundwater responses using a threshold-exceedance metric. The seven most influential parameters were integrated into a Bayesian framework (DREAM) to quantify uncertainty and generate probability maps of shallow groundwater conditions based on both instantaneous threshold exceedance and event duration. Results showed that parameter sensitivities depend strongly on the local hydrological processes represented by the monitoring configurations; for instance, the normalized μ ^ k ∗ of the Mühlbach riverbed conductance decreases from 19.90% for monitoring points located close to the channel to 11.29% for monitoring points located farther away. Spatial sensitivity mapping revealed pronounced heterogeneity, with hydraulic conductivity and riverbed conductance among the dominant parameters and maximum normalized sensitivities locally exceeding 50%. Posterior uncertainty of the effective zonal parameters reflected the spatial distribution of the monitoring network, with hydrogeological zones well represented by monitoring observations exhibiting better-constrained parameter estimates, while poorly monitored zones remained more weakly constrained and represent priorities for future network expansion. This integrated framework demonstrates how monitoring data can be leveraged to generate uncertainty-aware, probabilistic estimates of shallow groundwater conditions and groundwater-flood potential, accounting for both event probability and persistence.

title: Urban water system vulnerability under climate change, demand growth, and institutional friction
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Sara Alonso Vicario, George M. Hornberger, Adam Wiechman, Maurizio Mazzoleni, Margaret Garcia
abstract: Climate change and rising water demands are straining urban water systems designed under assumptions of stationarity. In this context, selecting adaptation strategies requires water utilities to navigate climate uncertainty alongside financial and regulatory constraints. To understand these challenges, we apply a dynamic systems model that conceptualizes an urban water system comprising users, a utility that operates the reservoirs, and a governing body responsible for infrastructure investments, rate setting, and demand curtailment. The model is used to assess how the City of Santa Rosa, California, can adapt to changes in seasonal streamflow driven by climate change and shifts in irrigation demand under different water management approaches. Across ten global climate models (GCMs), six project improved system performance, three indicate declines, and one shows no substantial change. Improvements are associated with GCMs projecting higher winter inflows and moderate summer reductions, whereas sharp spring and early-summer flow losses lead to performance declines. When future irrigation demands are included, all GCMs project a decline in performance, with only 40% of demand met and rate increases reaching up to 33% in the worst-case GCM. Delayed investments reduce minimum reliability without significant rate benefits, while more responsive management mitigates unmet demand and slightly reduces rate burdens. The results reveal trade-offs between objectives, such as the one between loss reliability and ease rate burden, depending on the management approach. This study provides valuable insights for Santa Rosa on how to plan for future changes that may affect its water supply and offers a transferable framework to support adaptation planning in other cities.

title: ARISE: a novel automated hybrid system for multi-timescale flood forecasting and operational early warning in northeast India
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Sagar Debbarma, Sameer Mandal, Arnab Bandyopadhyay, Aditi Bhadra
abstract: Reliable multi-timescale flood forecasting remains a critical need in data-scarce mountain river basins, where national warning systems provide insufficient lead time for anticipatory action. This study introduces ARISE (Automated River Intelligence System for Early-Warning), an automated hybrid flood forecasting and early warning system developed and operationally deployed in the Tlawng River Basin of Mizoram, Northeast India. ARISE integrates two sub-systems: a Gauge-to-Gauge (G2G) short-term sub-system that utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to forecast 24-hour downstream stage from real-time upstream observations, and an NWP-driven medium-term sub-system that combines XGBoost-based bias correction of ECMWF ensemble forecasts with a hybrid HEC-HMS–GRU–XGBoost model chain to forecast stage at 3, 5, and 7-day lead times. Both sub-systems share a quantile-based five-tier danger level classification. The G2G sub-system achieved NSE of 0.77 and RMSE of 0.78 m, while the medium-term sub-system achieved discharge NSE values of 0.763, 0.744, and 0.735 at 3, 5, and 7-day lead times, with near-zero PBIAS across all horizons. Retrospective hindcasts of three major flood seasons (2018, 2024, and 2025) showed that ARISE pre-signaled all Extreme Danger peaks at Warning level or above, expanding the warning window from 12 to 24 h to 7 days. Event-based verification for 2018–2022 gave Severe Warning POD of 0.62–0.71 and FAR of 0.20–0.38. Operated with the Irrigation and Water Resources Department of Mizoram under the World Bank-funded National Hydrology Project, ARISE delivers daily automated flood bulletins, demonstrating that reliable, institutionally coordinated flood early warning can be achieved in data-scarce mountain basins using open-source tools.

title: Investigating the spatial patterns in the dependence of daily rainfall depth on wet spell duration over Europe
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Carmelo Cammalleri, Eren Senyuz, Carmelo Agnese, Giorgio Baiamonte, Stefano Ferraris, Tommaso Martini
abstract: Daily rainfall amount and occurrence are often investigated separately, without accounting for the possible dependence of rainfall depth (h) on wet spell duration (ws). Here, we show that this dependence occurs across Europe and exhibits consistent spatial patterns. The approach adopted for modelling this dependence relies on a log-growth relationship between ws and normalized arithmetic (AM) and geometric (GM) means. Applications of this model at European scale using E-OBS daily gridded data between 1981 and 2020 closely reproduce the empirical conditional means, with mean absolute differences below 1 mm and relative differences smaller than 10%. By assuming that daily rainfall depths follow a Polylog distribution, the full domain of h|ws dependence is captured by only four parameters (AM, GM, and the two parameters of the log-growth function). A spatial cluster analysis of these parameters highlights three major regimes: “strong” dependence in the Mediterranean and the western coast of Europe, “weak” dependence over most of eastern Europe, and a transition “intermediate” dependence region in the middle. Decision tree and random forest models reproduce the broad spatial patterns of these three regions using a limited number of predictors: elevation, mean annual temperature, and frequency of wet days. This result highlights those regions where neglecting the h|ws dependence may lead to substantial differences (even larger than 10 mm on the 90-th quantile), but also suggests how the dependence patterns can be systematically associated with coherent hydroclimatic gradients, which reflect common rainfall-generating mechanisms, such as orographic effects, and may also be linked to large-scale teleconnection patterns.

title: Physics-guided dual-path deep network with differentiable Muskingum routing for multi-station streamflow forecasting: balancing accuracy and interpretability in a karst basin
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Yuting Mao, Jie Niu, Mingxia He, Xiaolin Gu, Xiaosong Cheng, Ya Wang, Sha Li, Pan Wu, Yong Fu, Qixin Wu, Dongdong Liu, Bill X. Hu
abstract: Accurate and interpretable streamflow forecasting remains a fundamental challenge in hydrology, particularly in complex karst basins characterized by strong nonlinearity and heterogeneous flow pathways. Physics-based models provide process understanding but are often computationally demanding and difficult to calibrate, whereas purely data-driven models achieve high predictive skill but lack physical consistency and interpretability. To address these limitations, we propose a physics-guided deep learning (PGDL) framework that integrates a dual-path runoff representation with a differentiable Muskingum routing scheme for multi-station streamflow forecasting. The model decomposes runoff into fast-flow and slow-flow components using a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network and a reservoir-based module, respectively. These components are subsequently routed through a differentiable Muskingum operator with learnable parameters, followed by a residual correction module to reduce systematic bias. Additional physics-inspired constraints, including water balance, recession behavior, and auxiliary baseflow supervision, are incorporated to enhance physical consistency. The proposed framework is evaluated at three hydrological stations in a representative karst basin of the Nanming River, China. Results show that PGDL achieves superior predictive performance, with an average NSE exceeding 0.95, outperforming a suite of advanced baselines, including ANN, CNN, LSTM, Transformer, GNN-based, and mass-conserving recurrent models. Beyond accuracy improvements, the model yields physically meaningful intermediate representations and stable routing parameters consistent with basin hydrological behavior. These findings demonstrate that integrating differentiable physical processes with deep learning provides a promising pathway toward accurate, interpretable, and operationally applicable streamflow forecasting in complex hydrological systems.

title: A hybrid approach combining PCA-APCS-MLR and MixSIAR for NO 3 − -N source apportionment in groundwater: insights from the Weishan Irrigation District of the lower Yellow River
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Weiyan Pan, Yang Liu, Fengsen Liu, Yuting Zhao, Chengwei Zhang, Yuying Geng, Zhenghe Xu
abstract: Groundwater nitrate contamination in agricultural irrigation areas threatens water security and sustainable development, yet its sources and transformations under anthropogenic and hydrological drivers remain poorly understood. In this study, focusing on the Weishan Irrigation District-the largest irrigation area diverting water from the Yellow River in its lower reaches, we collected 58 groundwater samples in wet and dry seasons and applied hydrochemical and isotopic analyses combined with PCA–APCS–MLR and MixSIAR to identify and quantify nitrate sources and transformations. Results found that nitrification emerged as the dominant nitrogen transformation process in groundwater, while denitrification was spatially localized and occurred mainly in the middle and lower reaches of the irrigation district. The PCA-APCS-MLR model revealed three dominant controlling factors influencing groundwater NO3 −–N concentrations: agricultural activities, mineralization-salinity-related hydrogeochemical processes, and manure and sewage inputs. The MixSIAR model quantified the contributions of specific nitrate sources and identified manure and sewage as an important nitrate source (42% in the dry season; 53% in the wet season), followed by chemical fertilizers (28% in the dry season; 27% in the wet season). The higher contribution of manure and sewage during the wet season suggested that seasonal recharge and irrigation-related water movement enhanced the mobilization and transport of anthropogenic nitrogen. Our findings elucidate the spatiotemporal dynamics of nitrate in irrigation districts and offer a scientific basis for pollution control in the Yellow River basin and analogous regions worldwide.

title: Shift in rooting depth under Tibetan Plateau Greening: hydrological insights from vegetation’s drought adaptation capacity perspectives
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Zhiqiang Tang, Qiang Liu, Liqiao Liang, Jifa Qin, Jianfei Wu, Yinhong Kang, Xuan Wang, Chunhui Li, Junlong Zhang
abstract: Climate-driven shifts in root-zone dynamics significantly alter the vegetation water strategy, thus influencing ecosystem drought adaptation, while the mechanistic links between root zone and drought resistance remain uncertain. We integrated Guswa’s model and the Mass Curve Technique (MCT) to quantify 2001–2020 spatiotemporal dynamics of water-optimal root depth (Zr) and root zone storage capacity (SR) in the Jinsha River Basin. Additionally, we used a critical cumulative water-deficit threshold to characterize drought resistance in evaporative functioning. The results show that: (i) Estimated water-optimal root depth (Zr) exhibited an increasing trend across 64% of the basin area during 2001–2020. At the basin scale, greater Zr was significantly associated with greater root-zone storage capacity (r2 = 0.86, p < 0.05), suggesting a greater potential for hydrological regulation. (ii) Enhanced root zone water availability serves to bolster ecosystem drought resistance. Specifically, drought resistance (DR) demonstrates a positive sensitivity to increased rooting depth Zr (slope = 1.86, p = 0.42) or higher SR (slope = 0.05, p < 0.05). (iii) Relationships among Zr, SR and DR differed among vegetation states: the equilibrium state exhibits stable root zone and greater tolerance of root water deficits; the excessive state demonstrates rapid Zr deepening and probably enhanced resistance; whereas the recoverable state experiences declined resistance despite Zr extension. The findings highlight that climate warming alters the root zone of ecosystems, thereby changing the original ecosystem’s drought resistance.

title: Analyzing the impacts of climate and land-use changes on blue-green water: Ranging from resource availability to compound drought risks
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Yue Qiu, Yongping Li, Guohe Huang, Zhipeng Xu, Jinjin Ma, Zhenyao Shen, Long Ma
abstract: The increasing concurrence of blue and green water deficits is emerging as a critical driver of compound drought risks under climate and land-use changes. The traditional assessment methods treat them separately and fail to capture nonlinear interactions, underestimating systemic collapse risks. In this study, an integrated Climate-Land-Hydrology-Risk-Attribution (abbreviated as CLHRA) framework is developed for (i) simultaneously reflecting the impacts of climate and land-use changes on blue-green water, (ii) quantifying nonlinear interaction of blue-green water as well as their compound drought risks via high-dimensional vine couple, and (iii) quantitative decoupling of compound drought risks and their synergistic driving forces. The CLHRA framework is applied to the “Ji”-shaped region of the Yellow River Basin, which serves as a globally representative microcosm for deeply human-modified drylands. Key findings indicate: (1) multi-scenario projections reveal a stark divergence between blue and green water responses where future green water maintains a rigid cross-scenario stability (336–364 mm/year) across divergent pathways, whereas blue water exhibits pronounced scenario sensitivity and high volatility, with upstream resources constrained to ∼ 30 mm/year due to intensive vegetation water consumption; (2) elevated atmospheric evaporative demand compromises land-surface buffering capacity, driving the mean green-to-blue water drought propagation probability to 68.2% across the study area (peaking at 85.0% in vulnerable sub-basins under ED-SSP585), thereby inducing widespread spatial proliferation of systemic joint drought risks; (3) climate dictates average water endowments (>70%), yet its nonlinear interaction with land use alterations acts as a synergistic amplifier, translating meteorological stress into systemic hydrological deficits. These insights underscore the necessity of transitioning from isolated land–water management to systemic trade-off optimization, offering a versatile paradigm to safeguard eco-hydrological resilience across global drylands.

title: Quantification of Zoige alpine wetland responses to climate change using attention U-Net
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Jiarong Fan, Ya Huang, Yanping Li, Zhenhua Li
abstract: Alpine wetlands are critical components of ecological security barriers and carbon sink systems. Understanding their responses to climate change is essential for regional ecological conservation and climate adaptation. This study applied an Attention U-Net model that integrates multi-source remote sensing, topographic, and climatic data to reconstruct wetland dynamics in the Zoige study region at 30 m spatial resolution from 2000 to 2019, focusing on changes in spatial extent, wetland-type composition, and transitions among wetland subtypes. To explore climatic sensitivities, controlled perturbation experiments were performed for temperature and precipitation independently and jointly, each as an independent model run without assuming linear superposition. The model achieved an overall classification accuracy of 97.93%. Relative to the 2000–2019 baseline, a 2°C warming was associated with up to a 50% reduction in modeled wetland area, with the fastest decline at this point; marsh and swamp showed the largest area losses, while flooded flat remained relatively stable. Precipitation effects were weaker than temperature effects: increased precipitation promoted wetland area expansion only up to 10%, beyond which the response saturated or reversed. Precipitation had a limited effect once warming exceeded 2°C, and modeled wetland degradation exhibited a spatial progression from edges to center and from steep slopes to gentle slopes. This study demonstrates the potential of deep learning-based approaches for exploratory sensitivity analysis of plateau wetland responses to climatic variables. However, as a data-driven model, the Attention U-Net captures statistical associations rather than physical processes, and model outputs become highly uncertain when climatic conditions deviate substantially from the historical training range. The identified climatic thresholds should be interpreted as model-inferred sensitivity signals rather than validated ecological tipping points, and require further verification using process-based models and field observations.

title: A probabilistic framework for modeling compound flooding hazard in coastal-inland transition zones
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Hossein Haghgou, Dingbao Wang, Norberto C. Nadal-Caraballo, Zhen Hu, Guirong Yan
abstract: Compound flooding arises from the simultaneous or successive occurrence of multiple flood drivers, such as heavy rainfall, extreme river discharge, sea-level rise, high tides, storm surge, and wave action. While flood hazard curves (FHCs) in distinct coastal and inland zones are typically well defined, with specific flood drivers dominating each zone, the FHCs in coastal-inland transition or compound flood zones are more complex due to the combined effects of multiple drivers. The dependency between coastal and inland flood drivers complicates the development of FHCs for compound flood zones. The objective of this study is to develop a probabilistic framework for constructing reliable coastal-inland flood hazard curves (CIFHCs) for compound flood-prone areas, even under sparse data conditions, by explicitly modeling the statistical dependency between coastal and inland drivers using bivariate copula functions. A compound zone along the St. Johns River in eastern Florida is examined to illustrate and demonstrate the proposed probabilistic framework. The resulting CIFHCs closely match those derived from observations, with an average deviation of approximately 10%, which reflects the consistency of the framework. This coupled framework is further applied to investigate how potential changes in the probability distributions of coastal and inland flood drivers, and their statistical dependency, influence hazards in compound flood zones. This type of analysis is essential for low-lying coastal communities, as it supports flood risk-reduction decision-making that accounts for the nonstationarity of climate and compound flooding hazard.

title: Adaptive symmetric projection lemmings algorithm for cascade reservoir power scheduling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Qingru Cao, Yonggang Wu, Yongqiang Wang, Xutong Sun, Li Sun
abstract: Cascade reservoir scheduling problems are characterized by multiple constraints, high dimensionality, nonlinearity, and non-convexity. To improve solution efficiency while ensuring optimization quality, this study proposes an Adaptive Symmetric Projection Lemmings Algorithm (ASPLA). This algorithm improves upon the Artificial Lemmings Algorithm framework by introducing three key mechanisms. First, an adaptive operator selection strategy is incorporated to dynamically adjust the probability of selecting different search strategies throughout the optimization process. Second, a symmetric projection mechanism is used to enhance particle recognition of potentially feasible regions. Third, a feasibility repair strategy guided by Lagrangian gradient information is developed, which significantly strengthens the algorithm’s ability to satisfy critical reservoir operation constraints such as initial and terminal storage limits. The performance of ASPLA was systematically evaluated using the CEC2022 test suite and two classical cascade reservoir scheduling cases. Statistical analysis confirms the high efficiency and robustness of the ASPLA. And ASPLA is applied to the hydropower-oriented operation of four cascade reservoirs in the lower reaches of the Jinsha River. The results show that ASPLA achieves the highest average hydropower generation and lowest standard deviation among the comparison algorithms across all three scenarios. Further analysis of reservoir water levels, hydraulic heads, turbine discharges, spillage, and power outputs provides a physical interpretation of the optimized reservoir operation processes. Together with the comparative optimization results, these findings indicate that the proposed ASPLA can obtain physically reasonable and relatively high scheduling solutions for cascade reservoir systems under different hydrological conditions.

title: Tidal-creek topography regulates storm-driven sediment redistribution and geomorphic change on a macrotidal flat
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Renzhi Li, Haifei Yang, Chao Gao, Bixuan Tang, Jingdong Chen, Ya Ping Wang
abstract: Tidal creeks route water and sediment across intertidal flats, yet how their topography organizes sediment redistribution during strong winds remains poorly understood. This study combined month-long measurements of waves, near-bed currents, and suspended sediment concentration (SSC) at a creek margin and an adjacent open flat with repeated topographic surveys on a macrotidal mudflat in Jiangsu, China. Strong-wind tidal cycles exhibited stronger wave forcing, higher SSC, and a weaker negative SSC–drag relationship than non-event cycles of comparable tidal range. Under strong-wind forcing, distinct along-creek and cross-creek responses emerged once sediment was mobilized. At the RD1 station along the creek margin, cross-creek ebb velocity remained lower during the below-bank stage, while elevated ebb-phase SSC enhanced the along-creek transport index despite comparable along-creek velocities between conditions. Over the 12-h integration windows, these responses yielded stronger ebb-directed along-creek and net landward cross-creek tendencies in the near-bed transport indices. Repeated profile measurements provided complementary evidence of spatially uneven bed adjustment, including concentrated creek-margin reworking and patchy inner-flat elevation gains, while surface samples collected between strong wind events showed localized coarsening and improved sorting. Together, these findings suggest that creek topography and changing water levels shape the pathways of wave-mobilized sediment during strong winds, helping explain spatially uneven geomorphic adjustment within tidal flat-creek systems.

title: Human proximity to rivers in China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Xuejing Zhang, Wenfang Cao, Dandan Zhao, Yanlong Guan, Pengfei Wang, Jeffrey J. McDonnell, Junguo Liu
abstract: River proximity shapes human settlement patterns and water resource dependence, yet the long-term changes of human–river proximity and their drivers remain poorly understood. Using high-resolution population data for ten reference years, we developed a Proximity to Rivers Index (PRI) to quantify changes in population-density gradients relative to major rivers across China from 1953 to 2020. Random Forest models and counterfactual scenarios were used to examine socio-economic and natural associations with PRI. Although China's population more than doubled, the median population–river distance remained close to 10 km. However, PRI became progressively more negative from 1953 to 2020, indicating strengthening population concentration near rivers without a substantial shift in the median population location. Basin-scale trajectories were heterogeneous: human–river proximity generally strengthened in northern basins, whereas several southern basins exhibited weakening or more complex trends. Socio-economic variables were more strongly associated with the long-term PRI change, particularly in northern basins, while natural variability was more closely related to fluctuations among reference years in several southern basins. Urbanization rate and GDP had the highest relative importance nationally. Urban settlements were consistently closer to rivers than rural settlements, whereas the relationship between per-capita GDP and river proximity varied among Eastern, Central, and Western China. These findings highlight the need for basin-specific management that coordinates urban development, river-corridor protection, water-resource allocation, and climate adaptation.

title: Preference-conditioned feature selection for interpretable multi-objective water-system operating policies
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Guang Yang, Matteo Giuliani, Zengchuan Dong, Pan Liu, Bin Xu, Andrea Castelletti
abstract: The operation of water resources is inherently complex, necessitating the reconciliation of competing objectives, the coordination of interconnected infrastructures, and adherence to various regulations and stakeholder perspectives. Multi-objective optimization methods have emerged as powerful tools for addressing these complexities by enabling decision-makers to balance conflicting goals. The effectiveness of these methods is contingent upon the input variables utilized in water resource operation models. However, decision-makers often find it challenging to understand how different input variables impact optimization performance regarding different objectives, thereby reducing the interpretability of these models and impeding their practical application in real-world contexts. In this regard, the careful selection of input variables can enhance both the efficacy and interpretability of multi-objective water resource operations. This paper assesses the significance of various input variables in water system operation models under differing decision-making preferences and extracts the most relevant information to alleviate conflicts among competing objectives. The approach is demonstrated on the GERD-Merowe-HAD reservoir system within the Nile River Basin, where the primary functions are hydropower generation and irrigation water supply at a strategic monthly planning scale. The framework is designed to support strategic policy design and input-variable screening, rather than to generate real-time gate-release schedules. A systematic feature selection framework that integrates Recursive Feature Elimination with Evolutionary Multi-Objective Direct Policy Search is employed to analyze the importance of various input variables in multi-reservoir operation. By linking input variable importance evaluations with multi-objective reservoir operation performance, we identify compact input formulations for operational policies tailored to specific decision-making preferences. The findings indicate that using selected input variables can mitigate conflicts between hydropower generation and irrigation water supply in the Nile River Basin, particularly when a lower irrigation deficit is desired. Furthermore, customizing reservoir operation policies with input variables chosen based on decision-making preferences can enhance the performance of the relevant objectives. The selected reduced-input policies also improve the trade-off performance relative to conventional input formulations, indicating that compact input sets can reduce policy complexity without sacrificing system performance. This proposed framework holds promise for improving the interpretability of machine-learning-based operational policies for water resource systems and fostering a stronger connection between these complex systems and their human operators. The transferable contribution is the feature-selection workflow itself; the specific selected variables should be re-evaluated for each reservoir system according to local objectives, constraints, available information, and decision scale.

title: Cropland and population exposure to extreme precipitation events in Central Asia under future climate change
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Tao Li, Fengjiao Song, Andrée De Cock, Jiayu Bao, Philippe De Maeyer, Ting Wang, Diwen Dong, Ye Yuan, Xiaoran Huang, Tao Yu, Naibi Sulei, Anming Bao, Peter Goethals
abstract: Central Asia (CA) is experiencing rapid warming and an intensifying hydrological cycle, with important implications for extreme precipitation events (EPEs). However, future changes in cropland and population exposure to EPEs remain insufficiently quantified in this climate-sensitive dryland region.
