The assembly operated continuously underground for nearly 600 h under ambient temperatures from 17.8 to −7.2°C, and at the 65 A near-steady condition, it delivered 29.1 kWth of subsurface heat with 4.4 kWe of exportable electricity, achieving a first-law combined heat and power efficiency of 55% and a second-law exergy efficiency of approximately 28%, with a heat flux of 3.2 kW m−1 over 9 m. The exergy analysis identifies the unreacted reformate stream as both the dominant thermodynamic loss and the principal fuel cost driver, and demonstrates that capturing this stream would raise the combined heat and power efficiency to approximately 66%, substantially improving project economics. These findings confirm that GFC technology holds a clear cost advantage over the grid-powered in-situ heating methods being evaluated for Chinese deposits, establish the electricity co-product as a meaningful revenue stream that supports commercial scalability under Chinese energy market conditions, and identify unreacted fuel recovery and anode exhaust recycling as the highest-return engineering interventions for advancing in-situ oil shale conversion toward full-scale deployment in China.

title: Trans-dimensional Bayesian electromagnetic inversion for geothermal reservoir characterization in South China: Uncertainty analysis of subsurface conductivity recovered from CSAMT data
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Shengqi Tian, Peng Xue, Rongwen Guo, Jianxin Liu, Keke Zhou, Yongfei Wang, Jihai Mo, Jianjian Li, Heming Su
abstract: Electromagnetic (EM) methods are highly sensitive to subsurface conductivity contrasts associated with clay alteration, fluid circulation, and fracture-controlled hydrothermal systems, and have therefore been increasingly applied to geothermal exploration and reservoir characterization in recent years. However, EM inverse problems are commonly characterized by significant non-uniqueness. Conventional deterministic inversion methods typically produce a single best-fitting model, providing limited ability to quantify model uncertainty or to evaluate the effects of measurement noise and incomplete data coverage on inversion results. To address these limitations, this paper presents a trans-dimensional Bayesian inversion framework for EM inversion problems in geothermal exploration. By sampling an ensemble of models from the posterior distribution, the framework enables quantitative evaluation of model-parameter uncertainty. Specifically, this study implements a two-dimensional reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (rj-MCMC) algorithm based on wavelet-domain tree-structured parameterization, allowing model complexity to vary adaptively during sampling so that the appropriate level of parameterization is determined by the observed data. The proposed method is first evaluated using a synthetic experiment based on a classical convective geothermal model, with particular emphasis on uncertainty caused by unknown model parameterization. It is then applied to field controlled-source audio-frequency magnetotelluric (CSAMT) data from a geothermal area in southern China. The results demonstrate that the proposed probabilistic inversion method can provide reliable geothermal reservoir characterization while offering quantitative uncertainty information for resource assessment.

title: 3D seismic imaging of a fracture damage zone controlling reservoir compartmentalization at the Raft River EGS using multi-azimuth walkaway VSP
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Benxin Chi, Kai Gao, David Li, Joseph Moore, Clay Jones, Lianjie Huang
abstract: Accurate imaging of steeply dipping fracture zones in crystalline enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) is critical for constraining permeability architecture and guiding stimulation design. However, such structures remain poorly resolved by conventional surface seismic methods. We present a fully three-dimensional (3D) elastic-waveform inversion–migration workflow applied to multi-azimuth walkaway vertical seismic profiling (VSP) data acquired in a deviated borehole at the Raft River EGS. The workflow integrates first-arrival traveltime tomography, multi-scale elastic waveform inversion (EWI), and elastic least-squares reverse-time migration (ELSRTM) to recover high-resolution compressional- and shear-wave velocity models and to image structural discontinuities in the crystalline basement. The results reveal a laterally continuous low-velocity anomaly, with shear-wave velocity reductions of 25–30%, consistent with fracture-induced mechanical weakening. Two steeply dipping discontinuities bound a 50–80 m wide fracture damage zone. Independent constraints from microseismic clustering and geochemical compartmentalization corroborate the geometry and structural significance of this feature. Synthetic modeling further confirms that structures of this scale are resolvable (∼30 m). These findings indicate that the Narrows structure is a distributed fracture damage zone rather than a discrete fault plane. By resolving fracture-zone geometry at the tens-of-meters scale using a single borehole, this workflow provides a practical and transferable approach for improving structural characterization, reducing uncertainty in permeability architecture, and supporting reservoir modeling and stimulation design in fractured crystalline EGS reservoirs.

title: Frictional response of thermally treated granite joints under oscillatory normal stress: implications for fracture stability in enhanced geothermal systems
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Wengang Dang, Shixiao Li, Yuyong Jiao, Yu Liu, Yunhan Sheng, Kang Tao, Linchong Huang, Hongfei Duan, Xiang Li, Yu Feng
abstract: In enhanced geothermal systems, thermally altered fractures may experience cyclic normal stress perturbations during injection, production, and seismic disturbance. However, the frictional response of thermally treated granite joints under oscillatory normal stress remains insufficiently constrained. To address this issue, this study employed a large DJZ-500 direct shear apparatus to conduct laboratory research on the granite joint that had experienced different temperature heat treatments (23–500 °C) under constant normal load (CNL) and dynamic normal load (DNL). The results revealed that the joint shear strength exhibited a nonlinear evolution process dependent on temperature. Both static and dynamic shear strengths showed initial thermal strengthening (23–200 °C), followed by severe thermal degradation (200–500 °C). Moreover, when the heat treatment exceeded 300 °C, the shear strength dropped below the pre-treatment strength. With increasing dynamic amplitude, dynamic shear strength changes from being higher than to lower than the corresponding static strength. We refer to this phenomenon as frictional strengthening-to-weakening transition. The degree of this frictional strengthening or weakening depends on the temperature. Through three-dimensional surface morphology and results of uniaxial compressive test, we propose a mechanism indicating that the non-linear variation of shear strengths depends on the coupled effects of joint roughness and matrix strength. These findings provide some mechanistic insights into the thermodynamic stability of hot dry rock faults and offer important references for optimizing geothermal energy extraction in deep hot dry rock faults.

title: An investigation of the effects of temperature and clay content on fault gouge material
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Aigerim Sekerbayeva, Ali Mortazavi, Randy D. Hazlett
abstract: To understand fluid flow and permeability characteristics under various clay contents and temperatures, artificially created fault gouge materials were experimentally studied. The aim of the study was to investigate the effects of clay content and temperature on the permeability behaviour of synthetic fault gouge materials under controlled laboratory conditions representative of relatively shallow subsurface storage environments. The mechanical and strength characteristics of the fault gouge material were determined using standard laboratory tests, while water was used as the fluid for permeability measurements under controlled experimental conditions. Temperature changes from 25 °C to 65 °C resulted in only minor changes in permeability under the examined conditions, whereas variations in clay content up to 30% significantly reduced permeability to approximately one order of magnitude, with the largest reduction observed between the 10% and 20% clay compositions, indicating the strong influence of clay-rich compositions on fluid-flow behaviour. Consistent with previous studies, confining pressure remained an important factor controlling permeability reduction. Unlike much of the previous work, which primarily focused on the confining pressure effect, this work examines the combined effects of clay content and temperature, integrating permeability and mechanical characterization. The study combines permeability measurements with uniaxial compression and direct shear testing within a consistent experimental framework. The results provide baseline experimental insights into the relative effects of clay content, stress, and temperature on fault gouge permeability under water-saturated laboratory conditions relevant to the initial assessment of fault behaviour in subsurface storage systems, including geological CO₂ storage.

title: Analytical modeling of tracer pulse tests with significant background concentration at the Utah FORGE geothermal site
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Mahmoud Abdellatif, Smith Leggett, Qingwang Yuan
abstract: Lithium (Li+) and cesium (Cs+) ions show rapid reversible adsorption and desorption on geothermal reservoir rocks, making them potential candidates for sorbing tracer tests to estimate the heat exchange surface area of the geothermal reservoir. However, water geochemistry data from the Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (Utah FORGE) project show significant background concentrations of Li+ and Cs+, which obscure the tracer recovery response. To address this problem, we extended the semi-analytical Reactive Transport Laplace Transform Inversion model (RELAP) to account for non-zero background concentration and to simulate positive, negative, and multiple tracer pulse tests within a unified background-aware framework. The modified model was first history matched to a previous conservative tracer test at Utah FORGE to estimate the governing flow parameters and provide a data-informed basis for subsequent design calculations. Results indicate that transport between the injection and production well at the Utah FORGE is better represented by a two-component upscaled transport structure than by a single equivalent pathway. Using the history-matched model, the analysis showed that the Li+ or Cs+ tracer mass required to produce detectable positive concentration perturbations is economically prohibitive. In contrast, a negative pulse design based on freshwater injection produces detectable negative perturbations in the tracer recovery response. Expressed in normalized concentration form, the breakthrough curves remain directly comparable to those of a positive tracer pulse and preserve the standard retardation-based interpretation. These results establish a methodological and design-oriented framework for background-aware tracer testing in geothermal reservoirs.

title: Learning with constraints: A physics-guided Bayesian framework for reliable geothermal temperature mapping in northeastern Italy
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Danial Sheini Dashtgoli, Michela Giustiniani, Martina Busetti, Claudia Cherubini, Guillermo A․ Narsilio
abstract: Reliable deep-temperature estimation remains a central challenge in geothermal exploration, particularly in sedimentary–carbonate provinces where borehole data are sparse and vertically imbalanced. These conditions lead to unreliable extrapolation and poor uncertainty characterization in classical interpolation and purely data-driven models. This study develops a physics-guided Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework that integrates heteroscedastic probabilistic learning with conductive heat-transfer constraints to reconstruct the 3D geothermal structure of the Lower Friulian Plain (NE Italy) using 849 irregularly distributed temperature measurements. To explicitly address depth imbalance and evaluate extrapolation performance, a depth-aware training and validation strategy was implemented, including controlled withholding of deep observations (1000–1200 m). The architecture combines Monte Carlo-dropout Bayesian inference with two physics-informed formulations, a monotonicity constraint enforcing non-negative vertical gradients and a gradient-band constraint bounding geothermal slopes within regionally plausible conductive ranges. The resulting models achieve high fidelity in the data-supported domain (<1000 m), with coefficient of determination (R2) ≈ 0.95–0.96 and root mean square error ≈ 2.6–2.8 °C, while classical and data-driven models show reduced reliability under extrapolation conditions. The monotonic BNN attains R2 = 0.877 and RMSE = 1.33 °C, and the gradient-band BNN produces physically consistent geothermal gradients (≈0.014–0.018 °C/m), aligning with regional heat-flow constraints. Both physics-guided models deliver near-ideal uncertainty calibration (≈97–99% prediction-interval coverage) and eliminate nonphysical deep-zone oscillations. Independent validation against the Grado-1 well confirms agreement within ±1 °C across the full 100–1200 m profile. The proposed framework enables extrapolation-robust and uncertainty-aware 3D geothermal mapping, providing a transferable approach for geothermal resource assessment in data-limited subsurface systems.

title: Curie-point depth, geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow estimation from spectral analysis of aeromagnetic data over Natron Rift Basin, Tanzania
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Neema Bernad Mjami, Obeid Saitabau Lemna, Cuthbert Kimambo, Sarah Ayeng’o, Ivanka Orozova-Bekkevold
abstract: The Natron Rift Basin (NRB) in northeastern Tanzania, situated within the eastern branch of the East African Rift System (EARS), is among the country's promising geothermal prospects and has been designated as a priority development area. However, research into its geothermal potential remains limited despite active geothermal manifestations and favourable tectonic features, including faults, fractures, hot springs and volcanoes. Specifically, localized investigations of the geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow have not yet been carried out. This study aims to estimate the Curie-Point Depth (CPD) within the NRB using spectral analysis of aeromagnetic data, focusing on the area bounded by latitudes 2° S - 3.6°S and longitudes 35.2° - 36.8°E. The estimated CPD ranges from 12 to 18 km below ground level. These CPD estimates were used to constrain the geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow in the area. The calculated geothermal gradient and heat flow range from 31 to 46.5 °C/km and 77.6 to 116.3 mW/m², respectively. The results indicate a widespread distribution of low- to medium-temperature geothermal resources in the NRB. A potential high-enthalpy heat source was identified beneath the volcanic belt to the south of Lake Natron. This study presents the first regional scale maps of geothermal gradient and heat flow in the NRB, with an approximate spatial resolution of 44 km between data points. The results are spatially coherent with major structural and volcanic features of the EARS in the study area. These findings improve the understanding of the NRB deep thermal structures and can be used to identify priority areas that may warrant further investigation for future geothermal exploration.

title: Synergistic effects of epoxy/PTFE/CNT hybrid nanocomposite coating against silica scaling and corrosion under varying geothermal flow conditions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Yurian Ariandi Andrameda, Khasani, Kusmono, Hendra Ardi Kurniawan, Herdian Ardi Febrianto, Kadek Wahyudi, Zaky Ahmad Aditya, Shad Abdelmoumen Serroune
abstract: This study presents the development of a multifunctional epoxy/polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)/carbon nanotube (CNT) hybrid nanocomposite coating designed to simultaneously mitigate localized corrosion and silica scaling in geothermal environments. Morphological and surface property evaluations identified an optimal formulation (Epoxy/PTFE40/CNT0.8) that successfully balances surface hydrophobicity (water contact angle of 139°) with enhanced adhesion strength (8.68 MPa), avoiding the nanoparticle agglomeration observed at excessive filler loadings. Thermal analysis demonstrated that the integrated CNT network acts as a physical diffusion barrier, modifying the matrix degradation into a stabilized two-stage process capable of withstanding continuous exposure up to 150 °C. Electrochemically, the optimized composite established a highly tortuous barrier against corrosive Cl⁻ ions, achieving a charge transfer resistance of 882.9 Ω·cm² (47% above neat epoxy), a corrosion protection efficiency of 94.05%, and a minimal corrosion rate of 0.0098 mm/year. Furthermore, the tailored micro/nano-topography formed by PTFE particles and CNT networks successfully prevented the mechanical interlocking of mineral deposits, delivering peak silica scaling reductions of 65.08% under Upstream (near-wellhead) brine conditions and maintaining a 50.92% mitigation efficiency under Downstream (near-pond) supersaturation conditions. Ultimately, this synergistic hybrid coating offers an effective and scalable strategy for simultaneously combating the dual threats of scaling and corrosion, extending the operational lifespan of geothermal infrastructure.

title: 2D magnetotelluric inversion and 3D resistivity visualization for geothermal system characterization: A case study of Mount Parakasak
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Eko Minarto, Fatony Zepanya
abstract: Mount Parakasak in Banten hosts promising yet underexplored geothermal resources. This study integrates two-dimensional magnetotelluric (MT) and time-domain electromagnetic (TDEM) surveys to delineate subsurface resistivity structures and characterize the geothermal system. Thirty-six MT soundings, corrected for static shift using TDEM data, were inverted to generate 2D resistivity sections. These sections were subsequently interpolated to construct a three-dimensional resistivity visualization constrained by geological and geochemical datasets. The results identify a conductive clay cap (∼100 Ω·m) overlying an upflow zone near the Kaipohan manifestation, corresponding to estimated reservoir temperatures of 240–260 °C. The Batukuwung hot spring defines an outflow zone with temperatures of 52–75 °C. The integrated interpretation indicates an active geothermal system and identifies promising drilling targets at approximately 1500 m depth. These findings provide a robust framework for geothermal exploration and resource assessment, supporting future geothermal development in Banten Province.

title: Imaging the resistivity structure of Nage Geothermal System, Flores Island, Indonesia through 3-D magnetotelluric inversion incorporating the sea effect
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Maryadi Maryadi, Asep Sugianto, Iqbal Takodama, After Helfert Pasaribu, Yan Mark, Supriyanto Supriyanto, Hideki Mizunaga
abstract: The geothermal potential of Flores Island, Indonesia, is significant but structurally complex, requiring advanced geophysical imaging to delineate active hydrothermal systems. However, in such island-arc settings, some magnetotelluric (MT) inversion attempts still neglect the influence of the highly conductive surrounding seawater, thereby generating artificial deep conductive anomalies that can lead to costly misinterpretations of geothermal features. In this study, a three-dimensional (3-D) MT inversion of the Nage geothermal system is presented, which is based on full-impedance data from 82 stations. The model domain explicitly incorporates regional bathymetry and the seawater body to account for the sea effect. The results delineate a massive conductive clay cap beneath the high-temperature FW fumarole, identifying it as the primary hydrothermal upflow zone. A distinct, shallower geothermal reservoir was also identified between the Keli (APK) and Nage (APN) hot spring complexes, which appears to be hydrologically partitioned from the primary upflow by an NE-SW-oriented fault that acts as a structural permeability barrier between the complexes. Furthermore, the model detects a deep resistive body, interpreted as older intrusive rock, beneath the Nage caldera. These findings yield a refined conceptual model of the Nage geothermal field and demonstrate that explicitly modeling the sea effect is crucial to preventing the misinterpretation of deep reservoir structures in coastal volcanic environments.

title: Thermomechanical Response of Weathered Granite Soils Surrounding Energy Geostructures under Cyclic Thermal Loading
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Hanh Nguyen-Cong, Ba Huu Dinh, Ju-Won Ryu, Gyeong-O Kang, Young-Sang Kim
abstract: Understanding the thermomechanical behaviors of geomaterials is crucial for ensuring the successful design and long-term performance of energy geostructures. This study investigated the response of an undisturbed, low-plasticity weathered granite soil (WGS) from Gwangju, Korea, a saprolitic soil derived from regional granite that behaves as a transitional soil between sands and clays, under cyclic thermal loading. A modified temperature-controlled oedometer was used to subject both normally consolidated (NC) and overconsolidated (OC) states to multiple-cycle drained heating (60 °C) and cooling (20 °C) tests at different preconsolidation pressures. The experimental results indicated that the NC-WGS exhibited irreversible thermal consolidation under a single thermal cycle, whereas the heavily OC-WGS primarily exhibited reversible thermo-elastic expansion. In addition, the magnitude of NC-WGS thermal consolidation was strongly stress-dependent, with the maximum volumetric strain during the first heating phase decreasing from 0.404 % at 240 kPa to 0.134 % at 640 kPa. Multiple thermal cyclic loadings produced accumulated consolidation in NC with rapidly diminishing incremental strain (thermal hardening-type stabilization), reaching 0.915 % and 0.825 % after three cycles at 240 kPa and 320 kPa, respectively, and 1.015 % after eight cycles at 640 kPa. In contrast, OC responses became nearly repeatable from the second cycle onward with negligible additional plastic strain. Even under repeated cycling, the low-plasticity WGS (plasticity index of 2.6 %) exhibits markedly lower thermally induced volumetric strain than high-plasticity clays, supporting long-term serviceability and structural safety throughout cyclic thermal operation in energy geostructures.

title: Enhancing identification of geothermal prospection in Yingshan geothermal field using machine learning and thermal infrared remote sensing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Xin Zhang, Zhentao Hong, Xianjun Xie, Yanxin Wang, Qiang Liu, Haijin Xu, Xiao Wang, Tianyu Ren, Peisong Dong
abstract: Improving the accuracy of land surface temperature (LST) retrieval from thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing and inverting the properties of subsurface geothermal reservoirs remain significant challenges. This has particularly constrained the integration of TIR remote sensing with other exploration methodologies, such as geochemical surveys. To address this issue, we derived thermal infrared information from Landsat 8 and MODIS data, with Sentinel-2 and SRTM data providing auxiliary optical and topographic features in the Yingshan geothermal field. Subsequently, we adopted the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model to perform spatial downscaling of LST. By establishing the optimal feature combination for temperature retrieval, we achieved high-precision surface temperature inversion and compared its performance with the traditional bilinear interpolation and DisTrad models. In parallel, we developed a processing workflow for altered mineral identification based on ASTER and Landsat 8 reflectance data. Finally, we conducted a comprehensive analysis integrating the downscaled LST, thermally altered minerals, and in-situ geochemical data including soil gas Rn, Hg, and geothermal gradient (GTG), to improve the accuracy of geothermal prospect targeting. The results show that the XGBoost model significantly enhanced the detail richness of the LST map, increasing the entropy value from 3.13 to 3.30, which outperforms the results of bilinear interpolation (3.12) and the DisTrad model (3.14). Validation against in-situ surface temperature measurements shows that the XGBoost model achieved a mean bias error (MBE) of -0.492 ± 0.2 °C and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.39 ± 0.0702 °C, which are significantly better than the results of the DisTrad model (MBE = 0.539 ± 0.2 °C; RMSE = 2.77 ± 0.0387 °C) and bilinear interpolation (MBE = 0.625 ± 0.2 °C; RMSE = 2.98 ± 0.0418 °C). Furthermore, the P-P plot analysis indicates that the XGBoost model significantly improved the identification accuracy for both the relatively high-temperature geothermal fields and the low-temperature vegetation-covered areas. Our TIR remote sensing analysis identified four types of hydrothermal alteration: propylitic, argillization, biotitization, and sericitization, all of which were validated by field investigations. In the focal research area, we identified five high-temperature anomalies, along with their corresponding thermally altered mineral anomalies. The results indicate that the geothermal reservoirs in the anomaly zones are dominated by medium-acidic and medium-low temperature environments. Moreover, through comprehensive integration with soil gas Rn, Hg, and geothermal gradient (GTG), we classified the thermal anomalies into three distinct types with complete quantitative signatures: (1) Type 1 (geothermal fields): showed LST anomalies of 23.3 ± 1.12–24.6 ± 1.22 °C, with the presence of surface hydrothermal alteration minerals, paired with elevated Hg and GTG; (2) Type 2 (hidden faults): had normal LST, with no detectable hydrothermal alteration minerals, but pronounced Rn anomalies; (3) Type 3 (heat island/conductive zones): exhibited extreme LST fluctuations, with no detectable hydrothermal alteration minerals, paired with elevated GTGs but weak geochemical anomalies. This classification result suggests that downscaled LST, when integrated with soil gas Rn, Hg, geothermal gradient, and structural information, can assist in distinguishing known geothermal fields from potential concealed structural or conductive zones. The XGBoost-based downscaling method, combined with hydrothermal altered mineral identification, can significantly improve the accuracy of geothermal exploration targeting, analyze the genesis of geothermal distribution at the initial exploration stage, and substantially reduce the cost of geothermal system exploration.

title: Thermal diffusivity and transient thermal response of the Sabatini volcanic succession: insights from the shallow geothermal field at the ENEA-Casaccia Research Centre (Roma, Italy)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Anna Carmela Violante, Marco Proposito, Giambattista Guidi, Simona De Iuliis
abstract: Understanding transient heat transfer in heterogeneous volcanic formations improves the design of shallow geothermal energy systems (SGES). However, the thermal behaviour of stratified volcanic successions remains poorly constrained due to lithological variability, porosity contrasts, and groundwater driven heat transport. This study investigates the thermal diffusivity and thermal response of the Sabatini volcanic succession (Central Italy) using laboratory measurements, in situ thermal tests and Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) monitoring at the ENEA-Casaccia shallow geothermal field. Thermal conductivity (λ), bulk density (ρ), and specific heat capacity (cp) were determined along a borehole and used to derive thermal diffusivity (α). DTS monitoring enabled characterised transient thermal evolution along the borehole. Thermal diffusivity values range from 4.2 × 10⁻⁷ to 7.1 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s. Highest values are associated with lava and sandy tuffs, whereas the lowest occur in fine-grained, clay-rich deposits. DTS monitoring during a 12 h thermal stimulation test revealed depth-dependent heterogeneity and contrasting cooling behaviours among lithologies. Saturated lava units showed rapid heat uptake and dissipation, while fine-grained tuffs and sandy silts retained thermal anomalies for up to 48 h, indicating higher thermal inertia and heat storage capacity. Results demonstrate that lithology, porosity and saturation control transient thermal behaviour in volcanic successions.

title: Entraining low-pressure geothermal fluid for power generation using a supersonic ejector: A case study from Theistareykir power plant
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Ximena Guardia, Egill Juliusson, Karl Emil Sveinsson, Hilmar Einarsson, Gudrun Saevarsdottir, Yonatan Afework Tesfahunegn, Maria Sigridur Gudjonsdottir
abstract: An ejector is a device without moving parts that uses a high-pressure fluid to entrain fluid from a low-pressure source, thereby mixing them to create a single flow at an intermediate pressure. Such a device was designed for geothermal power plant conditions by Reykjavik University and tested at the Theistareykir Geothermal Power Plant in Iceland, in collaboration with Landsvirkjun Power Company, in November 2024. The system used high-pressure saturated steam from well ThG-11 to draw in a lower-pressure, two-phase mixture (with a 20% steam quality) from well ThG-15. The ejector was designed using an analytical model to handle a primary steam flow of up to 2.90 kg/s, and it was tested across a wide range of operating conditions. During the tests, the pressure of the primary fluid (from well ThG-11) varied from 8.5 to 28.5 bar g , while the pressure of the secondary fluid (from well ThG-15) ranged from 1.8 to 9.1 bar g . The ejector successfully entrained the secondary flow when the pressure difference between the primary and secondary fluids ranged from 9.9 to 26.3 bar. The highest entrainment ratio (ER), defined as the secondary-to-primary mass flow ratio, across the entire data set was 0.38. This occurred at a primary fluid mass flow rate of 2.76 kg/s and a pressure of 28.5 bar g , with a secondary fluid mass flow rate of 1.05 kg/s at 6.6 bar g . At the ejector outlet, the mixed flow pressure was 9.9 bar g , representing a 3.4 bar pressure gain relative to the entrained secondary fluid. The exergy analysis for this peak condition revealed an additional exergy rate of 269.17 kW. This represents a 9.1% increase in the total useful energy delivered from this pair of wells at the testing conditions. Scaling to the full capacity of both wells suggests a potential additional exergy rate of 1.65 to 1.96 MW for the power plant, based on the stable experimental operating range. The analytical model used to design the ejector showed good agreement with the measured data for the primary fluid but poor agreement for the secondary fluid, particularly in times of low or no entrainment and when the secondary fluid pressure did not have stable conditions. Overall, these results are promising for future applications of ejectors in connecting high- and low-pressure geothermal wells.

title: Effects of reservoir permeability heterogeneity on the size of solute and thermal protection zone around a geothermal reinjection well in a porous reservoir, Hungary
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Bence Molnár, Daniele Pedretti, István Garaguly, Gábor Varga, Judit Mádl‑Szőnyi, Attila Galsa
abstract: Sustainable groundwater management requires accurate delineation of a protection zone (PZ) around wells. While PZ has been widely studied for solute protection zone (SPZ) of drinking water wells, the growing use of geothermal applications requires also the delineation of both solute and thermal protection zone (TPZ). In this study, the effects of reservoir heterogeneity on SPZ and TPZ size were investigated using numerical simulations around a deep geothermal reinjection well, where reservoir heterogeneity was studied by stochastic permeability distributions. In the first part of the study, synthetic simulations were performed to highlight the importance of the scientific question, where the role of the permeability heterogeneity scale, and the thermal retardation were examined. The SPZ and TPZ size was characterized by monitoring the evolving position of the solute and thermal front. In the main part, the theoretical findings were applied to a real geothermal project in Hungary, proposing a novel workflow where the heterogeneity scale was derived from seismic attributes and geophysical logs. The results show that the SPZ and TPZ size increases with the heterogeneity scale, indicating that a larger protection zone is needed, although the effect of heterogeneity decreases over time. Heterogeneity has significant effect on the TPZ extension especially on small time scale, so its investigation in heat transport cannot be neglected despite greater heat diffusion. The probability maps of SPZ and TPZ areas illustrate well the uncertainty caused by reservoir heterogeneity. Finally, results highlight that TPZ cannot be directly rescaled from SPZ because of the time-varying difference between apparent and effective thermal retardation.

title: Wet and dry faults at thrust fronts as indicators of paleofluid flow in the carbonates of the Geneva Basin (Switzerland, France)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): G.L. Cardello, M. Lupi, E. Carminati, C. Doglioni, M. Sartori, E. Samankassou, M. Meyer
abstract: Thrust fronts are common targets for geothermal exploration in foreland basins because they contain fractured reservoirs made of a floor thrust and a frontal anticline, eventually crossed by high-angle transfer faults, and minor thrust splays. Although regional fluid flow is also controlled by petrophysical properties and the geothermal gradient, the tectonic contribution is best understood through outcrop analogs. We investigate tectonic controls on paleo-circulation across the carbonate-rich thrust front systems surrounding Geneva to better understand present-day hydrothermal pathways. Structural mapping and mesostructural analysis identify high-angle “wet” (mineralized) and “dry” (non-mineralized) faults, revealing where paleofluids circulated and sealed voids. Fault geometry defines a hierarchical network. First-order faults (>2.5 km long), mainly NW-oriented tear faults, accommodated thrust front curvature and acted as primary conduits for mineralizing fluids, except where E-W and WNW faults intercept the thrust front. Second-order faults, which are 0.4–2.5 km long, are less continuous and rarely mineralized. This suggests limited fluid migration in such gregarious faults. The fabric of mineralizations ranges from syn-kinematic slickenfibers to post-kinematic vadose cements, depending on fault orientation, kinematics, offset, and segmentation. The presence of rebrecciated fabrics and multiple generations of syn-thrusting veins and polygenetic calcite in NW-striking faults at thrust fronts suggests that these faults represent fossil examples of transient builds-up of paleofluid overpressure and deformation. Conversely, W- to WNW-tear faults mostly represent alternated pressure-solution and discrete faulting. These findings provide a framework for identifying permeable zones in carbonate thrust fronts, offering practical guidance for assessing geothermal exploration in deformed foreland basins.

title: Temperature field and assessment methodology for a low-medium temperature geothermal field: 3D geological-geophysical modeling in the Xiong'an Area, Northern China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Na Peng, Yihao Wu, Hanqing Qiao, Jiangtao Han
abstract: Mid-low temperature hydrothermal systems are widely distributed in continental intraplate basins, and accurately characterizing their deep thermal structures is crucial for understanding regional geothermal genesis. As a typical intraplate field, the Xiong'an Area in North China possesses significant deep potential. However, previous studies focused on localized assessments of isolated shallow fields, lacking regional 3D simulations based on fine structural constraints, which restricts the understanding of deep heat transfer mechanisms.In this study, we integrated three deep seismic reflection profiles, one magnetotelluric (MT) profile, regional geological, and well-log data to construct a high-resolution 3D geological-geophysical model. Constrained by petrophysical data, we employed a Multi-source data integration approach to solve the 3D steady-state heat conduction equation, achieving high-precision geothermal simulation down to 5 km depth, validated by measured well temperatures.Our results reveal significant spatial differentiation in the regional thermal structure, primarily controlled by varying "caprock-reservoir" configurations. The northern region (e.g., Rongcheng and Niutuozhen fields) exhibits a "thin caprock-shallow reservoir" pattern ( 3 km). The 3D model indicates the southern deep system possesses a significantly higher geothermal gradient, forming a promising target for deep exploration. Furthermore, we identify a concealed deep geothermal prospect near the Raoyang depression. This study delineates reliable exploration targets and provides a universally applicable framework for modeling Multi-source data integration in intraplate geothermal systems.

title: Field demonstration and integrated productivity-economics assessment of multi-lateral geothermal wells enabled by directional steel shot drilling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Paromita Deb, Andreas Reinicke, Jan Jette Blangé, Morteza Esmailpour, Carlo Guarnieri Calo’ Carducci, Martin O. Saar
abstract: This study explores the potential of multi-lateral slim-hole drilling to enhance reservoir access and connectivity in fractured geothermal reservoirs. At the core of this work is Directional Steel Shot Drilling (DSSD), a technology that combines conventional mechanical drilling with the erosive action of pressure-accelerated steel shots. This approach enables the cost-effective construction of multi-directional boreholes from a single wellbore. The DSSD technology was piloted at the VersuchsStollen Hagerbach underground research facility in Switzerland. The test site provides access to fractured hard rock formations under realistic stress and pore-fluid pressure conditions. Two horizontal wellbores, each 125 m long, were drilled. Rates of penetration (ROP) increased up to 2–5 times depending on the steel shot concentration in the drilling mud. Controlled building rates under steering (∼ 3.8–6.6°/30 m) and stable trajectories under non-steering conditions (∼ 0.3° /30 m) were achieved. The pilot demonstrated several key aspects: straightforward retrofitting of DSSD on conventional drill rigs, effectiveness of the steering concept, efficient transportation of steel shots in the mud, and the resulting enhanced bit performance in hard rock. To assess field-scale implications, reservoir simulations and a techno-economic assessment were performed using a fractured carbonate reservoir case. A set of 1000 geological realizations was generated to capture uncertainty in permeability distribution. These models were used to evaluate thermal energy production for 20 years, employing single-, dual-, and triple-lateral well architectures. Median results indicated that adding a second lateral boosts production by 45 – 50%, while a third lateral leads to an additional 25 – 30% gain. The techno-economic evaluation shows corresponding reductions in the levelized cost of heat by ∼20% when moving from single- to dual-lateral configurations, and by a further ∼25% when a third lateral is added. Similarly, the specific capital cost declines by ∼24% from single to dual laterals and by an additional 16% for triple laterals. Results remain conditional on assumptions of geology, well design, economics, and scalability to greater depth.

title: A GIS-based geothermal heat cost index (GHCI) map for efficient energy planning in Europe
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Younes Noorollahi, Steffen Nielsen, Bernd Moller, Amir Naseri
abstract: In the present society, sustainable energy system development is a vitally important issue receives considerable attention. Central district heating systems supported by renewable energy sources would play an essential role in future energy systems. Geothermal energy, as a renewable energy source, can provide a reliable baseload energy supply for direct uses of heat, such as space heating. For future energy system planning the economic feasibility of such a geothermal district heating system is very important for its viability among other available renewable and nonrenewable energy resources. In this regard, the Levelized Cost of probable hydrothermal geothermal resources of European countries is evaluated using a modified GIS-based GEOPHIRES code. The cost of geothermal heat varies over a wide range according to the many local and global parameters that are affecting the produced heat cost. The results show that, for the resources at a depth of 1000 m the geothermal heat can be provided by 3.7–18 USD/GJ. Furthermore, for deeper geothermal resources (a depth of 2000 m) the heat can be provided at a lower cost and it is more widely available in most of the countries with a cost of 3.4-17 USD/GJ around Europe.

title: Comprehensive characterization of drill core, and geochemical alteration pathways of drill core from the Humu’ula groundwater research project, Hawaii, USA: II. Keamuku maneuver area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Pooja Sheevam, Wendy M. Calvin, Eric Haskins, Thomas Bristow
abstract: In 2013–2015, two deep wells, PTA-2 and KMA-1, were drilled in the Humu‘ula Saddle region of Hawai‘i for groundwater and geothermal exploration as part of a broader effort to understand the geological history and resource potential of subsurface environments on the island of Hawai‘i. This study focuses on the alteration mineralogy of the KMA-1 drill hole, complementing similar investigations conducted on PTA-2. Mineralogical analysis of KMA-1 involved a multi-scale characterization of aqueous alteration using bulk and high-resolution visible and short-wave infrared (VIS-SWIR) and long-wave infrared (LWIR) spectral imaging, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Several types of secondary phases, including alunite, jarosite, secondary hematite, and smectites, were identified. This study shows distinct zones of alteration interspersed with largely unaltered sections and that alteration is not progressive with depth. Field surveys showed widespread alteration and abundant sulfates, while high-resolution techniques like XRD and XRF detected smaller quantities in bulk rock. This discrepancy suggests that spectroscopic methods are highly sensitive to strongly absorbing, albeit minor, mineral phases. Sulfates are not correlated with confined groundwater units suggesting possible fumarole systems buried over time or acid-steam alteration during post-shield volcanic phases. This study contributes to ongoing efforts to characterize the mineralization associated with geothermal and groundwater systems in the Hawaiian subsurface, providing further insight into hydrothermal processes and alteration pathways.

title: Uncertainty quantification under data worth for the Delft campus geothermal project
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Yuan Chen, Guillaume Rongier, James Robert Mullins, Denis Voskov, Alexandros Daniilidis
abstract: Low-enthalpy geothermal doublets for direct-use heating are highly sensitive to subsurface heterogeneity and operational uncertainty. This study quantifies these uncertainties for the Delft campus geothermal system using an integrated workflow that couples geological modeling with GPU-accelerated, high-spatial-resolution reservoir simulation. Ensembles of three-dimensional regional-scale facies models of the Delft Sandstone Member, with and without conditioning to Geothermie Delft (GTD) well data, were generated using object-based modeling and sequential indicator simulation. Porosity was modeled by sequential Gaussian simulation, and permeability was derived from a nuclear magnetic resonance-based porosity–permeability correlation calibrated to GTD well data, yielding higher permeability than core-based correlations for porosity below 15%. Lorenz coefficients indicate strong variability in property distributions, resulting in a wide spread of production temperatures. In total, 2000 geological realizations were simulated over 50 years using the GPU-enabled open-source Delft Advanced Research Terra Simulator (open-DARTS) under maximum and 2025-demand production schemes. Conditioning to GTD wells adds considerable data worth by constraining uncertainty in production well bottom-hole temperature (BHT) and pressure (BHP), while keeping injection pressure within Dutch regulatory limits. SIS models exhibit greater temperature and pressure variability than OBM models due to lower sand-body continuity. Despite large 80% confidence intervals, P50 production temperatures remain comparable for conditioned models. Distance-based generalized sensitivity analysis identifies net-to-gross ratio and the porosity–permeability correlation as dominant controls on thermal response. The 2025-demand scheme delays cold-front propagation. Results demonstrate that ensemble-based, GPU-accelerated high-spatial-resolution simulations enable robust and efficient uncertainty quantification for direct-use geothermal systems, highlighting the importance of well conditioning and reservoir heterogeneity characterization in constraining thermal responses.

title: Thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland basin inferred from 3D conductive heat flow modelling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Belay Gulte Mino, Graeme Beardsmore, Mark A McLean
abstract: Understanding spatial and depth-dependent variations in thermal conductivity is essential for accurate geothermal modelling in sedimentary basins. This study investigates the thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland Basin, southeastern Australia, by integrating published thermal-property datasets with 3D steady-state conductive modelling using the open-source Underworld3 framework. Lithology-dependent mean thermal conductivity values for the Latrobe Valley Subgroup were derived from borehole lithological proportions and ranged from 0.56 to 1.21 W/m·K, reflecting strong lateral heterogeneity associated with variable coal content. The thermal model incorporates spatially variable land surface temperature (LST), interval temperature logs, bottom-hole temperature data, and laterally varying basal temperatures extrapolated using one-dimensional conductive heat flow models and interpolated across the basin. Model results predict surface temperatures ranging from approximately 11.54 to 20.68°C and laterally variable basal temperatures of approximately 120 to 256°C at 5,000 m depth, reflecting the combined influence of thermal conductivity, heat flow, and surface temperature variability. Temperatures at the top of the Cenozoic-aged geothermal source rock range from approximately 14 to 65°C, indicating favourable conditions for low-enthalpy geothermal applications. Model constraining against borehole temperature data demonstrates good agreement between measured and modelled thermal profiles. Volumetric heat-in-place calculations indicate that the Cenozoic-aged geothermal source contains maximum values of approximately 31 exajoules (EJ) of stored thermal energy. These results highlight the importance of incorporating spatially variable thermal conductivity and non-uniform basal boundary conditions into geothermal models and provide a refined framework for geothermal assessment in the onshore Gippsland Basin and other coal-bearing sedimentary basins.

title: Mapping hydrothermally altered minerals using Landsat-8 satellite data, along bambam-billiri-kaltingo axis, in Upper Benue Trough, Northeastern Nigeria
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Bello Yusuf Idi, Mukaila Abdullahi
abstract: The Northeastern Nigerian Upper Benue trough is characterized by hydrothermal and geothermal manifestation features. In this work, the hydrothermally altered mineral deposits are mapped as a reconnaissance survey of the most feasible regions for geothermal energy and oxide mineral exploration in the trough. Bands 2, 4, 5, 6 and 2, 5, 6, 8 of the Landsat-8 OLI are respectively used to highlight iron-oxide and clay/hydroxide-bearing minerals. Band-ratio composites are used to map the relative spatial distribution of the alteration zones. The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is been used to identify the desired spectral bands for Crosta analysis. Based on the eigenvector loadings of the PC components, PCA bands with the highest eigenvalue loadings of the opposite signs are used to map the spatial distribution of iron-oxide and clay/hydroxyl minerals. The plot of delineated zones of hydrothermal alteration indicates the occurrence of iron oxide predominantly within the Keri-Keri Formation in the Northwestern region of the area. The clay and hydroxyl‑bearing minerals occur mostly within the alluvium sediment of the Bima Formation in the Southern region of the area. The work is a guide for geothermal and hydrothermally altered solid mineral explorations.

title: Characteristics and constitutive model of segmented damage and fracture in granite under thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) condition
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Luping Cheng, Chun Wang, Yi Tan, Hao Li, Zonghong Zhou, Yumeng Ren, Juanjuan Li, Taihao Cui
abstract: Rock damage induced by uneven heating, stress, and water supply (three-uneven) from exothermic minerals and geothermal exploitation remains a critical challenge. Four controlling factors (heating temperature, immersion water temperature, heated section height ratio, and heating-immersion water cycle times) were used to simulate the three-uneven conditions. Cyclic heating-immersion water and segmented heat treatment mechanical tests were conducted on granite. Additionally, the concept of "segmented damage" is introduced to describe regionally differentiated physicochemical damage. Results show four stages in axial stress-strain curves: upward concave, linear, nonlinear post-peak, and downward rebound. The first two stages are significantly influenced by the four factors. Both compressive strength and elastic modulus decrease with increasing four factors, and the dominant failure mode is compression shear. The heating boundary is a tensile stress concentration zone, revealing tensile crack initiation. A smaller heated section height ratio causes more severe fracturing in the unheated section, and vice versa. Positioned acoustic emission method reveals crack initiation from tensile thermal damage at the heating interface, and damage fractures morphologies (V-shaped, Y-shaped, single inclined planes). Damage evolution exhibits phased characteristics similar to biological population growth: slow accumulation, accelerated development, and stabilization. Based on this, a damage variable for granite under THM conditions is defined using biological population growth theory, and a segmented damage constitutive model is established. Theoretical curves match experimental data, showing the model effectively describes and predicts pre-peak mechanical behavior and strength characteristics under THM conditions, especially in the compaction and elastic stages.

title: Spatial distribution and environmental implications of total and mobile heavy metals in soils contaminated by long-term chemical industrial emissions
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): Shodi Turdukulovich Kholikulov, Isomiddin Nuriddinovich Bobobekov, Halil Erdem, Cabir Çağrı Gence, Dilfuza Kholmatova
abstract: Aims This study evaluated the spatial distribution, accumulation relative to background levels, DTPA-extractable concentrations, and spatial autocorrelation of potentially toxic elements in soils surrounding the Samarkand Chemical Plant, a major phosphate fertilizer production facility. Methods Surface soil samples (0–30 cm) were collected at distances of 250–5000 m in four cardinal directions. Total and mobile concentrations of Cu, Zn, Pb, Co, and As were determined. Contamination was assessed using Contamination Factor (CF), Geo-accumulation Index (IGEO), and Pollution Load Index (PLI); DTPA-extractable concentrations were compared with the same fraction of the background soil, and spatial autocorrelation was examined using Moran's I. Results Potentially toxic element (PTE) concentrations significantly exceeded background levels, peaking within 250–500 m and decreasing with distance, particularly along western and northern transects. Maximum total concentrations reached 1250 mg kg−1 for Cu, 1320 mg kg−1 for Zn, 526 mg kg−1 for Pb, 520 mg kg−1 for Co and 410 mg kg−1 for As. CF and IGEO values calculated from total concentrations indicated high contamination levels at sampling points close to the facility, particularly for Cu, Pb, and Zn. Moran's I confirmed strong, positive spatial autocorrelation and clustered contamination. Strong correlations between total and mobile fractions indicated that mobile pools are directly controlled by total accumulation. Conclusions Elevated total and DTPA-extractable element concentrations in soils surrounding the facility indicate the need for continued environmental monitoring. The findings identify sampling locations that warrant further investigation, while site-specific assessments are required to determine ecological risks and inform remediation decisions.

title: Declining carbon intensity with inventory- and boundary-dependent inter-city disparity: A two-province audit in China
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): Yulong Luo
abstract: Regional carbon-intensity targets describe aggregate performance but do not indicate whether city intensities converge. We examine how the direction of inter-city disparity changes with spatial boundary and emissions-inventory construction during periods of aggregate intensity decline. We vary the emissions inventory, its grid allocation, the endpoint definition and spatial membership, holding years, GDP denominator, metrics and a pre-specified directional rule fixed. Guangdong is the primary test and Hubei a pre-specified external test province. The Zhou inventory covers a Guangzhou-centered six-city corridor for 2000–2022; a frozen 2003–2017 comparison adds Chen county emissions and EDGAR v8.1 under two grid allocations; Hubei contributes 17 units for 2013–2017. Six-city intensity fell 73.0% while Theil rose 117.6%, and all 31 city omissions retained that pattern within Zhou. At the six- and four-city scales all four Guangdong series agreed, but across 21 cities EDGAR Theil fell by 18.9% and 18.0% while Zhou and Chen Theil rose by 21.2% and 31.6%, so the all-boundary criterion failed. In Hubei, aggregate intensity fell by 24–28% under all four inventory-allocation series, whereas all eight Theil changes were small and inventory-dependent, within 5.8% of their starting levels; no probability model is available to assess their signs. Disparity direction thus agreed across constructions only at the Guangdong corridor scales and diverged at the Guangdong-wide and Hubei-wide boundaries, so reported convergence of city intensities should be checked against differently constructed inventories. Because the inventories differ in source lineage and accounting scope, the reversals cannot be attributed to any single accounting choice.

title: Atmospheric microplastic deposition and inhalation health risk assessment at a tropical university campus in Malaysia
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): Muhammad Imran Zaffar, Fang-Lee Lim, Sumathi Sethupathi, Siti Nurfahirah Muhamad, Jheng-Jie Jiang, Mohammad Adam Bin Adman
abstract: Atmospheric microplastic deposition remains poorly characterized in tropical inland environments, particularly at university campuses where diverse human activities generate and resuspend synthetic particles. This study reports thirteen weeks of passive sampling (February–April 2026) at four paired indoor and outdoor stations at Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman (UTAR), Kampar, Malaysia. Passive sampling was combined with fluorescence microscopy, micro-FTIR polymer identification, meteorological correlation analysis and an inhalation-based human health risk assessment. Outdoor stations recorded a mean daily deposition flux of 201.3 ± 165.8 particles/m2/day, and indoor stations a mean of 576.4 ± 262.8 particles/m2/day. Lecture Hall Outdoor recorded the highest outdoor deposition (222.5 particles/m2/day), whereas Canteen Indoor exhibited the greatest indoor accumulation (764.1 particles/m2/day). Fragments and beads were the dominant particle forms in the fluorescence counts, and the 1–50 μm fractions dominated the size distribution at all stations. Semi-synthetic rayon was the most frequent material among spectrally identified particles (52 of 77). Outdoor deposition showed moderate but non-significant positive correlations with wind speed (rs = 0.407), relative humidity (rs = 0.368) and cumulative rainfall (rs = 0.341). Under the applied exposure and toxicological assumptions, modeled Hazard Index (HI) values at all stations were below 1.0 when compared with a surrogate particulate benchmark, and an upper-bound cancer risk screening indicator (CRI), which assumes that all polystyrene mass is equivalent to styrene, was several orders of magnitude below the 10−6 value conventionally used for comparison. These screening-level indices are not estimates of actual health risk; they depend on air concentrations reconstructed from passive deposition, a limited spectrally identified subset and surrogate toxicological values, and should not be interpreted as evidence of safety. Precautionary measures such as frequent wet mopping may be considered for high-occupancy indoor sites, although their effectiveness was not evaluated in this study.

title: Nitrogen-related grey water footprint of the main crops in Buenos Aires: Agricultural pollution or nutrient gap?
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): María Macarena Arrien, Maite M. Aldaya, Corina Iris Rodríguez
abstract: The expansion of agriculture in Argentina has increased the demand for inputs such as synthetic mineral fertilisers, which has heightened stress on water resources through both their use and the associated pollution. In particular, the grey water footprint (GWF) can be used to estimate the volume of water required to assimilate pollutants derived from agricultural production, such as nitrogen from fertilisation. Therefore, the objective of this study was to estimate the anthropogenic nitrogen load and calculate the GWF of the main extensive crops (maize, wheat, barley, soybean, oat, and sunflower) in the central-southeastern region of Buenos Aires province from 2008 to 2018. A methodology based on soil nitrogen balance with local data was applied to assess the potential stress on water resources. Soybean, sunflower, and oat did not present GWF because of negative nitrogen balances related to biological fixation (soybean) or under-fertilisation (sunflower and oat), a situation that reflects a ‘nutrient gap’. In contrast, wheat, barley, and maize showed GWF values of 401, 281 and 351 m3/ton respectively, particularly in areas with low yields. It is concluded that, although a zero GWF reduces the risk of nitrate pollution, it may also indicate progressive soil degradation caused by net nutrient export. Therefore, particularly in degraded soils or soils with low nutrient reserve capacity, a key recommendation is to optimise fertilisation management through practices such as soil analysis, the use of organic fertilisers, and strategies that promote nutrient replacement.

title: Thermal physiology of Heterostegina depressa and its potential expansion in a warming Mediterranean Sea
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): Michael Lintner, Manfred Wildner, Michael Schagerl, Igor Niezgodzki, Wolfgang Wanek, Matthias Nagy, Petra Heinz, Jan Goleń, Jarosław Tyszka
abstract: Climate warming is reshaping the biogeography of the Mediterranean Sea and increasingly favours the establishment and range expansion of warm-affinity and non-indigenous species. We quantified the temperature dependence of physiological performance in Heterostegina depressa, a large benthic foraminifer that hosts obligate diatom symbionts, across 10–35 °C. Complementary measurements of photosynthetic performance, photosynthetically active area, chlorophyll-a and fucoxanthin, and assimilation of inorganic 13C and 15N revealed the highest overall performance around 25 °C and sustained activity between 20 and 30 °C, whereas both colder and warmer treatments strongly impaired host–symbiont functioning. These responses are consistent with previously reported thermal limits for H. depressa but extend them by integrating multiple physiological and metabolic endpoints. We combined the experimentally observed thermal window with Mediterranean seawater-temperature simulations to explore how the area thermally permissive for H. depressa may shift under warming. We interpret these maps as potential thermal suitability rather than predictions of realized distribution, because establishment also depends on light, depth, substrate, hydrodynamics, nutrient conditions, dispersal, and biotic interactions. The results place H. depressa within the broader tropicalization of Mediterranean biota, in which warming relaxes cold-season barriers for thermophilic taxa while increasing summer heat stress at the warm end of their thermal niche.

title: Projected climate warming reduces occurrence probability of the imperiled Athabasca rainbow trout
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1058 Author(s): Lee Frank Gordon Gutowsky, Tyana Ashlie Rudolfsen
abstract: Freshwater salmonids often occupy narrow ecological niches defined by tight physiological constraints, limited dispersal pathways, and strong dependence on local habitat conditions. As climate warming, land use, and habitat fragmentation reshape riverine environments, many species may shift distributions or experience population declines, creating species-specific conservation challenges. We integrated two decades of Athabasca rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) inventory data from Alberta, Canada, with geomorphic and anthropogenic predictors in a gradient boosting species distribution model and projected occurrence probabilities under moderate and high future air-temperature scenarios while holding non-climatic predictors constant. Mean August air temperature had the greatest relative influence in the final model, and fitted occurrence probability was highest across an intermediate range of about 12–15 °C. Mean predicted occurrence probability across the stream network declined from 0.205 under current conditions to 0.107–0.068 under future air-temperature scenarios, equivalent to reductions of 47.7–66.9%. Although 54.8–97.4% of future stream-network sampling points fell outside at least one predictor range represented in the training data, increasing uncertainty in the magnitude and spatial distribution of projected change, the direction of change was consistent across all scenarios. These declines are projected across a landscape also characterized by roads and watercourse crossings, highlighting potential conservation conflicts where recovery objectives intersect with ongoing land use. These conditional projections provide a spatially explicit basis for prioritizing monitoring and conservation planning where climate-associated declines and existing landscape pressures coincide.

title: Landscape controls on thermal buffering and heatwave amplification in temperate river systems under increasing hydrometeorological extremes
description: Publication date: 25 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1057 Author(s): Mariusz Ptak, Soufiane Haddout, Teerachai Amnuaylojaroen
abstract: Water temperature is a key parameter governing river ecosystem functioning and is changing markedly under climate warming. Understanding how rivers respond to heatwaves is increasingly important as these events grow in frequency and intensity, yet the mechanisms shaping riverine thermal responses remain poorly understood. This study analysed atmospheric and riverine heatwaves from 1971 to 2024 in four temperate lowland rivers with contrasting landscape settings: forested, agricultural and urban catchments, and a reach influenced by a nearby lake. Atmospheric heatwaves followed similar patterns across all catchments, whereas the rivers' thermal responses varied considerably. The same climatic signal was attenuated in the Drawa but amplified in the Warta, Prosna and Obra. The intensification of riverine heatwaves relative to atmospheric changes ranged from about 2% in the Drawa to 140% in the Obra. Atmospheric heatwave events and days increased significantly at all four stations (Mann–Kendall, p < 0.001), whereas trends in water heatwave days ranged from 0.05 to 1.77 days year−1 and were significant in the Warta, Prosna and Obra (p < 0.01) but not in the Drawa. These differences were associated mainly with local landscape and hydrological conditions. In the Drawa, a predominantly forested catchment and substantial groundwater inputs limited water warming and enhanced resilience to thermal extremes. By contrast, the Obra reach, downstream of a shallow polymictic lake, showed strong amplification consistent with the lake's influence. In the Warta, the urban heat island effect was weaker than expected because its higher discharge, relative to the agricultural Prosna, buffered warming. The results indicate that local catchment characteristics can either attenuate or amplify the effects of climate warming on river thermal regimes, and that landscape controls modulate the regional climate signal shaping riverine heatwaves. These findings highlight the need to incorporate landscape conditions into river adaptation strategies.

title: Anthropogenic degradation of local ecosystems under extreme explosive impacts: Coupled soil geochemical anomalies and aerosol forcing
description: Publication date: 25 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1057 Author(s): Pavlo Bosak, Alina Bratus, Andrii Havrys, Vasyl Loik, Marian Lavrivskyi, Andrii Voloshchyshyn, Oleksandra Pekarska
abstract: Extreme high-energy impacts on critical infrastructure generate unprecedented spatially coupled environmental anomalies. Traditional approaches to assessing technogenic hazards often consider soil degradation and atmospheric pollution as separate processes, which reduces the effectiveness of spatial planning for emergency response. The aim of this study is to quantitatively assess a coupled two-phase environmental anomaly caused by missile strikes in order to develop strategies for ensuring environmental safety and reducing disaster risk. An integrated two-level design was applied: a macroscale analysis of the acute atmospheric phase, based on Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI satellite monitoring and SILAM numerical dispersion modeling using 40,000 cores on the PUHTI supercomputer, was combined with targeted microscale profiling of the chronic pedological phase using XRF spectrometry along a high-resolution transect across the epicenter of an X-101 missile crater. It was established that the destruction of infrastructure generates extreme emission pulses, with CO increasing by up to 362.5% and SO₂ by up to 454.8%, as well as aerosol forcing that locally triggers extreme precipitation. At ground level, a persistent geochemical gradient was identified, characterized by local accumulation of potentially toxic elements (e.g., Sr up to 184 mg/kg and Cu with an anthropogenic enrichment factor of 2.6) and a critical shift in acid-base balance toward alkalinity, with pH reaching 7.8. The study demonstrates that high-energy explosions act as a systemic trigger of complex environmental degradation. The proposed methodology provides an objective scientific basis for spatially targeted reclamation and emergency risk management strategies.

title: Simultaneous quantification of microbial source tracking markers, pathogenic bacteria, and antibiotic resistance genes in river water using high-throughput quantitative polymerase chain reaction in West Java, Indonesia
description: Publication date: 25 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1057 Author(s): Annisa Andarini Ruti, Soichiro Hirai, Bikash Malla, Ahmad Soleh Setiyawan, Tjandra Setiadi, Eiji Haramoto
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of contaminants in environments such as river water is crucial for effective water quality management. In this study, high-throughput quantitative polymerase chain reaction (HT-qPCR) was used to simultaneously examine 21 targets, including 10 microbial source tracking (MST) markers, five pathogenic bacteria, three antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), one mobile genetic element, and two bacterial indicator genes. During the dry season (August–September 2023), river water samples (n = 24) were collected from eight points along a river in West Java, Indonesia, and processed by centrifugation, DNA extraction, pre-amplification, and HT-qPCR. Across all targets, R2 (coefficient of determination) ranged from 0.989 to 1.000 and efficiencies ranged from 90% to 113%, indicating high performance, except for crAssphage (efficiency of 146%), which was subsequently excluded from further analysis. From the remaining MST markers analyzed, human- and bovine-associated markers, except for BK polyomavirus, were detected at positive ratios ranging from 8% (2/24; 95% CI: 1–27%) to 50% (12/24; 95% CI: 29–71%), whereas none of the swine-associated markers were detected. Of the five pathogenic bacteria tested, only cpe-positive Clostridium perfringens was detected, with a positive ratio of 8% (2/24; 95% CI: 1–27%). Across river sites, intI1, sul1, bla CTX-M, and bla NDM-1 were detected at positive ratios of at least 46% (11/24; 95% CI: 26–67%). From Sites 3 to 8, bla NDM-1 showed a mean concentration of 5.1 ± 0.7 log10 copies/L. Abundances of bla CTX-M, sul1, and intI1, were comparable (Bonferroni-adjusted paired t-tests, all adjusted p > 0.05), with strong correlations (Spearman's rank ρ = 0.77–0.85, p < 0.05). In these samples, ARG abundance may be more closely linked to overall fecal bacterial loading than to a specific host source. The elevated abundance of ARGs and microbial markers at several sites suggested that localized pollution sources should be prioritized for mitigation.

title: Contrasting thermal tolerance in corals emerges from temperature-induced gene network rewiring and isoform switching
description: Publication date: 25 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1057 Author(s): Federica Scucchia, Pierrick Harnay, Hollie M. Putnam
abstract: Organismal thermal tolerance will shape future coral reef function, as ocean warming drives extensive stress and mortality through increasingly frequent marine heatwaves. This is among the most apparent phenomena on reefs, where marine heatwaves can devastate reef-building corals, the ecosystem engineers, driving the breakdown of the coral-algae symbiosis, or coral bleaching. Coral resistance to bleaching varies markedly among species, reflecting differences in physiology underpinned by molecular regulatory mechanisms that are initiated early during heat stress and influence longer-term bleaching outcomes. Gene expression plasticity enables transcriptional adjustments to environmental stress, while alternative splicing and isoform switching further expand molecular adaptability by altering transcript diversity and abundance. Because genes function within combinatorial networks, changes in these network members and in the identity of highly influential hub genes can reveal higher-order biological reorganization under stress. Yet, the contribution of isoform switching to gene network dynamics remains unknown in corals. Here we integrate physiological performance, gene network topology, hub genes dynamics, and isoform switching across three Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa, Montipora capitata, and Pocillopora acuta, with known differences in thermal sensitivity to identify molecular processes shaping acute thermal responses. We show that the interplay between expression plasticity, hub gene rearrangement, and isoform switching drives species-specific thermal tolerance. Species-specific thermal tolerance was associated with differences in energetic status, with the most thermally tolerant species, P. compressa, exhibiting the highest energetic reserves. Network analysis uncovered extensive rewiring and temperature-responsive hub genes turnover regulated by switches in isoform usage. P. compressa shows stable constitutive gene expression and continuous isoform adjustments across temperatures, while fine-tuning thermal response through dedicated hub genes. In contrast, the most thermally sensitive species, P. acuta, shows broad transcriptomic shifts and isoform switching controlling the reorganization of network leadership at high temperatures. Together, these findings identify isoform switching as an under-explored regulatory mechanism linking early molecular responses to coral thermal resilience and species persistence in warming oceans.

title: Redox states of the open ocean during the early Ediacaran and Cambrian Ages 1–3: constraints from vanadium isotopes
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Pei-Shan Sui, Wei Wei, Shao-Bing Zhang, Guang-Yi Wei, Yan-Yan Zhao, Tianchen He, Hong-Fei Ling, Fang Huang
abstract: The early Ediacaran and Cambrian Ages 1–3 witnessed multiphase biological innovations, in which oceanic oxygenation may have played crucial roles. However, detailed marine redox states during this period remain highly debated. Sedimentary vanadium (V) isotope geochemistry is an emerging redox proxy for tracing changes in global marine redox state. Here, we report leachate V isotope compositions (δ51Vleach) of black shales from the lower Ediacaran and Cambrian Stages 1–3 successions in the Yangtze Block, South China. The δ51Vleach variability in the lower Ediacaran succession was caused by changes in local V drawdown efficiency, while that of the Cambrian Stages 1–3 was mainly derived from the open-ocean seawater δ51V (δ51VOSW) variation in response to global marine redox change. Based on these sedimentary δ51Vleach records, we reconstructed temporal δ51VOSW variations during the early Ediacaran and Cambrian Ages 1–3. During the early Ediacaran, the δ51VOSW value (–0.45 ± 0.06‰) is significantly lower than the modern value, and then increases during the Cambrian Ages 1–3, eventually reaching the modern value with an average of 0.26 ± 0.33‰ at ca. 521 Ma. Model-based estimates suggest that the open ocean of the early Ediacaran (ca. 594–582 Ma) may have been extensively euxinic, where early organisms could have survived due to the low oxygen requirements for basic metabolism or local oceanic oxygenation. The oxygenation extent of the open ocean during the Cambrian Ages 1–3 (ca. 539–514 Ma) should have significantly increased, possibly approaching modern-like value under our preferred model assumptions at ca. 521 Ma, which may have promoted the first appearance and radiation of skeletal metazoans and the subsequent Cambrian Explosion.

title: Comparative study of anoxic dissolution of arsenopyrite, loellingite, and pyrite: Crystal structural controls on interfacial reactivity
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Pei Chang, Xiangyu Zhu, Minghao Tang, Jianchao Zhang, Xiancai Lu, Cong-qiang Liu, H. Henry Teng
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and redox reactions at mineral–water interfaces fundamentally govern trace metal mobility and geochemical cycles in O2-limited environment. However, predicting how interfacial reactivity and ROS generation shift across compositionally related dichalcogenide minerals, driven by varying anionic frameworks and crystal structures, remains unresolved. Here, we systematically investigated the anoxic dissolution of pyrite, arsenopyrite, and loellingite under varying pH conditions by integrating aqueous H2O2 quantification, macroscopic dissolution kinetics, and surface-sensitive analyses (XPS and zeta potential). We propose that in sulfide-bearing minerals (pyrite and arsenopyrite), alkaline conditions actively promote H2O2 generation, which suppress the passivating effect from nascent Fe(III)-O layers and accelerates dissolution. In contrast, sulfide-deficient loellingite exhibits suppressed H2O2 accumulation and decelerated arsenic release under alkaline conditions due to the formation of a stable Fe(III)-O protective layer. This divergence may reflect loellingite’s narrow band gap and polarizable electronic framework, which together with its edge-sharing structure, may facilitate internal charge redistribution that quenches surface ·OH before H2O2 formation. These findings provide a fundamental physical–chemical framework linking bulk crystal geometry to interfacial ROS dynamics, offering critical insights for predicting mineral-specific dissolution behavior and arsenic mobility in anoxic subsurface systems.
