title: N and O isotope fractionation reveals distinct pathways of dissimilatory nitrite reduction to ammonium
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Guojun Chen, Qinqin Hao, Yan Ru, Andreas Kappler, Raymond Jianxiong Zeng, Xiaomin Li, Zebin Hong, Fanghua Liu, Fujun Yue, Shiwen Hu, Tongxu Liu
abstract: Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) is a major pathway of nitrogen (N) retention, yet its isotope systematics remain poorly constrained. Although DNRA and denitrification (DNF) share the same nitrate reductases, they diverge fundamentally at the nitrite reduction step, which represents the key biochemical distinction between N retention and N loss. Understanding N and oxygen (O) isotope fractionation during nitrite reduction is therefore critical for constraining isotopic signatures associated with DNRA pathways. This study systematically investigates dual N and O isotope fractionation associated with fermentative and respiratory DNRA pathways mediated by key nitrite reductases. Using pure-culture experiments spanning cytoplasmic (NirB) and periplasmic (NrfA-based) DNRA pathways, together with a mechanistic kinetic model, we demonstrate that different DNRA pathways generate characteristic and distinguishable N and O isotopic fingerprints. NirB-based fermentative DNRA showed a ratio of the O- and N-isotope effects (the 18 ε:15 ε ratio) of 0.45 ± 0.05, while NrfA-type respiratory DNRA exhibited a ratio of 1.15 ± 0.75. In contrast, multi-subunit NrfA-NrfH and NrfA-NrfB systems displayed negative 18 ε:15 ε ratios (−0.23 ± 0.30 and − 0.25 ± 0.09, respectively), indicating inverse O isotope fractionation linked to complex electron transfer mechanisms. These characteristic isotopic signatures provide a quantitative framework for identifying previously uncharacterized DNRA pathways in biogeochemical N cycling.

title: A continuum formulation for nano-scale mineral dissolution with stepwave-driven surface dynamics
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): M. Starnoni, C. Recalcati, M. Riva, X. Sanchez-Vila, A. Guadagnini
abstract: We develop a continuum-scale framework to describe the evolution of dissolving mineral surfaces directly from nano-scale observations. Quantitative interpretation of mineral dissolution remains challenging because surface evolution arises from coupled actions of terrace retreat and crystallographically controlled step propagation, resulting in experimentally observed surface morphologies that are inherently heterogeneous and dynamic. We represent the fluid-mineral interface as a moving surface whose velocity is decomposed into normal and tangential components associated with terrace retreat and lateral step propagation, respectively. Uncertainty in the corresponding model parameters is quantified through a stochastic Monte Carlo inverse-modeling framework constrained by real-time Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) observations. The approach is applied to the analysis of dissolution of a calcite crystal monitored through time-resolved AFM imaging. Simulations can reproduce the key statistical and spatial characteristics of the evolving surface and the distribution of reaction rates. Inferred parameter distributions reveal a systematic increase in tangential step-propagation velocities during dissolution, highlighting the increasing contribution of lateral step migration to surface evolution. Our formulation is consistent with the established conceptual picture of stepwave-driven surface dynamics and observed surface evolution, and provides a quantitative and physically interpretable link between nano-scale surface morphology and the effective processes governing mineral dissolution.

title: Species-specific strontium distribution and environment in coccolithophores revealed by X-ray fluorescence and spectroscopy
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Hallam J.M. Greene, Jessica M. Walker, Gerald Langer
abstract: The Sr/Ca ratio of coccoliths is the most developed coccolithophore-related geochemical proxy; used to reconstruct coccolithophore productivity. A process-based understanding of this proxy is limited, because Sr partitioning models are mostly not independently constrained. It has recently been discovered that the lopadoliths of Scyphosphaera apsteinii display stripes of different Sr concentrations, contrary to model predictions. In this study we use XRF imaging to investigate the distribution of Sr across coccoliths from different coccolithophore families. We measured coccoliths from two Coccolithales species, Coccolithus braarudii and Calcidiscus leptoporus, and two Zygodiscales, Pontosphaera syracusana and Helicosphaera carteri. Only P. syracusana showed Sr stripes akin to the ones in S. apsteinii. Thus, we hypothesize that Sr stripiness is an invention of the Pontosphaeraceae. This family produces high Sr muroliths, whereas the other species investigated here produce comparatively low Sr placoliths. All species investigated so far, however, incorporate Sr into Ca sites of the calcite lattice in coccolith calcite, as opposed to other inorganic or organic phases, as evidenced by XANES. We conclude that the Pontosphaeraceae feature a more complex calcification mechanism than placolith bearing species, including time-dependent Sr partitioning, a process that is not captured by our current models.

title: Volcanically driven redox stratification and N–S–C cycling perturbation in a Late Triassic lacustrine system: controls on carbon sequestration efficiency
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Xianxu Fang, Kelai Xi, Yingchang Cao, Xiujuan Wang, Guanghui Yuan, Yuan You, Miruo Lin, Ke Li, Chao Liang, Keyu Liu, Fang Hao
abstract: Water-column redox structure fundamentally governs ecosystem dynamics, biogeochemical cycling, and ultimately sedimentary responses. Redox stratification recorded in deep-time organic-rich lacustrine shales was frequently perturbed by geological events, particularly volcanism, which enhanced deoxygenation and nutrient loading under recurrent volcanic inputs. However, the biogeochemical pathways by which ecological stress developed and persisted remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate the Upper Triassic Chang 73 Sub-member of the Yanchang Formation in the Ordos Basin, a continuous succession of organic-rich lacustrine shales deposited under episodic volcanic influence. Integrating sedimentological, paleontological and multi-proxy geochemical records, we reconstruct the vertical redox structure of the paleolake and assess its response to contrasting volcanic input fluxes. Our results reveal a stable three-layer redox stratification (oxic, suboxic, and euxinic) that couples nitrogen–sulfur–carbon biogeochemical cycling via a cascade of aerobic respiration, denitrification, anammox, Fe–Mn reduction, and sulfate reduction. Positive δ15Norg values provide direct evidence for a chemocline that restricts denitrification and anammox to the suboxic layer without interference from sulfate reduction below. As volcanic input flux increased from low to high, δ13Corg shifted from negative excursions reflecting internal recycling of 12C to positive excursions driven by Rayleigh fractionation. This shift marks the transition from weakened to efficient carbon sequestration. These contrasting redox states demonstrate that volcanic forcing regulated carbon sequestration through nutrient fertilization that elevated primary productivity, but it was the integrity of redox stratification that ultimately determined carbon burial efficiency. Accordingly, we develop an integrated redox‑ecological model linking the strength of external volcanic forcing, the feedbacks of internal biogeochemical cycling, and the efficiency of lacustrine carbon sequestration into a coherent system. This model provides a process-based explanation of how this integrity mediates ecological stress and governs carbon sequestration efficiency. Drawing on this deep-time eutrophic lake system, this study identifies critical redox thresholds governing ecosystem responses to nutrient enrichment and deoxygenation in modern lakes.

title: Nanoscale mechanisms of mesocrystal formation during non-classical heterogeneous growth of manganese (hydr)oxides on ferrihydrite
description: Publication date: 15 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 435 Author(s): Yixuan Yang, Qingze Chen, Chi Zhang, Haozhe Ma, Jing Liu, Jianxi Zhu, Runliang Zhu, Hongping He
abstract: Crystallization by particle attachment (CPA) is an important non-classical pathway of mineral growth that often produces mesocrystals composed of aligned nanoparticles, whose internal interfaces and defects can impart distinctive geochemical reactivity. Given that mineral nucleation and growth in nature commonly occur on pre-existing substrates, a key yet underexplored question is how CPA-mediated mesocrystal growth operates at such heterogeneous interfaces. Herein, we investigated the heterogeneous oxidation of aqueous Mn(II) on ferrihydrite, with a specific focus on the formation of manganese (Mn) (hydr)oxides mesocrystals via CPA. Our results show that Mn (hydr)oxides formed on ferrihydrite grew via oriented assembly into mesocrystalline nanowires. Specifically, Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles assembled via end-to-end or side-by-side manners to elongate or widen nanowires, respectively. Misorientations among component nanoparticles led to curved nanowires, whereas straight nanowires resulted from well-aligned interfaces. Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles with different crystallographic orientations, and even different mineral phases, can assemble into mesocrystalline nanowires featuring misoriented but crystallographically correlated interfaces. This assembly is rationalized by approximate lattice correspondence at particle junctions and further supported by molecular dynamics simulations revealing energetically favorable interfacial configurations. The assembly of Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles was likely initiated by their detachment from ferrihydrite surfaces, driven by the accumulation and release of stress and strain at mismatched Mn (hydr)oxide-ferrihydrite interfaces. Revealing numerous new atomic details of Mn (hydr)oxide CPA, our study links the assembly behaviors of Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles to the development of their mesocrystalline structures. We also integrate our new findings with previous studies and synthesize the mechanisms by which different mineral substrates regulate CPA of Mn (hydr)oxides. These findings advance the understanding of heterogeneous growth of Mn (hydr)oxides on iron (hydr)oxides at the nanoscale and contribute to a more integrated view of coupled Mn-Fe cycling in the environment. Our study also highlights the critical roles of substrate mineral surfaces in non-classical mineral growth.

title: Contrasting sulfide behaviors during mantle silicate and carbonate metasomatism: Evidence from Os isotopes and highly siderophile elements in K-rich and Na-rich basalts
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Zhao-Xue Wang, Zhu Yin Chu, Tian-Hao Wu, Jingao Liu, Sheng-Ao Liu, Peng Peng
abstract: The oxidative breakdown of sulfides in the mantle is essential for extraction of chalcophile/siderophile elements into basaltic magmas and their potential contribution to the formation of metal ore deposits. This breakdown process is commonly associated with melt/fluid metasomatism, but the nature of special metasomatic agents is not yet well-constrained. Here, we report a comparative analysis of radiogenic Os isotopes, Re and platinum group element (PGE) contents in Cenozoic intraplate basalts from Eastern China, through combining new data for ultrapotassic (K2O/Na2O > 3) and potassic (K2O/Na2O = 1–3) basalts with published data for sodic (K2O/Na2O < 1) basalts. The ultrapotassic basalts have highly radiogenic 187Os/188Os ratios (0.1586–0.2954), in contrast to the sodic basalts with modern mantle-like 187Os/188Os values (0.1221–0.1432). Along with the differences in Sr-Nd-Mg-Zn-Fe isotopic compositions, ultrapotassic basalts were sourced from the lithospheric mantle mainly metasomatized by recycled silicic sediments, while sodic basalts originated from the asthenospheric mantle dominantly hybridized by recycled carbonate sediments. The two types of rocks display strong contrasts in terms of Re-PGE. Ultrapotassic basalts have differentiated PGE patterns and low total PGE contents (e.g., (Pd/Ir)N = 1.76–5.27; Ir = 0.036–0.051 ppb), indicating sulfides as a crucial residual phase during mantle melting. In contrast, sodic basalts exhibit almost undifferentiated PGE patterns and elevated total PGE contents (e.g., (Pd/Ir)N = 0.39–2.62; Ir = 0.045–0.314 ppb), indicative of sulfide breakdown during melting. Potassic basalts exhibit Re-PGE patterns and contents falling between ultrapotassic and sodic basalts, supporting a mixing origin inferred from Sr-Nd-Mg-Zn-Fe isotopes. These observations reveal distinct behaviors of sulfides during mantle silicate versus carbonate metasomatism at different depths. Metasomatism by recycled, reduced silicic sediments causes ineffective sulfide extraction, and instead results in long-term storage of chalcophile/siderophile elements in the subcontinental lithospheric mantle, which are potential to be released during subsequent melting events. In contrast, carbonate metasomatism at deeper mantle is a mechanism by which chalcophile/siderophile elements are extracted into magmas, possibly through oxidation-enhanced sulfide breakdown associated with the reduction of recycled carbonate. Collectively, both types of mantle metasomatism can have contributed to the extraction of highly siderophile elements through distinct ways at different stages.

title: Lignin degradation products in stemflow dissolved organic matter of three deciduous tree species
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Dillon Siple, Robyn C. O’Halloran, Samantha Chittakone, Karl Kaiser, Delphis F. Levia, Yu-Ping Chin
abstract: Stemflow is meteoric water flowing down a tree trunk and is a significant yet understudied pathway for mobilizing dissolved organic matter (DOM) from forest canopies to the soil. We studied the role of stemflow as a major source of soluble lignin-derived compounds and their degradation products to forest ecosystems during leafed months. Stemflow samples were taken from three deciduous tree species: Liriodendron tulipifera L. (yellow poplar), Fagus grandifolia Ehrh. (American beech), and Betula lenta L. (sweet birch) for three separate rain events. Stemflow was analyzed for its DOM composition and properties, as well as its lignin degradation products. Lignin degradation product composition of stemflow was determined through oxidation of DOM extracts by cupric sulfate and analyzed using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry. Due to limited sampling, results discussed throughout this paper are preliminary, but show an apparent need for future research of lignin-derived compounds within stemflow. We found dissolved organic carbon-normalized lignin degradation products values 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than in river waters and several times higher than throughfall (rainfall that passes through the canopy). Previous research quantifying lignin in deciduous tree detritus found carbon-normalized lignin degradation values similar to stemflow. Thus, while plant detritus provides useful insights into the compositional nature of unaltered source material, stemflow may offer similar information with respect to lignin degradation products. Stemflow lignin degradation product composition showed high syringyl to vanillyl (S/V) ratios typical of angiosperm origin as well as high vanillyl acid to aldehyde (Ad/Al)V ratios. These high (Ad/Al)V ratios are attributed to the constant cycling of depolymerized lignin by microbial degradation with stemflow dissolving and mobilizing these compounds. Thus, stemflow’s role in transporting soluble lignin-derived compounds to soils warrants further investigation, with important implications for understanding terrestrial carbon cycling.

title: Electrostatic discharge triggers troilite‑to‑magnetite oxidation in Mars dust activity
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Xiaojia Zeng, Xiongyao Li
abstract: Electrostatic discharge in Martian dust storms may significantly drive the chemical alteration and cycling of surface materials. Troilite is expected on Mars from magmatic and meteoritic sources but remains undetected by rovers, raising the question of possible electrostatic discharge-driven alteration. However, this hypothesis lacks direct experimental support. In this study, we experimentally simulate electrical discharge under Martian conditions by exposing troilite to such discharge in a CO2 atmosphere at low pressure. We found that electrical discharge rapidly oxidizes troilite to magnetite (Fe3O4), forming a ∼ 100 nm thick, polycrystalline, defect-rich alteration layer on the troilite surface. This oxidation is driven by reactive oxygen species attack Fe-S bonds, displace sulfur, and convert the residual iron framework into magnetite. Such an electrical discharge-driven pathway offers a new water-free mechanism for magnetite formation on Mars, specifically active during the hyper-arid Amazonian epoch. This work also provides an additional explanation for the missing troilite in Martian soils and the widespread occurrence of magnetite in Martian dust. More broadly, this study expands our understanding of Martian surface evolution beyond water-dominated scenarios and highlights oxidative role of ongoing dust activities on present-day Mars.

title: Bomb- 14 C signals in Santa Barbara Basin sediments and radiocarbon constraints on terrestrial organic carbon
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Hanyue Xu, Hong-Chun Li, Da-Wei Li, Meng Yu, Hailong Zhang, William M. Berelson, Meixun Zhao
abstract: The anthropogenic bomb-14C signal (produced by nuclear bomb tests in the atmosphere during 1945–1964 yr CE) provides a powerful tracer for quantifying organic carbon (OC) dynamics in marine sediments. This study uses two 210Pb-dated box cores (SBB-190629 and SBB-8-2012) from the Santa Barbara Basin (SBB), and the measured total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen, δ 13C and Δ14C of TOC (Δ14CTOC) to track the propagation of bomb-14C signal. Although bulk sedimentary Δ14CTOC values were strongly negative (−384‰ to −64‰), a distinct Δ14CTOC enrichment (up to ∼90‰) was identified in both cores after 1960 yr CE. This enrichment is identified as a bomb-14C event through its temporal synchronicity with the Δ14C records of established atmospheric carbon dioxide and surface seawater dissolved inorganic carbon. To deconvolve this signal, we employed a series of mixing models. A δ 13C-based binary mixing model was used to quantify the marine and terrestrial OC fractions since 1815 yr CE. Subsequently, the time-parallel surface seawater dissolved inorganic carbon radiocarbon record was used as the marine end-member to reconstruct the Δ14C composition of terrestrial OC. Finally, through the application of a petrogenic-biospheric mixing model, we revealed a significant bomb-14C enrichment within the biospheric component of the terrestrial OC and quantified a stable, background contribution of 14C-free petrogenic carbon (∼18%). Our findings demonstrate the attenuation of the bomb-14C signal through a complex terrestrial-marine system can still be recorded on sediment in SBB. This study establishes a framework to disentangle the bomb-14C signal on marine, biospheric-terrestrial, and petrogenic-terrestrial components. It also provides an approach for interpreting radiocarbon data in continental margin sediments and for constraining carbon cycling processes across these dynamic interfaces.

title: Simultaneous formation of DNA and RNA nucleosides in shock-recovery experiments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Jiawen Zhao, Koichi Mimura
abstract: Whether RNA, DNA, or both emerged as the first genetic system remains an important question in origin-of-life research. The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA preceded DNA, whereas alternative scenarios allow for the coexistence of RNA- and DNA-related building blocks during early chemical evolution. A key chemical question is whether deoxyribonucleosides can be generated abiotically from molecular precursors that could have been available under prebiotic conditions. Meteorite impacts generate transient high-pressure and high-temperature conditions that can promote rapid chemical reactions in solid-state environments. Here, we investigate the formation of ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks from ribose and canonical purine and pyrimidine nucleobases under simulated meteorite impact conditions. Shock compression generated both ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks during a single shock event. Single- and dual-13C-labeling experiments confirmed the incorporation of carbon from both ribose and nucleobase. Experiments conducted under different reaction conditions showed that nucleoside yields and product distributions varied with mineral composition, organic loading, nucleobase composition, and water content. These results demonstrate that shock compression provides a solid-state reaction regime in which both ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks can be generated from common molecular precursors. This study provides experimental constraints on nucleoside formation and the environmental factors affecting this process under impact-driven conditions.

title: Thermodynamics of NaCl(aq) from 230 to 2000 K and from 0.1 to 10,000 MPa: Applications to Earth and Other Ocean Worlds
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): J. Michael Brown, Olivier Bollengier, Ula Jones, Steven D. Vance, Baptiste Journaux
abstract: We present a new Gibbs energy representation for aqueous NaCl, based on new sound speed and phase equilibrium measurements, using local basis functions. Throughout, NaCl(aq) denotes the bulk aqueous component — the sum of NaCl 0 , Na + and Cl − — rather than the neutral complex, with the degree of dissociation implicit in the measurements rather than imposed. This comprehensive equation of state, valid for pressures to 10 000 M P a , temperatures from 230 K to 2000 K , and molality to 7 m o l k g − 1 , allows us to address chemical processes within Earth and interior structure and evolution of large icy moons with possible oceans. The region below 500 M P a at temperatures above 500 K , which contains water’s saturation curve and critical point, is excluded for want of constraining measurements; within the domain represented the fluid is a single phase. In regimes unconstrained by data, it assumes near-gas behavior at high temperatures and volume mixing of water and salt at extreme pressures. Differentiation of the representation yields all equilibrium properties, including volumes, specific heat capacities, and chemical potentials. The model is validated by its accurate prediction of ice Ih and VI melting and brucite dehydration in saline solutions, and by its reproduction of antigorite dehydration in pure water through two changes in reaction product to beyond 6000 M P a . We describe three applications of the Gibbs energy representation. (1) The depth during subduction of the antigorite dehydration reaction in the presence of saline geofluids is estimated to be reduced by 2 k m to 4 k m per mole of NaCl in solution, substantially less than the up to 10 k m per mole implied by previously inferred pressure-dependent water activities. (2) A H 2 O − NaCl phase diagram to 1000 M P a and 230 K to 400 K identifies the pressure-variant eutectics for hydrohalite and disodium chloride decaheptahydrate, and places the cenotectic — the absolute limit of liquid stability — at 205 M P a , 235 K and 3.90 m o l k g − 1 , where the liquid coexists with ice Ih, ice II and disodium chloride decaheptahydrate rather than with hydrohalite. (3) Icy moons: structural models of Ganymede, Callisto, and two Titan cases with 1.90 m o l k g − 1 aqueous NaCl show that melting point suppression stabilizes ices II, III, V, and VI, and that ices II and III can be buoyant in the coexisting fluid, with the sense of the ice II contrast reversing between 50 and 100 g k g − 1 . The resulting co-occurrence of ices II and III, not previously reported, admits multiphase overturning and implies that salinity governs the geodynamics of these > 100 k m lithospheres. Finally, we set out how a bulk Gibbs energy surface interfaces with species-based frameworks such as HKF and the Deep Earth Water model, and propose that the pressure derivative of the surface can be used to constrain the degree of association at high pressure.

title: Coupled kinetics of Mn(II) oxidation and Cd sequestration on ferrihydrite with varying crystallinity
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Lizhu Xu, Meiying Huang, Tongliang Wu, Peixin Cui, Cun Liu, Yujun Wang
abstract: Ferrihydrite (Fh) serves as a crucial geochemical interface for Mn(II) adsorption-oxidation in various soils and sediments, influencing the fate of associated Mn and cadmium (Cd). However, the impact of Fh crystallinity on the coupled kinetics and mechanisms of Mn(II) oxidation and Cd sequestration remains incompletely understood, particularly regarding the kinetic interplay. Here, we systematically investigated these coupled reactions on two-line Fh (2LFh with low crystallinity) and six-line Fh (6LFh with high crystallinity). 2LFh has a lower isoelectric point, a lower conduction band potential (E CB), and more abundant vacancy defects, while 6LFh exhibits higher isoelectric point and E CB but fewer vacancy defects. Kinetic experiments across pH 6.0−8.0 revealed similar trends in Cd and Mn(II) removal, with the most pronounced effects observed at pH 8.0. Based on the most pronounced reaction extents observed at pH 8.0, we developed a kinetic model that quantitatively describes the crystallinity-dependent kinetic coupling in Fh-Mn(II)-Cd ternary system. Dissolved Cd(II) and Mn(II) were rapidly adsorbed onto both 2LFh (k Cd = 5.43 × 106 M−1 s−1, k Mn(II) = 5.28 × 102 M−1 s−1) and 6LFh (k Cd = 2.85 × 105 M−1 s−1, k Mn(II) = 1.37 × 103 M−1 s−1). Subsequently, Mn(II) catalytic oxidation by O2 proceeded preferentially on 6LFh via an electrochemical pathway, driven by its higher E CB. This facilitated the abundant formation of amorphous manganese oxide (AMO) and groutite nanorods. In contrast, Mn(II) oxidation on 2LFh predominantly yielded abundant AMO and moderate amounts of manganite nanowires. Although secondary MnOx formation on Fh surfaces transiently increased dissolved Cd(II) by 1.3−15.8% relative to the Mn-free system, the extractable Cd fraction progressively decreased by 2.1−24.0%, with substantial Cd immobilized in secondary MnOx. Mechanistically, the model captures these Mn(II) oxidation pathways and dynamic redistribution of Cd between Fh and MnOx surfaces. These findings highlight that Fe‑Mn redox cycling and secondary mineralization critically govern the fate of heavy metals in redox‑dynamic soil environments, with crystallinity-dependent reaction pathways providing key mechanistic insights.

title: Rapid changes to permeable continental shelf sediment pore water geochemistry in response to olivine addition as a marine carbon dioxide removal technique
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Matthew Quinan, Aaron Celestian, Nick Rollins, Zvi Steiner, William Berelson
abstract: Marine enhanced rock weathering using the silicate mineral olivine has emerged as a promising ocean alkalinity enhancement/marine carbon dioxide removal technique in recent years. However, we lack an understanding of olivine dissolution and the concomitant alkalinity production in a marine sedimentary environment, where much of the dissolution is likely to occur, and the geochemical feedbacks therein. Previous olivine enhanced rock weathering experiments have typically been conducted at high fluid-to-mineral ratios using sediments composed predominantly of olivine, conditions that are not representative of olivine addition to natural sedimentary environments. They have also generally been done over long time periods (i.e. weeks to months) to obtain steady state dissolution/alkalinity production rates, thereby looking past the early, transient impacts of fresh olivine addition to marine sediment. Our uncertainty is compounded by the heterogeneity of continental shelf sediments, where variations in composition, grain size, permeability, diagenetic reactions, and pore water flow are likely to produce spatially variable olivine dissolution and alkalinity production. To help close these knowledge gaps, we conducted experiments to investigate the impacts of olivine dissolution on sediment geochemistry immediately following addition to shelf sands under varying physical conditions, all producing consistent results. Olivine dissolution and/or ion exchange resulted in rapid alkalinity production, even at short fluid:mineral contact time (residence times) and low fluid:mineral ratios. However, the precipitation of secondary minerals (CaCO3, Fe oxides, and potentially phyllosilicates) consumed a substantial portion of the produced alkalinity (28–88%), while increasing pore water pH slowed further olivine dissolution/ion exchange. These saturation effects decreased the efficiency with which alkalinity was durably produced by olivine dissolution in the sediment.

title: A new view of Xe and Ne in the Paleoarchean atmosphere from paired noble gas isotopic and trace element analyses of Barberton cherts
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): K.A. Woody, R. Parai, D.A. Fike, C. Jones, G. Avice, M.H. Barickman, J.B. Rodriguez, X.J. Zhang, A.H. Knoll
abstract: The terrestrial atmosphere governs Earth’s habitability and remains our most accessible analogue to distant planetary atmospheres, making the evolution of its composition over Earth history a topic of great interdisciplinary scientific interest. Many different natural samples are capable of trapping and retaining atmospheric gases on billion-year timescales, providing a geochemical archive of bygone processes. These trapped gases record a progressive depletion in the abundance of xenon (Xe) accompanied by its isotopic fractionation in Earth’s Archean atmosphere. However, the detailed history of this loss and isotopic fractionation of Xe is imperfectly constrained, in part because calculations focus on the non-radiogenic light isotopes of Xe (which are the least abundant isotopes) to determine ancient atmospheric compositions. In this study, we employed the full spectrum of Xe isotopes measured in four cherts from the 3.55–3.26 Ga Onverwacht Group of the Barberton Greenstone Belt, South Africa to quantify Xe isotopic fractionation in the Paleoarchean atmosphere. First, we measured the concentration and spatial distribution of Te, Ba, U, and Th by secondary ion mass spectrometry in subsamples of each chert to estimate the expected composition of Xe produced in situ by nuclear reactions. We then analyzed chips of these subsamples for Ne, Ar, and Xe elemental and isotopic compositions. We find that Xe data from Onverwacht bulk cherts reflect mixing between Paleoarchean atmospheric Xe and modern atmospheric Xe, with minor inputs from Xe produced by U, Ba, and Te decay. A mixing model incorporating these five components and testing a range of possible Archean atmospheric compositions indicates that Xe in the ∼ 3.26–3.28 Ga atmosphere was fractionated by ≥ 19 - 3.2 + 3.1 ‰u−1 relative to modern air. Our results emphasize that even samples with noble gas compositions dominated by trapped ancient fluids may in detail reflect multicomponent mixing, and that estimates of the extent of mass-dependent Xe fractionation reported in previous studies are lower limits. Barberton chert 20Ne/22Ne ratios extend below the modern atmospheric ratio, which could reflect post-entrapment fractionation that preferentially retained heavy Ne isotopes, or may indicate the preservation of a trapped multi-component mixture including paleo-atmospheric 20Ne/22Ne that was subsequently raised by volcanic outgassing.

title: Halogen behavior during high-grade metamorphism and partial melting in the deep continental crust (Ivrea-Verbano Zone, NW Italy)
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Peng-Yuan Han, Madison S. Huising, Jaime D. Barnes, Michael A.W. Marks, Tao He, Fernando Bea, Zhao-Chu Hu, Roberta L. Rudnick
abstract: Halogen (F, Cl, Br, and I) concentrations and Cl isotope (δ37Cl) ratios in a suite of well-characterized amphibolite- to granulite-facies metapelites, metabasites, and associated leucosomes from the Ivrea-Verbano Zone (IVZ), Northwest Italy, document halogen behavior during high-grade metamorphism and partial melting of the deep continental crust. With increasing metamorphic grade, metapelites record a progressive decrease in F, I, and possibly Br concentrations, likely due to metamorphic dehydration. By contrast, Cl is slightly elevated in granulite-facies metapelites, suggesting a relatively Cl-rich environment in the lower crust. Together with previously reported high Cl contents (up to 0.3 wt%) in garnet-hosted melt inclusions produced during partial melting of metapelites, this suggests that the elevated Cl was present during peak metamorphism and partial melting. All samples (metapelites, metabasites, and leucosomes) exhibit scattered but relatively narrow δ37Cl values, ranging from −1.3 to + 0.8‰, indicating that minimal Cl isotope fractionation occurs during metamorphic dehydration, partial melting, and fluid infiltration in the deep continental crust. The inferred Cl-rich environment in the IVZ lower crust is consistent with the Cl enrichment observed in many other granulite terranes, suggesting that such fluids may be common. Moreover, halogens present in the lower continental crust, whether released by metamorphic dehydration or introduced from other parts of the crust and/or mantle, may have facilitated partial melting and the generation of granitic magma, playing a vital role in the chemical differentiation of the continental crust.

title: Lead isotopes trace interhemispheric transport of water masses and pollution to the tropical western North Atlantic Ocean
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Hui Xu, Tina van de Flierdt, Arianna Olivelli, Yee-Lap Leung, Alex Griffiths, Katharina Kreissig, Barry J. Coles, Dominik J. Weiss, Rebekah E.T. Moore, Rob Middag, Mark Rehkämper
abstract: The use of leaded gasoline significantly impacted North Atlantic seawater during the 20th century, leaving a legacy of pollution that remains traceable despite the global ban reached in 2021. This study presents new Pb concentration and isotope data from four depth profiles in the western tropical North Atlantic along Leg 2 of GEOTRACES section GA02 from 31.7°N to 1.2°N. The data capture atmospheric inputs and water masses from both hemispheres, revealing latitudinal variability in Pb isotope signatures in the upper part of the water column. In surface waters, low 206Pb/207Pb ratios (1.166–1.173) indicate South American and North African anthropogenic sources at the southern stations, and higher 206Pb/207Pb ratios (1.174–1.179) reflect anthropogenic North American and natural North African mineral dust inputs at the northern stations. A comparison of North Atlantic surface water data for 1981–1999 and 2010–2014 reveals distinct shifts in Pb concentrations and isotope ratios, confirming the effectiveness of Pb isotopes as tracers for identifying and tracking Pb sources over time in the North Atlantic. The Pb concentrations and isotopic signatures of central water masses (formed 4–15 years ago relative to sampling time) and intermediate water masses (formed 20–50 years ago) are consistent with the expected atmospheric Pb sources at the time and location of their formation, emphasizing the influence of both spatial and temporal variations in atmospheric Pb deposition. However, in the intermediate layer, where northern- and southern-sourced water masses mix, a deviation of the Pb concentration from the expected water mass mixing trend suggests removal of some dissolved Pb by particles. North Atlantic Deep Water exhibits persistent anthropogenic Pb signals from historical US and European emissions (20–30 years ago), while bottom waters within a nepheloid layer show evidence of natural Pb release from sediments. Overall, these findings suggest that Pb isotope ratios predominantly act as conservative tracers of water masses in the strongly advective western tropical North Atlantic Ocean.

title: Processes controlling δ 41 K variations in the weathering profile of granite: implications for continental weathering proxies
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Mei-Li He, Jun-Wen Zhang, Na Wu, Shi-Chao An, Jun Mu, Dong-Yang Xiong, Liang Guo, Rui Wang, Zhi-Qi Zhao
abstract: Potassium (K) isotopes are significantly fractionated during the chemical weathering of silicate rocks, and therefore represent a potential proxy for the intensity of weathering. However, the processes influencing the fractionation of K isotopes during the weathering of silicate remain unclear. This study analyzes the K isotope composition (δ41K) of a weathering profile that was developed based on granite obtained from southeastern China. The δ41K value exhibited a systematic decrease, from −0.44 ± 0.04‰ in the granite bedrock at the bottom to −0.68 ± 0.03‰ in the most weathered profile near the surface, to indicate significant fractionation of K isotopes during the weathering of the sample. As the degree of weathering increased (CIA: 52.2 ∼ 92.4), the δ41K value of the weathered products decreased, and yielded a strong positive correlation with τK,Ti (R2 = 0.76, p < 0.01), a strong negative correlation with CIA (R2 = 0.79, p < 0.01), and was a proxy for the formation of clay minerals (K/Al; R2 = 0.80, p < 0.01) (excluding the influence of upper-layer plant litter). These observations suggest that the formation of clay minerals leads to the preferential incorporation of isotopically lighter K. Although kaolinite might have adsorbed minor amounts of isotopically heavier K on its surface when pH ≥ 6, this had a limited effect on changes in the δ41K value in the weathering products. The mineralogical composition and 87Sr/86Sr ratios in the profile suggest that the differential weathering of the primary minerals occurred in this weathering profile. While plagioclase had isotopically heavier K compositions than the bedrock, the contribution of its weathering to the total K pool within the weathering profile was relatively limited. Moreover, K-feldspar and biotite yielded similar K isotopic signatures to that of the bedrock, the weathering of which did not significantly influence the δ41K values of the weathering products. Therefore, the differential weathering of the primary minerals had a negligibly small effect on variations in the δ41K values within the weathering profile. Moreover, the total organic carbon (TOC) content in the upper part of the profile (≤100 cm) exhibited a strong positive correlation with τK, Ti (R2 = 0.84, p < 0.01), while the δ41K values of the weathering products showed a significant negative correlation with the TOC (R2 = 0.51, p < 0.05) and K/Rb (R2 = 0.72, p < 0.01). The weathering products near the surface (≤100 cm) were primarily influenced by the input of plant litter with light K isotope compositions, while biogenic processes had a negligibly minor role at deeper depths. These results suggest that the preferential incorporation of isotopically light K is the critical process controlling K isotopic variations within the profile. These results explain the enrichment of light K isotopes as silicate weathering intensifies, and support their use as tracers of the intensity of chemical weathering.

title: Early diagenetic Mo-S isotope and trace metal systematics in organic-rich marine sediments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Ricardo D. Monedero-Contreras, Carolina Rosca, Francisca Martínez-Ruiz, Antonio Delgado-Huertas, Martin Wille, Stephan König
abstract: Molybdenum (Mo) isotope compositions have been widely applied as a paleoredox proxy to reconstruct past ocean deoxygenation, particularly from organic-rich sediments such as sapropels and Black Shales. Yet the extent to which early diagenetic processes influence Mo primary redox signals (concentration and isotope composition) remains insufficiently constrained. Here, we present high-resolution molybdenum (Mo) and sulfur (S) isotope compositions, as well as trace metal concentrations, to assess the influence of postdepositional processes, including redoxcline migration and mineral phase cycling on sedimentary Mo isotope records in a deep marine setting, precisely sapropel S1 from ODP Site 969 (Mediterranean Ridge). At this site, sapropel S1 provides an ideal natural laboratory as it exhibits: (i) a complete redox sequence from oxic/suboxic to anoxic and sulfidic conditions; (ii) evidence of early diagenetic modification; and (iii) a distinct triple-peak Mo concentration pattern, each deriving from specific syndepositional and postdepositional redox processes. The oxygen-depleted organic-rich and sulfide-rich intervals exhibit light Mo isotope compositions (expressed as δ98Mo relative to NIST-3134 + 0.25‰) ranging from −0.52‰ to as low as −1.63‰, as well as light S isotope compositions below −35‰ (expressed as δ34S relative to Vienna Canyon Diablo Troilite standard). These δ98Mo values are lighter than expected for organic- and sulfide-rich sediments and likely reflect additional early burial diagenetic fractionation driven by non-quantitative Mo thiolation and Mn redox cycling under weakly sulfidic conditions. The enrichment of Mn- and Fe-oxyhydroxide-associated trace elements (e.g., Co, Ni, Tl, and Cu) at or above the oxidation front, together with U enrichment beneath organic-rich sediments, supports a multistage redox-diagenetic framework involving Mn–Fe oxide cycling, sulfide mineralization, and element redistribution across dynamic redox boundaries. The coupled Mo–S isotope systematics further constrain variations in sulfide availability and sulfur cycling. It shows how incomplete Mo thiolation can modify the dissolved Mo pool, whereas S reflects a sustained sulfate supply under open-system sulfidic diagenesis. Together, these results show that the Mo isotope record of sapropel S1 at ODP Site 969 is a diagenetically integrated signal rather than a direct archive of depositional redox conditions, illustrating how primary signatures can be remodeled across dynamic redox boundaries. More broadly, this study provides a framework for interpreting strongly negative δ98Mo signatures in other organic-rich marine environments characterized by fluctuating redoxclines, weakly sulfidic conditions, and active Mn/Fe cycling.

title: Silicon isotope fractionation during non-stoichiometric dissolution of wollastonite: Insights into dissolution reaction mechanisms
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Cameron Wood, Anna L. Harrison, Jacques Schott, Franck Poitrasson, Jon K. Golla, Jean-Michel Brazier, Vasileios Mavromatis
abstract: Silicate weathering exerts a major control on element cycles including the carbon cycle, whereby dissolution of silicates on the continents removes CO2 from the atmosphere in the form of alkalinity. The process of silicate weathering has also gained attention recently as a potential strategy for mitigation of climate change if the rates of dissolution can be accelerated. In the present study we show that wollastonite (CaSiO3) dissolution rate and stoichiometry is pH-dependent, with faster rates at acidic pH and preferential release of Ca relative to Si at acidic pH but much slower at alkaline pH with slight enrichment of the fluid in Si relative to Ca. The substantial fractionation of Si isotopes occurring during dissolution at acidic pH (Δ30Sisolid-fluid (≥0.85‰) is consistent with the formation of a SiO2 altered layer via the preferential release of Ca vs Si followed by the progressive condensation of Q2 wollastonite SiO4 units into Q3 and Q4 units, but it contradicts the formation of a silica layer induced by wollastonite stoichiometric dissolution followed by amorphous silica precipitation. In contrast, at basic pH, the fluid is somewhat enriched in 30Si, consistent with fractionation during adsorption of Si oxyanions at the surface of possibly precipitated calcite. Ca isotope fractionation, in contrast, is negligible under most conditions, implying calcite precipitation, if present, occurred near to equilibrium. An important implication of the experimental results is that isotope fractionation can occur during net silicate dissolution. Therefore, Si isotopes, and their combination with the isotopes of other major elements, provide an opportunity to evaluate dissolution mechanisms.

title: Green rust controls dissolved iron during transformation to magnetite: provisional solubility products of chloride and sulfate green rust
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Neil L. MacPherson, Logan Swaren, Leslie J. Robbins, Manuel Schad, James M. Byrne, Andreas Kappler, Kurt O. Konhauser, Daniel S. Alessi
abstract: Green rusts (GR) are a group of reactive mixed-valent FeII/FeIII hydroxide minerals that play an important role in geochemical systems. Yet, the formation kinetics and environmental implications of the transformation process and products remain poorly constrained. In this study, batch solubility experiments were conducted on fully characterized chloride-rich [GR(Cl)] and sulfate-rich [GR(SO4)] green rust varieties to determine their provisional solubility products ( K sp ′ ). While GR is a metastable phase that transforms into magnetite (Fe3O4) over the course of days, the kinetics of this transformation are slow enough to make the K sp ′ valuable in predicting equilibrium aqueous iron concentrations. Solubility experiments of GR(Cl) and GR(SO4) were performed at circumneutral pH (7.6 – 8.6), two different ionic strengths (IS) representing low IS or ‘freshwater’ (ultrapure water) and high IS or ‘seawater’ (0.56 M NaCl), and at three aging time intervals: 0, 2, and 7 days. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy analyses demonstrated progressive transformation of GR to magnetite during this time interval. Solubility experiments yielded average K ′ sp values for GR at each of the three age intervals. Variations between the average K ′ sp as a function of age were statistically insignificant, thus the resulting average K ′ sp values for each GR age interval were combined to produce an overall mean log K ′ sp . The overall mean log K ′ sp ( C l ) values in low and high IS are −75.07 ± 1.39 and −76.22 ± 0.42, respectively, while the overall mean log K ′ sp ( SO 4 ) values in low and high IS are −119.72 ± 1.03 and −126.60 ± 1.07, respectively. Chemical speciation modeling of the concomitant dissolution of GR and magnetite demonstrated that dissolved Fe concentrations were almost entirely controlled by GR dissolution rather than magnetite, demonstrating that GR can dominate aqueous Fe concentrations even in the presence of magnetite.

title: Trace-element signatures in magnetite induced by iron-reducing bacteria
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Xiaohua Han, James M. Byrne, Andreas Kappler, Wei Lin, Yongxin Pan
abstract: Biogenic magnetite nanoparticles produced by microorganisms are ubiquitous in modern environments and likely abundant in ancient sediments such as banded iron formations and paleosols. While magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) synthesize intracellular magnetite with distinctive morphological, chemical, and magnetic biosignatures, dissimilatory Fe(III)-reducing bacteria (DIRB) generate extracellular magnetite that is nanoscale, aggregated, and often superparamagnetic, complicating its distinction from abiotic counterparts. To resolve this challenge, we systematically compared magnetite synthesized through abiotic Fe2+ aq-induced ferrihydrite transformation and biogenic transformation mediated by the DIRB Shewanella oneidensis MR-1. Ferrihydrite substrates were co-precipitated with 21 trace elements at concentrations of 0, 10, and 20 ppm to evaluate the combined effects of formation pathway and trace-element availability on magnetite particle size, Fe valence state, and trace-element partitioning. Transmission electron microscopy results showed that biogenic magnetite was consistently smaller than abiotic magnetite, with increasing trace-element concentrations further reducing particle size in both systems. Notably, trace elements induced opposite redox trends: abiotic magnetite became progressively oxidized due to substitution-driven Fe2+ oxidation, whereas biogenic magnetite became more reduced as microbially mediated Fe(III) reduction was enhanced. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analyses demonstrated distinct trace-element partitioning patterns: abiotic magnetite preferentially incorporated Mg, whereas the biotic solid aggregates were consistently enriched in Co and Cd, regardless of initial trace-element concentrations or post-synthesis washing treatments. Because the biotic solid aggregates contained both magnetite and bacterial biomass, their elemental compositions reflect both mineral and biological pools. Accordingly, our objective is to identify pathway-dependent trace element signatures of biogenic and abiotic magnetite formation rather than to quantify elemental incorporation into a pure magnetite lattice. The observed differences may represent the combined effects of trace-element substitution in the magnetite lattice and biologically mediated processes. Comparison with magnetite produced by MTB further highlights substantial interspecies differences in trace-element partitioning, reflecting how the degree of biological control shapes biomineralization. Collectively, the coupled signatures of particle size, Fe valence distribution, and trace-element partitioning establish a coherent geochemical framework for distinguishing abiotic and biogenic magnetite. These results provide new constraints for identifying extracellular microbial magnetite in modern and ancient sedimentary records, with implications for paleoenvironmental reconstruction and astrobiological exploration.

title: Anaerobic oxidation of methane coupled to manganese oxide reduction by ANME–2a in brackish coastal sediments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Robin Klomp, Thomas J. van Asselt, Evalien Baas, Thilo Behrends, Tom Berben, Reinier A. Egas, Marit R. van Erk, Niels A.G.M. van Helmond, Peter A.G. ter Horst, Isabel M.L. Rigutto, Thomas Röckman, Anna J. Wallenius, Olga M. Żygadłowska, Wytze K. Lenstra, Mike S.M. Jetten, Caroline P. Slomp
abstract: Methane (CH4) is a powerful greenhouse gas, and its emission from coastal systems is critically dependent on the balance between methanogenesis and CH4 removal. Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) coupled to sulfate reduction is a key pathway, but the role of alternative electron acceptors, such as manganese (Mn) oxides, and the underlying microbial physiology remain elusive. Here, we examine the potential for Mn–driven AOM (Mn–AOM) in brackish coastal sediments at two sites in the Bothnian Sea. The overlapping presence of CH4, Mn oxides, dissolved Mn, and anaerobic methane–oxidizing archaea (ANME) of the clade ANME–2a in sediment zones at the two sites points towards potential for Mn–AOM. Laboratory incubations of sediment from these zones using 13C–labelled CH4 revealed stimulation of AOM upon addition of the Mn oxides birnessite and pyrolusite at one of the two sites. X–ray absorption spectroscopy of the sediment confirmed reductive dissolution of the added Mn oxides during the incubations. A role for cryptic sulfur cycling could be excluded since the addition of molybdate, an inhibitor for sulfate reduction, did not affect the Mn–AOM activity. In all incubations where AOM was stimulated by Mn oxides, members of ANME–2a were the only methanotrophs and increased in relative abundance compared to the start and control. Metagenomic analysis revealed that the ANME–2a genome encoded for all genes involved in the reverse methanogenesis pathway, and eleven multi–heme c–type cytochromes (MHCs), which could mediate extracellular electron transfer. Several MHCs of the ANME–2a were similar to MHCs of freshwater metal–reducing ANME–2d, suggesting similar mechanisms for metal–driven AOM across ANME clades. We conclude that ANME–2a can couple Mn oxide reduction to CH4 oxidation in brackish coastal sediments. Our results highlight that this process needs to be considered when studying CH4 dynamics in coastal systems.

title: Pressure-dependence of viscosity and structure of nepheline melts: implications for mobility of alkaline silicate melts under continental rifts
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Qi Chen, Bin Zhao, Aaron Wolfgang Ashley, Young Jay Ryu, Tony Yu, Yanbin Wang
abstract: Primitive nephelinitic magmas are among the most silica-undersaturated alkaline melts generated in continental rifts. However, high-pressure viscosity and structural constraints for their nepheline-rich component remain sparse. Within the Na-aluminosilicate system, nepheline is the silica-poor endmember required to evaluate how pressure, H2O, and silica influence melt rheology along the nepheline-jadeite-albite join. Here, we report in situ falling-sphere viscosity measurements on nepheline melts with 0.2 and 3 wt% H2O at 0.6–7 GPa and ≤ 1980 K. We also perform in situ X-ray scattering measurements on nepheline and nepheline + silica melts under similar conditions to constrain their structures. Our results show that nepheline melt viscosity decreases strongly from ∼0.6 to 5 GPa and then increases slightly at higher pressures. Increasing H2O from ∼0.2 to 3 wt% lowers the melt viscosity by ∼0.2–0.4 log units, corresponding to a reduction by a factor of ∼1.6–2.5, over comparable pressure–temperature conditions. X-ray scattering shows no resolvable pressure-dependent shift in the position of the first-neighbor T-O peak (T = Si + Al), whereas the first sharp diffraction peak (FSDP) shifts to higher Q values with pressure for both nepheline and nepheline + silica melts. This provides direct evidence for the reorganization of intermediate-range structure. Nepheline melt shows a smaller pressure-induced FSDP shift than nepheline + silica and literature jadeite melts, broadly paralleling its weaker viscosity reduction relative to jadeite and albite melts. Pressure-induced changes in Al and possibly Si coordination may also contribute to the weaker viscosity reduction. We apply our constraints to a primitive nephelinitic melt analog for the Labait volcano (Tanzania). We find that ≤ 3 wt% H2O increases both melt mobility and calculated percolation velocity by up to a factor of ∼50 relative to the dry case. These results indicate that volatile enrichment can be crucial to promote extraction of deep nephelinitic melts beneath continental rifts.

title: Calcium isotope systematics during multistage seafloor alteration of abyssal peridotites: insights from the Gakkel Ridge
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Jia-Wei Xiong, Chuan-Zhou Liu, Yin-Zheng Lin, Yang Xu
abstract: Calcium is readily mobilized and redistributed during seafloor alteration of abyssal peridotites, yet the associated isotope effects of serpentinization and carbonation are difficult to distinguish from inherited magmatic signatures. Here we combine thermodynamic modelling and whole-rock geochemistry with selective leaching experiments to disentangle these contributions in a petrographically classified suite of Gakkel Ridge peridotites. Thermodynamic melting calculations coupled with internally consistent mineral–melt fractionation factors provide a reference frame for both Ca contents and isotope compositions. Relatively fresh peridotites have δ 44/40Ca values of 0.88–0.94‰, slightly below the predicted residual values, consistent with minor carbonate addition and/or prior melt–rock interaction. In contrast, serpentinized peridotites lacking visible carbonate generally record substantial Ca loss and span a wide δ 44/40Ca range of 0.59–1.19‰. Calculations of selective orthopyroxene and clinopyroxene consumption yield distinct isotope trajectories depending on the evolving Ca contributions of the two pyroxenes and the adopted mineral–fluid fractionation factors. None of the results reproduces the lowest measured values, which likely reflect inherited magmatic signatures and/or unmodelled kinetic effects. In carbonated samples, carbonate-rich leachates account for ∼ 59–100% of whole-rock Ca, with δ 44/40Ca values down to − 0.11‰ in aragonite-dominated fractions and up to 1.43‰ in calcite-dominated fractions. Carbonate addition can thus dominate the whole-rock isotope budget, with the direction of the shift set by the dominant polymorph. These results collectively show that altered oceanic mantle is highly heterogeneous in Ca isotope composition, and that carbonated oceanic mantle spans both light and heavy signatures. This pre-subduction heterogeneity should be considered when interpreting Ca isotope evidence for recycled carbonate in the deep Earth.

title: Trace element distribution in coarse-grained Ca-Al-rich inclusions by femtosecond LA-ICP-MS: Implications for U-Pb chronology
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Merel E. Onderwater, Elishevah M.M.E. van Kooten, Glenn J. MacPherson, Alexander N. Krot, Martin Bizzarro
abstract: Calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs) in chondritic meteorites are the first solids that formed in the Solar System, as established by U-Pb chronology. After initial condensation, coarse-grained CAIs (Compact Type A, Type B, Type C) experienced melting, resulting in igneous partitioning and spatial redistribution of trace elements among constituent minerals. Understanding these distributions is essential for identifying trace-element host phases and interpreting U-Pb ages. Rare earth elements (REEs) and the actinides Th and U are particularly informative tracers, yet actinide behavior in coarse-grained CAIs remains poorly constrained. Further, the decay of short-lived 247Cm to 235U (t1/2 = 15.6 Myr) complicates U-Pb age determination of bulk CAIs, but its impact at the mineral scale remains elusive. Here, we present major- and trace-element distribution maps of six coarse-grained CAIs mainly composed of melilite, Al,Ti-pyroxene, anorthite and spinel (±forsterite) from CV3 (Vigarano-type) chondrites acquired by femtosecond laser ablation ICP-MS. In CAIs lacking perovskite or hibonite, our results show that Al,Ti-pyroxene is the dominant host of U, Th, and most REEs, with strong enrichments observed toward pyroxene grain edges, whereas light REEs reside in melilite. Trace-element zonation reflects igneous fractional crystallization and is overprinted by melt evaporation, which caused depletion of the most volatile REEs (Yb, Eu, Ce) and U in CAI outer regions and rims. Using Nd and Th distribution maps as proxies for Cm, we model the effects of 247Cm-235U decay on mineral-scale U isotopic compositions. Variable Cm-U partitioning among coexisting minerals is predicted to generate resolvable inter-mineral 235U/238U variations, with the largest excesses in melilite. These variations can produce apparent U-Pb age offsets of ∼0.1–1.0 Myr when U isotopic compositions and radiogenic Pb are derived from isotopically distinct mineral reservoirs, but generally remain small (< 0.15 Myr) when using bulk U isotopic compositions. Our results demonstrate that fractional crystallization and melt evaporation exert a primary control on U distribution and isotope systematics in igneous CAIs and provide new constraints on the interpretation and robustness of high-precision U-Pb chronology of the earliest Solar System solids.

title: Molecular mechanisms of cadmium isotope fractionations during adsorption onto todorokite
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Hui Yin, Xinran Yan, Kideok D. Kwon, Chuanwei Zhu, Wentao Wang, Juhyeok Kim, Wei Li, Jingyuan Ma, Jiangshan Li, Ping Wang, Mingxia Wang, Guohong Qiu, Peng Cai, Hanjie Wen
abstract: Todorokite (Tdr), a tectomanganate with a 3 × 3 tunnel structure, controls the adsorption behavior and isotope fractionation of Cd2+ in marine and terrestrial environments. However, the underlying mechanisms of these processes remain poorly constrained. Here, we elucidate how ionic strength governs Cd isotope fractionation during adsorption onto Tdr by integrating batch adsorption experiments, Cd K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectroscopy, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The adsorption density of Cd2+ onto Tdr gradually increases with pH, but decreases greatly with increasing ionic strength from 0.1 M to 0.72 M NaNO3. Cd2+ adsorption preferentially enriches lighter Cd isotopes in the solid phase relative to the aqueous solution. This fractionation is linked to distortions in Cd2+ coordination environments upon adsorption, as revealed by EXAFS and DFT. Increasing ionic strength reduces the magnitude of Cd isotope fractionation (Δ114/110Cdsolid‑solution) from −0.46 ± 0.05‰ to −0.26 ± 0.07‰, which closely correlates with a shift in Cd2+ binding configurations from tunnel-center sites to corner sites, as captured by classical MD simulations. At low ionic strength, Cd2+ forms a mixture of outer-sphere complexes in tunnel centers and inner-sphere complexes at edge and corner sites. Elevated ionic strength promotes partial dehydration of Tdr tunnels and enhances inner-sphere complexation at corner sites, thereby dampening isotope fractionation. These findings resolve the adsorption-induced Cd2+ isotope fractionation mechanisms and identify ionic strength as a key control on Cd2+ partitioning and isotopic signatures during interactions with tectomanganate minerals in the environment.

title: Stable cerium (Ce) isotope fractionation during sorption onto common iron oxides and implications for Ce redox proxies
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Weiming Ding, Wei Ren, Yanyi Yang, Tingying Xu, Xin-Yuan Zheng
abstract: Stable cerium (Ce) isotopes (142Ce/140Ce) have recently emerged as a promising proxy for redox changes in modern and ancient environments. However, robust interpretation of Ce isotope data from natural samples is hampered by the lack of constraints on Ce isotope fractionation during sorption of aqueous Ce onto iron oxides – ubiquitous minerals that strongly influence the Ce cycle in nature. Here we report results from a series of controlled laboratory experiments designed to quantify stable Ce isotope fractionation during sorption of aqueous Ce(III) onto four common iron (oxyhydr)oxides, including ferrihydrite, goethite, hematite, and magnetite. Complementary synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) analyses were employed to assess Ce valence states on mineral surfaces, while a series of isotope exchange experiments using an enriched 142Ce tracer were conducted to constrain Ce isotope exchange kinetics and the mechanism underlying the observed fractionation. XANES analyses show no detectable Ce(III) oxidation during sorption onto ferrihydrite, goethite, or magnetite, but nearly complete oxidation of Ce(III) to Ce(IV) on hematite. The observed oxidation of Ce(III) on hematite surfaces demonstrates that Fe oxides can contribute to Ce redox transformations, complicating interpretations of Ce valence states alone as redox indicators. The 142Ce-tracer experiments provide unambiguous evidence for rapid Ce isotope exchange between dissolved and sorbed Ce, regardless of Ce valence state on Fe oxide surfaces, with near-complete Ce isotope exchange typically achieved within 2 days. These results indicate that isotopic equilibrium may be attained rapidly during Ce sorption onto Fe oxides. Heavy Ce isotopes are preferentially retained in the aqueous phase, and the inferred equilibrium fractionation factors between aqueous and sorbed Ce (Δ142Ceaq–sorbed) increase in the order: hematite (0.071‰) ≈ goethite (0.077‰) < magnetite (0.118‰) < ferrihydrite (0.174‰). The magnitude of the observed fractionation does not correlate with Ce oxidation on mineral surfaces, suggesting that changes in Ce valence state are not the only control on stable Ce isotope fractionation. Instead, the fractionation appears to be closely linked to the Ce sorption affinity of oxide minerals, with greater affinity corresponding to larger fractionation, indicating an important mineralogical control on equilibrium Ce isotope fractionation during sorption. Together with previously quantified Ce isotope fractionation during sorption onto manganese oxides, this work provides a framework for interpreting δ142Ce variations in Fe- and Mn-oxide-bearing sediments, particularly those formed in aqueous environments with low Ce concentrations. Although further study is needed to fully constrain the effects of solution chemistry and post-depositional alteration, the mineral-specific Ce isotope fractionation identified here provide first-order constraints for interpreting Ce isotope variations in Precambrian banded iron formations (BIFs). A simple mass-balance model predicts that the onset of Mn oxidation on the early Earth can generate greater δ142Ce variability in seawater and coeval BIFs than Fe-oxide sorption alone. A closed-system diagenetic model further indicates that primary Ce isotope signatures preserved in BIFs are relatively robust against complete reset by later fluid alteration. These results highlight the potential of stable Ce isotopes to trace the emergence of Mn oxidation in Earth’s early oceans.

title: Recycling of juvenile arc crust in an ancient convergent margin revealed by Hg isotopes
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Han Qi, Jun-Hong Zhao, Runsheng Yin, Anbo Luo
abstract: Recycling of newly formed arc crust at convergent margins is critical to the long-term balance between growth and destruction of the continental crust. However, identifying this process in ancient convergent systems remains challenging because direct geological evidence is rarely preserved. Here, we measure Hg stable isotopes and Nd–Hf radiogenic isotopes in subduction-related igneous rocks from the Neoproterozoic (870–730 Ma) active continental margin of the Yangtze Block in South China to investigate the recycling of juvenile arc crust. Both mafic rocks and granitoids exhibit variable whole-rock Δ199Hg values that largely overlap the depleted-mantle range, ranging from −0.13‰ to +0.15‰ (mean = −0.04 ± 0.15‰, 2SD) and −0.18‰ to +0.11‰ (mean = −0.05 ± 0.14‰, 2SD), respectively, suggesting variable contributions from mantle-, marine-, and terrestrial-derived Hg. Samples with negative Δ199Hg signatures show variable but mostly positive whole-rock εNd (−3.4 to +6.4) and positive zircon εHf (+1.8 to +14.7), and all samples with Δ199Hg below the depleted mantle range (< −0.10‰) have positive εNd values (+0.3 to +3.1). These combined isotopic characteristics indicate that terrigenous sediments formed by weathering and erosion of juvenile arc crust and carrying terrestrial-derived Hg were recycled into the mantle source of arc magmas. Such recycling was likely achieved through subduction of arc-derived trench sediments and/or tectonic erosion of forearc materials. The results of this work suggest that recycling of newly formed arc crust in convergent margins may have been an overlooked means of crustal destruction throughout Earth’s history.

title: Multi-site Li diffusion and coupling to Cr, REE, and P in garnet: Experimental data and implications for interpreting diffusion profiles in natural systems
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): E.M. Bloch, A. Devoir, O. Müntener, R. Hervig, J.J. Barnes, M.J. Kohn
abstract: We present diffusion experiments on almandine and spessartine garnet conducted at 700–900 °C and 1 atm under Ni–NiO fO2 buffering, designed to evaluate the role of coupled substitution and defect chemistry in controlling Li mobility. Experiments employing source powders doped with Li and either REE or P demonstrate that Li diffusion varies systematically with the identity of the coupled species. In REE-doped systems, Li profiles evolve over the same length scale as REEs and yield diffusivities consistent with established REE diffusion rates, indicating that Li transport is limited by the slower trivalent cation flux. In contrast, undoped Li-out diffusion experiments produce substantially longer Li profiles over identical timescales, reflecting faster transport. Comparison with published inversions of multielement diffusion in natural garnets reveals no clear inconsistency between those natural datasets and experimentally derived slow REE diffusivities, supporting application of the Li–REE results to natural systems. Lithium–Phosphorus experiments yield extremely short P diffusion profiles, consistent with a much slower Li mechanism involving P on the tetrahedral site. Additional experiments reveal fast Li transport associated with multi-site diffusion behavior and with processes linked to Cr redistribution. Across all experiments, effective Li diffusivity varies by at least three orders of magnitude as a function of experimental conditions and substitution mechanisms. These results demonstrate that Li diffusion in garnet cannot be described by a single Arrhenius relationship but instead reflects a spectrum of coupled and multi-site diffusion mechanisms. The dataset presented here likely captures only a subset of the mechanisms active in natural systems and Li diffusivity may span an even broader range than we observe here. Consequently, quantitative interpretation of Li diffusion in natural garnets requires consideration of multiple diffusion mechanisms, potentially including processes not yet characterized, and should be approached with appropriate caution.

title: Sedimentary and redox controls on pyrite sulfur isotopes in oxic–suboxic continental shelf sediments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Xin Chang, Tiegang Li, Zhifang Xiong, Chengguo Guan, Yu Gu, Houjie Wang, Guangchao Zhuang, Xiting Liu
abstract: Pyrite links sedimentary processes with the biogeochemical sulfur cycle and is widely used for reconstructing past redox and depositional environments. However, the controls on pyrite formation and its sulfur isotopic composition (δ34Spyr) in dynamic continental shelf settings, particularly under fluctuating oxic–suboxic conditions, remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate a late Pleistocene–Holocene sedimentary succession from the mud wedge off the Shandong Peninsula (Yellow Sea), which provides a high-resolution archive of glacial–interglacial environmental change, to resolve the relationship between δ34Spyr and shelf sedimentary evolution. We combine sulfur isotope measurements with redox-sensitive trace metals (U and Mo) and previously published sedimentological and geochemical data. Bulk δ34Spyr shows systematic variability associated with several depositional and diagenetic factors. First, δ34Spyr covaries with sedimentation rate, total organic carbon content, and water depth, indicating an important influence of depositional dynamics on pyrite formation and apparent isotopic fractionation. Second, more oxidizing conditions during the Holocene sea-level highstand coincide with generally higher δ34Spyr values, consistent with redox-related changes in sulfur burial. Third, localized sulfur cycling possibly related to anaerobic oxidation of methane may have contributed to elevated δ34Spyr in discrete intervals through isotopic mixing. These results indicate that bulk pyrite sulfur isotopes in oxic–suboxic continental shelf sediments primarily record sedimentary evolution and local diagenetic sulfur cycling, while redox-related variations in sulfur burial may further influence their stratigraphic pattern. This study provides a well-constrained example of δ34Spyr behavior in a non-euxinic shelf environment and emphasizes that depositional and early diagenetic processes must be explicitly considered when applying pyrite sulfur isotopes to paleoenvironmental reconstructions.

title: Synergistic effects of montmorillonite and microbial consortia on Cr(VI) reduction
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Yi Zhou, Guocheng Lv, Yunpu Zhao, Xiaotong Yang, Meng Liu, Xuelian Yu, Hongli Chen, Xiaoyan Li, Libing Liao
abstract: Cr(VI) contamination poses a serious threat to ecosystems and human health, making bioremediation strategies that leverage mineral–microbe interactions one of the most critical remediation approaches. Here, we systematically describe the synergistic role of montmorillonite (Mnt) and an indigenous microbial consortium in driving Cr(VI) transformation under simulated groundwater conditions. In batch experiments, abiotic systems with Mnt or sterilized biomass showed negligible or limited Cr(VI) removal, whereas the Mnt–microbe system achieved nearly complete Cr(VI) removal in Cycle 1 and maintained consistently high removal efficiencies over three consecutive redox cycles. RT-qPCR analysis revealed an adaptive strategy whereby the chromate efflux transporter gene chrA was upregulated in the late stage while the intracellular reductase gene yieF remained continuously expressed, concurrent with a strong enrichment of Gammaproteobacteria (from 11.35% to 89.90–96.35%) within Mnt-provided microhabitats. Advanced spectroscopy (XRD, XPS, EXAFS) and microscopy, together with a quantitative Cr mass balance, demonstrate that the main reduction product is Cr(III), which is retained through three pathways: (i) retention of Cr(III) compounds on solid surfaces, (ii) interlayer fixation of Cr(III) within Mnt, and (iii) coprecipitation of Cr(III) with Fe(oxyhydr)oxides. These results highlight a combined mechanism whereby Mnt acts as a chemical buffer, structural host, and ecological scaffold, providing a robust, field-relevant strategy for in situ remediation of Cr(VI)-contaminated aquifers and soils.

title: Triple oxygen isotopes in precipitation reveal kinetic isotopic fractionation driven by turbulence in atmospheric river storms
description: Publication date: Available online 18 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Erik J.H. Oerter, Jory Lerback, Jake Harm, Rebecca J. Lazarus, Ate Visser
abstract: Atmospheric river (AR) storms are outsized in their hydrologic importance, especially along continental coastal environments. A better understanding of the physical processes occurring during precipitation generation will improve predictive capabilities of precipitation forecasts. The triple oxygen isotopic composition of precipitation is a useful tracer of the physical processes affecting precipitation because the derived Δ′17O parameter can help distinguish between equilibrium isotope exchange and kinetic fractionation. While the effects of kinetic fractionation have been interpreted from deuterium-excess (d-excess) values, this effect in d-excess is temperature dependent. Because Δ′17O values are relatively insensitive to temperature, the effects of kinetic fractionation are more easily interpretable from the Δ′17O values. Together, the coupled use of both Δ′17O and d-excess values provides complementary information. We collected precipitation at ∼1 hr intervals during a very strong land-falling AR event in mid-latitude west-coast North America, and analyzed these samples for δ2H, δ17O, δ18O, d-excess, and Δ′17O values. We observed a distinct V-shaped pattern (decrease followed by increase) of Δ′17O values through the storm progression, whereas δ2H, δ18O, and d-excess values produced an L-shaped pattern (decrease with no increase). We put these storm data into the context of daily precipitation samples collected at the same site over a 5 year period. Along with complementary meteorological data and analyses, we determined that post-condensation evaporation and re-condensation cycling of precipitation was a dominate process during the Early, pre-frontal passage phase of the AR storm. After frontal passage, we find that Rayleigh-type distillation and equilibrium condensation are the dominant processes in the 2021 AR storm. Thus, the triple oxygen isotope composition of AR precipitation is an important indicator and tracer of physical processes occurring within AR storms.

title: Reconfiguration of natural organic matter by MnO 2 in frozen matrices
description: Publication date: Available online 18 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Peizeng Yang, Jingqi Ruan, Jie Chen, Bin Gao, Deyang Kong, Junhe Lu
abstract: While mineral-carbon interactions have been largely studied at ambient temperatures, their dynamics in frozen environments remain unclear. Here, we unveil that the transformation of natural organic matter (NOM) by β-MnO2 was drastically accelerated in frozen matrices under mildly acidic conditions. This enhancement is driven by the freeze-concentration effect, which expels reactants into liquid-like grain boundaries, thus significantly increasing their local concentrations and acidifying the microenvironment. This pH shift profoundly enhances the redox potential of MnO2, facilitating its reactions with NOM, yielding structurally more complex oligomers and polymers, and hydroxylated and quinone-like derivatives.
