Consequently, extensive molecular reorganization occurs, accompanied by a marked decrease in formula count (from 5130 to 2841) and increase in intensity-weighted average molecular weight (from 326.546 to 443.286 Da) but with relatively stable total organic carbon. Concurrently, the reduction of Mn(IV) to dissolved Mn(II) induced by NOM is also accelerated in ice. This previously overlooked cryochemical pathway can alter the reactivity, mobility, and bioavailability of organic carbon. In a warming climate with intensified freeze–thaw cycles, these findings are critical for predicting carbon fate in cold regions.

title: Titanium isotopic insight into variable melt source contributions within the Aleutian Island Arc
description: Publication date: Available online 18 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Emma G. Ling, Sarah M. Aarons, Zhe James Zhang, Linqing Huang, Aleisha C. Johnson, Mauricio Ibañez-Mejia, Gene Yogodzinski, Nicolas Dauphas, Peter Kelemen
abstract: Titanium (Ti) isotopes are a well-established tracer of magmatic differentiation capable of providing useful insight into the magma series and geodynamic setting of rock formation. Titanium isotope fractionation is sensitive to magma conditions such as oxygen fugacity, water content, and the initial geochemical composition of a melt, however during plate subduction the relative contribution of the partial melt from the subducting slab on the Ti isotopic composition of the resulting melt is still under exploration. In this study, we use a suite of samples from two relatively modern, well-characterized sites from the Aleutian arc to probe how formation processes (e.g., partial melting versus fractional crystallization/magma recharge mixing) influence the measured Ti isotope compositions. We present Ti isotopic compositions for 18 volcanic samples from two Aleutian arc sites: Western Aleutian seafloor lavas from the Ingenstrem Depression, and lavas from Korovin Volcano on Atka Island. Samples dredged from the Ingenstrem Depression span a relatively narrow range in Ti isotopic composition (δ49Ti = +0.031 to + 0.147 ‰) with a relatively muted trend in Ti isotopic composition with respect to increasing silica content (SiO2 = 50.41 to 66.30 wt%). The samples from Korovin Volcano span a larger range (δ49Ti = -0.021 to + 0.355 ‰) and include more pronounced Ti isotopic variations with increasing silica content (SiO2 = 50.38 to 64.09 wt%). We use thermodynamic modeling (THERMOCALC software 3.53c) to predict isotope fractionation and show that the rocks from Ingenstrem Depression formed through melt-fluxed melting whereby between 0–70% of cool, hydrous-siliceous partial melt of subducting mid ocean ridge basalt (MORB) in eclogite facies mixes with mantle peridotite as it is heated and decompresses in the mantle wedge. In contrast, the Korovin Volcano dataset is likely formed by fractional crystallization from basalt to dacite with a potential role for recharge mixing of mantle derived melts. The data presented here suggest both a mantle wedge and subducting slab contribution for rocks from Ingenstrem Depression, further highlighting how Ti isotopes can be used to elucidate mass transfer in subduction zones and quantify variable source contributions in arc magmas, thereby providing significant insight into rock formation processes beneath Earth’s surface.

title: Adsorption mechanisms of carbonate on goethite: Density functional theory models of IR spectra and implications for surface complexation modeling
description: Publication date: Available online 17 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): James D. Kubicki, Mario Villalobos, América X. Cruz-Valladares
abstract: Understanding carbonate-goethite (α-FeOOH) surface interactions is crucial for describing adsorption-mediated mechanisms of many anions and cations on goethite, in view of the ubiquitous geochemical nature of both components. In the present work, we investigated, using computational approaches (Density Functional Theory) in conjunction with experimental infrared spectroscopy, possible mechanisms of carbonate adsorption onto goethite. Energy minimization calculations with the VASP code using periodic slab models for the two crystal faces of goethite revealed that there is a slight preference for the monodentate (Mono) complex that interacts with adjoining positively-charged triply-coordinated surface –OH groups, as compared to the bridged bidentate (BB) complex, but within the typical errors of the method, suggesting that both complexes have similar probabilities to form. Additional Gaussian 16 calculations on extended molecular clusters yielded a higher probability of the Mono surface complex to forming on the (101) face, while on (210) (Pnma standard crystallographic setting) the BB complex was largely preferred. The IR signals theoretically generated for each complex on each face yielded three possible surface configurations that matched closely the experimental IR signals of carbonate adsorbed on goethite: A BB complex on face (101), BB complexes on both faces (101) and (210), and Mono and BB complexes on face (101) plus a BB complex on face (210). This latter combination was tested with a unified CD-MUSIC surface complexation model. This model has been successfully applied to goethite for several anions and cations including protons, on goethites of different particle sizes and thus different reactive surface site densities. The CD-MUSIC model yielded adequate simulations of the experimental adsorption data across different conditions, with similar affinity constants for the three complexes, and contributions from each complex that were similar to those predicted by the cluster model. The results of this work tying theoretical models to experimental data revealed the importance of using case-specific surface configurations that are not necessarily applicable to similar environmental minerals, in this case for Fe(III) (hydr)oxides.

title: Hydrological and biogeochemical impact of a dynamic freshwater lens on the carbonate geochemistry in a sandy subterranean estuary
description: Publication date: Available online 16 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jiawei Liu, Zijun Wu, Bradley A Weymer, Qianqian Wang, Qiyue Gu, Yuanqing Chen, Zhonglin Ma, Yiqing Wang, Bulderxen Huate, Guanlin Li, Jiangtao Li, Nicole Kowalski, Michael Ernst Böttcher
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is an important pathway for dissolved carbon delivery to the coastal ocean and a potential driver of coastal acidification; however, the controls on the sources and transformations of SGD-derived carbon remain poorly constrained for sandy beach aquifers under contrasting seasonal conditions. Here, we integrated geochemical, geophysical, and microbial approaches to investigate a permeable subterranean estuary (STE) on the northern coast of the subtropical Beibu Gulf, South China Sea. The contrasting wet and dry seasons provided a natural setting to examine coupled hydrological–biogeochemical processes affecting the dissolved carbonate system. A freshwater lens was observed during the wet season, when precipitation was higher, whereas it was largely absent from the supratidal beach zone during the dry season. This seasonal contrast was associated with changes in salinity distribution, end-member mixing, and carbonate chemistry within the STE. Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), total alkalinity (TA), and Ca2⁺ exhibited non-conservative behavior across salinity zones. Geochemical and microbial evidence suggested sulfate reduction during the wet season, whereas aerobic respiration appeared to be a more important pathway for organic matter degradation during the dry season. CO2 outgassing and carbonate dissolution–precipitation likely further modified the carbonate system in both seasons. SGD-derived DIC fluxes averaged (4.0 ± 0.5) × 105 mol d−1 in the wet season and (5.0 ± 0.4) × 105 mol d−1 in the dry season, comparable to DIC inputs from the adjacent Fengjia River. Most groundwater TA/DIC ratios were below 1 and lower than those of offshore seawater in the Beibu Gulf, consistent with SGD contributing to coastal acidification. The acidifying potential of SGD appeared higher during the dry season, possibly reflecting a larger contribution of inland-derived freshwater SGD and associated shifts in biogeochemical pathways. The estimated [TA–DIC] flux indicates that SGD may have had a stronger acidifying influence than that of the Fengjia River during the dry season. Overall, these findings highlight the seasonal evolution of transient freshwater lenses as a factor that can modulate carbon cycling, export, and acidification potential in sandy beach aquifers, and underscore the need to integrate SGD and its biogeochemical impacts into regional carbon budgets and carbonate chemistry assessments for unvegetated sandy coastal systems worldwide.

title: Spatiotemporal variability of Tungsten-182 in the Hawaiian Plume
description: Publication date: Available online 14 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Lori N. Willhite, Nicole M.B. Williamson, Valerie A. Finlayson, Dominique Weis, Richard J. Walker
abstract: As a product of the decay of short-lived 182Hf (t½ = 8.9 Myr), 182W isotopic compositions in Earth’s rock record reflect processes that occurred during the first ∼60 Myr of the Solar System. Modern mantle plume-derived ocean island basalts have µ182W values (parts-per-million deviation from the bulk silicate Earth; BSE) that range from BSE estimates to values as low as ∼-25. The range of µ182W in some mantle plume-derived systems indicates variable contributions of an ancient component with low μ182W. The expression of the anomalous component in mantle plumes has implications for its size, viscosity, fusibility, distribution, and density. The Hawaiian mantle plume is well characterized with respect to chemical and isotopic variations for a range of elements, as well as magmatic flux, over the ∼5 Myr rock record represented by the volcanoes of the Hawaiian archipelago. To examine the physical nature of the anomalous component in this major plume system, we analyzed 35 basalts from across the archipelago for μ182W values and paired these data with complementary major-trace element and other isotopic data. These data, together with previously published data, indicate that Hawaiian plume-derived lavas were characterized by pulses of isotopically anomalous material, such that the component that hosts negative µ182W was either not always present or did not always contribute to melt production over the 5 Myr period. Of greatest note, the Hawaiian plume expresses large µ182W deficits during distinct time periods, at approximately 5 Ma in Kaua‘i and at present-day Kamaʻehuakanaloa, creating an inverted “u” shaped pattern of µ182W versus distance along the archipelago. Bulk Silicate Earth-like to moderate negative µ182W values (+1 to −14.5) appear at ∼1 Ma in Lānaʻi. Hawaiian volcanic centers lack clearly resolved µ182W anomalies at West Ka‘ena, Wai‘anae, Ko‘olau’s Makapu‘u section, Haleakalā, and Kohala. The negative µ182W anomalies at ∼5 Ma and present day correspond with rapid increases in magmatic flux of the Hawaiian plume, suggesting that the entrainment and expression of anomalous µ182W could be related to variations in the thermal structure of the plume. The Loa and Kea trends that are characterized by distinctive variations in the compositions of long-lived radiogenic isotope systems do not show resolvable differences between their µ182W systematics, indicating that the diverse contributions of recycled materials to the plume did not strongly affect the µ182W values of plume melt products. The attenuation of µ182W anomalies due to mixing with components with normal µ182W is unlikely to account for the distribution of µ182W along the archipelago. During the intervals when µ182W anomalies were minimal, the region of melting did not sample the anomalous component, most likely because it was irregularly entrained in the mantle plume.

title: Manganese-mediated ROS amplification drives oxidative dissolution of stibnite under dark abiotic conditions
description: Publication date: Available online 13 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Tongliang Wu, Linfang Zhu, Meiying Huang, Cun Liu, Yihang Huang, Song Wu, Zimeng Wang, Peixin Cui, Yujun Wang
abstract: Although oxidative dissolution of stibnite (Sb2S3) governs antimony (Sb) mobilization in many subsurface environments, the abiotic mechanism responsible for sustained oxidation in dark systems remains unresolved. Here, we show that interfacial activation of molecular oxygen (O2) on Sb2S3 generates surface-derived superoxide (O2 •−), which is coupled to Mn-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) reactions and markedly accelerates oxidative dissolution under dark conditions. Kinetic experiments showed that dissolved Mn(II) substantially enhanced Sb2S3 weathering, increasing the apparent Sb(V) release rate from 1.45 ± 0.52 × 10−10 mol m−2 s−1 in the absence of Mn(II) to 7.69 ± 1.13 × 10−10 mol m−2 s−1 at 1 mM Mn(II). Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed O2 •− generation on the Sb2S3 surface, and density functional theory calculations showed favorable electron redistribution from surface Sb sites toward adsorbed O2, supporting an interfacial electron-transfer mechanism. In the presence of Mn(II), H2O2 accumulation was greatly enhanced, consistent with Mn-mediated conversion of O2 •− to H2O2. This process was accompanied by the formation of poorly crystalline mixed-valence Mn (oxyhydr)oxide phases, progressive elemental sulfur accumulation, and increasing Sb–O coordination, indicating coupled oxidation of both reduced sulfur species and Sb(III). This O2 •−-initiated, Mn-mediated pathway provides a mechanism for accelerated Sb2S3 oxidation under dark, Mn-rich, mildly alkaline conditions.

title: Low-Ca olivine antecrysts as fingerprints of recycled oceanic crust and possible pyroxenite destruction beneath the southern East Pacific Rise region
description: Publication date: Available online 13 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Annie Chien, Peng Jiang, John M. Sinton, Zhaoshan Chang, Shiqiang Huang, Ethan Warnes, Jacqueline E. Dixon
abstract: Lavas from the 13°S to 23°S southern East Pacific Rise (SEPR) exhibit significant compositional heterogeneity along and near the ridge axis, as well as the off-axis Rano Rahi Seamounts and the west-northwest trending Pukapuka Ridge. This heterogeneity has been attributed to “plume-like” materials or “entrained mantle heterogeneity”, likely involving recycled components. However, whether recycled oceanic crust (ROC) is a major recycled component and whether the mantle beneath the SEPR is lithologically heterogeneous (i.e., presence of pyroxenite) remains poorly constrained. In this study, we examine textures and geochemical (major, minor, and trace element) compositions of olivine phenocrysts in lavas from the representative SEPR regions, via integrated EPMA and LA-ICP-MS techniques and fractional crystallization (FC) modeling. Our results reveal distinct olivine populations characterized by their zoning patterns and Ni-Ca compositions. FC modeling of the Ni-rich olivine endmember (the high-Ni trend) favors high-pressure FC at approximately 1.0 GPa, potentially reaching 1.5 GPa, under relatively oxidized conditions (up to ΔQFM +2) and with initial H2O contents of up to approximately 0.5 wt.%. A distinct group of reversely zoned olivines exhibit low-Ca cores (∼310 to ∼1160 ppm Ca) that plot along the high-Ni trend and cannot be explained by repeated mafic recharge or diffusion-driven re-equilibration. These low-Ca, reversely zoned olivine cores are interpreted as olivine antecrysts and occur exclusively in the isotopically anomalous region at 18°–19°S, characterized by elevated 87Sr/86Sr and low 143Nd/144Nd. Together with evidence from other trace elements (Li, Zn, Sc, Ti), these low-Ca olivine antecrysts can be best explained by crystallization from deep-sourced, Ca-poor melts derived from ROC-metasomatized mantle. Despite the inferred involvement of ROC, olivine first-row transition-element ratios, including Mn/Fe, Zn/Fe, and Mn/Zn, provide no clear evidence for a preserved pyroxenite source lithology but instead support a peridotite-dominated source. The apparent absence of a recognizable pyroxenite signature despite ROC involvement may reflect either insufficient ROC relative to peridotite to form pyroxenite initially or possible pyroxenite destruction through complete melting and assimilation into the surrounding peridotite, thereby forming refertilized peridotite. In the latter scenario, ROC-derived chemical and isotopic signatures may persist after the original lithological identity has been erased. These findings highlight the value of olivine textures and in situ geochemistry as complementary to glass and whole-rock analyses, revealing potential olivine-scale fingerprints of ROC involvement and providing insights into ROC fate and associated mantle processes that may be obscured by bulk compositions. Together with studies of pyroxenite in other geological settings, our findings raise the possibility that pyroxenite destruction may be a globally widespread process that contributes to mantle geochemical and lithological heterogeneity in both plume-influenced and plume-absent oceanic and continental settings.

title: Oxygen isotopic and chemical composition of chromites in the unique Washington County iron meteorite and implications for classification
description: Publication date: Available online 12 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Manfred Vogt, Daniel Mahr, Andreas Pack, Mario Trieloff
abstract: The ungrouped iron meteorite Washington County, so far unique for hosting solar-wind derived He and Ne within its metal, contains previously undocumented µm-sized chromite inclusions, extremely enriched in Mn and with highly variable oxygen isotopic compositions. The chromites of ≤ 13 µm in diameter occur as isolated, angular to subangular grains, which are erratically but frequently distributed within the metal of the iron meteorite. 76 inclusions were characterized by SEM–EDS, micro-Raman spectroscopy and electron microprobe analyses as Mn-bearing chromites (FeCr2O4), containing several wt% MnO, and manganochromites ((Mn,Fe)(Cr,V)2O4) with up to ∼ 27 wt% MnO, representing the Mn-richest natural chromite ever reported. δ18O, δ17O and Δ17O values of ten Mn-bearing chromites and five manganochromites were determined by Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) to reveal potential genetic associations with other meteorites. The δ18O values of individual chromite inclusions, with spatial distances of only a few millimeters, range from −3.52‰ to + 20.38‰, defining a huge measured isotopic spread – unprecedented among differentiated meteorites – while the mean Δ17O value of −0.07 ± 0.13‰ (2σ) is indistinguishable from the Terrestrial Fractionation Line (TFL). The measured oxygen isotopic spread shows no systematic relationship with chemical composition of the inclusions as both low- and high-Mn chromites show δ18O variations of ∼ 22‰ and ∼ 24‰, respectively. However, because potential matrix-dependent and other analytical effects cannot be fully quantified, the magnitude of the intrinsic isotopic variability remains uncertain. If a substantial component is intrinsic, the δ18O and δ17O variations are consistent with kinetic isotope fractionation during oxygen diffusion when chromites formed by solid-state exsolution within the FeNi metal upon cooling. Δ17O values overlap with those of enstatite chondrites, aubrites, and other non-carbonaceous (NC) meteorites but differ from most carbonaceous (CC) meteorites. A comparative analysis of oxygen isotope trends in NC versus CC meteorites shows that Δ17O values support classification of Washington County as NC-iron, suggesting a common formation region in relation to the NC population. Further literature review reveals additional NC-irons (i.e., irons of groups IIAB, IIG, IIIAB, IVA and IAB) that might, like Washington County, contain volume-correlated solar-type noble gases, potentially consistent with more intense exposure to solar irradiation in the inner solar system and incorporation of solar signatures preferentially into NC parent bodies.

title: Role of alkalis in carbonatite melt-mediated rare earth element mineralization
description: Publication date: Available online 12 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jia-Dong Ma, Hao-Cheng Yu, Isra Ezad, Li Zhou, Xing Ding, Ming-Qian Wu, Yi-Xue Gao, Zhong-Hai Fan, Shan-Shan Li, Kun-Feng Qiu, Jun Deng
abstract: Although recent studies have established a melt–fluid evolutionary framework for REE mineralization in carbonatitic systems, the role of sodium (Na), a principal alkali component, in fluid saturation, REE partitioning between melt and fluid, and REE mineral crystallization remains incompletely constrained. To evaluate the role of Na during REE mineralization, we conducted high-pressure, high-temperature experiments at 550–650 °C and 100 MPa, investigating the crystallization of REE minerals and fluid saturation in a simplified CaCO3-Na2CO3-LaF3 system containing 10 or 20 wt% bulk Na2CO3, with corresponding CaCO3 contents of 70 or 60 wt% at a fixed LaF3 content of 20 wt%. Experiments were run either as anhydrous compositions or fluid-bearing with the addition of pure H2O, a 3.3 mol L−1 NaCl aqueous solution, or a 1.7 mol L−1 Na2SO4 aqueous solution. Run products contained calcite and quenched carbonatitic melt, together with variable assemblages of bastnäsite, carbocernaite, and a Ca–F phase. Vapor cavities in fluid-bearing runs are interpreted as evidence of a separate fluid phase. Comparative experiments showed that, at a given temperature, increasing the bulk Na2CO3 content from 10 to 20 wt% results in increasing carbonatitic melt fraction. The higher bulk Na2CO3 content is also associated with greater inferred H2O retention in the carbonatitic melt. In fluid-bearing experiments, REE minerals crystallized within the quenched carbonatitic melt rather than within vapor cavities. Fluid–melt partition coefficients calculated from mass balance ranged from 0.05 to 0.13 for La and 0.09 to 0.31 for F. Chlorine- and sulfur-bearing components introduced through the addition of fluids were also detected in the quenched carbonatitic melt. These results show that REE are preferentially retained in the melt and that REE minerals crystallize primarily within the carbonatitic melt during melt–fluid coexistence. In bastnäsite-bearing experiments, carbonatitic melts with higher Na2O contents also contained higher La2O3 concentrations, suggesting that higher Na may enhance the capacity of carbonatitic melts to retain dissolved REE during REE mineral crystallization. The species of crystallizing REE minerals in the carbonatitic melts varied with bulk Na2CO3 content and temperature. In the high-Na system (20 wt% bulk Na2CO3), carbocernaite was dominant (12.9 vol%) at 550 °C, whereas only minor bastnäsite crystallized (2.9 vol%) at 600 °C. In the low-Na system (10 wt% bulk Na2CO3), bastnäsite crystallized from 550 to 650 °C (4.8–9.9 vol%). These relations suggest that higher Na availability favors alkali–REE carbonate crystallization, whereas lower Na availability favors bastnäsite crystallization in carbonatitic systems. Together, these findings indicate that primary REE mineralization remains melt-dominated during melt–fluid coexistence rather than shifting toward hydrothermal control. Within this melt-dominated framework, Na influences melt persistence, fluid saturation, REE retention in carbonatitic melts, and the crystallization of REE minerals during melt–fluid evolution in carbonatitic systems

title: Crystallographic controls and growth-rate effects on trace-element uptake in natural sphalerite
description: Publication date: Available online 11 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Chen Wei, Max Frenzel, Richard Wirth, Joachim Krause, Viktor Bertrandsson Erlandsson, Lin Ye, Frank Melcher, Zhilong Huang
abstract: Compositional zoning in minerals is increasingly exploited to reconstruct growth histories and decipher the processes and mechanisms of ore formation. Sphalerite is an important host of the critical metals Ga, Ge, and In, and commonly exhibits complex compositional zoning that may record the incorporation and partitioning of these elements during crystal growth. However, growth texture, such as sector zoning, can produce remarkable compositional differences among crystallographically nonequivalent but time-synchronous growth sectors. So far, this texture and its key control factors have been largely overlooked. Here, we combine electron backscatter diffraction, electron microprobe analysis, laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry, and transmission electron microscopy to investigate sector-zoned sphalerite crystals from Gorno (Italy), Huize (China), and Elmwood (USA). The results show clear elemental partitioning of tri- and tetra-valent cations (e.g., Ga3+, Ge4+, and Sb3+) between crystallographically distinct but time-equivalent growth sectors. Specifically, these elements are preferentially incorporated into different crystallographic face families in the following order: {111} > {110} > 1 ¯ 1 ¯ 1 ¯ } > {100}. Monovalent cations (e.g., Cu+, Ag+, and possibly Tl+) are positively correlated with the highly charged cations, probably due to incorporation for charge compensation. In contrast, divalent cations generally show weak sectoral partitioning, with Cd2+ and Hg2+ showing somewhat opposite enrichment patterns. These selective elemental uptakes appear to be governed by the crystallographic structure of sphalerite and modulated by the kinetic effects imposed by hydrothermal growth environments. Importantly, they can arise without changes in bulk fluid compositions, thermodynamic conditions (incl. T, pH, pH, fS2), with no detectable involvement of accessory phases. This impacts trace element-based thermodynamic proxies and hydrothermal history reconstructions, complicates the use of experimental partition coefficients, and warrants evaluation of crystallographic effects on isotope fractionation. Our study provides a framework to recognize and evaluate such textures in sphalerite, applicable to other minerals with analogous textures, improving the robustness of trace element (isotope)-based interpretations.

title: FROM slab dehydration to arc magmatism: tracing continuous fluid release with molybdenum isotopes in forearc serpentinite
description: Publication date: Available online 11 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Fu-Qiang Dai, Yi-Xiang Chen, Ren-Xu Chen, Zi-Fu Zhao, Yu Wang, Jie Li, Thomas Pettke, Trevor J. Falloon
abstract: Isotopic evidence remains scarce for the contribution of forearc serpentinite to the source of arc magmas. In this study, we present new Mo contents and isotopic ratios for serpentinites from the Tonga-Kermadec forearc, to explore the behavior of Mo during forearc serpentinization and its role in arc magma formation. Our results reveal that the Tonga-Kermadec forearc serpentinites are enriched in fluid-mobile elements (e.g., U, As, Sb, Mo), and most samples exhibit heavy Mo isotopic compositions with δ 98/95MoNIST3134 ranging from −0.27‰ to 1.84‰. Molybdenum-As-Sb-Sr-U contents in these serpentinized peridotites show two different variation trends with their δ 98/95Mo values, indicating that their protoliths were metasomatized by different-stage forearc fluids with divergent Mo systematics. Rayleigh dehydration modelling using proximal oceanic crust materials indicates that forearc fluids released from sediments and/or altered oceanic crust at various depths can effectively account for the Mo isotopic endmember compositions observed in these serpentinites. We suggest dragged-down forearc serpentinite is the most important heavy Mo carrier for fluid-rich arc front magmas (especially in cold subduction zones). This study offers new insights into the Mo cycling process in subduction zones and highlights the role of forearc serpentinites in the formation of arc magmas.

title: Chromium isotope systematics of ferromanganese nodules: implications for the marine chromium cycle
description: Publication date: Available online 10 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Xi Yu, Ziyao Fang, Xiaoqing He, Liang Yi, Chenglong Deng, Huiqiang Yao, Liping Qin
abstract: Ferromanganese nodules play a crucial role in the marine cycle of many trace metal elements and significantly affect the isotope composition of these elements in seawater. Chromium (Cr) is a redox-sensitive element, and its isotope system has been widely used to trace the redox conditions of paleo-environments. Previous studies have shown that the Cr isotope compositions of ferromanganese nodules are notably lower than those of seawater, but the mechanisms behind this isotope fractionation and their implications for the marine Cr cycle are still debated. In this study, we examined ferromanganese nodules from the Western Pacific Ocean along with Cr adsorption experiments, and combined selective leaching, scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry analyses to explore the sources of Cr in the nodules and the geochemical processes that influence their Cr isotope compositions. The adsorption experiments show that during the uptake of Cr(VI) by manganese (Mn) oxides, lighter Cr isotopes are preferentially incorporated into the solid phase, leading to an equilibrium Cr isotope fractionation of about − 0.90‰ (Δ53CrMnOx−solu). However, this process alone cannot fully explain the low Cr isotope values and their substantial variability observed in our nodule samples (δ53Cr, −0.82‰ to − 0.20‰). Selective leaching results indicate that only a limited fraction of Cr is associated with readily leachable mineral phases, indicating the presence of additional Cr reservoirs. Iron (Fe) oxides may incorporate isotopically light dissolved Cr(III), potentially contributing to the negative bulk δ53Cr values. Meanwhile, in situ analyses reveal substantial Cr enrichment in Si- and Al-rich components, including authigenic clays and detrital materials, suggesting that these components represent additional important Cr reservoir. Our findings suggest that the Cr isotope compositions of ferromanganese nodules reflect the combined influences of multiple processes involving different Cr species and mineral phases. Consequently, the relationship between nodule and seawater δ53Cr is more complex than previously assumed, making it difficult to directly reconstruct paleo-seawater Cr isotope compositions from ferromanganese nodules. These findings highlight the importance of Cr speciation and mineralogical controls when interpreting Cr isotope records in Fe-Mn-rich sediments as proxies for past ocean redox conditions.

title: Hydrated mantle source and low-pressure differentiation control the formation of gold-enriched magmas
description: Publication date: Available online 9 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Deng-Yang He, Hao-Cheng Yu, David Hernández-Uribe, Olivier Namur, Meng-Fan Yang, Shan-Shan Li, Guo-Long Yan, Kun-Feng Qiu, Jun Deng
abstract: Crustal magmatism is widespread on Earth, yet only a relatively small proportion of magmatic systems become enriched in gold (Au) during differentiation to form Au deposits. How mantle source properties and crustal differentiation jointly control this selectivity remains poorly quantified. Here, we combine thermodynamic modeling with trace element mass-balance calculations to trace the generation and preservation of Au-fertile magmas from mantle source to upper crust. Our results show that high Ba/Zr ratios in Au-related magmas are source-controlled rather than differentiation-driven, indicating the hydrated, metasomatized mantle as a prerequisite for generating Au-fertile magmas. This is consistent with an extensive positive correlation between Au concentrations and Ba/Zr ratios of natural arc magmas. Hydrous and oxidized melting of metasomatized mantle can accelerate residual sulfide exhaustion at low melting degrees and generate primary mantle melts containing tens of ppb Au. Modeled magmas with H2O > 4–6 wt% reproduce the U/Yb and Nb/Y signatures of natural Au-related magmas and favor delayed sulfide saturation, indicating that H2O-rich melts are critical for maintaining Au fertility during crustal differentiation. Consistent with this, mass balance calculations show that, in evolved melts containing 1 wt% MgO, the 8 wt% H2O-rich model retains an additional 26% of the initial Au inventory relative to the 2 wt% H2O-poor model. Modeled Cu/Zr and Cu/Y systematics further reveal that, compared to high-pressure differentiation in thick crust, low-pressure magma evolution in thin crust suppresses premature sulfide saturation and FeO depletion, exerting a first-order control on the preservation of magmatic Au fertility. Along the hot-zone path in thick crust, >82% of the initial Au is removed, whereas low-pressure paths allow magmas to ascend to <5 kbar without substantial Au depletion (<10%). Cu/Zr and Cu/Y ratios also identify different evolution and formation processes for magmas associated with Au and Cu mineralization, respectively. The decreases in both ratios of modeled magmas caused by sulfide saturation during fractional crystallization reproduce the low Cu/Zr and Cu/Y array of Au-related magmas, whereas assimilation of 10%–20% pre-existing sulfide-bearing cumulates reproduces the high Cu/Zr and Cu/Y array of Cu-related magmas. Collectively, our findings establish a hierarchical framework, in which hydrated fertilized mantle generates Au-rich parental melts, and high melt H2O contents and low-pressure differentiation in thin crust preserve Au fertility during ascent to shallow crustal levels.

title: Vanadium isotopic compositions in organic-rich sediments and the implications for constraining ancient marine redox evolutions
description: Publication date: Available online 9 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Siqi Li, Sean Newby, James McManus, Silke Severmann, Jeremy D. Owens
abstract: As a novel redox proxy, authigenic sedimentary vanadium isotope signatures (δ51Vauth) have been suggested to be sensitive to benthic redox conditions and have the resolution to identify low-oxygen environments. Importantly, these low-oxygen environments are associated with ecological significance due to increased oxygen stress on marine ecosystems. However, some aspects of V isotopes remain poorly constrained, including the potential influence from early diagenetic processes under varying redox gradients, which could complicate the interpretation of sedimentary V isotopic signatures in reconstructing ancient marine redox conditions. In this study, sedimentary δ51Vauth values were measured across a range of depositional environments that have varying levels of bottom water oxygenation and early diagenetic processes. Sediments and pore fluids were collected from six sites located around the eastern Pacific oxygen minimum zone along the California and Mexico continental margins, encompassing a range of benthic redox conditions from oxic to anoxic, as well as having variations in organic carbon burial rates. The data show that sedimentary δ51Vauth values appear relatively consistent with core depth at each site, regardless of the potential for V remobilization between sediments and pore fluids. We interpret this vertical consistency reflecting limited V release from sediments during early diagenesis. Thus, variations in sedimentary δ51Vauth across the studied sites dominantly correspond to the local redox conditions. In the oxic settings at Patton Escarpment and San Clemente Basin, V is primarily scavenged by manganese (Mn) and iron (Fe) oxides, and sedimentary δ51Vauth values range from approximately –1.10‰ to –1.40‰. This variability is plausibly influenced by specific oxide mineralogy or the relative abundances of Mn and Fe oxides. At low-oxygen (bottom water [O2] <∼20μM) and anoxic sites—Catalina Basin, San Pedro Basin, San Blas Basin, and Soledad Basin—authigenic V has previously been suggested to be mainly delivered via organic particles, although contributions from Fe oxides may also play a role in authigenic V enrichment. A general trend of higher sedimentary δ51Vauth values occurring with more reducing conditions suggests a redox-dependent isotope fractionation. Notably, sites with similar bottom water redox conditions, i.e., near anoxic (bottom water [O2] at ∼3 μM) and fully anoxic, but different organic carbon burial rates and Fe enrichments, display similar sedimentary δ51Vauth values. Furthermore, the sedimentary δ51Vauth values documented at Soledad Basin, where no significant V depletion is observed in either bottom waters or pore fluids, closely approach the values reported for surface sediments in the euxinic Cariaco Basin. This suggests that, in Cariaco Basin, V isotope fractionation is not primarily driven by water column H2S accumulation or Rayleigh fractionation derived from V depletion as proposed in previous research. Therefore, anoxic and euxinic environments both exhibit an isotope offset of around -0.4‰ relative to seawater. Overall, our findings demonstrate that sedimentary δ51Vauth signatures are sensitive to local redox conditions—particularly across the oxic to anoxic conditions—and are relatively resistant to alteration during early diagenesis, across a wide range of porewater redox conditions from oxic to sulfidic conditions. These findings highlight the potential of V isotopes as a robust proxy to diagnose local redox variations. Integration with other local and global redox proxies can provide a more comprehensive framework for reconstructing ancient marine redox evolution.

title: Zinc behavior during carbonated peridotite melting
description: Publication date: Available online 7 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Zhongxing Sun, Xiaolin Xiong, Jie Tang, Chunguang Wang
abstract: The characteristic high δ66Zn (≥0.3–0.4‰) of intraplate alkaline basalts indicate derivation from carbonated peridotite or a mixed peridotite + carbonated eclogite source. Moreover, these basalts also exhibit high Zinc (Zn) contents. Zn behavior should thus offer strong potential for tracing carbonated peridotite involvement in their genesis. A significant knowledge gap exists, however, as mineral-melt Zn partition coefficients (D Zn) during carbonated peridotite melting are scarce. Here D Zn between mineral and carbonate/carbonated silicate melt were experimentally determined at 3 GPa and 1300–1450 °C. Integrating our results with literature data reveals that melt MgO and SiO2 contents well correlate with mineral-melt D Zn. We quantified these relationships by parameterizing mineral-melt D Zn as function of melt MgO and SiO2 contents. Using our new D Zn values, we modeled Zn behavior during carbonated peridotite melting. The modeling results indicate that partial melts derived solely from carbonated peridotite consistently contain less than ∼100 ppm Zn. This is insufficient to explain the high Zn contents (∼120 ppm) observed in high-δ66Zn intraplate alkaline basalts. In contrast, mixing of peridotite-derived melts with melts derived from eclogite + Zn-rich carbonate provides a viable mechanism to account for the high Zn contents in these high-δ66Zn intraplate alkaline basalts. Therefore, a mixed peridotite + carbonated eclogite mantle source might represent a suitable origin for intraplate alkaline basalts exhibiting high δ66Zn values.

title: Zircon saturation in damp hot rhyolites
description: Publication date: Available online 6 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Julian-Christopher Storck, Ben Ellis, Edgar A. Cortes-Calderon, Marcel Guillong, Olivier Bachmann
abstract: Zircon is a key mineral for understanding evolved magmatic systems, yet its presence in hot, silicic magmas challenges conventional models of zircon saturation. Volcanic rocks of the Columbia River–Snake River Plain–Yellowstone hotspot track, for example, contain notable quantities of zircon despite having high temperatures, low crystallinities, and moderate zirconium (Zr) contents, conditions under which magmas are theoretically predicted to be zircon-undersaturated. This study investigates how and where zircon forms and persists in such seemingly unfavorable environments. We focus on the Castleford Crossing ignimbrite, one of the youngest and hottest eruptions in the Central Snake River Plain, to reconstruct the final stages of its thermal and crystallization history. New time–temperature constraints are derived from an integrated approach combining zircon U–Pb geochronology, mineral thermometry, and thermodynamic modeling. Two-Fe-Ti-oxide and pyroxene thermometry yield magmatic temperatures of > 910 °C and ∼ 930 °C, respectively. These estimates converge with calculated zircon saturation temperatures, consistent with the low pre-eruptive H2O contents (∼1–2 wt%) of these rhyolites. Textural observations show that over 75% of zircon crystals are attached to or included within oxides, pyroxenes, and plagioclase. This spatial association suggests that zircon nucleation is facilitated in microns-thick, supersaturated diffusive boundary layers enriched in Zr and characterized by a lower “M factor” (major-element cation ratio) adjacent to growing major phases. U–Pb dating by LA-ICP-MS across multiple units reveals very little scatter beyond analytical uncertainty, indicating a minimal antecrystic component, a finding corroborated by ID-TIMS data from the same units. While most zircons crystallized in near equilibrium with the evolving host melt, a small fraction, distinguished by high U and Ti contents, likely reflects fast disequilibrium growth. Collectively, our results demonstrate that zircon saturation in these hot magmas is possible, although it is achieved primarily through the creation of transient, Zr-rich microenvironments. This mechanism reconciles the presence of largely autocrystic zircon in these hot Snake River Plain rhyolites and has broader implications for interpreting zircon geochronological data in terms of magma fluxes in high-temperature silicic systems. In particular, the short zircon crystallization histories recorded by the large ignimbrites of the Snake River Plain and Yellowstone province are likely due to poor preservation potential of zircons in such high-T, and relatively dry rhyolitic magmas, not to unusually high magma production rates.

title: Dehydration processes of stagnant slab within the mantle transition zone revealed by geochemistry of olivine-hosted melt inclusions
description: Publication date: Available online 4 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Junfu Zhang, Yang Yu, Jie Tang, Feng Wang, Wenliang Xu
abstract: Nearly 50% of subducted plates may stagnate in the mantle transition zone (MTZ), forming the big mantle wedge (BMW) structure. Fluids or melts released by subducted stagnant slab within the MTZ intensively influence the physical–chemical nature and evolution of the upper mantle in a BMW system. However, dehydration processes of stagnant slab within the MTZ are unclear. Here, we present geochemical and H-B isotopic data of olivine-hosted melt inclusions from Early Oligocene-Miocene basalts in eastern Northeastern China (ENC), with an aim of constraining the dehydration processes of subducted stagnant slab in the MTZ within the BMW system. The olivine-hosted melt inclusions in OIB-like basalts (33–21 Ma) exhibit low water contents in primary melts (545–965 ppm) and mantle sources (116–202 ppm), coupled with low H2O/Ce ratios (7.96–13.6) and low δD values (−406 ‰ to −191 ‰), implying that the water in mantle sources is mainly contributed by ancient sediment-dominated dehydration in the MTZ. The olivine-hosted melt inclusions in weak-arc like basalts (11 Ma) exhibit relatively high water contents in primary melt (5780–6381 ppm) and mantle source (354–390 ppm), with elevated H2O/Ce ratios (135–166) and upper mantle-like δD values (−119 ‰ to −78 ‰), suggesting that the water in mantle source is mainly contributed by the young lower oceanic crust-dominated dehydration in the MTZ. Additionally, the melt inclusions in the ENC basalts also exhibit variable δ11B values (−17.10 ‰ to −0.08 ‰). The heavy B isotopic compositions of a small amount of melt inclusions from 33 Ma and 11 Ma basalts indicate the contribution of subducted serpentinite dehydration. The water contents in mantle sources of 33 Ma and 21 Ma basalts are lower than those in mantle sources of the early Cenozoic basalts, which is consistent with the transition from an active continental margin setting to trench-arc-basin system and formation of the northeastern (NE) Asian BMW, whereas the increase of water contents in mantle sources from 33 Ma to 11 Ma basalts could reflect the initial stagnance of subducted Pacific slab to formation of the NE Asian BMW as well as the transformation from ancient sediment-dominated dehydration to young lower oceanic crust-dominated dehydration, which is closely related to the evolution of the NE Asian BMW.

title: Beyond bulk sediments: extracting salinity signals from Sr/Ba ratios in complex marginal-marine settings
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Xia Zhang, Xiaotian Zhang, Yue Cai, Rong Hu, Guyue Tan
abstract: Sedimentary successions in modern to sub-modern marginal-marine environments are valuable archives of climatic and environmental change. However, paleosalinity reconstruction in these settings is often compromised by lithological heterogeneity, complex sediment sources, hydrodynamic processes, and diagenetic overprinting. Using a well-constrained postglacial succession (∼15 ka to present) from the Qiantang River coastal system, we test and refine Sr/Ba-based salinity proxies, that have been widely used in fine-grained siliciclastic successions. To investigate occurrence modes and interfering factors of Sr and Ba, we analyzed bulk sediments, grain-size fractions, and selective chemical extracts using dilute acetic acid (HAc), ammonium carbonate (AC), sodium acetate (NaAc), and ammonium acetate (AA). Our results show that Sr/Ba ratios in the 1.50) environments. Nevertheless, this ratio tends to overestimate salinity in high-energy settings, where clay winnowing preferentially removes exchangeable Ba. We therefore apply a correction using the relative proportion of the coarse-grained sensitive end-member (FEI). The FEI-normalized SrAC/BaHAc ratio shows enhanced sensitivity to relative sea-level variations and successfully identifies the MFS. This refined multi-proxy framework is well-suited for modern to sub-modern marginal-marine settings where exchangeable fractions are largely preserved, and confounding influences can be corrected through integration with sedimentological analyses. For ancient or diagenetically altered successions, where exchangeable fractions are severely modified but within a closed system, bulk Sr/Ba proxies in fine-grained successions remain a promising alternative, provided that carbonate-rich and/or barite-bearing intervals are treated with caution. This conclusion is supported by the general consistency observed between the Si/Al-normalized Sr/Ba<10μm ratios and the refined exchangeable proxies. Overall, this multi-proxy approach circumvents confounding factors and offers practical utility for paleoenvironmental and relative sea-level reconstruction in complex modern to sub-modern marginal-marine settings. More broadly, the methodological framework might offer a reference point for analogous investigations in other contexts, depending on site-specific preservation conditions of exchangeable fractions.

title: Potassium isotope dichotomy in hydrogenetic ferromanganese crusts: phase-specific archives of seawater signatures or authigenic processes?
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jiayang Chen, Weiqiang Li, Tianyu Chen, Yang Qu
abstract: Stable potassium (K) isotopes offer valuable insights into K cycles at various scales. Hydrogenetic ferromanganese (Fe-Mn) crusts, precipitated from seawater and enriched in K, could serve as potential marine K isotopic archives. To evaluate this potential, we conducted detailed investigations of the elemental and isotopic characteristics of K in two hydrogenetic Fe-Mn crusts from the northwestern Pacific Ocean floor over the past 80 million years. Sequential extractions reveal two major K-bearing phases: exchangeable K mainly in Mn oxyhydroxides (62.8 ± 8.9%) and structural K in silicates (32.6 ± 9.3%), with other phases contributing less than 5%. The δ41K values of the exchangeable K, ranging from −0.09 ± 0.04‰ to 0.35 ± 0.05‰, are higher than those of silicate K, which range from −0.71 ± 0.06‰ to −0.34 ± 0.05‰. Notably, the δ41K values of exchangeable K in the two crusts exhibit inconsistent temporal variations. This indicates that exchangeable K in Fe-Mn crusts is susceptible to local diagenetic processes, undermining its reliability as a proxy for long-term seawater δ41K changes. In contrast, the δ41K values of silicate K show consistent temporal trends, correlating with changes in distances between the sample sites from the Hawaiian hotspot. This suggests that the isotopic ratios of silicate-bound K in Fe-Mn crusts can record seafloor authigenic processes, and the growth of authigenic minerals in Fe-Mn crusts appears to be mainly influenced by basaltic volcanic detritus from hotspots. This study reveals a fundamental elemental and isotopic dichotomy of K in Fe-Mn crusts, demonstrating that 1) hydrogenetic Fe-Mn crusts are unlikely to be robust recorders of seawater K isotope evolution, and 2) silicate-bound K can be a sensitive tracer for seafloor authigenic processes and hotspot-related volcanism.

title: Lithospheric mantle derivation and depth-dependent endowment of Neoarchean orogenic gold in the Yilgarn Craton
description: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Qingfei Wang, David I. Groves, Runsheng Yin, Shiyu Liu, Carl Brauhart, Lin Yang, Huajian Li, Neal J. McNaughton, Kunfeng Qiu, Yongbo Peng, Jun Deng
abstract: The Yilgarn Craton represents one of the largest Precambrian orogenic gold provinces globally. The Kalgoorlie and Kurnalpi terranes, dominated by mesozonal-epizonal deposits, host the bulk of the gold, whereas the South West and Youanmi terranes, dominated by hypozonal deposits, are far less endowed. The source of auriferous fluids has long been debated between models involving crustal metamorphic devolatilization at mid-crustal levels and magmatic-hydrothermal processes near the crust-mantle boundary, whereas the causes for the marked regional endowment contrast remain poorly understood. Here we present integrated Hg, multiple S, and Sr isotope data to reveal that these four terranes share a common lithospheric mantle source and that their contrasting gold endowment relates to distinct depth-controlled mineralization processes. Non-zero Δ33S values of gold-related sulfides (−0.09 to 0.81 %) are comparable to those of granites across all terranes. This implies that lower-crustal components were involved in the source, arguing against a model involving a mid-crustal metamorphic fluid source. The Δ199Hg values of native gold and sulfides range from negative to positive and center near zero, indicating that lithospheric mantle metasomatized by oceanic sediments with significant input of continental crust is the most plausible source for the auriferous fluid. This is supported by elevated (87Sr/86Sr)i ratios of hydrothermal apatite. Critically, Δ199Hg values are similar between the well-endowed Kurnalpi Terrane and the poorly endowed South West and Youanmi terranes, confirming a common lithospheric mantle source. In striking contrast, δ202Hg values are markedly higher in mesozonal-epizonal deposits (0.11–1.79 %) than in hypozonal deposits. This distinction is attributed to fluid phase separation during mesozonal and epizonal mineralization at middle-upper crustal levels, whereas isotopically light Hg was preferentially partitioned into the vapor phase and lost, leaving the residual fluids enriched in heavy Hg isotopes. In contrast, the greater depths of hypozonal mineralization effectively inhibited such phase separation. Collectively, these interpretations suggest that the primary control on gold endowment is not source heterogeneity but rather the current exposed crustal depths of the terranes.

title: Dissolved organic matter decouples Fe(II) oxidation from arsenic immobilization: radical localization, mineral disorder and colloid stabilization
description: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Junhao Niu, Valentina Erastova, Xinghao Wang, Yanwei Wang, Juan Gao
abstract: Arsenic contamination of paddy soils and shallow aquifers threatens drinking-water safety and staple-crop production worldwide, and its severity is set by Fe-As coupling at subsurface oxygenation fronts. Where oxygen periodically infiltrates reduced layers, Fe(II) oxygenation generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and fresh Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides that jointly oxidize mobile As(III) and sequester the resulting As(V). How dissolved organic matter (DOM), a ubiquitous constituent of redox-dynamic environments, disrupts this natural attenuation circuit remains insufficiently resolved at the molecular scale. We examined straw-derived DOM across C/Fe molar ratios of 0–10 during aerobic oxidation of 1 mM Fe(II) in synthetic solutions at pH 5.5–7.5, combining radical quenching, kinetic modelling, XRD, Fe K-edge XAS and STEM-EELS. Converging quenching and modelling evidence indicates that As(III) oxidation proceeded predominantly via hydroxyl radicals generated at the Fe-mineral – water interface (·OHsurf) rather than via the freely dissolved pool. Increasing DOM progressively relocated ·OH generation to aqueous Fe(II)-DOM complexes, where radicals were scavenged before reaching surface-associated As(III); the Fe(II) utilization efficiency for As(III) oxidation accordingly declined from 0.33% to 0.13%. A transition near C/Fe ≈ 5 for rice straw-derived DOM separated two geochemical regimes: below it, micron-scale lepidocrocite aggregates settled and retained arsenic, whereas above it, ferrihydrite–organic nanocolloids of 160–360 nm carrying approximately 40% of total As remained suspended. We identify that DOM controls As fate through coupled effects on the spatial partitioning of radical generation, iron mineral transformation, and colloidal stabilization, and propose C/Fe stoichiometry as a governing chemical parameter for predicting arsenic fate in redox-fluctuating environments.

title: Manganese mineralization driven by dynamic oceanic redox fluctuations: insights from chromium isotopes
description: Publication date: Available online 29 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Qiang Chen, Xuefei Liu, Qingfei Wang, Fangge Chen, Xuefei Sun, Lei Liu, Jun Deng
abstract: Sedimentary manganese (Mn) deposits are valuable archives of paleoceanographic redox conditions and biogeochemical cycles, yet the mechanisms controlling Mn precipitation remain debated. Here, we present mineralogical, geochemical, and Cr isotopic (δ53Cr) data from the Late Carboniferous Ortokarnash Mn deposit (NW China) to constrain its genesis and link redox fluctuations to Mn mineralization. Mn-bearing layers are hosted in organic-rich marlstones with δ53Cr values of 0.46 ± 0.03‰, comparable to those of modern euxinic sediments (Cariaco Basin: 0.53 ± 0.21‰). Together with low redox-sensitive element abundances and abundant fine-grained framboidal pyrite, these signatures indicate wall-rock deposition under euxinic conditions. In contrast, relict primary Mn oxides within Mn carbonates, elevated δ53Cr values (average 1.08‰), and positive Ce anomalies indicate that Mn carbonates formed via diagenetic reduction of Mn oxides originally precipitated in oxic bottom waters. We link these redox oscillations to episodic ventilation and self-regulation of restricted basins during transgressions. Large-scale sea-level rises introduced oxygenated surface waters, transiently oxygenating the basins, while subsequent upwelling of Mn(II)-rich anoxic deep waters drove rapid Mn(II) oxidation. Enhanced nutrient supply during transgressions increased primary productivity and benthic oxygen consumption, promoting diagenetic Mn-oxide reduction and Mn-carbonate formation in anoxic pore waters. This study highlights repeated regional redox fluctuations as a key driver of major Mn carbonate deposits, establishing them as robust archives of local marine redox oscillations throughout Earth’s history.

title: Controls on organic matter fractionation and arsenic sequestration by Fe(III)-clay-humic coprecipitation
description: Publication date: Available online 27 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Hongling Bu, Hanjie Chen, Ziming Xu, Dong Liu, Peng Yuan, Manjia Chen, Shujie Hu, Fangyuan Meng, Chengshuai Liu
abstract: Coprecipitation of iron(III), clay minerals, and organic matter (OM) is a ubiquitous interfacial process in aquatic-terrestrial critical zones including wetlands, riverine sediments, and estuaries, where it governs organic carbon cycling and the subsequent environmental fate of metalloids such as arsenic (As). Molecular fractionation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) during this coprecipitation modulates carbon persistence, and the resulting composites control subsequent As sequestration, yet the mechanisms by which clay minerals shape DOM fractionation and the resulting As sequestration remain unclear. Here we use a ternary model system of Fe(III), montmorillonite (Mnt), and humic substance (HS) to investigate how clay alters Fe–OM coprecipitation and subsequent As uptake. We find that Mnt surfaces promote the heterogeneous nucleation of poorly crystalline ferrihydrite in intimate spatial association with clay edges, producing a defective Fe–OM–Mnt interface that imposes strong molecular selectivity on DOM removal. ESI-FT-ICR-MS shows that CHONS-rich ligands are preferentially scavenged from solution, while aliphatic-like molecules remain in the residual DOM. The same interface that sorts DOM also controls As sequestration. TEM-EDS mapping shows that As is spatially associated with clay-derived Si and Al domains within the composite, rather than segregated as discrete iron oxide particles. We propose that As binds to edge-anchored Fe sites bonded to the Mnt surface through ≡Mnt–O–Fe–OOC–HS linkages, rather than to bulk ferrihydrite. These findings indicate that clay minerals are not inert spectators in Fe–OM coprecipitation but active participants that restructure the interfacial environment and thereby alter the partitioning of both organic carbon and As

title: Zinc isotope evidence for intrusive Siberian Traps magmatism during the end-Permian mass extinction
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Na Li, Mengchun Cao, Guolin Xiong, Yi-Bo Lin, Mohammad N. Gorgji, Dongxun Yuan, Guangyi Wei, Thomas J. Algeo, Quan-feng Zheng, Hua Zhang, Shu-zhong Shen
abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction (EPME) coincided with catastrophic changes in global climate, the carbon cycle, marine redox conditions and nutrient cycling. Volcanism associated with the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province (STLIP) is widely recognized as a primary driver of these changes. However, the mechanisms by which different modes of magmatism influenced marine biogeochemical cycles remain incompletely resolved. Here, we present high-resolution zinc isotope (δ66Zn) records through the Permian-Triassic transition from two well-preserved marine carbonate successions located on opposite margins of the Paleotethys Ocean: Dajiang (South China) and Abadeh (Iran). Despite marked differences in paleogeographic setting and depositional environment, both sections display comparable δ66Zn ranges and coherent stratigraphic trends. Both records exhibit a pronounced negative δ66Zn excursion of ∼0.5–0.6‰ in the uppermost Permian that is closely associated with the onset of the negative δ13C excursion, indicating a broadly coeval perturbation to the marine zinc and carbon cycles prior to the EPME. Carbonate-hosted δ66Zn values records remained perturbed throughout the lowermost Triassic, suggesting that disruption of the marine Zn cycle in shallow-marine environments extended beyond the initial biotic crisis. Mass-balance constraints indicate that changes in biological utilization alone are insufficient to explain the observed isotopic shift. We suggest that a sustained input of isotopically light Zn to the ocean–atmosphere system is likely to account for the excursion, plausibly linked to large-scale sill-complex intrusions and contact metamorphism associated with STLIP magmatism. Sustained low δ66Zn values following the extinction coincided with an enhanced influx of isotopically light Zn during peak thermogenic devolatilization, whereas reduced deposition of Zn-bearing organic matter likely represented a secondary effect on the marine Zn cycle. Our results demonstrate that shallow-marine carbonates preserve first-order changes in shallow seawater δ66Zn associated with large-scale perturbations of the marine Zn cycle and highlight the role of prolonged, sill-dominated intrusive magmatism in altering marine Zn source-sink balance during the end-Permian environmental crisis.

title: Multi-Stage Carbonatite Magmatism Drives Rare Earth Element Enrichment
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Lucas Tatnell, Andrea Giuliani, Isra Ezad, Christopher M Fisher, Mohammed Bouabdellah, Stephen Centrella, Laurent Sapor, Marco Fiorentini
abstract: Rare earth elements (REE) are crucial for the green-energy transition, with the largest REE deposits occurring in carbonatites. Either magmatic differentiation or hydrothermal remobilization are considered primary mineralizing mechanisms for ore-grade REE enrichment. Here, we test and quantify the hypothesis that during protracted carbonatite magmatism, late carbonatitic brines/brine-melts from younger magmatic events strip REE from previously crystallized primary calcite (± apatite ± REE phases), progressively concentrating REE in the fluid phase. We demonstrate quantitatively that primary calcite in the Twihinate carbonatite complex, Morocco, loses > 50% of its ∼ 0.1 wt% REE during reaction with late carbonatitic brines/brine-melts. Textures and carbonate chemistry show that removal of REE from calcite by these fluids occurs throughout the complex. Mass balance implies that enough calcite is available to source all required metal for ore formation. Comparable observations across carbonatites worldwide indicate that remobilization of REE from primary calcite (± apatite ± REE phases) by residual magmatic fluids may represent a fundamental mechanism for REE mineralization in carbonatite systems.

title: Recycling of terrestrial mercury in modern subduction zones: constraints from Hg-Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Dian-Bing Wang, Ping-Ping Liu, Runsheng Yin
abstract: Mercury (Hg) isotopes, particularly mass-independent fractionation (MIF; expressed as Δ199Hg), serve as a powerful tracer for tracking the recycling of surficial materials into Earth’s deep interior. However, the contribution of terrestrial Hg to modern subduction zones remains poorly understood. Here we present new Hg–B–Sr–Nd isotopic data for volcanic rocks from eight stratovolcanoes and the Toba super-sized volcanic system, all located along the Sumatra segment of the Sunda arc. Sumatra volcanic rocks have negative Δ199Hg values (from −0.19 to −0.02‰), indicating an input of terrestrial Hg. Their mass-dependent fractionation (MDF; expressed as δ202Hg) ranges from −2.08 to −1.07‰, lower than that of the Mesozoic basement on Sumatra (−0.05‰). Together with Sr-Nd isotope constraints indicating minor crustal contamination, these observations rule out a crustal origin for the negative Δ199Hg anomalies and instead reflect a mantle source modified by recycled terrestrial Hg. The near-zero Δ199Hg values of the Nicobar Fan sediments (−0.01 to 0.03‰) indicate that the recycled terrestrial Hg in the mantle source is unlikely to originate from the Nicobar Fan but more likely reflects locally derived Sumatran terrigenous sediments. Three-endmember mixing models coupling Δ199Hg with Sr–Nd isotopes further indicate that the subducted sediment contribution was dominated by Nicobar Fan sediments but included a smaller proportion of Sumatra terrigenous component carrying the negative Hg-MIF signature, with total sediment additions of <5 wt% beneath the Sumatra stratovolcanoes and ∼5–10 wt% beneath the Toba volcanic system. Boron isotopes indicate slab-derived fluid additions of ∼0.01–1.0 wt% and ∼0.01–0.05 wt% beneath Sumatra stratovolcanoes and Toba volcanic systems, respectively. Mass-balance calculations show that fluids containing ∼20 ppb to 3.3 ppm Hg could reproduce the average Δ199Hg value of the Sumatra volcanic rocks, indicating that slab-derived dehydration fluids are potential carriers transferring terrestrial Hg into the mantle wedge. Near the slab tear zone, sediment melts generated during the diapiric ascent and partial melting of subducted sediments result in the enriched Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of the Toba volcanic rocks. Our results demonstrate that Hg isotopes, when integrated with Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics, serve as a sensitive tracer for distinguishing recycling of various components in subduction zones.

title: The effect of pressure and temperature on the fluid/melt partitioning of porphyry ore metals
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Ivano Gennaro, Alexandra Tsay, Zoltán Zajacz
abstract: A major fraction of the total Cu, Mo, and Au mined worldwide is derived from porphyry ore deposits, with Ag representing an abundant by-product from the exploitation of these deposits. The relative endowment of these metals is linked to deposit depth, with Au-rich deposits forming in the shallowest levels of the crust while Mo-rich deposits form deeper. These deposits are fed by magmatic-hydrothermal fluids derived from magma chambers which likely sit 5–15 km below the surface, but attainment of fluid saturation at greater depths has also been proposed. These deposits display a general depth-dependent metal endowment. To determine the effect of pressure (P) and temperature (T) on the ability of the fluid phase to extract these metals from the melt, experiments were conducted in cold-seal pressure vessels and a piston cylinder apparatus covering a range of P (150–700 MPa) and T (760–950 °C) conditions at which fluid exsolution is most likely to occur in crustal magma reservoir systems. Experimental capsules were composed of a Au-Ag-Cu alloy as the source of metals and contained a synthetic rhyolite glass, fluid of 1 or 12 mol Cl/kg H2O, and natural quartz chip for the entrapment of synthetic fluid inclusions. Metal solubilities in the melt and fluid phases increase roughly linearly with increasing T; Cl concentration only affects the solubility of metals in the fluid phase. Fluid/melt partition coefficients of Cu, Ag, and Au decrease monotonically with increasing T and are generally unaffected by P at a fixed fluid salinity. Chlorine and Mo partitioning into the fluid increase by a factor of 4 with P increasing from 150 to 500 MPa at low fluid salinities but decrease slightly at high fluid salinities. Empirical functions were fit which describe the solubility, fluid/melt partitioning, and metal/Na exchange of Cl, Cu, Ag, Au, and Mo as functions of T and P. A simplified magma degassing model based on these equations reveals that ore metal extraction from magmas is the most effective at upper crustal emplacement depths and relatively high initial water concentrations.

title: Hydrothermal experiments reveal methanol, ammonia, and methylamines as tracers of pH and temperature with potential application to Enceladus, Europa, and other icy ocean worlds
description: Publication date: Available online 13 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Kirtland J. Robinson, Everett L. Shock, Sean P. Sylva, Jeffrey S. Seewald
abstract: Icy ocean worlds in our solar system are prime targets in the search for extraterrestrial life. Enceladus and Europa are icy moons with evidence of global subsurface oceans in contact with rocky interiors, which may provide habitable environments for chemotrophic life. However, the interaction between water and rock and any changes in fluid chemistry are poorly constrained because the icy shells of these moons inhibit direct sampling of subsurface aqueous environments. Characterization of subseafloor processes may depend on chemical signatures in materials that are transported to accessible sampling locations near the surfaces of these icy ocean worlds. Here we present a theoretical framework where organic compounds likely to be present at icy ocean worlds can be utilized as tracers of geochemistry if they approach metastable equilibrium abundances, which we test with laboratory experiments. We use thermodynamic calculations of aqueous solutions to demonstrate that abundances of methanol, ammonia, and methylamines (compounds selected based on Enceladus’ plume data) should approach steady state ratios based on reversible substitution reactions that are systematically controlled by pH and temperature. We test these calculations by performing laboratory hydrothermal experiments ranging in temperature (175-325°C) and pH (∼3.5–7.0), demonstrating that chemical concentration measurements alone can be used in predictive models to accurately constrain the different conditions across experimental systems. As examples, with experiments conducted at 250°C, we demonstrate that the chemical tracers in a pH ∼ 3.5 solution predict a pH ≤ ∼5.0 and a temperature of ∼ 225-250°C, while the tracers in a solution at pH ∼ 7.0 predict a pH of ∼ 6.0–7.5 and a temperature of ∼ 200-275°C. Notably, all of our high-temperature experiments are cooled to room temperature prior to analysis, indicating that the hydrothermal signal (i.e., the ratio of chemical species) is preserved due to the slowing of reaction kinetics at lower temperatures, which may be analogous to hydrothermal fluids that vent into icy oceans. Similarly, we also performed a partial-cooling experiment that shows a tracer signal produced at 325°C remains largely preserved for a year after the experiment was cooled to 175°C. We compare experimental results from gold reaction vessels to experiments previously conducted in glass vessels to assess the effects of experimental vessel type and find only minor differences in product distributions over time. Overall, our findings provide additional motivation to target small organic molecules for analysis on future missions to icy ocean worlds in order to constrain subsurface geochemical parameters critical to habitability.

title: The importance of deep reactions between ascending komatiite and pre-existing protocratonic lithosphere for the chemistry of Archaean peridotites and greenstone belt volcanics: insights from reaction experiments
description: Publication date: Available online 9 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Rodrigo Freitas Rodrigues, Balz S. Kamber, Gregory M. Yaxley, Emma L. Tomlinson, Sandra Piazolo, Nathan R. Daczko
abstract: The cratonic lithospheric mantle is the buoyant 200–250 km deep root that enabled ancient continents (cratons) to survive for billions of years. The root stabilised due to extensive melting, erupting magnesian magmas at surface. However, peridotite xenolith samples from the cratonic mantle exhibit far more variable olivine/orthopyroxene and MgO/SiO2 ratios than expected from residues after melting of fertile mantle, exemplified by enigmatic dunites and orthopyroxene-rich harzburgites. Similarly, Archaean ultramafic lavas (komatiites) also show wider MgO/SiO2 variability than could be expected from shallow olivine fractionation. In addition, many komatiites have unexpectedly complex radiogenic isotope systematics, inconsistent with high-degree melting of refractory mantle. Thermodynamic modelling has suggested that these complexities could arise during deep (2–5 GPa) melt-solid reactions. Here, we present high-pressure layered experiments (3 GPa) involving the reaction between komatiite juxtaposed against harzburgite. The melt-bearing reactions yielded layered charges, wherein the initial komatiite layer (original, unreacted composition) was transformed into orthopyroxene-rich harzburgite following the reaction, and the original harzburgite layer resulted in the formation of dunite, with mineral modes and Mg-number depending on temperature. The solid residues of the reacted layers (orthopyroxene-rich and olivine-rich) are compositionally and mineralogically analogous to natural cratonic harzburgites and dunites, respectively. Thermodynamic modelling indicates that the MgO/SiO2 variability of the residues could be further increased by reacting the komatiite with fertile lherzolite instead of harzburgite. Solid-melt reactions markedly altered the composition of the incoming komatiite melt, with basaltic komatiite and komatiitic basalt formed at lower temperatures and modified high-Mg komatiites at higher temperatures. The melts exhibit the very wide range of MgO/SiO2 seen in ultramafic lavas in Archaean greenstone belts. Consideration of rare earth element and Hf partitioning suggests that assimilation of protocratonic ancient harzburgite into invading komatiite will be much more strongly seen in radiogenic Hf than Nd (or Ce) isotope ratios. Although both the original solid (harzburgite) and the incoming melt (komatiite) are ultramafic, their chemical contrast is sufficient to drive metasomatic reaction, likely partly due to the presence of a percolating melt. The reactions require higher temperatures than attained in the post-Archaean mantle, explaining both the sharp demise of komatiites after 2.5 Ga and the highly refractory nature of Archaean harzburgites and dunites. Ancient proto-cratonic mantle is one plausible candidate harbouring radiogenic signatures of Hadean silicate differentiation. The reason why these signatures are most commonly found in Archaean mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks may relate to the secular drop in maximum plume temperature, which has compromised the capacity of younger melts to sample this reservoir via assimilation.

title: Post-operative exposure to air pollution and colorectal cancer survival: A multi-center cohort study in southwestern China
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 520 Author(s): Lang Wang, Chang Liu, Xiong Zhou, Jinshan Liu, Jian Xie, Man Zhang, Zhihu Xu, Botian Chen, Xiaoyu Liu, Rongbin Xu, Dong Peng
abstract: Evidence linking post-operative air pollution to colorectal cancer (CRC) survival remains limited. This multi-center cohort study included 7068 patients undergoing radical resection for CRC at four hospitals in Chongqing, China. Over a median follow-up of 56 months, 1540 all-cause deaths occurred. Residential exposures to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), inhalable particulate matter (PM10), ozone (O3), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and carbon monoxide (CO) were obtained from CHAP, whereas PM2.5 constituents, including sulfate (SO4 2-), nitrate (NO3 -), ammonium (NH4 +), organic matter (OM), and black carbon (BC), were obtained from TAP. Time-varying Cox models assessed associations between 1-year lagged moving-average exposures and all-cause mortality. In fully adjusted models, each 5 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 and PM10 was associated with higher mortality, with hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.079 (95% CI: 1.045–1.115) and 1.050 (95% CI: 1.027–1.074), respectively. These associations were generally consistent across two-pollutant and sensitivity analyses. The inverse association observed for O₃ warrants cautious interpretation. Among PM2.5 constituents, OM showed the most consistent positive association (HR per IQR increase: 1.088; 95% CI: 1.028–1.152) and remained significant in residual and remaining-mass models. These findings link particulate pollution to CRC survival and highlight the potential relevance of PM2.5 constituents, particularly OM.

title: Redox-differentiated bank filtration is associated with enhanced sulfamethoxazole transformation but sustains persistent transformation products
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 520 Author(s): Jimmy Köpke, Caglar Akay, Simon Klaes, Julia Huchthausen, Luise Henneberger, Lorenz Adrian, Chang Ding, Aki Sebastian Ruhl
abstract: Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is a frequently detected antibiotic that challenges drinking water production by bank filtration and managed aquifer recharge. Although redox conditions influence antibiotic transformation, their long-term effects on transformation products (TPs), microbial communities, and residual toxicity remain poorly understood. This long-term study integrates parent compound attenuation, TP formation, microbial community composition, and cytotoxicity to provide a comprehensive assessment of SMX fate during continuous-flow subsurface treatment. Laboratory-scale bank filtration columns were operated for 589 days under initially oxic and subsequently redox-differentiated conditions. No SMX transformation occurred under fully oxic conditions. Following methanol amendment and redox differentiation, SMX transformation was consistently observed, peaking in the oxic–anoxic transition zone and continuing under anoxic conditions. Twenty TPs, predominantly derived from modifications of the isoxazole and aniline moieties, exhibited distinct spatial formation and persistence patterns. Endpoint microbial community composition differed among sampling zones and SMX treatments, including enrichment of Meiothermus (class Deinococci) in the high-concentration treatment. Despite partial SMX attenuation, enriched influent and effluent extracts from the high-concentration treatment showed comparable cytotoxicity. These findings demonstrate that long-term redox differentiation is associated with enhanced SMX attenuation but also persistent TP formation and residual cytotoxicity, highlighting that parent compound removal alone is insufficient to evaluate micropollutant attenuation and environmental risk in bank filtration and managed aquifer recharge systems.

title: Environmental persistence, bioaccumulation, toxicity and priority of fluorinated liquid crystal monomers
