abstract: Biocrusts are among the earliest biological covers established during mine tailings recovery, yet their roles in regulating microbial communities and soil multifunctionality under metal stress are poorly understood. We investigated algal and moss crusts developed along a tailings abandonment chronosequence spanning 4, 6–9, 13, and 30 years in a gold mine tailings pond to analyze their effects on heavy metals, microbial communities, and soil multifunctionality, and identified distinct recovery pathways. Soil multifunctionality was 3.96–9.18-fold higher in biocrusts than in bare sand, with algal and moss crusts showing stronger N- and C-cycling functions, respectively. Heavy metals, particularly Cd, Hg, and Pb, accumulated in biocrusts, whereas bioavailable fractions remained low (0.03%–27.12% of total concentrations), indicating limited metal mobility despite surface enrichment. Biocrusts significantly reshaped microbial community structures, with assembly shifting from stochastic processes during early recovery toward deterministic homogeneous selection at later stages; bioavailable Cd acted as an important environmental filter in moss crusts. PLS-PM revealed that soil multifunctionality in algal crusts was mainly associated with heavy metal accumulation, bioavailability, and microbial richness, whereas moss crusts were linked to soil texture improvement, metal bioavailability, and microbial network complexity. Overall, biocrusts enhance soil multifunctionality through metal availability regulation and microbial network restructuring, providing a sustainable strategy for metal mine tailings restoration.

title: Prioritization of high-risk PFAS based on comprehensive toxicity indexing and cascade features distillation
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Gan Miao, Tian Qiu, Xinya Gu, Fengjiang Sun, Jian Ding, Yurong Cui, Lin Lu, Ziyuan Li, Peijie Sun, Tian Yi, Yuebin Lv, Meian He, Xiaoting Jin
abstract: The rapid expansion of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) has far outpaced their toxicological characterization, leaving critical gaps in human health risk assessment. Current evaluations predominantly rely on single acute endpoints, failing to capture internal persistence, bioavailability, or chronic health effects. Here, we establish a human health-oriented, multidimensional framework integrating four complementary hazard dimensions: internal persistence, physiological distribution potential, acute lethality and chronic toxicity, to prioritize PFAS based on cumulative risk potential. A systematic assessment of 2213 OECD-listed PFAS identifies PFAA precursors and related compounds (PFAA-PFs) as the highest-risk category, ranking first in overall scoring and leading the PMT and P/MT classification with a share of 87%. To unravel the structural basis of these rankings, we develop a cascade features distillation framework that identifies three dominant structural drivers: halogen substitution (nX), molecular topological complexity (SRW10), and electronegativity-weighted autocorrelation (ATS4e), collectively explaining > 47% of toxicity gain. Targeted in vitro validation across risk-stratified PFAS demonstrates strong concordance between predicted rankings and experimentally derived benchmark doses (IC50, BMD10 and BMDL10), confirming the framework's predictive power. This work delivers a mechanistically interpretable, experimentally validated framework for large-scale PFAS toxicity prioritization, offering a scalable strategy to inform evidence-based regulation and sustainable chemical design.

title: Chloramine trade-off in bromide-impacted water: Fewer brominated trihalomethanes but more brominated nitrogenous byproducts
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Yuwei Wu, Huan Liang, Shumin Zhu, Yangtao Wu, Lingjun Bu, Shiqing Zhou, Wenhai Chu
abstract: In source waters with elevated bromide levels, chloramine has replaced chlorine to mitigate the formation of regulated brominated trihalomethanes (Br-THMs). However, the coexistence of chloramine and bromide potentially generates substantial amounts of brominated nitrogenous DBPs (Br-N-DBPs), which remain unregulated. Herein, we conduct a comparative analysis of overall toxicity and high-molecular-weight (HMW) Br-N-DBPs formed during chlor(am)ination in bromide-impacted waters. Compared to chlorination, chloramination reduces Br-THM concentrations and the number of HMW DBPs by 48.98% and 11.19%, respectively, while increasing overall cytotoxicity (the 50% maximal effect concentration (EC50) value) by 10.64%. Although the total number of HMW DBPs decreases, the proportion of Br-N-DBP formulas (CHNOBr + CHNOClBr) rises from 17.39% (415 of 2387) in chlorination to 32.41% (687 of 2120) in chloramination. This enhancement is driven by more diverse reactive intermediates and unique nitrogen-involving transformations during chloramination, yielding a wider variety of HMW Br-N-DBP formulas. Consistently, precursor tracking reveals a broader spectrum of SRNOM components involved in chloramination than chlorination (1548 vs. 1224). This work highlights the need for a more comprehensive evaluation of the reduction in regulated Br-THMs, the increase in cytotoxicity, and the enrichment of unregulated HMW Br-N-DBP formulas during the transition from chlorination to chloramination in bromide-impacted waters.

title: Characterizing crop-differentiated hazardous pollutant emissions from residue open burning: An integrated multi-source satellite and phenological metrics coupling approach
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Ying Zhou, Caixu Yang, Wanting Zhang, Jianlei Lang, Wenhan Zhang, Wenyue Zhang, Dongsheng Chen, Shuiyuan Cheng
abstract: Crop residue open burning (CROB) is a significant global source of hazardous air pollutants, posing acute and chronic health risks and transboundary pollution episodes. Current remote sensing-based emission estimates generally overlook crop-type differences and apply uniform combustion parameters, limiting the characterization of crop-specific combustion and emission heterogeneity. To address this gap, we developed a crop-specific emission estimation framework by integrating multi-source satellite-derived fire radiative power (FRP) data with crop distribution and phenological information to characterize crop-specific variations in combustion characteristics and emission spatiotemporal patterns. The results showed that different crop residues exhibited distinct combustion characteristics. Specifically, the maximum burning duration for wheat residue (9 h) was shorter than that for rice and corn (13 h), while rice and corn residues showed faster FRP growth and reached their peak FRP earlier during combustion. These differences indicate that crop residues exhibit distinct FRP temporal evolution patterns, underscoring the necessity of adopting mathematical distribution models and combustion parameters that can characterize crop-specific burning behaviors. In terms of emissions, corn residue burning dominated CROB emissions, contributing 43.0%-67.3% of various pollutants, and its PM2.5 emission per unit residue yield (emission intensity) was 1.3–1.5 times higher than those of rice and wheat. Substantial regional heterogeneity was observed; for the same crop, PM2.5 emission intensity varied by up to 16 times across different regions. This study provides a methodological framework for crop-specific CROB emission estimation and develops a high-resolution, crop-specific emission inventory, offering essential data support for air quality modeling, health risk assessment, and targeted CROB management.

title: Oxygen vacancy-regulated Lewis acidity and water activation govern hydrolase-like catalysis in CeO 2 nanozymes
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Yisong Qi, Lei Wang, Zhijie Chen, Dongle Cheng, Huaqing Liu, Chongyang Ren, Xiaoqiang Cao, Fei Li, Longlong Zhang, Yanlong Wang
abstract: CeO2 nanozymes are promising artificial hydrolases for organophosphate remediation, yet the link between oxygen-vacancy content and hydrolysis kinetics remains unclear. In this work, CeO2 nanorods with controlled oxygen vacancies were fabricated to build defect-based structure-activity relations. Using p-nitrophenyl phosphate as substrate, the sample with 29.05% Ce3 + fraction and high oxygen vacancies exhibited a 1.5-fold enhancement in hydrolase activity relative to low-vacancy CeO2 nanorods, by improving both substrate affinity and catalytic turnover. Mechanistically, Ce3+-vacancy sites activate water while Lewis-acidic Ce4+ polarizes phosphoryl groups, promoting nucleophilic attack and P-O bond cleavage. This vacancy rich nanozymes can realize the colorimetric detection of paraoxon by monitoring the released p-nitrophenol, accompanied by the partial degradation of organophosphorus pollutants with vacancy dependent characteristics. Here, we show that the combination of vacancy regulated Lewis acidity and water activation regulates hydrolase-like catalysis, providing a defect engineering strategy for artificial hydrolases.

title: Tire rubber-derived contaminant 6PPD-quinone induced male-biased reproductive toxicity in zebrafish ( Danio rerio )
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Zhuo Li, Yuxuan Chen, Xiangxiang Huang, Fengxiao Hu
abstract: N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine-quinone (6PPD-Q), an ozonide derivative of the tire antioxidant N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD), has been frequently detected in surface waters in recent years. However, the potential reproductive toxicity of 6PPD-Q in fish remains unknown. In this study, zebrafish larvae at 3 h post-fertilization (hpf) were exposed to 0, 0.2, 2, and 20 μg/L of 6PPD-Q for 120 days until sexual maturity. Our results revealed that 6PPD-Q induced significant sex-specific reproductive toxicity in zebrafish. In females, except for the declined proportion of mature oocytes observed in the highest concentration group, 6PPD-Q did not significantly affect the gonadosomatic index (GSI), ovarian development and cell apoptosis, hormonal level and offspring development. However, in males, GSI, spermatogenesis, 11-KT and androstenedione (ASD) levels, and fertility were significantly reduced, especially in the 2 and 20 μg/L groups, accompanied by increased apoptotic cells in testes. Additionally, transcriptions of hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis genes including esr1, esr2b, ar, star, cyp11a1, cyp17a1, hsd3b2, and cyp19a1a were disrupted. Molecular docking analysis showed stronger binding affinity of 6PPD-Q to the androgen receptor (AR) than 11-KT, which was further verified through the microscale thermophoresis (MST) and dual-luciferase reporter assays. Collectively, 6PPD-Q exerts significant male reproductive toxicity by disrupting the HPG axis and sex hormone synthesis, and retards testis development and spermatogenesis through competitive binding to AR.

title: Endogenous iron activation driven by microbial competitive release enhances electrogenic petroleum hydrocarbon degradation via boosted oxygen influx at soil-water interface
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Xin Yu, Xiaoyu Zhu, Xiaodong Chen, Yun Zhang, Yinghao Shi, Xiaolin Zhang, Bingyang Liu, Qian Zhao, Dejun Wang, Wenqing He, Xiaojing Li
abstract: Microbial extracellular electron transfer enhances the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbon (PH), however how the electron flow regulates iron cycling and PH removal remain unclear. This study confirmed a "competitive release" effect of biome that activated endogenous iron to create favorable conditions for subsequent colonization of electroactive bacteria. Sterilization, employed as a tool to simplify microbial community structure, triggered a "competitive release" effect by eliminating fast-growing competitors, which enriched electroactive bacteria and increased the cumulative electron flux by 27% (4157 C, 2.59 × 10²² e) over 203 days. This finding verified the role of microbial interactions in electrogenic removal (72–93% reduction). Furthermore, electron transfer shifted the in-situ soil redox potential from a reductive (< 100 mV) to an oxidative state (200–400 mV), and increased its diffusion depth and concentration at the soil-water interface, thereby enhancing the aerobic PH removal. In parallel, a consortium dominated by iron and oxygen redox was established, particularly in sterilized soil with more electron flux. Consequently, Desulfitibacter and Pseudomonas as capable taxa were enriched in sterilized soil while Guyparkeria and Salinimicrobium in non-sterilized soil. In conclusion, biocurrent-mediated iron redox established a superior electron transfer pathway to specialize PH removal in terms of the dissolved oxygen in soil.

title: Antibiotic removal and antibiotic resistance gene modulation in a pyrite-based bioelectrochemically enhanced constructed wetland
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 519 Author(s): Jie Peng, Nuerla Ailijiang, Qiongling Mao, Jiali Chang, Zhiming Zhang, Abudunaibi Abulake, Yue Zhang, Xifeng Tu
abstract: Antibiotic residues and the environmental dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) pose persistent threats to aquatic ecosystems and public health. A pyrite-based bioelectrochemically enhanced constructed wetland (PBE-CW) was developed to evaluate the removal of enrofloxacin (ENR) and sulfamethoxazole (SMX), responses of resistance-related genetic elements, pyrite interfacial transformation, plant responses, and microbial functional potential. At 1.2 V, ENR and SMX removal efficiencies reached 87.33 ± 3.13% and 99.85 ± 0.32%, respectively. Independent batch experiments showed that applied voltage enhanced ENR and SMX transformation in the pyrite system, accompanied by stronger 1O2 signals and multiple intermediates. During long-term operation, pyrite surface oxidation was accompanied by Fe/S dissolution and migration, enrichment of genera associated with electroactivity, Fe/S transformation, and antibiotic degradation, and increased abundances of genes related to extracellular electron transfer (EET), Fe/S cycling, and aromatic compound transformation. Meanwhile, target ARGs and intI1 generally showed lower absolute abundances in the anoxic zone and lower relative abundances in the aerobic zone. Overall, PBE-CW enhanced antibiotic removal and showed potential for modulating resistance-related risks through the integration of pyrite, bioelectrochemical processes, and rhizosphere interactions.

title: Quantitative monitoring of DNAPL source-zone evolution in heterogeneous sand-clay aquifers via deep learning fusion of time-lapse ERT and induced polarization
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Fansong Meng, Jinguo Wang, Yun Yang, Yaping Qi
abstract: Dense non-aqueous phase liquids (DNAPLs) form highly irregular source zones in saturated heterogeneous sand-clay media, where conventional single-method geophysical surveys are limited by insufficient spatial resolution and clay-induced electrical background interference, and standard inversion remains inadequate for quantitative characterization of contaminant distributions. This study develops a data-model integration framework that couples petrophysical constraints with a U-Net architecture, fusing time-lapse cross-borehole electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) and time-domain induced polarization (TDIP) to map multi-source electrical parameters directly to DNAPL saturation. Because clay distribution governs DNAPL migration pathways, chargeability and normalized chargeability are incorporated as petrophysical medium-background constraints. For the demonstration case, time-lapse fusion outperforms static fusion by a wide margin, raising the intersection over union from 0.27 to 0.63 and reducing the boundary displacement distance from 0.81 to 0.23 m. Across a fixed subset of 150 stochastic realizations, the normalized-chargeability constraint further reduces the boundary displacement distance by 6.65–7.50% relative to unconstrained time-lapse fusion, and its advantage in image-domain MSE emerges at the 5–10% observation-noise levels representative of field acquisition. Increasing observation noise from 1% to 10% raises the image-domain MSE by 28–34%, while ±10% single-factor perturbation of the petrophysical parameters changes the evaluation metrics by at most 2.34%. In the synthetic sand–clay scenarios considered here the framework shows promising performance for monitoring source-zone evolution, and provides a basis for future laboratory and field validation.

title: The importance of eventflow sampling for river load estimation of trace contaminants
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Nikolaus Weber, Steffen Kittlaus, Katarina Kozlica, Radmila Milačič Ščančar, Jörg Krampe, Matthias Zessner, Ottavia Zoboli
abstract: The accurate quantification of riverine contaminant loads is essential for assessing mitigation measures, pollution transport to downstream recipients (lakes, seas, countries) and for substance balance model validation. However, monitoring programmes based on regular, low-frequency grab samples often fail to adequately capture high-flow events (hereinafter referred to as eventflow). Ignoring these periods introduces significant bias into load estimation. To address this limitation, we developed and validated a targeted sampling strategy that combines high-frequency in-situ measurements with flow-type composite sampling, enabling accurate load estimation with reduced analytical effort. We tested this approach across three rivers with varying catchment characteristics and applied it to quantify seasonal and annual loads of trace contaminants representing different emission pathways and transport behaviours, including total and dissolved potentially toxic elements (PTEs), such as Hg, Ni, Pb, Cu, Cr, Zn, Cd, and As; pharmaceuticals; perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs); and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs). We derived the eventflow contributions to annual loads and quantified the potential bias from conventional sampling that misses eventflow periods. Our results demonstrate that eventflow sampling and its proper representation in load estimation are essential for particle-bound and hydrologically responsive contaminants. Excluding eventflow samples led to substantial underestimation of total PTEs loads ( ∼ 50% on average). For river systems dominated by diffuse inputs, PFCA loads were underestimated by ∼ 30% and pharmaceuticals by 28%–55%. In contrast, for river systems with substantial wastewater treatment plant inputs, the bias of dissolved PTEs, pharmaceuticals, and PFSA remained modest (typically within ± 15%), reflecting the dominance of steady point pathway contributions. The results demonstrate that our targeted sampling strategy provides a validated, cost-effective solution for accurate load estimation of trace contaminants.

title: Source-zone-informed numerical modeling of DNAPL transport and remediation in fractured media: From process representation to credible prediction
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Yuqing You, Fuyun Huang, Xiaoqing Shi, Chuanyin Jiang, Di Deng, Jie Zhou, Xiaoguang Wang
abstract: Dense non-aqueous phase liquids (DNAPLs) in fractured media remain difficult to predict because the source-zone architecture controlling dissolution, matrix storage, and remediation response is rarely directly observable or uniquely identifiable. This review frames numerical modeling of DNAPL transport and remediation as a source-zone-informed hydrological prediction problem. We synthesize the spatiotemporal lifecycle of contamination and compare continuum, discrete-fracture, and hybrid representations alongside inverse and surrogate-assisted approaches. Across the reviewed studies, prescribed source architectures, scale-dependent constitutive relations, and scarce independent field validation limit predictive credibility. Greater geometric or process detail therefore does not necessarily improve forecasts. For pump-and-treat, surfactant-enhanced remediation, thermal treatment, chemical oxidation, and enhanced bioremediation, we assess how process representation, treatment-induced feedbacks, and observation requirements affect prediction. Cross-domain comparisons with karst hydrology, radionuclide migration, petroleum reservoir simulation, and geological carbon storage identify transferable strategies for inferring hidden structure, representing long-term exchange, and updating coupled models. The resulting fit-for-purpose framework links prediction targets to model structure, priority observations, and uncertainty outputs. It emphasizes independent testing and iterative model-observation-inversion workflows, treating remediation operations as diagnostic perturbations as well as interventions. Future priorities are shared lifecycle datasets, cross-scale tests of effective relationships, and efficient inference across alternative source and process hypotheses. These developments are needed to distinguish sustained source depletion from temporary concentration suppression and strengthen the evidence supporting hydrological and remediation decisions.

title: Driving mechanisms of rainfall recharge intensity on hydrological response and nitrate source evolution in a karst spring system
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Shuna Sun, Mingming Luo, Xiangyu Peng, Wenhui Zhao, Haoyang Li, Xiaoyang Liu, Hengquan Wang
abstract: Karst groundwater is a vital global freshwater resource, and rainfall-driven recharge plays a critical role in controlling groundwater flow and solute transport. This study investigated the Qinglongkou Spring (QLK Spring) system in western Hubei Province, China. Hydrological responses and nitrate sources under different rainfall intensities were examined using high-frequency hydrological monitoring, hydrochemical analyses, dual nitrate isotopes (δ15N-NO3 − and δ18O-NO3 −), and the MixSIAR Bayesian mixing model. Results indicate that rainfall intensity is a major factor influencing hydrodynamic responses and nitrate transport in the karst system. The high-intensity rainfall event (mean intensity 9.5 mm·h−1) activated conduit flow and preferential flow pathways, resulting in a 1.5 h response lag and a peak spring discharge of 2990.7 L·s−1. In contrast, the low-intensity rainfall event (mean intensity 2.4 mm·h−1) showed a 7.5 h response lag and a lower peak spring discharge of 1347.9 L·s−1, reflecting slower recharge with a greater contribution from diffuse infiltration and fracture flow. Hydrochemical variations were jointly controlled by dilution and water-rock interactions. Solute fluxes responded synchronously to discharge during the high-intensity rainfall event, whereas stronger water–rock interactions during the low-intensity rainfall event produced relatively high solute concentrations but low fluxes. Ammonium-based fertilizers and soil organic nitrogen were identified as the primary potential nitrate sources. During the high-intensity rainfall event, the sum of the posterior mean contributions from these two sources exceeded 65%, whereas during the low-intensity rainfall event, the posterior mean contribution of ammonium-based fertilizers decreased to 15.7%–16.4%, accompanied by increased contributions from atmospheric deposition and manure/sewage. The high-intensity rainfall event was associated with rapid mobilization and high-flux export of agricultural nitrate, whereas the low-intensity rainfall event showed greater source mixing and biogeochemical buffering, resulting in a more balanced source contribution pattern. These findings indicate that rainfall intensity can substantially influence nitrate source contributions and transport dynamics by modifying recharge pathways, hydraulic connectivity, and water residence times, providing insights for groundwater quality management and non-point source pollution control in karst regions.

title: Virus transport mediated by microorganisms and micro-nano bubbles in soil
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Weipeng Liu, Fengxian Chen, Liqiong Yang
abstract: Public health threats from pathogenic viruses remain a persistent societal concern. Viruses enter soils through irrigation, manure application, or aquifer recharge, with their subsurface transport and fate determining the associated public health risk. While soil microorganisms are a key ecosystem component, their role in virus transport remains a critical knowledge gap. This study aims to investigate the influence of soil microorganisms on virus transport and to evaluate the feasibility of using micro-nano bubbles (MNBs) to mitigate virus transport. We selected two model viruses with different isoelectric points (MS2 and ΦX174) and performed column experiments, varying microbial activity (native vs. inhibited) and the presence of MNBs (with vs. without MNBs). We observed enhanced transport for both viruses in soil with repressed microbial activity, which was attributable to the lower abundance of microbial cells. The virus with the higher isoelectric point (ΦX174) exhibited more pronounced transport changes, with recovery differing by ~62.49 percentage points between the two treatments. Furthermore, MNBs could hinder virus transport by providing air–water interfaces. This effect was more pronounced when microbial activity was inhibited, with MNB addition reducing MS2 recovery by ~14.52 percentage points. This study reveals the distinct roles of microorganisms and MNBs in virus transport and underscores the importance of considering biological processes when assessing the fate of viruses in soil.

title: Lacustrine groundwater discharge drives antibiotic fluxes in large shallow lakes: From a hidden sink to a secondary source
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Jiamei Zhang, Yu Wang, Gege Cai, Fazhi Xie, Yuyang Zhu, Zhiqiang Xie, Xing Chen, Guolian Li, Shan Li, Xin Luo
abstract: Intensified human activities have exacerbated antibiotic pollution in large freshwater lakes. Although multiple pathways can transport antibiotics into lakes, the contribution of lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) to surface water contamination remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the migration of antibiotics across surface water and groundwater in Chaohu Lake, the fifth-largest freshwater lake in China, with a specific focus on LGD contributions. Overall, antibiotic concentrations were higher in surface water than in groundwater, with both water bodies exhibiting elevated levels during the dry season. Utilizing a 222 Rn mass balance model, LGD was significantly stronger in the dry season, driving a substantial groundwater-derived antibiotic flux to the surface water (72.62 μg/(m2·d)) dominated by quinolones. Moreover, among the input pathways quantified in this study, LGD was estimated to account for 73.01–96.22% of the quantified antibiotic inputs. Positive matrix factorization and structural equation modeling indicated distinct pollution drivers: surface-water antibiotics were mainly associated with wastewater-treatment-system-related inputs in the wet season (32.92%) and domestic-sewage-related inputs in the dry season (26.11%), whereas groundwater antibiotics showed substantial associations with livestock-breeding-related inputs (26.86–28.60%), and antibiotic occurrence in both water bodies was also associated with nitrogen and phosphorus levels. Ecological risk assessment indicated that algae were the most sensitive receptors and that ciprofloxacin was the principal risk contributor for both water bodies. These findings elucidate how seasonal variation regulates the key pathways by which antibiotics enter surface water, and highlight that groundwater serves not only as an antibiotic sink but also as a critical secondary source for surface water contamination. Ultimately, effective prevention and mitigation of antibiotic pollution in shallow lakes must inherently integrate the management of LGD and adjacent input rivers.

title: Multi-response optimization of TCE remediation using blended surfactants: A combination of Taguchi design, resistivity method, and ANN
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zhihang Jin, Hanle Liu
abstract: Chlorinated dense non-aqueous phase liquids (DNAPLs) such as trichloroethylene (TCE) are among the most persistent contaminants in groundwater. Because of their high density, low aqueous solubility, and high toxicity, TCE that infiltrates below the water table forms long-term source zones that are difficult to locate and to treat. Surfactant-enhanced aquifer remediation (SEAR) flushes an aqueous surfactant solution through the contaminated zone to lower the interfacial tension and solubilize or mobilize the trapped DNAPL, and its performance depends strongly on the subsurface conditions and on the operating parameters chosen. In this study, an L9 orthogonal array was used to optimize the operating parameters of a blended SDS/TX-100 system in laboratory-scale, one-dimensional sand-column experiments. The resistivity change rate and the remediation pore volume (PV) were selected as response variables. Single-response Taguchi analysis indicated that the injection rate had the greatest influence on the resistivity change rate, while the mixing ratio dominated PV. Multi-response optimization under equal weighting yielded the optimal combination: α = 1.0 (pure SDS), total concentration 3.0 g/L, and injection rate 3 mL/min. The ANN model achieved R2 values of 0.845 (resistivity change rate) and 0.661 (PV) via leave-one-out cross-validation. The results demonstrate that the integrated framework of real-time resistivity monitoring, Taguchi optimization, and ANN prediction provides a practical, data-driven methodology for SEAR process design.

title: Effectiveness of PFAS remediation strategies on AFFF impacted soils under different climates and soil characteristics
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Colin McKay, Ilka Wallis, John Hutson
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) widespread use as a component in aqueous firefighting foams (AFFF) has created environmental legacies for airports, airbases and other industrial sites. PFAS released during historical AFFF use has often migrated into the unsaturated zone, which then acts as a long-term source for sustained PFAS contamination of groundwater, and surface water pollution at many affected sites. Accordingly, the vadose zone has become a critical target for remediation. This study used numerical unsaturated zone simulations to quantify PFAS migration under a range of practical onsite remediation measures, across a large range of climates and soil conditions. A 70-year simulation timeframe emulating a hypothetical AFFF application history, combined four climatic regions, four soil types and three soil sorption capacities for PFOS, PFHxS and PFOA. Simulated remedial options included full and partial soil stabilisation, clay capping, and natural dilution and attenuation. Results show that climate strongly controls PFAS mobility and remediation timeframes: under tropical conditions, rapid PFAS migration shortens the available window for remedial intervention, whereas under drier climates migration is slower, but low-level PFAS discharge below the treatment horizon can persist for decades. Full-profile stabilisation together with a surface cap markedly reduced PFAS leaching, lowering cumulative fluxes to less than 10% relative to stabilisation alone, or less than 2% of flux from untreated soils. Partial stabilisation was less effective due to continued leaching from deeper, untreated, portions of the soil profile. Combining partial stabilisation with a cap generally provided little additional reduction in cumulative downward PFAS export compared with capping alone. Simulations also revealed that upward wicking of PFAS occurred into clay caps, potentially providing a source for ongoing PFAS surface runoff from capped source zones. Wicking was mitigated when caps were underlain by stabilised soil. Overall, model outcomes highlight that combining soil stabilisation and hydraulic control offers the greatest containment, but optimal remediation design and timing depend strongly on local climate and soil properties.

title: Reactive transport of the rare earth element neodymium (Nd) using surface complexation models: Assessing the fate and transport of an emerging 21st century environmental contaminant
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Jaxon Dii Horne, Larissa Costa, Christopher D. White, Karen H. Johannesson
abstract: We investigate the transport of the rare earth element neodymium (Nd) in a hypothetical, shallow groundwater system via a series of numerical experiments that leverage surface complexation models (SCM) simulating N d 3 + sorption onto goethite (α-FeOOH) and hydrous ferric oxide (HFO). Neodymium is a key critical metal necessary for the manufacture of permanent magnets and thus can make up a substantial proportion of electronic waste. One-dimensional reactive transport models are constructed that simulate advective-dispersive transport, mineral dissolution/precipitation, aqueous complexation, and sorption/desorption of Nd along a modeled flow path. Models assume an imbibition phase where Nd-polluted water (1 μmol kg−1) infiltrates the aquifer, which initially contains groundwater that is nearly devoid of Nd. Subsequently, the aquifer is flushed with the nearly Nd-free water to evaluate the behavior of a Nd plume along the flow path and to assess the time that might be required to remediate the aquifer. Simulations produce sharp sorption fronts with long tails typical of strongly sorbed solutes. Models run in the presence or absence of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) reveal that Nd transport is strongly affected by aqueous complexation with carbonate anions [i.e., NdC O 3 + + Nd C O 3 2 − ], which may inhibit sorption of the aquo ion, N d 3 + . However, SCMs that also include NdC O 3 + sorption, predict enhanced retardation along the flow path. This knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport of Nd in aquifer systems, namely whether only the aquo ion sorbs or if aqueous complexes also sorb, requires additional investigations.

title: Hydrogeochemical patterns, driving factors and probabilistic health risks of karst groundwater in the Feicheng fault region (Eastern China): Revealed by self-organizing map and optimized forward model
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Changsuo Li, Wenqiang Zhang, Jing Li, Shuai Gao, Yue Teng, Jinxiao Wang, Jun Li, Guoli Yang
abstract: The identification of karst hydrogeochemical patterns, driving factors, and associated health risks is critical for balancing karst groundwater resources and human health, and for managing poor-quality groundwater influenced by natural conditions and anthropogenic emissions. This study integrates hydrogeochemical parameters with the self-organizing map, optimized forward model, and Monte Carlo model to identify hydrogeochemical patterns and assess their driving factors and probabilistic health risks in the Feicheng fault region. The results reveal that natural conditions (e.g., topography and mineral types) and anthropogenic emissions jointly constrain the complex hydrogeochemical patterns in the study area. In low-lying areas, karst groundwater is closely associated with pore water and exhibits high ion concentrations. It is primarily influenced by evaporite dissolution (50.0 ± 10.2%) and carbonate dissolution (26.6 ± 7.70%), followed by agricultural and residential emissions (18.6 ± 11.6%). In the basin margins near piedmont areas, karst groundwater is partly affected by fracture water and shows low ion concentrations. Carbonate dissolution, mainly of calcite, plays a crucial role in karst hydrogeochemical patterns (45.2 ± 10.1%). Given the significant non-carcinogenic risks to the native population, especially younger individuals, diffuse NO3 − pollution in karst groundwater should be prioritized for management and prevention. This study highlights the capability to reveal the hydrogeochemical driving factors of karst groundwater using an integrated method, and provides systematic insights for sustainable management of karst groundwater resources.

title: Pistia stratiotes alters diuron partitioning and metabolite formation: evidence from plant-mediated processes
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Maria Carolina Ramírez Hernández, Mateus Alencar Bezerra Silva, Lucrécia Pacheco Batista, Jesley Nogueira Bandeira, Breno De Holanda Almeida, Jarlan Lucas dos Santos Silva, Darcio Cesar Constante, Daniel Viana de Freitas, Paulo Sergio Fernandes das Chagas, Claudinei da Cruz, Daniel Valadão Silva
abstract: Herbicide contamination in aquatic systems is commonly assessed through changes in water concentrations, potentially overlooking redistribution among environmental compartments and metabolite formation. Here, we investigated the environmental fate of diuron in aquatic microcosms with and without Pistia stratiotes, integrating diuron partitioning among water, sediment, and plant tissues with DCPMU formation, bacterial abundance, and plant physiological responses under environmentally relevant and elevated exposure levels (2.5, 10.0, and 25.0 μg L−1). In non-vegetated systems, diuron rapidly partitioned into sediment, which represented the main reservoir and was associated with progressive DCPMU formation. In contrast, the presence of P. stratiotes substantially altered diuron partitioning, reducing sediment retention and increasing accumulation in plant tissues, particularly roots, while bacterial abundance increased in water and sediment. These findings indicate that macrophytes can modify contaminant distribution and create alternative compartments for diuron retention and associated transformation processes. Despite physiological stress, P. stratiotes maintained diuron accumulation with limited translocation to shoots. Overall, reductions in water concentrations did not necessarily indicate contaminant attenuation, as diuron was redistributed among sediment and plant compartments and remained associated with metabolite formation. These findings highlight the importance of considering contaminant partitioning, plant accumulation, and transformation processes when assessing herbicide fate and persistence in vegetated aquatic systems.

title: Multi-scale approach to understanding and predicting environmental reactivity in the context of ISR
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Marine Bonnet, Niya Grozeva, Nicolas Seigneur, Sophie Guillon, Bayarmaa Purevsan, Natsagmaa Jadambaa, Mathias Gex, Clémence Besançon, Valentin Robin, Pierre Grizard, Michaël Descostes
abstract: In situ recovery (ISR) is a worldwide mining technique which accounts for more than 52% (in 2024) of global U production, thanks to its cost-effectiveness. However, where an ISR process uses sulfuric acid (H2SO4), local underground exploited aquifers' water quality can be affected by low pH and high concentrations of SO4. Hydrogeochemical processes controlling this groundwater changes are studied here in the context of the planned exploitation of the Zoovch Ovoo deposit in Mongolia, using a multi-scale approach comparing real data with models. At the laboratory scale, experimental data combined with a 1D reactive transport model (RTM) demonstrate that ion-exchange reactions on clay minerals surface are the main geochemical mechanism governing groundwater chemistry (pH and major ions). To consider system heterogeneity and the spatial impact of the ISR process, field data from two pilot cells were combined with a 3D reactive transport model. The model successfully reproduced the field data by considering both ion-exchange and dissolution-precipitation reactions of the mineral phases, especially calcite and gypsum, necessary to explain the water chemistry at larger scale. Vertical and lateral fluid excursions out of the pilot cells were observed depending on the system heterogeneity. This study demonstrated that the relative importance of the various processes investigated depends on the time and distance scales probed. For the short term and U production, heterogeneities and ion-exchange are crucial for explaining the changes in groundwater chemistry. A better understanding and quantification of these processes will help operators optimize production and long-term environmental remediation strategies.

title: Canopy exchange processes enhance acid-neutralizing capacity in subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Shui-Xia Li, Zhi-Yun Jiang, Yi-Hua Xiao, Han-Wen Zhang, Meng-Di Wu, Tong-Zheng Chen, Zhi-Gao Fu, Jing Li, Si-Yi Zhang
abstract: Forest canopy serves as the first interface for atmospheric deposition into ecosystems, thereby playing a crucial role in regulating hydrological processes and associated water chemical cycles by means of canopy exchange processes. However, it remains poorly understood how canopy exchange processes alter chemical processing of rainwater, such as the acid-neutralizing capacity (ANC) in acidic areas. This study examined the hydrological partitioning and associated chemical composition in a typical subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest in southern China. Hydrological components, including rainfall, throughfall, and stemflow, were measured and sampled from January 2020 to December 2021, and the canopy exchange process was then estimated using a canopy budget model. Results showed that pH and ANC increased in throughfall but decreased in stemflow. During the dry season, throughfall exhibited significantly higher neutralization capacity (ΔpH = 1.11 ± 0.89; ΔANC = 0.11 ± 0.13 meq L−1), whereas in the wet season, the neutralization capacity of throughfall was substantially weaker (ΔpH = 0.07 ± 0.85; ΔANC = 0.03 ± 0.09 meq L−1). In contrast, stemflow showed persistent acidification across both seasons (dry-season ΔpH: −1.29 ± 1.01; wet-season ΔpH: −1.18 ± 0.69), with its ΔANC significantly below zero in the wet season (−0.07 ± 0.09 meq L−1, p = 0.009). The canopy budget model indicated that most solutes (except F−) were leached from the forest canopy, with K+ exhibiting the most pronounced canopy leaching effect. In addition, canopy exchange contributed positively 83% to acid-neutralizing capacity (ANCNTF) of net throughfall flux. Among ions mediating canopy processes, Ca2+, K+, Mg2+, and F− all made positive contributions to the acid neutralizing capacity of canopy exchange (ANCCE) in both dry and wet seasons, with K+ contributing the most (31.43% in the dry season and 25.52% in the wet season). In contrast, NO₃− and Cl− exhibited negative contributions: the negative effect of NO₃− was stronger in the wet season (−20.69%) than in the dry season (−0.63%), whereas Cl− showed the opposite pattern (dry: −12.03%–; wet: −12.03%). Our results suggest that the forest canopy may play a significant role in mitigating the effects of atmospheric acid deposition. This finding contributes to a better understanding of forest eco-hydrological processes and could have important implications for forest management in similar subtropical regions globally.

title: Vadose-zone control of PFOS delivery to groundwater: Explicit unsaturated-zone transport with solid-phase and air–water interfacial sorption
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Vahid Rafiei
abstract: Quantifying PFOS retention in the unsaturated zone beneath contaminated sites requires a model that simulates how much PFOS the unsaturated zone holds and when PFOS first reaches groundwater. Both determine how long a source keeps feeding the aquifer and when watershed and site assessments need an explicit unsaturated zone. We modified the unsaturated-zone transport of MODFLOW 6 to simulate solid-phase and air–water interfacial sorption, each dependent on water content, and drove it at two sites with daily percolation from SWAT+. We applied it at three sites that differ in depth to water, infiltration and water content: two firefighting-foam sites and a tannery legacy source. At the shallow site, the same released mass was run once through the unsaturated zone and once directly to the water table. In a simulated 6.4–6.9 m column (3.0–4.3 m measured nearby), 63–83% of the PFOS released in 1971–1994 was above the water table in 2024, and its median crossing was delayed by at least 42 years; PFOS in the deep aquifer was 70–83% lower in 2017. Without sorption the two runs agreed within 0.2%, so the delay is sorption, not water movement. An advection–dispersion screen shows that 1/10,000 of the source concentration first reaches the water table within a median of 18–38 years at a dispersivity of 10% of the depth, against a median transit of 83–182 years. A single travel time answers neither question: a screen must report when PFOS is first detected and how long the unsaturated zone feeds the aquifer.

title: Machine learning prediction of arsenic natural background level heterogeneity in shallow groundwater: Integrating in-situ hydrochemistry and spatial proxies at the meso-scale
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Laura Landi, Joel Podgorski, Michael Berg, Marco Rotiroti, Chiara Zanotti, Alessandro Amorosi, Enrico Dinelli, Maria Filippini
abstract: Geogenic arsenic (As) contamination poses a major environmental concern, yet mapping its Natural Background Levels (NBLs) remains challenging in data-scarce, human-impacted regions within heterogeneous sedimentary aquifers. NBLs are essential for distinguishing natural from anthropogenic contributions and for establishing threshold values in environmental policy and groundwater management. This study applies a Random Forest (RF) algorithm to predict arsenic NBL exceedance of the WHO guideline (10 μg/L) in shallow groundwater of the Ferrara province (Po Plain, Italy). Three model configurations were tested using: (i) in-situ hydrochemical variables (hydrochemical model), (ii) spatially continuous variables (geospatial model), and (iii) a combination of both (mixed model). The mixed model achieved the highest performance (AUC = 0.88), followed by the hydrochemical model (AUC = 0.86). The geospatial model performed slightly lower (AUC = 0.83) but enabled the generation of a continuous 50 m-resolution probability map, identifying 17% of the area as potentially exceeding 10 μg/L. Iron, redox potential and dissolved oxygen were the dominant hydrochemical predictors, while organic carbon, clay content, and surficial geology were the dominant spatial variables, reflecting geochemical and sedimentary controls on As mobilization through reductive dissolution processes. Elevated exceedance probabilities are identified in the northeastern sector, proximal to the Po River Delta, and in peat-rich central areas. This study demonstrates that spatially continuous variables can effectively complement hydrochemical data for continuous NBL mapping, capturing meso-scale heterogeneity that single, groundwater body-scale values conventionally adopted in European NBL frameworks are unable to resolve, thus offering a useful tool for contamination assessment and groundwater management.

title: A capillary microporosity framework for modeling the fate and transport of PFAS in concrete
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): K. Schmeltzer, C.J. Newell, P. deBlanc, S. Jacob, J. McDade, R. Caird, G. Dooley, J. Gamlin, E. Kainer, C. Leong, J. Scalia, C. Shackelford
abstract: Concrete pads impacted by aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) represent long-term sources of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) to stormwater runoff that require environmental impact assessment. However, existing assessment models have not reproduced field observed PFAS concentration profiles. Accordingly, a new mechanistic model for PFAS assessment (CAPCON) based on a capillary microporosity framework for PFAS transport within concrete is proposed. The proposed CAPCON model includes dual-domain diffusion within water-filled capillary pores together with episodic PFAS release to runoff driven by wetting and drying cycles based on site-specific climatic conditions. Comparison of CAPCON modeled versus measured PFAS concentration profiles from concrete cores recovered from two field sites with contrasting climatic and PFAS loading conditions resulted in good agreement (log-RMSEs of 0.03 to 0.36). The calibrated CAPCON model also captured the characteristic first-flush pattern observed in field-measured sheet-flow runoff tests, although first-flush magnitudes were overpredicted for three of the four site/compound combinations. Results indicate that climate influences PFAS transport in concrete. In wetter climates, deeper water penetration into concrete increases the extent of water-filled capillary pores, enabling faster diffusive transport through the capillary region and deeper PFAS penetration. In drier climates, diffusion is slower within unsaturated, lower-permeability regions of the concrete, resulting in greater near-surface accumulation. The proposed CAPCON framework provides a mechanistic basis for evaluating PFAS transport and release from concrete pads under variable climatic conditions and offers improved capability for assessing long-term environmental impacts of AFFF-impacted concrete pads.

title: Ammonium transport in zeolite and zero-valent iron columns: Experiments and tempered fractional modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Xiaoxiao Hao, HongGuang Sun, Xuantong Fan, Shuai Yang, Yuncong Yan
abstract: Ammonia nitrogen contamination in groundwater poses risks of eutrophication and drinking-water quality deterioration. Understanding ammonium transport in reactive porous media is critical for predicting its subsurface fate. This study utilized batch adsorption experiments, column transport tests, and a tempered one-sided density (TOSD) transport model to investigate the transport behavior of ammonium in two reactive media—zeolite and zero-valent iron (ZVI)—which serve as model systems for in-situ groundwater remediation. The results of the batch adsorption experiments for zeolite and ZVI were consistent with the pseudo-second-order and pseudo-first-order kinetic adsorption models respectively. Both adsorption isotherms conformed the Freundlich model, and the results indicated greater ammonium uptake by zeolite than by ZVI. The column breakthrough curves exhibited anomalous transport behavior, and the TOSD model (a fractional-order modeling framework) accurately described the transport experimental data, proving the applicability of the TOSD method in describing the anomalous transport of ammonium ions. The model fitting parameters suggested that adsorption and rate-limited mass exchange may be the plausible factors influencing ammonium retention. This study provides experimental evidence and modeling tools for ammonium ion transport in reactive media, which is significance for mitigating groundwater pollution.

title: Aquitard-breaching conduits control salinity dynamics and variable-density contaminant transport in coastal aquifer-aquitard systems
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zihao Zhang, Leyu You, Jiaxu Zhang, Jina Yin, Jie Yang, Alicia Wilson
abstract: Contaminant transport from semi-confined aquifers to coastal waters is an emerging environmental concern, yet its prediction remains challenging due to the complexity of coastal aquifer systems. In coastal environments, aquitards are breached by conduits formed through natural processes or anthropogenic disturbances, enhancing hydraulic connectivity between otherwise isolated aquifers. Despite their widespread occurrence, the impacts of conduits on salinity distributions and land-derived contaminant migration from semi-confined aquifers to coastal waters remain poorly understood. This study systematically investigates the influences of an aquitard-breaching conduit on salinity dynamics and land-derived contaminant transport in coastal aquifer-aquitard systems. The conduit is represented as a high-permeability pathway through the low-permeability aquitard. Results show that a conduit enhances seawater intrusion into semi-confined aquifers relative to no-conduit conditions, irrespective of conduit locations. Notably, a conduit situated near an underlying saltwater wedge induces saltwater up-coning from that wedge, establishing a hydraulic connection between the overlying and underlying wedges. This up-coning redirects both freshwater-density and saltwater-density contaminant plumes from predominantly horizontal migration to vertically oriented pathways toward the ocean. In the absence of up-coning, plume behavior diverges by density contrast: freshwater-density contaminants preferentially discharge through the conduit, whereas saltwater-density plumes partition between upward discharge via the conduit and seaward transport within the semi-confined aquifer. Compared to no-conduit scenarios, conduits consistently facilitate the export of freshwater-density contaminants, whereas a conduit without saltwater up-coning can prolong the residence time and discharge duration of saltwater-density contaminants and reduce their peak efflux. These findings demonstrate a dual role for aquitard-breaching conduits in modulating seawater intrusion and contaminant fate, providing new insights for managing coastal groundwater systems.

title: Contrasting hydrological states are associated with sediment bacterial community variation and micropollutant biodegradation potential in a river-connected floodplain lake
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): You Li, Xue Yin, Jiao He, Yuanyuan Zhao, Changhui Wang, Leilei Bai
abstract: Hydrological contraction is a defining feature of river-connected floodplain lakes, but its association with sediment bacterial communities and contaminant biodegradation potential remains incompletely understood. During one observed wet-to-dry transition in Dongting Lake, China, we combined sediment physicochemical and enzyme measurements, pre-incubation bacterial community analyses, and standardized microcosm assays of 17α-ethinylestradiol biodegradation potential (EBP30) in sediments. As mean local water coverage decreased from 76.4% in the expanded state to 35.2% in the contracted state, dry-period sediments generally exhibited higher TOC, Fe(III), potential dehydrogenase activity, and field estrogen concentrations. Wet-period sediments showed higher bacterial richness, diversity, and community-level niche breadth and lower compositional dissimilarity and dispersion, whereas dry-period communities exhibited greater relative contributions of dispersal limitation and environmental selection, together with a denser, less modular, and more positively cohesive correlation network. Despite reduced alpha diversity, EBP30 increased from 0.76 ± 0.06 μg g−1 during the wet period to 0.93 ± 0.18 μg g−1 during the dry period, with the largest wet-to-dry increase in East Dongting Lake. Partial least-squares path modeling (PLS-PM) and site-blocked cross-validation indicated that EBP30 was more closely associated with bacterial compositional indicators, dry-period-associated taxa, and sample-level network cohesion than with taxonomic richness alone. A sensitivity PLS-PM using site-level water coverage retained similar explanatory power and identified a supported negative total association between water coverage and EBP30. These findings identify hydrological state as an important correlate of sediment microbial functional potential and emerging-contaminant fate in dynamic floodplain lakes.

title: How do stabilized river meanders affect microbial communities and water quality in urban rivers?
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Dantong Zhu, Jiaxing Zeng, Jiajie Su, Shoushu Liu, Zhuoyin Lu, Saiyu Yuan, Xianglong Wei, Hongwu Tang, Xiangju Cheng
abstract: Urban river meanders are frequently stabilized and hardened for flood control, thereby substantially altering their natural hydrodynamics and ecological functions. However, the influence of such engineered bends on sediment microbial communities, key players in nutrient cycling and thus water quality, remains poorly understood. Here, we integrate 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, co-occurrence network analysis, and community assembly modeling to investigate seven stabilized meanders along Guangzhou's Yangmei River during a single summer sampling campaign. We found that bend-position-related habitat differences were associated with the spatial organization of microbial diversity and putative co-occurrence patterns. Mid-bend sections showed ecological patterns consistent with stronger local hydraulic disturbance, while post-bend sections were more consistent with relatively depositional habitat conditions. Mid-bend sediments, associated with relatively high hydraulic energy, exhibited the lowest α-diversity and distinct co-occurrence patterns, consistent with greater local hydraulic disturbance than at pre- and post-bend sites. Within the sampling campaign, spatial differences in water chemistry were more closely associated with external nitrogen and phosphorus inputs, whereas the spatial heterogeneity of benthic microbiota was more strongly linked to localized hydrodynamic conditions. Co-occurrence patterns also varied among bend positions along the meander transition. Neutral-community modeling suggested that stochastic processes played an important role in bacterial community assembly during the sampling period. Complementary βNTI–RCbray null-model analyses identified dispersal limitation as the predominant inferred process, whereas heterogeneous selection contributed relatively more in post-bend depositional sediments. Our findings highlight local heterogeneity in benthic habitats and water–sediment exchange conditions within stabilized meanders, which may influence local nutrient dynamics. These results suggest that bend-scale hydraulic conditions and microbial habitats warrant consideration in urban river restoration.

title: Coupled sediment and microplastic fluxes revealed by check-dam sediment records
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Kazem Nosrati, Fatemeh Lak, Zahra Etminan, Adrian L. Collins
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, yet their redistribution through erosion and accumulation within sediment-retention structures remains poorly quantified. This study quantified MPs in sediments retained behind check dams and examined their relationships with sediment storage and erosion-related sediment yield at the catchment scale. Twenty check dams in a semi-arid mountainous catchment in northeastern Iran were investigated. Sediment storage ranged from 531 to 9828 Mg (mean: 2683 Mg), while specific sediment yield ranged from 16.2 to 855.4 Mg km−2 yr−1 (mean: 247.1 Mg km−2 yr−1). MPs were detected in all sediment samples, with concentrations ranging from 800 to 5240 particles kg−1 dry sediment (mean: 2702 particles kg−1). Estimated MP inventories ranged from 9.0 × 108 to 2.4 × 1010 particles per check dam. Strong positive relationships were observed between specific sediment yield and estimated MP yield (r = 0.99, p < 0.01) and between accumulated sediment mass and estimated MP inventory (r = 0.80, p < 0.01), indicating a close association between sediment dynamics and MP redistribution. Fibrous MPs dominated the assemblage (86.6%), and the 500–1000 μm size class accounted for the largest proportion of detected particles (44.7%). Raman spectroscopy confirmed several polymer types within the analyzed subset. Overall, the findings show substantial accumulation of sediment-associated MPs behind check dams and indicate that erosion-driven sediment mobilization may represent an important pathway for MP redistribution in erosion-prone catchments. However, the persistence of this retention may depend on the stability of accumulated sediments, which can potentially be remobilized during high-energy hydrological events.

title: Non-reactive solute transport in coupled macro-meso-micro porous system: experiments and HYDRUS-2D modeling with GSA-PEST integration
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Aman Chandel, Deepak Swami, Nitin Joshi, Jiri Simunek
abstract: This study investigates the processes governing tracer transport in a stratified porous medium, which produces asymmetric breakthrough curves (BTCs) with multiple inflection points. Such complex BTCs are often analyzed using multi-porosity or multi-permeability flow and transport models. However, these models introduce increased parameter complexity and associated sensitivity, necessitating thorough evaluation. In this context, we coupled the Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) and Parameter Estimation (PEST) with the DualPerm (DP) HYDRUS module to quantify parameter sensitivity and enhance BTC representation. A micro-aquifer experiment was conducted on a stratified porous medium using a non-reactive tracer for testing the capabilities of the developed framework. The sensitivity analysis aimed to examine how different model parameters contribute to different segments of the asymmetric BTC. This analysis revealed that the fracture and immobile domain parameters dominate early tracer breakthrough (64% of the total sensitivity). In comparison, the matrix parameters and the porosity of the immobile region contributed 48% of the total sensitivity during the rising limb period. The prolonged tailing limb was primarily influenced by the matrix parameters (porosity and permeability, 91% sensitivity), with the porosity of the immobile region adding only 4%. It was also established that BTC-based parameter estimation emphasizes peak concentration, but often overlooks critical features like mass recovery, solute residence time, and spatial variance. An alternate approach, which is based on cumulative solute mass recovery, showed efficiency in capturing complex features of experimental BTCs such as inflection points, peak timing, and long-tailing behavior. The proposed framework enhances the capability of the HYDRUS (DualPerm) module to investigate various flow and transport processes, improving mass recovery estimation compared to conventional BTC-based methods.

title: Effect of entrapped water on NAPL migration in unsaturated fractures
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Song Xue, Qingteng Fan, Zexiong Zhou, Zhibing Yang, Gang Liu, Biao Li
abstract: The migration of non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPL) in unsaturated fractures involves NAPL-water-air three-phase displacement. Understanding the impact of entrapped water on this migration process is crucial for predicting NAPL flow and solute transport in the fractured vadose zone. This study presents visualized flow experiments to systematically investigate NAPL (n-octane) invasion behaviors in initially dry and water-entrapped unsaturated single fractures by varying fracture inclination angle and injection flow rate. The experimental results reveal that entrapped water fundamentally shifts NAPL flow patterns from fingering flow in dry fractures to film flow propagating along entrapped water droplets in water-entrapped fractures. Compared to fingering flow in dry fractures, film flow in water-entrapped fractures exhibits enhanced lateral expansion, longer fracture penetration time, higher breakthrough saturation, larger perimeter-area ratio, and stronger ability to invade large-aperture channels. The morphology of the film flow is jointly regulated by injection flow rate and fracture inclination angle. Lower flow rates and larger inclination angles result in thinner films, while sufficiently high flow rates at small inclination angles can trigger a transition from film flow to fingering flow in the main flow channels. We also find that the distribution of NAPL-occupied apertures consistently follows a normal distribution, independent of flow rate and fracture inclination angle, and aligns with the statistical properties of the fracture aperture field. These findings elucidate the regulatory role of entrapped water on NAPL migration and advance the mechanistic understanding of NAPL invasion in unsaturated single fractures, thereby informing groundwater contamination risk assessment and remediation design.

title: Environmental fate of ciprofloxacin in agricultural soils under realistic irrigation water matrices: kinetic, column transport, thermodynamic, mechanistic and machine learning insights
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Saurabh Kumar, Lucas Joseph Makuni, Renu Meena, Nitin Khandelwal
abstract: The combined influence of soil properties, irrigation water chemistry, and transport processes on antibiotic fate remains poorly understood. Here, ciprofloxacin (CIP) retention, transport, and remobilization were investigated in three agricultural soil types under four different irrigation water matrices using batch, column, thermodynamic, mechanistic, and machine-learning approaches. At elevated concentrations (10 mg/L), all soils exhibited comparable retention capacities, whereas substantial differences emerged at extremely elevated concentrations (150 mg/L), with maximum adsorption capacities following the order black soil (≈17.6 mg/g) > alluvial soil (≈15.6 mg/g) > red soil (≈10.4 mg/g). Transport behaviour differed markedly among soils, with retardation factors following the order black soil (7.9) > alluvial soil (2.24) > red soil (1.4). After 180 pore volumes, relative breakthrough remained below 0.03 in black soil but reached 0.25 and 0.45 in alluvial and red soils, respectively. Rainfall flushing further revealed contrasting environmental outcomes, with black soil strongly immobilizing CIP, red soil promoting rapid transport, and alluvial soil acting as a persistent contaminant leaching reservoir. Thermodynamic analyses indicated predominantly endothermic adsorption with enhanced spontaneity at elevated temperatures. FTIR and zeta potential analyses identified surface complexation, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and cation bridging as the primary retention mechanisms. Random Forest modelling identified soil type as the dominant control on CIP retention, accounting for ~92% of total feature importance (R2 = 0.96–0.97). These findings demonstrate that soil properties govern CIP fate and determine contrasting pathways of sequestration, persistence, and groundwater contamination risk.

title: Substrate-explicit coupled modeling of organic matter degradation and sulfide production using a generalized kinetic approach
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): P. Trinchero, A. Nordström, M. Calpe, G. Román-Ross, A. Costa-Solé, O. Silva, G. Deissmann
abstract: In natural subsurface systems, Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) is a potent reducing agent, as it sustains and catalyzes a number of microbially-mediated reactions. One of such reactions, namely the reduction of sulfate to sulfide mediated by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) is particularly relevant for the evaluation of the long-term stability of deep geological repositories (DGRs) for spent nuclear fuel. Some of these proposed DGRs will be hosted at great depth in fractured crystalline rocks where sulfide, potentially produced by SRB, is practically the only oxidant of relevance for the copper canisters used to safely store and keep isolated the radionuclides from the natural environment. One important limitation to this reaction is substrate availability, as the DOM that typically infiltrates, e.g. from overlying surficial sediments, is typically bound in complex polymeric organic compounds (cellulose, starch, proteins, fats, etc.) that cannot be directly used by SRB. A further intermediate step is therefore needed which consists in the degradation of ’complex’ organic matter into ‘simpler’ organic substrates. This intermediate step is performed by a different microbial group (typically acetogens and/or fermenters) that acts on a substrate characterized by significant heterogeneity. Previous studies have documented that the organic carbon substrate typically comprises thousands of species depending on the type of subsurface environment. In this study we argue that the evaluation of microbially mediated sulfate reduction by means of reactive transport modeling should explicitly account for the substrate heterogeneity. However, explicitly accounting for thousands of chemical species of complex organic matter presents two significant challenges. The first is how to parameterize each individual reaction. The second is how to include this large number of species in the mass balance calculations. The first challenge was addressed through the development of a Generalized Kinetic Model (GKM) that formulates all rates as a function of a universally accepted rate of electron transfer along with the underlying stoichiometry of each individual metabolic reaction. The computational challenge was overcome by using weight-based reaction rates. In practice, we solve transport and mass balance for the equivalent total concentration of complex organic carbon while retaining information on the underlying substrate and associated microbial population through the use of two weighting functions, which are updated on lagged time based on mass balance. The numerical framework is first verified and then applied to simulate sulfide production in a single fracture–matrix system. Important modeling outcomes, such as the dependence of SRB activity on the degradation of a complex organic substrate and the role of the matrix as a temporary storage term for substrates, are derived.

title: Seasonal changes in petroleum NSZD biodegradation rates associated with water table fluctuations within the zone of soil contamination
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Michael J. Donn, John L. Rayner, Kaveh Sookhak Lari, Andrew King, Greg B. Davis
abstract: Natural Source Zone Depletion (NSZD) is widely used to manage petroleum-contaminated sites, but estimating NSZD rates is challenging because most methods rely on short period, averaged or point-in-time measurements. These can be misleading due to seasonal variability in biological activity, moisture and water table fluctuations influencing NSZD rates. Here we utilise continuous inground sensor measurements and light non-aqueous phase liquid (LNAPL) distributions from cores to understand seasonal processes affecting NSZD rates. Linked to multiphase modelling these data are used to test the hypothesis that seasonal NSZD variations result from LNAPL distributions and water table fluctuations. Using ~3.5 years of continuous oxygen and temperature data across four fuel types, NSZD rates were shown to vary by up to an order of magnitude seasonally. Rates ranged from 0.1 to 0.8 kg/m2/y for diesel to ~5 to 13 kg/m2/y for aviation gasoline, with broadly comparable trends between oxygen- and temperature-based methods. Rising water tables generally reduced NSZD rates at the diesel, gasoline, and crude oil sites by inundating the LNAPL depth distribution and disconnecting it from oxygen in the vadose zone. In contrast, at the aviation gasoline site, where LNAPL persisted above the maximum water table, NSZD rates remained high or increased. Modelling reproduced observed trends at the diesel site and showed that NSZD rates are influenced by the exposure of LNAPL to the vadose zone air phase (i.e., oxygen), with inundation suppressing rates, while exposure enhanced it. This is further supported by soil core TPH measurements that show loss of shorter chain TPH ranges at shallower depths above and within the zone of water table fluctuation relative to deeper in the formation. Continuous monitoring and modelling have provided insights into the dynamic NSZD rate estimates, indicating that care is needed to align field measurements with conceptualisation of LNAPL distributions and water table dynamics.

title: Reactive solute transport driven by coupled stress fields affected by injection pressure and permeability during in-situ chemical oxidation remediation of contaminated groundwater
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Guiyao Xiong, Zhiyu Jiao, Xiaobin Zhu, Qi Zhang, Yun Zhang, Yun Yang, Shujun Ye, Jinguo Wang, Jichun Wu, Brent Sleep
abstract: Groundwater contamination at the site is worsening, and in-situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) has been widely adopted for contaminated groundwater remediation due to its low environmental risk and low cost. Through laboratory experiments and field simulations, we optimized the system for TCE degradation using activated sodium persulfate and explored how injection pressure and formation permeability affect TCE remediation. The results show that both sodium citrate (TCD) and citrate (CA) chelating agents can increase TCE oxidation by persulfate, with optimal molar ratios of Na2S2O8:TCD:Fe2+:TCE of 20:10:10:1, and Na2S2O8:CA:Fe2+:TCE of 20:5:10:1, achieving high TCE removal rates of 97% and 98%, respectively. Pressurized injection increases the hydraulic gradient and flow velocity, thereby enhancing advection and mechanical dispersion, especially in high-permeability media. In low-permeability media, pressurization also modifies porosity and tortuosity and increases the effective diffusion coefficient, which is relatively more important for solute transport. Pressure-induced permeability changes were limited under the tested 0.1–1 MPa range and were secondary to advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. In layered subsurface systems, placing horizontal wells at the interface between high- and low-permeability layers was more effective in delivering oxidants to contaminated regions than vertical wells. In summary, higher-pressure oxidant injection improved remediation in the simulated low-permeability formations by increasing advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. The relative contributions were site-specific, and diffusion enhancement was not the sole controlling mechanism. The numerical model can effectively simulate ISCO of TCE by accounting for the multi-field-coupled stress field. It can provide valuable insights for designing groundwater remediation projects.

title: Diffusion of inert and reactive tracers: Overview of the DIR field experiment in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay rock (France)
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): V. Blin, M. Descostes, J. Radwan, E. Tevissen, T. Grangeon, T. Fierz, C. Frechou, P. Brisset, M. Filippi, C. Landesman, S. Ribet, P. Meier, M. Saint-Jalmes, R.V.H. Dagnelie, S. Dewonck, J.-C. Robinet
abstract: The geological disposal of radioactive waste is under investigation in several countries, especially in Europe. In this field, clay-rich sedimentary rocks are promising natural barriers to limit and delay the release of radionuclides toward the biosphere, due to their diffusion-driven transport and retention properties. In addition to laboratory studies, field studies in Underground Research Laboratories (URL) represent a significant value to strengthen safety demonstrations. In this context, the DIR experiment (Diffusion of Inert and Reactive tracers) was developed and implanted in the Meuse/Haute-Marne URL located in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay-rich formation. Over 6 years, several diffusion experiments were performed with radioactive tracers: HTO (tritiated water), 36Cl−, 125I−, 22Na+, 134Cs+, assessing the behaviour of neutral, anionic and cationic species. The evolution of each radiotracer activity was monitored in the injection borehole, from at least 100 days up to 3 years. Overcoring of the rock at the end of the experiments allowed the accurate characterization of radiotracer profiles. An overview of the DIR experiment is provided here, illustrating the large amount of data gathered in 4 specific boreholes at two different depths: −445 and − 495 m, within the Callovo-Oxfordian geological layer. The modelling of experimental results allowed the quantification of diffusion properties parallel to the bedding of the rock for the studied radionuclides. Diffusion parameters for HTO are in agreement with those determined on samples using the conventional through diffusion method. Anions are partially excluded from porosity with quantified values 0.3 < ε a(anion)/ε(H2O) < 0.6. On contrary, the diffusion of cations is limited by their adsorption on clay surfaces with the evidence of surface diffusion processes. The sensitivity analysis on adjusted parameters provided additional insights on the local properties, such as homogeneity of the diffusion plume and the limited extension of the damaged zone surrounding boreholes: L EDZ ~ 1–3 cm. Still, further field experiments are necessary to measure diffusion in such EDZ and to improve accuracy on the diffusion anisotropy ratio.

title: Oxidative sulfide weathering and weak mineral attenuation controlling arsenic mobility in a crystalline aquifer
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Swati Ganveer, Kamal Lochan Pruseth, David Anand Aind
abstract: This study investigates the source–sink dynamics and hydrogeochemical controls governing arsenic fate and transport within a fractured crystalline aquifer system. The hydrogeologic framework is characterized by spatial heterogeneity in redox conditions and persistent undersaturation with respect to key Fe-, sulfate-, and Ca-bearing mineral phases.
