abstract: Indoor exposure to 222Rn depends not only on the mean concentration but also on temporal concentration variation in relation to room occupancy. Therefore, hourly radon data, when combined with space-use information, can provide a basis for occupancy-weighted exposure assessment. This study analysed hourly 222Rn concentration time series in two residential rooms in Da Lat: an upper-floor room without direct ground contact and with a direct opening to outdoors, and a lower-level, basement-like room with ground contact and indirect air exchange through an adjacent space. During the sequential monitoring segments, the enhanced natural air-exchange state had a lower mean 222Rn concentration than the closed state in both the basement-like room (154.6 versus 433.1 Bq m−3; 64.3% lower) and the upper-floor room (50.8 versus 89.3 Bq m−3; 43.1% lower). An exploratory one-zone mass-balance analysis yielded higher fitted effective removal parameters, aeff, under enhanced exchange (0.499 versus 0.315 h−1 and 0.338 versus 0.213 h−1, respectively), consistent with faster apparent radon removal. In the basement-like room, the effective source-related term, Eeff, was also lower under enhanced exchange (2348 versus 4945 Bq h−1); however, this parameter represents a model-inferred source–removal balance rather than an independently measured source strength. These findings support systematic, long-term investigations, prioritising lower-level, ground-contact and poorly ventilated rooms.

title: Low-methoxyl pectin–Ca 2＋ gelation as a sample solidification protocol for marine radioactivity monitoring by HPGe gamma spectrometry
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yejin Lee, Hyunsung Kim, Myeongsik Shin, Gyoung Jun Choi, Jun Yoo, Ku Kang
abstract: Marine radioactivity monitoring requires rapid, reliable sample preparation methods that remain functional aboard ships and other mobile platforms. Liquid seawater samples, however, are prone to geometric instability and spillage during vessel motion, which degrade HPGe gamma spectrometry measurement quality. We developed a solidification procedure based on low-methoxyl (LM) pectin and controlled Ca 2 + supplementation, which converts seawater into a mechanically stable, leak-resistant gel through egg-box cross-linking. Under the optimised condition (1.4 g LM-pectin per 28.26 g seawater, 300 rpm, 120 min), the gel formed a mechanically stable cylindrical counting geometry (diameter 60 mm, fill height 10 mm) under the selected preparation condition. Paired activity retention, calculated from measurements of the same sample before and after solidification of Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety (KINS) proficiency-test samples, was 100.2 ± 6.1 % for 137 Cs ( n = 8 ), 95.5 ± 6.6 % for 134 Cs ( n = 7 ), 97.0 ± 4.9 % for 241 Am ( n = 8 ), and 97.2 ± 2.4 % for 60 Co ( n = 3 ) across a gamma-energy span of 59.5–1332.5 keV. All 26 paired determinations remained within the 80–120% screening range, and 24 of 26 were consistent with complete retention within their expanded uncertainty ( k = 2 ). The procedure uses food-grade reagents, requires no pre-evaporation or specialised equipment, and completes gelation within two hours. With minimum detectable activities of a few Bq kg − 1 for a 28.26 g sample counted for 30,000 s, the protocol is intended for rapid shipboard screening of elevated-activity samples in emergency situations rather than for routine low-level monitoring. These results support further shipboard validation of gel-based sample preparation for environmental radioactivity surveys.

title: T-Rex: the transportable radon-222 explorer for environmental or public health studies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Raghav Hariharan, Cynthia Leung, Alan D. Griffiths, Ot Sisoutham, Scott D. Chambers
abstract: We describe the development and testing of a “suitcase sized” 100 L two-filter dual flow-loop radon monitor, weighing ∼18 kg, flow rate ∼5 L min−1, Rn-222 sensitivity ∼0.02 s−1∙(Bq∙m−3)−1, temporal resolution 30-min, and operational range ∼0.3 – 30,000 Bq∙m−3. Its portability and sensitivity make it an ideal “crossover instrument” between the needs of the Public Health and Environmental research communities. Pending traceable calibration in a controlled climate chamber, here its performance was compared with a 200 L two-filter monitor (1.65 m tall, ∼80 kg), sampling outdoor air over 3 weeks during which radon varied between 0.14 Bq∙m−3 and 9.1 Bq∙m−3. The distribution (10th/50th/90th percentile) of absolute hourly bias was 0.03/0.19/0.54 Bq∙m−3. A separate comparison was made with an AlphaGUARD PQ2000 Pro and DF2000 over 8 days during which radon ranged from 0.6 Bq·m−3 to 9.9 Bq·m−3. The reported 8-day average radon was 3.5 ± 1.97 Bq·m−3 (100 L monitor), 4.01 ± 2.92 Bq·m−3 (PQ2000 Pro) and 4.24 ± 2.65 Bq·m−3 (DF 2000). Daily mean absolute bias reached 1.7 Bq·m−3, and absolute bias of 6-hourly means reached 3.2 Bq·m−3. For the PQ2000 and DF 2000, hourly counting uncertainty reached 30 % at 6 Bq·m−3 and 4.5 Bq·m−3, respectively (c.f. manufacturers reported detection limit of 2 Bq·m−3). The 100 L monitor reached 30 % counting uncertainty at 0.3 Bq·m−3. While this does not meet the measurement criteria for Global Atmosphere Watch “baseline” monitoring (detection limit ≤0.05 Bq∙m−3), the monitor would be well suited for many environmental monitoring purposes and portable enough for indoor use.

title: Calibration of the NDUSRM series and further measurements of 236 U/ 238 U isotopic ratios in the Ewing collection
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Thomas L. Bailey, David Lund, Griffin Mulcahy, Alistaer Zhou, Noah Cabanas, John P. McDonaugh, Ruchi Rathod, William Von Seeger, Philippe Collon
abstract: 236U is one of the rarest isotopes of uranium, occurring in ores with an abundance below 1 × 10−9. Due to a wide variety of geological factors, the 236U content in a given uranium ore body is considered to be a unique “fingerprint” like signature, with applications in nuclear forensics and geophysics. Its low abundance though is only detectable via Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS), capable of measuring 236U/238U ratios below 1 × 10−11. Improvements to the AMS setup at the University of Notre Dame’s Nuclear Science Laboratory, have greatly improved its detection limit, enabling measurements across the entire 236U/238U ratio range found in natural ores. A description of the improvements is presented. A survey of the 236U/238U ratio of various ores from North American and African mines was conducted with the improved setup, using in house reference standards to quantify the measurements. A new detection limit of 1 × 1 0 − 12 was established.

title: Regional exposure to ageing nuclear infrastructure in Europe: Examining plume trajectories and dispersion for the 45-year old Almaraz Nuclear Power Plant under present and future climates
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Angelo Alves, Diogo Costa, Vanda Salgueiro
abstract: Severe accidents at nuclear power plants may release radionuclides whose atmospheric dispersion transcends national borders. Many of Europe’s reactors were commissioned between the late 1970s and the mid-1980s and now operate well beyond their original design life, often under licences extended into the 2030s–2040s. Taking the Almaraz Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) in western Spain – one of at least 17 ageing European reactor sites aged 40–57 years – as a representative case, this study assesses the European-scale atmospheric exposure to a hypothetical severe release of Fukushima-analogue magnitude under current and projected climate conditions. The Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model was used to compute 48 h forward trajectories and three-dimensional 137Cs dispersion plumes, driven by ERA5 reanalysis (2014–2024) and by 19 CMIP6 SSP5-8.5 simulations bias-corrected with the MBCn multivariate procedure for 2041–2070, using the 137Cs emission inventory of Source Term 5 (JAEA-Katata-6h). Under historical forcing, the dispersion is organised into three recurrent transport modes – westward or near-source (towards Portugal and the eastern Atlantic), eastward (towards the Iberian interior and the western Mediterranean) and northward to north-eastward (towards France) – with opposite seasonal cycles: the westward mode dominates autumn and winter, whereas the continental modes peak in summer. The westward and near-source clusters are also the slowest and shallowest, favouring boundary-layer transport and near-source deposition, so the highest concentrations occur in compact, slow-moving plumes, whereas the fast long-range clusters produce the broadest and most dilute ones. Under SSP5-8.5 the three modes persist, but the winter transport loses its long-range Atlantic reach and concentrates over Portugal and the western Iberian Peninsula, while the summer transport re-orients towards the western Mediterranean as the eastward mode strengthens and the northward mode weakens. Future peak concentrations increase in winter and autumn, decrease in spring and diverge in summer, with higher peaks systematically paired with more compact, near-source plumes. These seasonally and quantile-dependent shifts indicate that historically-informed emergency-preparedness planning may misjudge future transboundary exposure at Almaraz, warranting periodic re-assessment under updated climate projections. The seasonal patterns themselves are site-specific, but the assessment framework is directly transferable to the other long-operating European reactors that will remain in service for decades.

title: Radioecological dynamics in high-altitude ecosystems: Sources, processes, risk, and early-warning systems in mount Aragats
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Nona Movsisyan
abstract: This review presents an integrated conceptual framework describing radionuclide behavior in mountainous environments by synthesizing previously fragmented studies from Mount Aragats into a unified radioecological monitoring framework. Using Mount Aragats as a representative high-altitude ecosystem, the review integrates radionuclide sources, environmental processes, monitoring strategies, spatial modeling, and radiological assessment within a common perspective. Mountain regions function as dynamic orographic traps, where altitude-dependent atmospheric processes, complex topography, and heterogeneous geology govern radionuclide deposition, redistribution, and long-term retention across multiple environmental compartments, including atmospheric particulate matter, snow, soils, mosses, and river sediments. Methodological approaches adapted for complex terrain-including altitude-based sampling, baseline and background definition, geochemical indicators, regression modeling, Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, and ecological risk assessment – are synthesized into a unified framework. These approaches improve the interpretation of spatial variability, identify the principal environmental drivers, distinguish natural background from anthropogenic inputs, and support more robust environmental assessment. The synthesis of long-term investigations from Mount Aragats demonstrates that reliable baseline establishment, combined with a process-based understanding of radionuclide behavior, is fundamental for environmental monitoring in mountainous regions. This review provides a transferable methodological approach for mountain radioecology supports environmental surveillance, baseline reassessment, anomaly detection, nuclear emergency preparedness, and early-warning systems in mountainous regions influenced by both natural and anthropogenic radiation sources.

title: Transport of 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant accident-derived 137 Cs to the tropical North Pacific
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Mutsuo Inoue, Daichi Koshiishi, Yuichiro Kumamoto
abstract: The impact and transport patterns of the 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant (FDNPP) accident-derived radiocesium in the tropical North Pacific remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the latitudinal and vertical distributions of the concentrations (activities) of 137Cs, 226Ra, and 228Ra in this tropical area (8°–10°N) in April–May 2025. We observed low 228Ra concentrations in surface and mixed layers (< 0.5 mBq/L), indicating that the influence of seawater from the coastal area was not dominant, even near the eastern coast of the Philippines. 137Cs concentrations at the surface in the tropical area exhibited moderate variations (1.0–1.2 mBq/L) with the highest concentrations observed at a depth of 200 m (1.7–2.3 mBq/L). Additionally, the surface and 200 m depth fractions of FDNPP accident-derived 137Cs were 0.25–0.4 and 0.35–0.6, respectively. By 2025, FDNPP accident-derived 137Cs was partially transported across the tropical North Pacific by westward currents (e.g., the North Equatorial Current). These findings can be used to elucidate current radionuclide dynamics in tropical areas.

title: Validation of the ray-tracing Monte-Carlo code tRAYcy for geometry and coincidence-summing corrections in environmental gamma-ray spectrometry
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Felix Diel, Marc Breidenbach, Spencer Behling, Herwig Marschelke, Marcus Neuer
abstract: Accurate determination of radionuclide activities in environmental samples requires the detector response to be known for the specific detector–sample geometry, and requires correction for the matrix and density differences between calibration and sample as well as for true coincidence summing (TCS). We demonstrate the scientific validity and practical applicability of the ray-tracing Monte-Carlo code tRAYcy for these tasks by analysing two international proficiency-test materials with assigned reference activities: a soil matrix ( ρ = 1.70 g cm −3 ) and a ground green-tea matrix ( ρ = 0.62 g cm −3 ), both measured in 1l Marinelli geometry on a 40% relative-efficiency N-type HPGe detector calibrated with an aqueous mixed- γ source. Activities were evaluated under successive correction strategies — no correction, geometry (efficiency-transfer) correction, TCS correction, and the two combined — and, additionally, using a sourceless mathematical calibration in which the full-energy-peak efficiency was simulated directly for the sample geometry rather than transferred from the measured source. Uncorrected analyses showed systematic deviations of both signs, with absolute deviations reaching approximately 11%. Fully corrected results agree with the assigned reference values within 4% for 40K, 60Co, 133Ba, 134Cs, and 137Cs. Larger deviations were observed for 241Am in the soil sample (6.6%) and 210Pb in the green-tea sample (-7.7%). The mathematically calibrated activities reproduce the assigned reference values, showing that a physically modelled efficiency can replace a matched calibration source. Finally, complete synthetic spectra generated for both samples in single simulations reproduce the principal measured spectral structures across the investigated energy range, including nuclide-specific contributions, summing features, escape structures, and the Compton continua. Localised discrepancies remain in the low-energy X-ray region and below prominent high-energy peaks. The results show that physically motivated Monte-Carlo modelling delivers accuracy consistent with the assigned reference values for real environmental matrices.

title: A Life-course screening-factor framework for radionuclides in drinking water: identifying when adult-based screening is conservative, representative, or non-conservative
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Alaaddin Alnajjar, Majd Hawwari
abstract: Adult-based drinking-water screening is practical for routine radiological assessment, but it reduces life-course exposure to a single adult reference condition. This simplification cannot determine whether the adult factor represents chronic lifetime-average exposure or whether the limiting annual dose occurs during infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, or late life. A life-course screening-factor framework was developed for 17 radionuclides, with published reference results for Ra-226 and Ra-228 incorporated for comparative context. Chronic ingestion at 1 Bq L−1 was modeled over 70 years using age-specific intake rates and age-dependent ingestion dose coefficients; screening performance was evaluated using Rpeak = Fpeak/Fadult and Rlife = Flife/Fadult. Adult-based screening was neither uniformly conservative nor uniformly non-conservative. Lifetime-average underestimation (Rlife > 1) occurred for Ra-224, Pb-210, Po-210, I-131, Sr-90, and Th-228 among the newly analyzed radionuclides; the published Ra-228 reference case showed the most pronounced bias overall (Rlife ≈ 2.04). Uranium isotopes, Am-241, Cs-134, Cs-137, Pu-239, Th-230, and Th-232 were conservative for lifetime-average exposure, while C-14 and tritiated water were approximately adult-representative. Peak-dose blind spots were identified for Ra-224 (severe infant peak; Rpeak ≈ 15.8), Th-228, Po-210, I-131 (young-child thyroid peak), and Sr-90 (two-peak skeletal-growth pattern). Uranium isotopes and Am-241 showed mixed behavior: conservative for lifetime average but with missed infant dose maxima. Pb-210 and Ra-228, despite identical adult-based screening factors, produced substantially different cumulative lifetime doses (44.4 mSv versus 71.4 mSv at 1 Bq L−1), demonstrating that adult-based equivalence does not guarantee equivalent chronic exposure. These findings demonstrate that adult-based drinking-water screening performance is radionuclide-specific and metric-specific. True lifetime-average underestimation occurs when Flife exceeds Fadult, whereas Fpeak identifies age-specific exposure windows hidden by adult-only screening. The proposed Flife and Fpeak factors provide a practical life-course extension to adult-based screening for drinking-water radiological protection.

title: Indoor radon exposure and ventilation-driven mitigation in a high-rise residential unit using source-term-informed monitored-zone assessment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Min-Jun Kim, Chang-Hyeon Kim, Won-Jun Jang, Jae-Oh Shim
abstract: Increasing airtightness in high-rise residential buildings can enhance indoor radon accumulation when persistent indoor source terms are combined with limited air exchange. This study evaluated indoor radon accumulation and ventilation-driven reduction in four monitored zones of one newly constructed high-rise residential unit using multi-point detector measurements during actual energy-recovery ventilator (ERV) operation at nominal settings of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 h−1, complemented by chamber-derived surface-associated radon source information and zone-specific air volumes. Paired pre-ERV concentrations ranged from 496 to 1010 Bq m−3. The combined mean detector-level reductions were 79.2%, 81.5%, and 84.0% at the three nominal settings, respectively. Relative to the 0.3 h−1 tests, the 0.5 h−1 tests had higher mean reductions and fewer residual detector locations above 148 Bq m−3, whereas the 0.7 h−1 tests had the highest combined mean reduction and shortest average response time. Multi-point measurements showed an 18.6% corner-to-center difference under closed-door conditions, indicating spatial non-uniformity within the monitored unit. The first-order mass-balance calculation was retained only as a descriptive setting-level consistency check (combined-mean RMSE 4.37 percentage points; MAE 3.11 percentage points). Effective in situ ACH was not independently verified, and each room-level condition was tested once; therefore, between-setting differences are interpreted within the tested campaign rather than as isolated causal effects of ventilation rate.

title: A rapid atmospheric radionuclide dispersion prediction and dose assessment method based on the physics-aware spatio-temporal neural operator
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Zihui Yang, Boang Ge, Xiao Wang, Jue Wang, Ziwen Mo, Yuchen Li, Yihang Sun, Bin Zhang
abstract: Rapid prediction of atmospheric radionuclide dispersion is essential for emergency decision-making and radiation protection in nuclear accidents. Although computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods provide high accuracy, their limited efficiency makes it difficult to meet timeliness requirements. To address this limitation, this study proposed a method for rapid atmospheric radionuclide dispersion prediction and radiation dose assessment based on a physics-aware spatio-temporal neural operator (PA-STNO). Within the proposed model-based method, condition encoding represents variations in meteorological and release conditions, spatio-temporal attention enhances plume-evolution and spatial-structure features, the Fourier Neural Operator backbone models long-range transport dependencies, and a physics-aware composite loss improves the representation of high-concentration regions, plume boundaries, and overall concentration-mass consistency. Multi-condition tritium dispersion data generated with OpenFOAM were used for model training and evaluation. On the primary test set, PA-STNO achieved a Relative L2 of 0.21, an FAC2 of 0.92, and a Plume IoU of 0.82, while substantially improving prediction speed. The model also outperformed the baseline models, and a supplementary comparison with a conventional Lagrangian dispersion model showed reasonable agreement, with a mean absolute relative deviation of 8.36%. The predicted fields were further used for radiation dose assessment, linking rapid concentration prediction with dose calculation and supporting the preliminary assessment of dispersion consequences and radiological impacts.

title: Equilibrium in segments of natural decay series in NORM samples from the Czech Republic: 238 U – 234 U – 230 Th and 232 Th – 228 Ra – 228 Th
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Tereza Doksanská, Alena Kelnarová, Mahulena Kořistková
abstract: Industrial processing of mineral resources can lead to the redistribution and concentration of naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM). In the Czech Republic, hazards associated with the release of NORM from industrial facilities, its handling, and long-term exposure are assessed by comparing activity concentrations of 10 long-living radionuclides with the associated clearance levels. Six radionuclides are determined by gamma-ray spectrometry: 238U, 226Ra, 210Pb, 228Ra, 228Th, and 40K. Activity concentrations of four radionuclides – 234U, 230Th, 210Po, and 232Th – are derived using a set of estimative equations. These equations frequently lead to overestimation of 230Th and 232Th, and underestimation of 234U. The aim of this work was to study the equilibrium in the first segments of the uranium (238U −234U – 230Th) and thorium (232Th – 228Ra – 228Th) decay series, and to propose an updated set of estimative equations for 234U, 230Th, and 232Th for materials that satisfy the equilibrium condition in the given segments. Importantly, materials originating from different industrial processes were assessed individually, and all materials included in this study were released from workplaces in the Czech Republic. In total, 48 samples from 7 workplace types were split into 8 material categories. For each sample, gamma-ray spectrometry was used to determine 228Ra, and 228Th, and alpha spectrometry to determine 238U, 234U, 230Th, and 232Th. Activity ratios for each radionuclide pair within the given decay segment were assessed using orthogonal distance regression and/or by evaluating the activity ratios. Material categories exhibiting radioactive equilibrium in both decay segments were ashes and slag from coal combustion plants, samples utilized in cement manufacturing, old building materials, drilling muds, and waste from zircon and zirconia processing. In contrast, sludges, sinters and filter materials from water treatment facilities, along with waste from oil and gas transportation and processing, were identified as materials with disturbed equilibrium in the 238U −234U – 230Th and 232Th – 228Ra – 228Th decay segments.

title: Contact dose rate as an operational screening parameter for NORM oily sludge segregation on offshore oil and gas platforms
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Marcelo Macedo Valinhas, Marco Aurélio dos Santos, Francisco Cesar Augusto da Silva
abstract: On offshore oil and gas platforms, limited space, time and logistics create significant challenges for the characterization and segregation of NORM waste. This raises a practical question: can routine contact dose rate measurements, already incorporated into offshore radiological protection practices, provide sufficient information to support safe waste segregation decisions before oily-sludge drums leave the platform? This study evaluates the use of contact dose rate (CDR) measurements as an operational parameter for NORM oily-sludge drum segregation and risk-informed waste-management decisions. A historical dataset comprising 22,782 drum records from Brazilian offshore production was analyzed, including 8304 drums with offshore CDR measurements subsequently reassessed onshore and characterized by in situ gamma spectrometry. Offshore and onshore dose rates showed a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.827; R 2 = 0.684; p < 0.001). A multiple regression model without an intercept, based on 226Ra and 228Ra activity concentrations, showed a strong fit (R 2 = 0.8353). For drums with CDR ≤ 0.5 μSv·h−1, the statistical assessment quantified the probability of exceeding radionuclide-specific activity concentration criteria, providing a basis for evaluating uncertainties associated with dose-rate-based segregation and exemption decisions. The findings support the use of CDR as an operational waste-management parameter that may also support exemption from regulatory control under the applicable regulatory conditions, reducing reliance on systematic gamma spectrometric characterization. The study provides quantitative evidence that may contribute to discussions on the refinement of risk-informed regulatory approaches for NORM waste management in the oil and gas industry.

title: Review on algae-derived biopolymers to remove radionuclides from aquatic systems: sorption mechanisms, kinetics and stability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Govindharajan Sattanathan, Selvarajan Ramganesh, Jeyaseelan Aravind, Srinivasan Venkatesh
abstract: The carboxyl, sulfate, phosphate and hydroxyl groups on algal biomass and its polysaccharides bind uranium, caesium, strontium and radium. The reported uranium capacities for brown macroalgae vary greatly depending on pH and pretreatment, ranging from roughly 150 to 560 mg/g. Green macroalgae and immobilized microalgae report much smaller uranium capacities, typically in the range of 75-290 mg/g. Certain microalgae remove 88-95% of dissolved 137Cs within 48 h. However, these values mostly stem from acidic, single-solute batch experiments. When the same material is used to test actual effluents, removal rates drop, often dramatically. This review evaluates algae as a feedstock for functional polymers, combines capture mechanisms with the aqueous chemistry that governs them, and re-evaluates how isotherm, kinetic, and thermodynamic models are interpreted. The review then compares the quantitative and qualitative data regarding engineered hydrogels and composites, including their stability, regeneration, and response to competition from other ions. Finally, the loaded sorbent is viewed as secondary radioactive waste, and column operation, life-cycle burden, and traditional alternative options are placed within this context. Maximum capacity is less important than selectivity in real water and safe end-of-life management as critical evaluation criteria.

title: Natural and technologically enhanced radioactivity (NORM/TENORM) in soils, mining residues and waters of mining areas worldwide: a systematic review and multivariate synthesis of the 1976–2026 literature
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Edmundo Escareño-Juarez
abstract: Mining and mineral processing redistribute naturally occurring radionuclides and can generate technologically enhanced naturally occurring radioactive material (TENORM). A PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of the 1976–2026 literature was combined with a quantitative, multivariate synthesis of activity concentrations reported in abstracts. Of 60,242 records from seven bibliographic sources, including the IAEA INIS database, and citation searching, 16,689 were eligible and 1308 studies from 103 countries provided 4532 values (4276 study-level records). In mining-impacted soils, geometric means of 226Ra(238U), 232Th and 40K were 56.7, 38.1 and 306 Bq kg−1; medians exceeded the UNSCEAR world medians by 11% and 26% for 226Ra(238U) and 232Th, whereas 40K was 18% lower. Uranium mining showed the highest soil 226Ra(238U) (geometric mean 324 Bq kg−1) and tin/rare-earth/mineral-sand operations the highest 232Th (78.9 Bq kg−1). The 232Th/226Ra(238U) ratio was lowest in phosphate and uranium operations (medians 0.30 and 0.56) and 0.7–1.4 in the other industries. After adjustment for industry, region and publication year, tailings and residues contained 6.6 times more 226Ra(238U) than soils, and 31% of tailings records exceeded 1 Bq g−1. Uranium exceeded the WHO drinking-water guideline (30 μg L−1; a yardstick for mine waters) in 45% of groundwater and 83% of mine-water records, and 53% of mine-water records exceeded 1 Bq L−1 of 226Ra. The median outdoor effective dose from soils was 0.072 mSv y−1. In this abstract-level dataset, the largest enhancements and guideline exceedances occurred in residues and mine waters and differed among industries; harmonised reporting would enable full-text meta-analysis.

title: Measurement intensity and regulatory effectiveness in radon governance: A comparative analysis of the United States and Europe
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Robert Bobkier, Peter Bossew, Petros Koutrakis, Ewa Katarzyna Czech, Konstantin Kovler
abstract: Measurement intensity, understood as the capacity of a regulatory system to generate exposure-relevant data at scale, is a revealing indicator of how legal frameworks translate scientific knowledge into protective action. Radon is a leading environmental carcinogen, yet the U.S. and Euratom Community legal systems have responded to the same body of scientific evidence through structurally different regulatory architectures. These architectures have produced deep asymmetrical levels of measurement intensity, thereby substantively shaping the foundations upon which mitigation, optimization, and enforcement rest. The present study examines the development of radon governance in the U.S. and Europe through a combined doctrinal, empirical, and regulatory lens. Drawing on U.S. national radon datasets, European Indoor Radon Maps and an analysis of epistemic capacity, it demonstrates that regulatory effectiveness is not strictly correlated with legal stringency. The U.S. federal-state-market architecture, combining non-binding federal guidance with state disclosure rules, transaction-driven testing, and private-market incentives, has generated reported measurement volumes more than one order of magnitude above the currently documented European map-based dataset, together with substantially greater reported mitigation activity. These gross outputs do not, by themselves, establish a net reduction in the number of high-radon dwellings or in population risk, but they demonstrate a markedly greater capacity to generate exposure-relevant information and activate remedial pathways. The Euratom Community has developed a codified framework under Directive, 2013/59, but exhibits structurally lower testing rates, largely because mandatory workplace duties are concentrated within Radon Priority Areas and because comparable mechanisms for embedding household testing in ordinary social and economic routines remain limited. The article concludes that measurement intensity can function as a structural diagnostic of epistemic and remedial capacity, revealing how divergent normative designs generate distinct pathways for converting scientific insight into concrete public-health protection.

title: 210 Pb ex in lacustrine sediments: A half-century global synthesis (1977-2024)
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Renaldo Gastineau, Floriane Guillevic, Palak Aggarwal, Anthony Foucher, Olivier Evrard, Christine Alewell, Robert Sabatier, Pierre Sabatier
abstract: Unsupported 210Pb (210Pbex) is a naturally occurring radionuclide widely used to establish sediment chronologies spanning the past ∼150 years, thereby providing high-resolution temporal frameworks for palaeolimnological reconstructions. Since the late 1970s, numerous hypotheses have been advanced to explain the environmental and climatic controls on 210Pbex deposition in lakes, yet no comprehensive synthesis of the accumulated empirical evidence is available. Here, we compile a global database of 210Pb measurements from 670 lacustrine sediment cores from studies published between 1977 and 2024 CE, encompassing 530 lakes across 61 countries and all continents except Antarctica. Before 2000 CE, approximately 85% of the sediment cores studied were located in the Northern Hemisphere. This proportion declined to 45% after 2000, reflecting a geographic expansion of 210Pb-based chronologies use toward the Southern Hemisphere. Using this dataset, we first assess the bivariate relationships between the 210Pbex surface activities, depositional fluxes, inventories, and individual environmental covariates, such as mean annual precipitation, land/ocean ratio, latitude and elevation. We then apply ordinary least squares multiple linear regression (OLS) and random forest (RF) models to rank the drivers of spatial variability in 210Pbex deposition at the global scale. The RF models outperform the OLS; the surface activity, flux and inventory models have low to high explanatory power for interpretation (R2 = 0.21, 0.35 and 0.66, respectively). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) indicate that elevation is the dominant predictor of both fluxes and inventories, followed by latitude and mean annual precipitation. These findings demonstrate that large-scale atmospheric processes primarily govern global patterns of lacustrine 210Pbex deposition. This study provides the first quantitative, data-driven global assessment of the environmental controls on lacustrine 210Pb deposition, enhancing the robustness and comparability of 210Pb-based chronologies worldwide.

title: Reshaping millennial-scale human–water relationships: A multi-disciplinary synthesis of the Yellow River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiting Zuo, Lu Liu, Junxia Ma
abstract: Study region Yellow River Basin, China, a large sediment-laden river system shaped by millennia of human activities, environmental changes, and river management. Study focus Recent reviews have documented Yellow River flood history and anthropogenic disturbances in considerable detail, yet their relevance to long-term socio-hydrological governance remains insufficiently synthesized. This review integrates historical, archaeological, paleoenvironmental, ecological, hydrological, geomorphological, and governance evidence to re-examine the millennial-scale evolution of human–water relationships in the basin. New hydrological insights for the region The synthesis identifies four broad stages: adaptive coexistence (ca. 2070 BCE–581 CE), agricultural expansion and landscape transformation (581–1368 CE), sediment-driven vulnerability and hydraulic dependence (1368–1949 CE), and engineering regulation and ecological restoration (since 1949 CE). Across these stages, increasing human pressure and changing ecological buffering capacity altered erosion, sediment accumulation, and river-system responses, while increasing hydraulic dependence during periods of heightened vulnerability. Governance correspondingly shifted from localized adaptation toward basin-scale coordinated regulation, water–sediment management, and ecological restoration. These stage transitions reflect changing feedbacks among climatic variability, human interventions, ecological conditions, fluvial processes, and institutional arrangements, offering a long-term socio-hydrological perspective on hydrological vulnerability and sustainable management in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Afghanistan's water security crisis: Coupled hydroclimatic stress, groundwater depletion, water quality risks, and institutional constraints
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sajid Ullah, Rujun Chen
abstract: Study region Afghanistan is an arid to semiarid country where river flow variability, precipitation fluctuations, limited groundwater recharge, irrigation demand, and snow and glacier dynamics constrain water availability. Changes in these processes at the basin scale directly affect national water security. Study focus This review synthesizes peer-reviewed and gray literature published from 2017 to 2025, integrating hydrogeological, water-quality, remote sensing (RS), geographic information system (GIS), and hydroclimatic studies. It evaluates surface-water availability, groundwater quantity and quality, and the impacts of climate variability and water-management practices on Afghanistan’s water resources. New hydrological insights for the region The reviewed studies demonstrate significant spatial variability across Afghanistan’s major river basins. The Kabul River Basin (KRB) is the most well-documented hotspot of groundwater stress, with reported declines of up to 1.5 m yr⁻¹ , reduced storage, excessive abstraction, and deteriorating water quality. In contrast, the Helmand River Basin (HRB) and Panj-Amu River Basin (PARB) are strongly controlled by cryospheric processes, with snowmelt contributing approximately 77% and 74% of annual river flow, respectively. Changes in snow persistence, glacier conditions, runoff timing, and drought patterns threaten surface-water reliability and groundwater recharge. Overall, Afghanistan’s water crisis stems from the combined effects of hydroclimatic variability and anthropogenic pressures. Significant uncertainties persist in poorly monitored basins, underscoring the need for improved monitoring networks, recharge assessments, and integrated water-resource management.

title: Joint flood diversion impacts of semi-restoration polder areas and flood storage and detention areas on the complex river-lake system of Poyang Lake, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tianfu Wen, Chao Deng, Fei Xu, Linus Zhang, Mou Leong Tan, Jing Li, Yang Xia
abstract: Study region Poyang Lake, the largest freshwater lake in China, is a complex river-lake system hydraulically connected to the Yangtze River. Semi-restoration polder areas (SRPAs) and flood storage and detention areas (FSDAs) constitute the two principal flood diversion systems for mitigating extreme floods in the region. However, the joint effects of these two types of flood diversion areas under different flood hydrographs remain insufficiently understood. Study focus This study employed a physically based large-scale two-dimensional hydrodynamic model that explicitly incorporated both SRPAs and FSDAs to investigate their joint flood diversion effects in the Poyang Lake system. Three representative extreme flood events (1954, 1998, and 2020), representing distinct flood hydrograph characteristics, were selected to evaluate flood diversion performance through comparative hydrodynamic simulations. Multiple indicators, including water-level reduction, time lags, and flood losses, together with a fuzzy optimum selection model, were adopted to identify optimal flood diversion schemes and reveal coupled hydrodynamic mechanisms unique to Poyang Lake. New hydrological insights for the region The effectiveness of joint flood diversion is fundamentally governed by flood hydrograph characteristics. Temporal hydrodynamic responses, including water-level reduction, time lags, and inundation dynamics, varied substantially among the three representative flood events, highlighting the importance of flood evolution and diversion timing in coordinated flood management. Spatially, water-level reductions were generally greater in the broad main lake than in the narrow outlet channel, where backwater effects from the Yangtze River may constrain the effectiveness of flood diversion. Coordinated operation of SRPAs and FSDAs can effectively reduce critical water levels and alter the timing of critical-water-level exceedance, with pronounced combined peak attenuation observed under the steep single-peak flood. Most importantly, the comparison across the three flood events reveals that hydrodynamic coupling between SRPAs and FSDAs varies with flood hydrograph characteristics, ranging from strong synergy to relatively independent regulation. This finding helps explain the variations in diversion benefits among historical floods in Poyang Lake and highlights the need to account for flood evolution and the temporal relationship between diversion processes when evaluating joint flood diversion schemes. These insights provide a scientific basis for adaptive flood diversion operation, integrated floodplain management, and flood risk mitigation in Poyang Lake and other river-connected lakes worldwide.

title: A lag-aware and interpretable two-stage framework for identifying dominant precipitation-related predictors in the data-scarce Mekong River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xi Weng, Tianshan Zeng, Yiqun Sun, Dongdong Gao, Qiongfang Li, Xiaogang Tian, Nengmin Zhu, Hongle Shi
abstract: Study area The Mekong River Basin is a data-scarce transboundary basin where sparse, unevenly distributed, and temporally discontinuous gauge observations hinder reliable precipitation estimation, particularly under strong subregional hydroclimatic heterogeneity. Research focus This study developed a lag-aware and interpretable two-stage framework to identify dominant precipitation-related predictors across the basin. In the first stage, transfer entropy (TE) was used to preliminarily screen candidate predictors by assessing directional lagged dependence from each candidate variable to precipitation over 1–7-day lags. In the second stage, tree-based machine learning and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to quantify predictor contributions within the fitted models and diagnose predictor structures across subregions and rainfall regimes. New hydrological insights The framework reduced a high-dimensional candidate predictor space to compact sets of 10–15 inputs. Under a common sample-based split, the compact models achieved a mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.232, compared with 0.275 for models using the complete preliminarily screened sets, and performed better overall than conventional feature-selection alternatives. Across subregions, cloud microphysical variables aloft and lower-atmospheric moisture variables were recurring contributors to modelled precipitation. Convective available potential energy (CAPE) and directional transport-related predictors also played important roles. In the heavy-precipitation subset (≥90 mm day−1), transport-, flux-, and energy-related predictors became more prominent in the fitted-model SHAP rankings. This rainfall-regime contrast provides a useful diagnostic of regional precipitation processes, although the heavy-precipitation results remain exploratory because of the limited number of gauge-day samples.

title: Identifying phreatic aquifer recharge sources and evaluating groundwater quality: Application of an end-member mixing analysis with statistically guided tracer selection in the Zishui River estuary
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Pengyu Fu, Xue Ping, Xing Liang, Menggui Jin, Zhikai Chang, Liqun Sun, Xin Zhang, Zhixin Zhang
abstract: Study region The Zishui River estuary, located in Hunan Province, China, is a transition zone from hilly-hillock areas to alluvial plain, where phreatic aquifer recharge processes are complex and their impacts on groundwater quality remain insufficiently understood. Study focus Identifying groundwater recharge processes is critical for resource management and groundwater quality regulation. Traditional End-Member Mixing Analysis (EMMA) involves subjective tracer selection, and previous studies have often separated recharge-source identification from groundwater-quality assessment. To reduce subjectivity in tracer pre-selection, we applied an EMMA workflow supported by Student’s t-test-based tracer screening. We quantified contributions of four recharge components: precipitation, confined groundwater, surface water, and anthropogenically modified recharge, and evaluated recharge-quality links using hydrogeochemical and isotopic data. New hydrological insights for the region Hill-hillock areas dominated by rainfall (contributing >50% of recharge) exhibit low pollution due to rapid water renewal, whereas most plain zones (with ~40% confined groundwater input) face high geogenic contamination risks (like As and Mo). Transition zones recharged by anthropogenic sources (up to 60% of total recharge) face severe threats from nitrogen and heavy metals (Co, Se, Ag, and Cd). The proposed workflow provides a transparent statistical basis for tracer pre-selection and supports the assessment of recharge-related groundwater-quality patterns in the Zishui River estuary, offering useful implications for groundwater protection in similar basins.

title: Groundwater-dependent vegetation reveals potential groundwater discharge zones in data-scarce alpine headwaters of the Yellow River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fen Gou, Gaihong Jia, Yingying Yao, Shuitao Guo, Yiqing Wang, Zhenjiang Wu, Fang Ji, Michele Lancia, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Study region The headwaters of the Yellow River in the Tibetan Plateau. Study focus Groundwater discharge sustains alpine headwater ecosystems by maintaining baseflow and buffering the effects of climate variability and drought. However, its regional distribution remains difficult to constrain because of complex terrain, permafrost conditions, and sparse groundwater observations. This study used groundwater-dependent vegetation (GDV) as an ecological indicator of persistent subsurface water supply to identify potential groundwater discharge zones. We integrated GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage anomalies, Sentinel-2 optical indices, Sentinel-1 radar indicators, and hydro-topographic variables to constrain GDV mapping during low-water-storage periods and infer potential spring discharge zones. New hydrological insights for the region Terrestrial water storage anomalies showed strong spatial heterogeneity during 2002–2023, with trends ranging from −2 to 12 mm yr⁻¹ and low-water-storage months accounting for 21%–73% of the study period. High-confidence GDV was concentrated along the Yellow River mainstream, river-valley wetlands, lake margins, and fault-related zones. We identified seven high-confidence springs, 55 potential springs, and broader groundwater discharge zones. These inferred discharge features showed contrasting spatial organization across the basin: the central and western regions were characterized by sparse, point-like potential springs, whereas the southeastern region was dominated by continuous belt-like diffuse discharge along river valleys, wetlands, and shallow groundwater systems. This framework provides a basis for targeted spring surveys and for assessing groundwater-dependent ecosystems under ongoing permafrost degradation.

title: Seasonal variations in nitrate sources and transformation indicators in the upper Xiangjiang River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yuxin Qin, Ziqiang Yang, Bing Li, Junxing Chen, Ruotong Xiong, Xia Jiang, Jia Wang, Liang Wang, Mingke Luo
abstract: Study region The upper Xiangjiang River Basin in China; the Xiangjiang River is a tributary of the middle Yangtze River. Study focus By integrating hydrochemistry, dual nitrate stable isotopes (δ15N–NO3 - and δ18O–NO3 -), and the Bayesian mixing model MixSIAR, this study characterized seasonal and spatial variations in nitrate, indicators of nitrogen transformation, and source contributions across the study area. We compared nitrate source characteristics with studies from the upper, middle, and lower Yangtze River Basin. New hydrological insights for the region Nitrogen pollution in the upper Xiangjiang study area showed pronounced seasonal and spatial variability. Mean TN and NO3 -–N concentrations during the rainfall season were 2.22 and 1.73 mg N L−1, respectively, substantially higher than 0.42 and 0.13 mg N L−1 during the regular season. Hydrochemical and dual-isotope patterns were consistent with nitrification contributing to nitrate formation, while no spatially coherent isotope signal of net denitrification was evident in surface waters. MixSIAR identified soil organic nitrogen (SON) as the largest nitrate source in both seasons, contributing 45.2% in the rainfall season and 52.6% in the regular season, followed by manure and sewage (M&S) at 33.5% and 37.0%, respectively. These results indicate that nitrate in the upper Xiangjiang River Basin is jointly influenced by soil nitrogen pools and manure/sewage-related inputs, with nitrate concentrations, spatial patterns, and source contributions varying substantially between seasonal hydrological settings.

title: The regulation mechanism of North Atlantic Oscillation on precipitation in the Tibetan Plateau: An isotopic perspective
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Baijun Shang, Feng Wang, Hui Gao, Tonggang Fu
abstract: Study region: The Tibetan Plateau (TP), known as the "Asian Water Tower," plays a critical role in shaping Asian hydrological cycles and maintaining regional ecological security. Study focus: The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is closely associated with precipitation patterns over the TP and, by modulating the westerly circulation, leads to distinct precipitation processes over the northern and southern TP. In this study, we use observed precipitation stable isotopes in conjunction with the IsoGSM model to elucidate the mechanisms by which the NAO regulates the inverse precipitation patterns between the northern and southern TP. New hydrological insights for the region: During NAO events, circulation anomaly signals propagate eastward, resulting in lower precipitable water content (ΔPWC) over the southern TP and higher ΔPWC over the northern TP, generating an inverse precipitation pattern between the southern and northern TP. The northern local meteoric water line (LMWL) has a slope of 7.63 and an intercept of 5.53, while the southern LMWL has a slope of 7.57 and an intercept of 7.06. The slopes of the southern and northern LMWLs are both lower than the Global Meteoric Water Line (GMWL) slope, which may suggest relatively high temperatures in the moisture source areas. In contrast, the differing intercepts reflect distinct atmospheric processes, with subsidence associated with anticyclonic systems dominating the southern TP and ascending motion associated with cyclonic systems dominating the northern TP. Based on precipitation stable isotopes, this study improves the understanding of NAO impacts on precipitation processes and provides a reference for simulating atmospheric circulation effects on precipitation patterns over the TP.

title: Anthropogenic disturbance reconfigures carbon cycling pathways in mountain-lake continua: Insights from hydrochemistry, isotopes, and microbial communities
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zuobing Liang, Yi Jin, Tao Hu, Zhengliang Yu, Yumei Yan, Zaizhi Yang, Yifan Xu, Xin Xiong
abstract: Study Region Two adjacent mesoscale stream catchments (Streams W and L) draining the Lushan Mountain massif (29°26′-29°41′N, 115°52′-116°08′E) in Jiangxi Province, subtropical China, into the Bali Lake and Poyang Lake basins. Spanning a continuous elevation gradient from alpine headwaters (>1000 m) to lowland lake margins (<20 m), the two catchments share a humid subtropical climate and broad geological setting but differ in land-use intensity, local lithology, and anthropogenic pressure, together forming a natural mountain–lake continuum. Study Focus Anthropogenic activities profoundly affect biogeochemical cycles in freshwater ecosystems, yet their specific effects on carbon dynamics in subtropical mountain–lake continua remain incompletely characterized. This exploratory spatial study compares carbon cycling between the two catchments to help separate anthropogenic disturbance from natural variation. Twenty-four stream water samples (12 per catchment), collected in January 2025, were analyzed using an integrated framework combining hydrochemical analysis, stable carbon isotopes (δ¹³CDIC), Bayesian DIC source apportionment (MixSIAR), EEM-PARAFAC optical characterization of dissolved organic matter (DOM), and 16S rRNA microbial community sequencing. The objectives were to characterize hydrochemical differences and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) sources, resolve spatial variation in DOM composition and bioavailability, and explore associations between bacterial community structure and DOM components along the continuum. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Stream W displayed elevated NO₃⁻, Cl⁻, and SO₄²⁻, consistent with domestic sewage and agricultural runoff, whereas Stream L was more strongly influenced by natural carbonate weathering, although lithological contrasts between the catchments also contribute to the observed patterns. DIC varied with elevation in both streams; Bayesian apportionment estimated sewage as the primary DIC contributor in Stream W (median 70.4%, 95% CI: 58–81%) and soil-CO₂-driven carbonate weathering as dominant in Stream L (median 54.8%, 95% CI: 43–67%). PARAFAC resolved four DOM components: Stream W showed a higher proportion of labile components and a more systematic downstream evolution, while Stream L exhibited greater spatial heterogeneity consistent with discrete point-source inputs. Exploratory microbial analyses revealed genus-level community differences and system-specific DOM-taxa associations warranting experimental follow-up. These results provide a spatial baseline indicating that diffuse-source and point-source disturbance may call for different management approaches in subtropical mountain–lake continua, pending validation by longitudinal monitoring.

title: How reliable are satellite precipitation products in extreme events? Insights from the “23•7” rainstorm in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei Region
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zitong Zhou, Qian Ma, Yan Guo, Guocan Wu, Ying Li, Ge Gao, Lingjun Liang
abstract: Study region The Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei (BTH) region experienced the July 2023 “23·7” extreme rainstorm, characterized by complex rainfall evolution. Study focus A process-oriented framework was developed to evaluate eight satellite precipitation products against observations from 174 rain gauges. The evaluation examined intensity-dependent detection and estimation, rainfall-peak representation, temporal phase matching using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), and spatial structure using the Structure–Amplitude–Location (SAL) method. New hydrological insights for the region During the “23·7” extreme rainfall event, satellite errors varied systematically with rainfall intensity. Overestimation dominated at 0.1–0.8 mm h⁻¹ , while systematic underestimation emerged above 4.0 mm h⁻¹ . Peak detection rates ranged from 53.3% to 77.3%, with most timing errors occurring within ±1 h. Peak-to-peak alignment reduced the negative bias relative to same-time evaluation, indicating that temporal phase mismatch contributed to the apparent underestimation, although residual biases remained after alignment. Spatially, median SAL location errors were below 0.05 for all products, while discrepancies were more evident in structure and amplitude. Overall, the results from this event reveal that intensity-dependent errors manifest differently across temporal and spatial dimensions.

title: Contrasting spatiotemporal patterns of assimilatory nitrate, phosphate and N 2 O emission in hilly and plain rivers
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Renhua Yan, Yuxin Zou, Ao Wang, Jiacong Huang, Qing Zhu, JiaLong Yan, Junfeng Gao
abstract: Study region Zhonghe Watershed, a northwestern upper sub-watershed of the Taihu Basin, Southeast China, and a key drinking water source for the Yangtze River Delta. Study focus This study quantifies the diel and seasonal variations in assimilatory nitrate, phosphate, and N2O emission fluxes in hilly and plain rivers during wet and normal periods. The research aims to understand the underlying mechanisms driving these processes and identify the key environmental factors influencing nutrient transformation and water-air N2O emission. New hydrological insights for the region Hilly river exhibit higher nitrate assimilation rates and lower N2O emissions compared to plain river, primarily due to its steeper gradients, stronger hydrodynamics, and higher dissolved oxygen concentrations. The diel and seasonal variations in assimilation of nitrate and phosphate and N2O emission are influenced by factors such as light, temperature, and hydrological conditions. For example, nitrate assimilation is higher during the day due to light-driven photosynthesis, while N2O emissions are higher during the wet season due to increased nutrient loads and reduced dissolved oxygen concentrations. The study identifies key environmental factors influencing nutrient transformation and N2O emission, including nitrate and phosphate concentrations, dissolved oxygen, pH, and hydrodynamics. These findings provide valuable information for developing effective management strategies to mitigate eutrophication and N2O emissions in the region.

title: Synergistic effects of multiple factors on surface runoff initiation time at mountainous hillslopes: A case study in the upper reach of the Danjiangkou Reservoir, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiaoxia Tong, Li Li, Wenfeng Ding, Dongguo Shao, Jianming Li, Longzhang Fang, Fuyuan Liu, Jinquan Huang, Guanhua Zhang, Qianjin Dong
abstract: Study region The Guanshan River watershed, China. Study focus Predicting surface runoff initiation time (T sur ) is critical for flash flood early warning in mountainous watersheds. We quantified how rainfall intensity (RI), slope gradient (S), soil thickness distribution pattern (STDP), and initial soil moisture (θ ini ) jointly regulate T sur through 72 laboratory simulations and 26 field plots. Three-way ANOVA decomposed the main and interaction effects, and two threshold models derived from the fitted T sur model (CR and CR+ASM) were validated on independent field plots. New hydrological insights for the region T sur decreased with RI and θ ini , each following a power function. The accelerating effect of S depended on RI: raising S from 5° to 15° and 25° shortened T sur by 60.5% and 75.1% at 30 mm/h but only 33.0%–66.0% at 120 mm/h, reflecting a shift from lateral-drainage to infiltration excess. RI×S and the STDP-involving interactions explained 19.19%–20.07% and 30.96%–34.87% of T sur variance, showing STDP acts as a pathway regulator, not a direct control. The fitted T sur model yielded cumulative rainfall (CR) thresholds CR 1–CR 4 that partition runoff generation into three stages; which differed between thick and thin soil layers (CR 4 = 38.64 vs. 32.67 mm) because CR alone ignores the initial storage deficit. Reformulating this criterion as CR + ASM ≥ W crit nearly eliminated this difference (≤2.32 mm) and reproduced runoff initiation under extremely dry conditions where rainfall-only indicators failed.

title: A scenario-neutral framework for regional drought risk management to assess climate change impacts in a large river basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiyoung Kim, Ji Eun Kim, Seung Beom Seo, Tae-Woong Kim
abstract: Study region The Seomjin River basin, one of South Korea’s large river basins, exhibits significant spatial variability in hydrological drought conditions across its sub-basins. Study focus This study proposed a regional drought risk assessment framework that integrates the joint drought management index (JDMI), which enables comprehensive assessment of drought risk, with a scenario-neutral approach that enables sensitivity analysis across a wide range of plausible climate futures. A total of 209 climate stress time series were generated by combining 19 precipitation and 11 temperature scenarios and were applied to 15 sub-basins of the Seomjin River in South Korea. A response surface was generated using the maximum JDMI estimated from runoff time series derived from the climate stress time series. Subsequently, response surfaces were used to assess climate change impacts for shared socioeconomic pathways (i.e., SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5). New hydrological insights into the region under study Hydrological drought severity in the Seomjin River basin was found to be governed primarily by precipitation change, whereas temperature exerted a secondary, amplifying influence under precipitation-deficit conditions. The proposed JDMI-based framework identified 1992–1996 as the most severe drought episode among the 47 five-year moving windows (1974–2024) in the Seomjin River Dam basin (#4001), with a maximum JDMI of 2.168 corresponding to a severe drought stage and an estimated annual water deficit of 13.6 × 106 m3. Two independently documented historical droughts in the 1994–1998 and 2015–2019 windows were classified as severe and moderate drought stages, with JDMI-based water deficits of 13.1 × 106 and 11.0 × 106 m3 per year, respectively. Mean reservoir storage in these windows was 18.02 × 106 and 13.29 × 106 m3 below the long-term mean, providing independent evidence of drought impacts. A comparison of observed and simulated low-flow deficits showed substantial underestimation of deficit volumes, indicating uncertainty in absolute deficit estimates. When 18 CMIP6 GCMs were mapped onto the response surfaces, an average tendency toward drought mitigation appeared from the near future (2025–2060) to the far future (2061–2100). However, under SSP5–8.5 in the far future, the projections spanned all drought stages (D0–D4). These results indicate that greater inter-model spread, rather than a change in mean drought severity, is the dominant challenge for drought risk management in the basin.

title: Evaluating the influence of reservoir storage dynamics on runoff processes using multi-source remote sensing automation: Jiaoyi Basin case study
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xingyu Wu, Ke Zhang, Xiaoji Shen, Xuejun Yi, Haijun Wang, Wei Gao, Cuiying Chen, Wei Liu, Shen Wang
abstract: Study region The Jiaoyi Basin (3345.12 km²) in Shandong Province, China, contains five small and medium-sized reservoirs, three of which lack continuous storage observations. The study covers 2018–2022. Study focus We developed an automated waterbody-extraction method combining iterative Otsu thresholding with Random Forest object recognition and a Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 storage-fusion method. In total, 1016 satellite scenes (690 Sentinel-1 and 326 Sentinel-2) were used across the five reservoirs. The methods were developed and evaluated at the two data-rich reservoirs using 392 scenes (278 Sentinel-1 and 114 Sentinel-2) and then applied to the three data-scarce reservoirs. Reconstructed daily storage was analyzed using lagged Spearman correlation, the Reservoir Influence Index (RI), and reservoir-aware Grid-Xinanjiang (GXAJ) simulations. New hydrological insights for the region Waterbody extraction achieved a coefficient of determination (R²) up to 0.9103 and Kappa up to 0.9848, while storage fusion reduced normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) by 0.0609 and 0.0429 in the validation period at Tangcun and Xujiaya, respectively. The five-reservoir RI was 0.09, and peak storage-change–streamflow correlations were 0.29–0.53, indicating detectable but modest daily regulation. Incorporating reservoir dynamics increased Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) by 0.01 and reduced peak-flow and absolute runoff-volume errors by 1.6 and 1.1 %age points, respectively, mainly improving peak and recession simulations.

title: Assessing dynamic variations in snow accumulation and ablation for hydrological processes in northwest arid China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chuan Wang, Zhi Li, Yupeng Li, Gonghuan Fang, Fan Sun
abstract: Study region The arid region of Northwest China has experienced pronounced warming and wetting under climate change. snowpack exhibits significant spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and changes in snow accumulation and ablation strongly influence regional solid water resources and snowmelt runoff. Study focus Using ERA5-Land daily snow water equivalent (SWE) reanalysis data, this study quantifies the rates, durations, and long-term evolution of snow accumulation and ablation during 1951–2022 and investigates their primary climatic drivers. New hydrological insights for the region The multi-year average snow accumulation rate (1.07 mm/d) is lower than the ablation rate (1.63 mm/d), with both peaking in the Altay, Ili-Tianshan, and Kunlun Mountains, indicating strong topographic control. Over the past 72 years, accumulation rates increased slightly, whereas ablation rates decreased, both exhibiting elevation dependence. Low-rate events dominate both phases, with a shorter accumulation period and a longer ablation period. Atypical processes, including ablation during the accumulation phase and accumulation during the ablation phase, are widespread, particularly in alpine regions. Snow accumulation and ablation are jointly controlled by maximum snow water equivalent (SWEmax), peak SWE timing, and snow phenology. Total snow accumulation increased slightly, whereas total ablation shows spatial heterogeneity. Reduced ablation during the accumulation phase and enhanced accumulation during the ablation phase increase regional solid water storage. These findings improve understanding of asymmetric snow dynamics and support snowmelt runoff simulation and water resources management.

title: Mekong River sediment decline, downstream reassembly, and weakening sediment exchange with Tonle Sap Lake
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Bo Liu, Khosro Morovati, Zilong Zhao, Hongling Zhao, Guangheng Ni, Fuqiang Tian
abstract: Study region Mekong River Basin. Study focus Dam expansion has disrupted Mekong sediment transport, yet mainstream sediment decline, downstream reassembly, and sediment exchange with Tonle Sap Lake are often studied separately. We combine long-term suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) observations, period- and hydrograph-limb-specific rating curves, and daily discharge reconstructed by a coupled hydrological–hydrodynamic model at Chroy Chang Var (CCV; delta apex) and Prek Kdam (PK; Tonle Sap gateway). Rating-curve and reconstructed-discharge uncertainties are jointly propagated to quantify changes from pre-dam (1962–1992) to post-dam (2010–2024). New hydrological insights for the region Mean annual suspended sediment load (SSL) at Chiang Saen declined by 85.7%, from 68.00 [95% uncertainty interval: 64.78, 71.46] to 9.75 [9.06, 10.41] Mt yr⁻¹ . Yet post-dam SSL at CCV was 54.55 [50.81, 58.90] Mt yr–1, of which Chiang Saen represented only 17.9% and cumulative net interstation changes 82.1% [80.6, 86.3%]. These are net reach-scale changes, not identified sediment sources or historical recovery. At PK, mean lakeward SSL was 2.41 [2.26, 2.56] Mt yr–1 and the mean inflow-minus-outflow balance was −0.59 [−0.87, −0.33] Mt yr–1. Lakeward SSL and reverse-flow volume declined significantly and covaried, although shared discharge dependence partly explains this correlation. Reconstructed flow-weighted SSC showed no significant trend, whereas observation-based evidence for declining SSC was model-dependent. The modern Mekong shows upstream depletion, downstream reassembly, and weakening sediment connectivity with Tonle Sap Lake.

title: Revealing the spatio-temporal evolution and driving mechanisms of watershed vegetation ecosystem stability using a novel integrated framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiping Yao, Shengzhi Wang, Haoyu Xue, Xu Luo, Guoqiang Wang, Shen Qu, Xiaoman Jiang, Zhendong Yang, Wenxing Zhang, Xiaojing Zhang, Ruihong Yu
abstract: Study region The Hunhe Basin lies in the Inner Mongolia section of the Yellow River Basin, China, a typical arid and semi-arid watershed where large-scale ecological restoration has greatly increased vegetation cover while intensifying pressure on limited water resources. Study focus Reconciling restoration and water sustainability requires disentangling how vegetation ecosystem stability (VES) responds to external climatic drought and internal water deficit. We developed an ecological resilience (ERes) model analogized to Hooke’s Law that integrates climatic dryness degree (CDD) and vegetation water deficit pressure (VWDP). CDD, VWDP and ERes are quantified from water imbalance and residual vegetation growth capacity, with slope trend and sensitivity analysis isolating key ERes controls. Applied across Hunhe Basin over 1982–2020, we disentangle VES dynamics and underlying drivers. New hydrological insights for the region CDD dominated ERes variations in spring and summer, whereas VWDP, the imbalance between vegetation available water (surface runoff and soil water) and ecological water demand, controlled ERes in autumn, winter, and annually, making water deficit the core driver of VES decline. Restoration improved VES in northern and eastern restoration zones (ERes II→III/IV), but excessive afforestation under water-limited conditions caused marked decline (−0.51 < SlopeERes < −0.45) in western and northeastern areas. Positive CDD–VWDP feedbacks propagated stability loss across most of the basin (−0.52 < SlopeERes < −0.30), indicating that restoration intensity must match regional water availability.

title: Natural matrix effects on the transport of chlorinated phenols through Danube alluvial sediments
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tamara Apostolović, Marijana Kragulj Isakovski, Irina Jevrosimov, Jelena Beljin, Peng Zhang, Srđan Rončević, Snežana Maletić
abstract: Study region Six layers of Danube alluvial sediment were collected at the Petrovaradinska ada groundwater source near Novi Sad, Serbia. This permeable alluvial system is relevant to riverbank filtration and drinking-water protection because surface water–groundwater exchange may transport organic micropollutants. Study focus Sorption and transport of 4-chlorophenol (4-CP), 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP), 2,4,6-trichlorophenol (2,4,6-TCP), and pentachlorophenol (PCP) were examined using natural Danube water. Batch sorption and column transport experiments were combined with isotherm modelling and analysis of sediment-property relationships. Results were compared with previous experiments using a synthetic aqueous matrix. New hydrological insights for the region Sediments were predominantly sandy, containing 70–93% medium sand, 0.85–2.4% clay, 0.06–0.23% total organic carbon, and specific surface areas of 0.76–2.14 m² g⁻¹ . Sorption equilibrium was generally reached within 12–24 h. Retardation was compound- and layer-dependent: 1.45–2.80 for 4-CP, 1.35–2.45 for 2,4-DCP, 1.00–1.50 for 2,4,6-TCP, and 2.40–4.60 for PCP. Maximum sorption capacities were generally lower in Danube water than in the synthetic matrix, indicating that natural-water constituents influence contaminant partitioning. Overall, the sediments provide limited and variable protection, highlighting the need to account for sediment heterogeneity and water composition when assessing contaminant transport and groundwater vulnerability.

title: Elevation-dependent threshold effects of social-ecological-landscape factors on water supply service flow in a plateau mountain city
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qingpu Li, Xiaoqing Zhao, Yuju Ran, Zixiang Sun, Zexian Gu, Yuenan Wang
abstract: Study region Kunming, a typical plateau mountain city in southwestern China facing severe water scarcity. Study focus Water supply service flow (WSF) is the potential water supply service transferable downstream after local demand is satisfied. This study simulated the direction and quantity of WSF in 2010 and 2023 across four elevation gradients. An Extreme Gradient Boosting model with Shapley Additive Explanations (XGBoost-SHAP) and a piecewise structural equation model identified the dominant drivers of WSF and their threshold effects, that is, the driver values at which a factor's influence on WSF reverses between positive and negative. New hydrological insights for the region Between 2010 and 2023, the water supply–demand deficit area expanded from 5.85% to 11.33% and total WSF quantity declined by 36.79%. The dominant drivers of WSF were elevation gradient-specific: ecological and landscape-pattern factors controlled Gradient I, ecological factors controlled Gradient IV, and socioeconomic and ecological factors jointly controlled Gradient II and Gradient III. Each key driver showed a gradient-specific threshold; in Gradient IV, for example, the precipitation threshold sustaining WSF fell from about 978 mm in 2010–894 mm in 2023. Overall, these elevation-dependent thresholds and driving mechanisms provide a scientific basis for spatially differentiated water-resource management.

title: Impact of soil moisture intrinsic signal structure on agricultural drought forecastability in the Yangtze River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Lue Zhou, Gengxi Zhang, Thian Yew Gan, Huimin Wang, Jinbai Huang, Shuai Zhou, Jin Zhao
abstract: Study region Yangtze River Basin (YRB). Study focus This study examines how two intrinsic temporal properties of soil-moisture drought signals are associated with realized forecast skill: persistence-related singularity structure, characterized by the maximum singularity strength (α max), and multifractal complexity, quantified by the singularity-spectrum width (Δα). A Joint Standardized Soil Moisture Index (JSSI) was constructed across five accumulation scales, and multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MF-DFA) was used to characterize multiscale temporal structure. Support Vector Regression (SVR), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) models were selected to forecast JSSI at 1-, 3-, and 6-month leads. New hydrological insights for the region the maximum singularity strengths (α max) and width of the singularity spectrum (Δα) show the most consistent associations with forecast skill and significant spatial organization across the basin. At the 1-month lead, α max provided the clearest common direction of skill variation, while responses to Δα were more model dependent. Cross-model agreement was strongest at the 3-month lead, with correlations among fitted forecastability surfaces of 0.993–0.999. At the 6-month lead, α max remained a common organizing axis, while the association with Δα became increasingly architecture dependent. Geopotential, long-term mean LAI, and soil type jointly explained 36.62% and 43.35% of the spatial variation in α max and Δα, respectively. Overall, soil-moisture temporal structure provides an important context for drought forecastability.

title: Depth-dependent seasonal associations of runoff and evapotranspiration with soil ice in the source region of the Yellow River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Lei Song, Yanping Li
abstract: Study region The Source Region of the Yellow River (SRYR) is an alpine permafrost basin on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau and provides a setting for examining depth-dependent seasonal associations between soil ice, runoff, and evapotranspiration (ET). Study focus Using monthly WEB-DHM-PF soil ice simulations (1964–2024), observed basin outlet runoff, and reanalysis ET, this study examined annual phase associations and seasonal segmented relationships within the upper 0–2 m profile. Lagged correlation, segmented model comparison, and Bootstrap assessed when runoff and ET correspond to soil ice, where supported relationships occur across regions and depths, and how low ice slope direction and statistical support vary. New hydrological insights for the region Soil ice associations with runoff and ET mainly reflected the annual freeze and thaw cycle, with phase correspondence varying systematically with soil depth. Runoff associations extended through most of the soil profile in the degraded region but were concentrated in the shallow and middle zones of the stable region, whereas ET showed a relatively continuous vertical phase structure in both regions.
