This study reassessed groundwater ages and reconstructed groundwater evolution in the coastal sedimentary sequence of the Rokkasho area, Shimokita Peninsula, northeastern Japan, using multiple environmental tracers. Groundwater samples were analyzed for major dissolved constituents, stable isotopes, 3 H, 14 C, 36 Cl/Cl, and dissolved noble gases. Corrected 14 C ages of fresh groundwater were evaluated using hydrogen isotope ratios and noble-gas recharge temperatures, whereas the residence time of deep saline groundwater was assessed using the 36 Cl/Cl method. Fresh groundwater occurs from the shallow subsurface to approximately 180 m below sea level. Corrected 14 C ages range from modern to about 35 ka and are consistent with paleoclimatic variations inferred from δ 2 H values and noble-gas recharge temperatures, supporting the reliability of the age correction. Deep saline groundwater exhibits 36 Cl/Cl ratios close to secular equilibrium, indicating residence times of at least 400 ka. In the upper part of the low-permeability formation, groundwater chemistry indicates mixing among freshwater, fossil seawater, and relatively younger seawater. These results suggest that seawater infiltrated into the shallow formations during marine transgression, whereas older fossil seawater was preserved in deeper, low-permeability strata. Subsequent uplift and sea-level regression promoted freshwater flushing of the shallow aquifer while preserving mixed saline groundwater at intermediate depths. The combined use of multiple groundwater-dating techniques provides a robust reconstruction of long-term groundwater evolution at the Rokkasho site.

title: Influence of tile-drainage water on groundwater nitrate concentrations within a saturated riparian buffer zone
abstract: Abstract Saturated riparian buffers (SRBs) are edge-of-field conservation practices that divert tile drainage into riparian soils to reduce nitrate delivery to streams, but the long-term response of saturated-zone groundwater to repeated tile-water inputs remains uncertain. This study evaluated 6 years of tile-flow, nitrate-nitrogen (NO 3 -N), and chloride data from an SRB in central Illinois to determine whether tile diversion altered groundwater NO 3 -N concentrations or caused multi-year nitrate accumulation. Groundwater samples from upgradient wells, representing background conditions, were compared with downgradient wells influenced by SRB distribution tiles. Mixed-effects models showed no significant relationship between daily tile-flow volume and groundwater NO 3 -N concentration and no significant difference between upgradient and downgradient groundwater. A 5-week lag analysis also showed no NO 3 -N response to prior tile flow. In contrast, chloride, used as a conservative tracer, increased with prior tile-flow volume, indicating hydraulic connectivity between diverted tile water and downgradient groundwater. The decoupling of chloride and NO 3 -N responses suggests that nitrate was attenuated within the SRB rather than simply diluted while transported to the monitored wells. During September and November no-flow periods, downgradient NO 3 -N concentrations remained low and did not increase progressively across years. These results indicate that the SRB sustained nitrate attenuation over multiple years without measurable dissolved NO 3 -N accumulation in the monitored shallow groundwater.

title: Sedimentary organic carbon contents control the nitrate reduction potential in a Holocene aquifer: Evidence from batch incubations
abstract: Abstract Groundwater quality is increasingly threatened by nitrate (NO 3 − ) contamination from agricultural activities. In many aquifers, NO 3 − is attenuated through microbially mediated reduction coupled to the oxidation of reduced constituents in the aquifer matrix. However, predicting NO 3 − turnover at the aquifer scale remains difficult because electron donors such as organic carbon and reduced sulfur species are heterogeneously distributed and reliable proxies for NO 3 − reduction potential are lacking. To address this challenge, batch experiments were conducted using eight facies types from a previously characterized tufaceous Holocene aquifer in southwestern Germany. The facies exhibited a wide range of solid-phase organic carbon contents (SOC 0.5–40.1 wt.%). NO 3 − reduction in batches was assessed by monitoring temporal changes in NO 3 − , sulfate (SO 4 2− ), and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations. NO 3 − reduction followed a two-phase pattern: An initial rapid, nonlinear decrease likely driven by readily bioavailable DOC, followed by a linear decline consistent with zero-order kinetics. Long-term NO 3 − reduction rates showed a strong positive relationship with solid phase organic carbon (SOC) ( R 2 = 0.69) across all microcosms ( n = 40) and facies ( n = 8). Experimental reduction rates were combined with facies-specific horizontal groundwater flow velocities to estimate NO 3 − turnover distances and times for an initial concentration of 50 mg L −1 NO 3 − . The results demonstrate that NO 3 − attenuation is controlled by both biogeochemical and hydraulic factors. The study highlights SOC as a key proxy long-term NO 3 − reduction potential and demonstrates the value of facies-based approaches combined with reaction-kinetic modeling for assessing groundwater quality at the aquifer scale.

title: Estimating groundwater levels and their associated uncertainty through spatiotemporal kriging of groundwater-level data
abstract: Abstract Sustainable groundwater management requires, among other factors, reliable monitoring of groundwater levels (GWLs) and their spatiotemporal evolution in an aquifer with meaningfully quantified uncertainty. Geostatistical methods can estimate GWL surfaces directly from available groundwater monitoring data. This contrasts with groundwater flow modeling, which requires much more detailed data. This study estimates spatiotemporal GWL maps and quantifies associated uncertainties by spatiotemporal kriging, which combines spatial interpolation with temporal gap filling and noise filtering. The central hypothesis is that including hydrogeological information in kriging improves GWL predictions. To test this hypothesis, spatiotemporal trends and soft information inspired by hydrological understanding are included. These include digital elevation models, river exchange components, and the confinement status of aquifers. To test the necessity of full statistical involvement through Bayesian hyperparameter inference, universal kriging is operated in a fully Bayesian framework and then compared to simpler approaches like non-Bayesian and residual space–time kriging. The approach is demonstrated for the Wairau Plain aquifer, New Zealand, where the spatiotemporal GWL estimates can be compared with transient simulation results from a numerical groundwater flow model. The results indicate that space–time kriging is a valuable tool to estimate transient GWL maps, where auxiliary hydrogeological information is highly useful, that the fully Bayesian treatment of universal kriging is worth the effort, but that a posterior (Bayesian) uncertainty of geostatistical hyperparameters is close to irrelevant.

title: Groundwater sustainability in hyper-arid regions: Integrated groundwater modeling of Qatar’s aquifers under climate change and management scenarios
Hydrochemical characteristics and mixing processes of the multi-aquifer system in a coal mining district, northern Anhui Province, China
Temporal variability of stable isotopes in groundwater: A multi-year seasonal analysis and comparison with groundwater levels in the Piedmont Po Plain (NW Italy)
Assessing the worthwhileness of efficiency enhancement methods mitigating buoyancy flow in high-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage
abstract: Abstract High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) presents a promising approach for achieving a temporally and spatially balanced, continuous energy supply. A key challenge in HT-ATES systems is the density-driven buoyancy flow, which can result in considerable heat losses and reduced energy efficiency, or thermal recovery efficiency. This study explores two strategies for mitigating the effects of buoyancy flow: adjusting the working fluid’s salinity and modifying the production well screen length, under varying intensities of buoyancy flow. Numerical simulations are employed to evaluate the recovery efficiency and pumping energy requirements across a range of fluid salinities and screen lengths over multiple HT-ATES operational cycles. Under conditions of high intensity of buoyancy flow, the impact of different fluid salinities on thermal front evolution and associated hydrodynamic processes is analyzed. Recovery efficiency exhibits a nonmonotonic response to fluid salinity, with the maximum improvement reaching 36.5% at an increase in salinity of 6%. At a moderate intensity of buoyancy flow, altering fluid salinity proves ineffective due to the formation of a buffering layer, where cooled saline water separates the injected fluid from the surrounding groundwater. Comparatively, modifying fluid salinity is found to be more effective than adjusting the production well screen length. For both strategies, the additional pumping energy required is negligible relative to the gain in recovered heat. The number of operational cycles has minimal influence on the heat plume’s location and morphology. Furthermore, owing to the additional preferred pathways and irregular-shape fronts, the recovery efficiency enhancement methods are found more effective in heterogeneous aquifers.

title: Unraveling the interactions between shallow and deep aquifers through analysis of groundwater chemical trends: insights from the Piedmont Po Plain (NW Italy)
abstract: Deep aquifers are essential groundwater resources for human activities, and their exploitation has intensified in recent years, as shallow aquifers generally exhibit a higher occurrence of contaminants compared to deep aquifers. The aim of the study is to examine the interactions between shallow and deep aquifers using hydrochemical approaches, considering the spatiotemporal distribution and trends of physicochemical parameters, major ions, heavy metals, pesticides and specific hydrochemical indices in deep aquifers over the 2000–2021 period in Piedmont (NW Italy). In the Piedmont Po Plain, a shallow phreatic aquifer hosted in fluvial deposits overlies deep confined and semiconfined aquifers, hosted in transitional and marine complexes. Results highlight (1) an increase in physicochemical parameter values and major ion concentrations; (2) enhanced introduction of pollutants, such as pesticides; (3) increased CO 2 levels, leading to increased concentrations of some major ions and decreased concentrations of Fe 2+ and the calcite saturation index (SI calcite ); and (4) intensified ion exchange processes. In conclusion, the increasing trends in physicochemical parameter values and major ion concentrations confirm an increase in the recharge of deep aquifers from overlying shallow aquifers, likely driven by the intensified exploitation of deep groundwater resources. This work represents one of the first regional studies of deep aquifers in the Piedmont Po Plain to analyze both physicochemical parameter and major ion trends and the significant role of interactions with shallow aquifers, providing valuable insights for local authorities, particularly as deep aquifers are expected to be increasingly exploited in the future for agricultural and drinking-water purposes.

title: Groundwater evaporation in an Andean salt flat: A new methodological approach in a brine mining context
Anomalously high wellhead temperatures relative to natural springs in the Niujie Geothermal Field, Yunnan (China): Hydrochemical and structural controls
Re-evaluating coastal salinization in the Mitidja Plain, northern Algeria, using vintage VES data: Statistical clustering and 3D inversion
Correction: How does rewetting propagate through restored peatlands? An integrated surface–subsurface modelling analysis of water–table dynamics
The beginning of groundwater use by hominins and its key to migrations by Homo erectus out of Africa
abstract: Abstract Despite growing acceptance of the importance of groundwater use by hominins, there has been little hydrogeological investigation into the controls on groundwater availability as relevant to their evolution and geographic dispersal. This study integrates available fossil and stone tool data with hydrogeological landscape reconstruction and conceptualisation to develop understanding and constraints on the earliest use of groundwater by hominins and early migrations between Africa and Eurasia. It is proposed that the first bipedal human ancestors, appearing in the fossil record in Central and East Africa between 6 and 7 Ma, learned from other mammals how to find and access shallow groundwater in ephemeral streambeds. The first evidence of hominin associations with groundwater discharge from springs is from around 2–4.5 Ma in the East African Rift System (EARS), these locations likely being critically stable hydro-refugia within the driest parts of precession-dominated climatic cycles. The first migrating hominin species appears to have been Homo erectus , with those in the EARS leaving in waves as small bands from around 1.9 Ma at the end of a humid period in the Arabian Peninsula. It is proposed that the most hydrologically plausible routes linking the EARS to Eurasia are via Red Sea crossings and then through the Arabian Peninsula moving along the strike of regional aquifers which would have provided perennial groundwater even over long climatically arid periods. The paper demonstrates the fundamental importance of groundwater for early hominin communities during a critical period in the evolution of human physiology and consciousness.

title: A two-stage clustering algorithm for generating digital cores for grouting in highly fractured rock foundations
Resolving 3-D aquifer architecture through assimilated lithological and geophysical data: Insights from multilayered alluvial systems of the Ganga–Mahananda floodplain, eastern India
Hydrochemical characteristics, origins, and health risk assessment of fluoride in groundwater in the Biliu River Basin, Liaodong Peninsula, China
Effect of bioturbation–induced riverbed morphological changes on groundwater/surface-water exchange in mountain rivers
Characterization of subsurface groundwater pathways from treated wastewater effluent infiltration along the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
abstract: Abstract Recharge of treated wastewater to the environment is increasingly becoming a component of water resources management, especially in water-limited areas such as the Grand Canyon. Treated wastewater from the Grand Canyon South Rim Wastewater Treatment Plant has been discharged to a dry wash located along the surface expression of a fault for decades, but the fate of the wastewater is unclear. Previous research suggested possible connections between the treated wastewater discharge sites and springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon, particularly Monument spring. Additional investigations presented in this report add further evidence to the connection between the wastewater and Monument spring, utilizing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, artificial sweeteners, and stable isotopes of water. A dye trace established the first direct connection between wastewater and Monument spring where the dye added to treated wastewater took about 4–6 months to move through the subsurface and was detectable for 5 months. The persistence of wastewater tracers over time and the timing of dye movement suggests a fast subsurface flow pathway. On the basis of geologic observations of faults and jointing, groundwater flow follows a possible combination of karst and other structural pathways. The dye and wastewater tracers were monitored at other springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon and the combination of repeated dye detections and multiple wastewater tracers were only found at Monument spring. Multiple lines of evidence provide a robust tracer suite to support evidence of structural/karst controls on preferential flowpaths; faults alone are unlikely to explain the flow pathway.

title: Numerical simulation of the impact of tunnel drainage on matrix–conduit water exchange in the karst aquifers of Panzhou City, China
Quantifying water origin of a Mediterranean urban karst aquifer using storm event typology and high-frequency physicochemical signatures
Estimating multi-decadal groundwater levels using incomplete well records in confined and unconfined aquifers of the southern San Joaquin Valley, California (USA)
Hydrochemistry of confined aquifers in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy: Regional patterns, trends, and drivers
abstract: Abstract Confined aquifers are considered to be protected from surface contamination, yet intensive abstraction and long-term land-use pressures may alter their quality, especially in coastal areas. This study characterises the hydrochemistry of the multilayered confined aquifer system of the lower Friulian Plain (NE Italy), where groundwater is extensively exploited and locally affected by anthropogenic stressors. The study combines hydrochemical data from 1996 to 2025 from the monitoring activity of Regional Environmental Protection Agency of Friuli Venezia Giulia (ARPA FVG) and new samples collected in 2024–2025, compiling 1210 samples from 103 wells. The aim is to determine how recharge sources, residence time, and human activities control groundwater quality. Hydrochemical families were identified using major ions, redox-sensitive species, organic micropollutants, stable oxygen isotopes, and multivariate statistics. Three groundwater families were recognised: submodern waters, with hypoxic conditions, low to absent contaminant load and likely associated with recharge dating back to the late Würmian glacial period; modern-pristine waters, which are characterised by oxidising conditions, are SO 4 2− -rich, and show low to absent NO 3 − and pesticide concentrations; and modern-impacted waters, which are similar to the latter but display elevated NO 3 − concentrations, lower pH values, and detectable anthropogenic contaminants. Long-term trends indicate that although NO 3 − concentrations are overall stable or slightly decreasing in shallow aquifers, slowly increasing trends occur in deeper wells and near the margins of the NO 3 − plume, suggesting downward and lateral migration of impacted modern groundwater. Cl − concentrations show no increasing trends in coastal wells, indicating no evidence of active seawater intrusion.

title: Validating a numerical model for calco-carbonic reactive transport in a laboratory-scale fracture analog
abstract: Abstract Calco-carbonic reactive transport controls the dissolution of limestone by carbonic acid, a key process shaping the hydraulic and geochemical evolution of carbonate aquifers. Quantitative understanding of the coupling between flow, transport, and chemical reactions is essential for predicting karstification under variable hydraulic gradients, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 partial pressures, and pH. To support model validation, laboratory experiments were conducted in a 1 m $$^2$$ 2 vertical karst-fracture analog with variable aperture, representing a simplified hydrogeologic fracture domain. Numerical simulations reproduced these experiments under controlled discharge, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 concentration, and acidity. The coupled reactive transport models capture feedbacks between forced convection, diffusion, and density variations, linking reactive interface dynamics with evolving flow fields. Simulated and measured calcium and carbonate ion concentrations showed good agreement, indicating that diffusive transport at the water–limestone interface primarily limited dissolution. Insights from the combined modeling and experimental framework refine laboratory-scale design, improve interpretation of dissolution kinetics, and strengthen the basis for upscaling to field-scale carbonate aquifers. The results enhance prediction of permeability evolution, flow-path development, and $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 - $$\text {H}_{2}\text {O}$$ H 2 O -rock interactions in karst systems.

title: Mechanical and chemical rehabilitation of groundwater abstraction wells clogged by iron and manganese precipitates in Finland
abstract: Résumé Le colmatage des puits de captage d'eau souterraine survient généralement lorsque le fer et le manganèse dissous dans l'eau précipitent sur les éléments du puits, entraînant une baisse du débit. En Finlande, ce phénomène est marqué car les sols sont riches en fer et en manganèse, et les aquifères sédimentaires quaternaires recouverts d'argile présentent généralement une carence en oxygène. Une nouvelle approche de réhabilitation des puits, combinant traitements mécaniques et chimiques, a été appliquée à quatre puits de captage d'eau souterraine situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés en Finlande. D'après les analyses par fluorescence X (XRF), les précipités responsables du colmatage étaient composés de Fe₂O₃, SiO₂, MnO et P₂O₅. Les réhabilitations mécaniques et chimiques ont toutes deux permis d'augmenter considérablement les débits (de 68 à 6 692 %) ; même les puits totalement colmatés ont affiché une nette amélioration de leur débit après l'intervention. À l'issue de la réhabilitation mécanique, les crépines des puits présentaient un niveau de propreté modéré. La réhabilitation chimique a permis un nettoyage supplémentaire des crépines, libérant totalement les fentes et réduisant la turbidité. Le traitement chimique a entraîné une augmentation de la conductivité électrique, de la teneur en sulfates ainsi que des concentrations en fer et en manganèse (dissous et totaux) dans l'eau, en raison des réactifs utilisés et de la dissolution du fer et du manganèse contenus dans les précipités. Toutefois, la qualité de l'eau est revenue à ses niveaux initiaux après une journée de pompage suivant le traitement. Cette méthode de réhabilitation est applicable aux puits de captage situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés, au sein d'aquifères constitués de sable et de gravier à forte conductivité hydraulique. Néanmoins, des études complémentaires sont nécessaires pour mieux comprendre le processus de colmatage ainsi que l'applicabilité de ces méthodes de réhabilitation dans des contextes hydrogéologiques et des environnements redox variés.

title: Sustainable groundwater management in coastal areas: Modelling saltwater intrusion dynamics in Muravera, Italy
abstract: Abstract The coastal alluvial aquifer of Muravera, in south-eastern Sardinia (Italy), is affected by intense saltwater intrusion that seriously threatens freshwater supply. As groundwater overexploitation is often the main process controlling saltwater intrusion dynamics, it can strongly exacerbate salinization, making sustainable groundwater management essential to safeguard these resources. Reliable hydrogeological models based on robust datasets are powerful tools to support decision-making. This work develops a variable-density groundwater flow and solute transport model to analyse saltwater intrusion into the coastal aquifer of Muravera. Four simulation scenarios were implemented. The first reconstructs the historical evolution of salinization over the period of 1999–2023, whereas the other three extend the simulations to 2050 to quantify the various effects of different groundwater abstraction practices and to test a mitigation scenario. Two modelling codes were coupled to support the analysis. Groundwater recharge was computed using the Soil–Water-Balance (SWB) code and subsequently used as input to the iMOD-WQ code, which simulates variable-density flow and salt transport using SEAWAT. This coupling explicitly captures temporal and spatial recharge variability, which is often oversimplified in other approaches. The results indicate that groundwater abstractions for rice-field irrigation exerts a stronger influence on salinization dynamics than drinking-water abstractions. The mitigation scenario attenuates groundwater salinization in the plain, providing useful insights for future groundwater-management strategies.

title: Groundwater modeling to evaluate saltwater intrusion and freshening processes identified from hydrochemistry in a coastal groundwater system in Vietnam
Correction: Socio-hydrogeology: The past, present, and future of a people-centred and place-based approach to groundwater science
Advancing hydraulic conductivity estimation in the Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group using borehole NMR logging
abstract: Abstract The Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group is an important aquifer in the United Kingdom (UK) for groundwater and geothermal energy applications. Hydraulic conductivity ( K ) is essential for understanding groundwater movement, contaminant and heat transport in aquifers. Pumping test and borehole nuclear magnetic resonance logging (BNMR) were conducted in three boreholes drilled into the Sherwood Sandstone to determine K . BNMR provides information on the water-filled porosity and pore space geometry, and compared to conventional methods, it is an effective way to estimate K at a high vertical resolution. Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (T-C) were used to estimate K using the standard empirical constants initially developed for petroleum reservoir applications. K SDR and K T-C were upscaled to the larger volume represented by K pumping for comparison. Both the standard SDR and T-C equations underestimated K by at least two orders of magnitude because of the limited transferability of their empirical constants to shallow groundwater systems, as they were derived for petroleum reservoir rocks rather than near-surface materials. The fits between the K SDR , K T-C and K pumping were optimised using a semi-constrained least-squares approach to obtain a set of site-specific parameters for the Sherwood Sandstone Group. The new K SDR and K T-C estimates, based on site-specific parameters, are within an order of magnitude of the K pumping . This study presents the first reported SDR and T-C constants for the Sherwood Sandstone Group, which may be used to estimate a more reliable NMR-derived high-resolution hydraulic conductivity in other locations where this formation is present.

title: Isotopic assessment of the origin of fresh and saline groundwater in the highly exploited, predominantly fossil Mekong Delta aquifer in Ca Mau, Vietnam
Estimating specific yield from GRACE-based storage change and groundwater levels across India
Mining-induced overburden fracture development and its control on preferential groundwater flow
Hydrochemical differences and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, North China
abstract: Abstract The periphery of the Jinan Pluton, North China, contains abundant cold-water and geothermal karst resources, constituting a natural observatory for investigating karst water origins and hydrogeochemical evolution. To advance the understanding of the occurrence pattern and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, a total of 36 samples of karst groundwater were collected and analyzed for hydrochemical constituents via ion chromatography (IC) and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), and isotopic composition. The results are as follows: (1) Along the south-to-north regional groundwater flow path, cold-water and geothermal karst groundwaters around the Jinan Pluton exhibit significantly distinct hydrochemical types. From shallow cold-water karst (spring water) to deep geothermal karst systems, the hydrochemical types become progressively more complex, accompanied by a continuous increase in the extent of water–rock interaction. (2) Within the geothermal field north of the Yellow River, the observed gradual increase in total dissolved solids (TDS) of geothermal karst water from west to east can be attributed to two main factors. First, the geothermal karst water in the western segment of the geothermal field receives significant recharge from the Yellow River. Second, the karst water level in the eastern segment of Jinan is the lowest across the study area, making it the convergence center of regional karst groundwater flow, which results in a relatively isolated hydrogeological environment with respect to the surface. This study reveals karst water hydrochemical evolution near the Jinan Pluton to guide water resource utilization and protection.

title: Leveraging machine learning tools to minimize uncertainties of physically based regional-scale groundwater models: A case study on precision modeling of groundwater levels in the Bist-Doab region, India
Hydraulic stimulation geometry governs information efficiency and parameter identifiability in hydraulic tomography: A comparison of dipole and sequential pumping tests

Old water, rapid responses: Process-based hydrogeological domains reveal hydraulic–age decoupling and implications for recharge assessment in a complex aquifer system of the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa
abstract: Abstract Groundwater-level fluctuations are commonly used as recharge indicators because groundwater-level rises are often assumed to represent additions of recently recharged water to aquifer storage. In heterogeneous, multilayer aquifer systems, this assumption remains uncertain because groundwater-level variations may also reflect hydraulic connectivity, pressure transmission, storage redistribution, and groundwater mixing. Misinterpretation of groundwater-level behavior may consequently bias recharge estimates and groundwater-resource assessments. This study evaluated relationships among groundwater-level behavior, groundwater residence times, and hydrogeological process domains within the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa. Groundwater hydrographs, tritium-derived groundwater ages, and a domain-based conceptual framework were integrated to investigate spatial variability in groundwater flow and recharge processes. Piston-flow (PF) apparent ages ranged from 0 to 60 years, whereas exponential–piston flow model (EPM)-derived mean transit times (MTTs) ranged from 2 to 80–100 years across hydrogeological domains. Recharge-dominated systems showed strong seasonal groundwater-level responses despite the coexistence of young and broad groundwater-age distributions and highly variable hydrograph responses, reflecting mixed recharge and storage influences. Structurally controlled systems showed rapid hydraulic responses despite prolonged groundwater residence times, suggesting pressure transmission independent of groundwater transport times. Residence-time-dominated systems were characterized by older groundwater and subdued hydrograph responses associated with prolonged storage. Groundwater-level response rate showed a weak and statistically non-significant relationship with MTT (Pearson's r = − 0.307, p = 0.460), demonstrating hydraulic–age decoupling and indicating that recharge assessments based solely on groundwater-level fluctuations may substantially misrepresent groundwater recharge processes in structurally complex multilayer aquifer systems.

title: Evaluating the long-term efficacy of subsurface cutoff walls as a barrier against seawater intrusion in unconfined island aquifers under various climatic-stress scenarios
Seasonal fluctuation of spring outflows in contrasting lithological and geomorphological environments of the western mid-hill region, Nepal
Groundwater potential zoning in the Grande River Basin: A semi-arid region of Northeast Brazil
abstract: Abstract Seasonal water scarcity in western Bahia, Brazil, has led to increased dependence on groundwater resources; however, basin-scale hydrogeological measurements remain insufficient for preliminary assessments. This study presents a geographic information system-based groundwater potential map for the Grande River Hydrographic Basin (GRHB), where groundwater potential is defined as a relative index reflecting conditions favorable for recharge and subsurface storage, rather than a direct measure of aquifer productivity. Ten hydrogeological and terrain proxy layers, derived from existing datasets and remote sensing, were standardized and integrated using an analytic hierarchy process weighting scheme and a weighted linear combination. The resulting index was classified into five groundwater potential categories. The very high- and high-potential classes account for 48.08 and 25.41% of the basin, respectively, while the moderate class accounts for 19.90%, and the low- and very low-potential classes together comprise 6.59%. Spatial association with available well locations was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis and the area under the curve, which yielded a value of 0.821, indicating that wells are more frequently located in areas with higher index values. Additionally, a groundwater abstraction-pressure proxy, derived from wells with reported daily abstraction volumes, was used to identify potential stress areas where high favorability coincides with concentrated abstraction activities. These outputs serve as a first-order screening tool to guide field verification, monitoring, and targeted data acquisition across the basin.

title: Macroscopic and mesoscopic characteristics of non-Fickian solute transport in rough fractures

Steady-state semi-analytical solutions for assessing the shape of the freshwater–seawater interface induced by a finite-sized underground physical barrier and a pumping well in a sloping coastal aquifer

Application of the new preconsolidation head and safe pumping buffer concepts to groundwater management for preventing land-subsidence recurrence in an overexploited aquifer system: A case study of Taiyuan City, northern China
Integrating geophysical and underwater robotic surveys with transport and geochemical modeling to assess the Solotvyno salt mine hazard in the Transcarpathia province of Ukraine
abstract: Abstract The Solotvyno salt mine in West Ukraine presents significant environmental and infrastructural risks due to uncontrolled salt dissolution following mine flooding, causing ground subsidence, sinkhole formation, and transboundary contamination of the Tisza River. This study employs an innovative multidisciplinary approach to characterize subsurface conditions and contamination pathways. The UX-1Neo autonomous underwater robotic platform conducted 14 dives in two flooded mine shafts, revealing intact main shaft structures but worrying blockages in horizontal passages, distinct haloclines at different depths (60 m in ventilation shaft 9, 140 m in shaft 10), and evidence of ongoing salt crystallization. Ground geophysical surveys such as electrical resistivity tomography, very low frequency radio-magnetotellurics and horizontal loop electromagnetics identified compromised protective clay layers (“pallag”) and potential air-filled voids, explaining accelerated dissolution and surface deformation. Hydrodynamic and contaminant transport modeling quantified salt fluxes (~ 2000 m 3 /day through “pallag” zones, ~ 13–15 m 3 /day from direct mine leakage) and confirmed dissolution rates of approximately 5.0–5.5 m 3 /day of rock salt, driven by both anthropogenic influences and natural gradients toward the Tisza River. NETPATH mixing models revealed variable contamination throughout the system, with the Black Moor area showing highest vulnerability (up to 27.4% mine water contribution) while the Tisza River maintains relatively good water quality despite measurable contamination (1.97% mine water). The suggested approach provides critical insights into risk assessment and remediation planning, representing a significant advancement in monitoring and managing complex environmental hazards associated with abandoned salt mines.

title: Ascertaining controls on spring discharge: Implications for the revival of drying springs in the Middle Hills region of Nepal
Groundwater occurrence and quality in a hyper-arid desert: Insights from high-resolution electrical resistivity surveys in Tharparkar, Pakistan
abstract: Abstract The Tharparkar District in Pakistan is among the world’s most water-scarce regions, characterized by its hyper-arid climatic conditions and the absence of perennial surface water resources. Understanding the occurrence of groundwater potential and its quality is therefore critical, particularly in remote regions where hydrogeological information remains limited. This study characterized groundwater resources using 576 high-resolution electrical resistivity survey (ERS) probes up to a depth of 300 m, conducted from 2017 to 2020. Complementary hydrochemical investigations included laboratory analysis of 168 groundwater samples collected from dug wells and 672 soil samples up to a depth of 0.60 m. Results demonstrated that the water table lies at depths of 2–15 m (26% of the area), 16–30 m (23%), and 31–90 m (51%). Interpretation of ERS data revealed that approximately 10% of the groundwater resources, covering the southern parts of Diplo, Islamkot, and Nagarparkar Talukas, are suitable for drinking at a depth of 25 m, with around 3% classified as fresh and 7% as slightly saline. Groundwater salinity increases with depth, as 51% of the area shows high salinity at depths of 26–50 m and very high salinity at depths of 51–200 m. Arsenic and fluoride concentrations exceed permissible limits in 10 and 28% of the groundwater samples, respectively. These findings provide robust geophysical and hydrochemical evidence to guide targeted groundwater development, water quality mitigation strategies and inform policy interventions, aimed at enhancing water security and safeguarding the health of communities living in severely water-stressed desert regions.

title: The spatiotemporal evolution and controlling factors of the groundwater environment: Insights from long-term monitoring of Tongzhou District, China
Integrated geochemical characterization and multicomponent modeling for reservoir temperature estimation in the Boğazlıyan Geothermal Field (Central Anatolia, Turkey)
Correction: Isotopic investigations on identification of atmospheric moisture origins and evaluation of runoff source contributions to the Upper Beas River Basin in the western Himalayas
Understanding groundwater flow in a buried valley and bedrock aquifer system in Kurikka, Finland, using hydrochemical indicators and residence time tracers 3H and 14C
abstract: Abstract Growing demand for groundwater in western Finland has drawn attention to a regional network of buried valleys with high potential for domestic and municipal water supplies. This study aims at understanding the groundwater flow in the buried valley and bedrock aquifer system using hydrochemical data and residence time indicators ( 3 H, 14 C). A multivariate statistical analysis (hierarchical clustering on principal components) revealed six water groups reflecting the origins and different stages of groundwater evolution. Overall, a modern groundwater component (< 60 years old) and active flow system are present in all parts of the system. Longer residence times are found deeper within the buried valleys ( 3 H-free waters) and at greater depth in a few locations in the bedrock ( 14 C ages > 5000 years). The occurrence of geochemically evolved waters in the deeper, downgradient areas of buried valleys indicates suitable (in terms of quantity and quality) and safe (low vulnerability) water supply relative to demand. More broadly, the multi-tracer approach provides insights into the geochemical evolution of groundwater, revealing groundwater flow conditions, geological history and aquifer unit composition. Residence time indicators also illustrate the relative hydraulic isolation of buried valleys, which has implications on vulnerability and sustainable exploitation. To fully clarify the exchanges between bedrock and granular aquifers, a sampling scheme targeting deep flow paths beneath the Paloluoma and Kyrönjoki valleys would be necessary. This study will support the development of a numerical model of the aquifer system and contribute to informing future management decisions.

title: Towards global groundwater recharge estimation from GRACE-constrained GLDAS-CLSM data
abstract: Accurate estimation of groundwater recharge at regional to global scales is essential for sustainable water resource management, yet current methods lack consistency. This study introduces the groundwater storage fluctuation (GSF) method to derive gross recharge, total discharge (including both natural and human-related outflows that cannot be distinguished without additional data), and net recharge from GRACE-constrained GLDAS-2.2 CLSM groundwater storage (GWS) anomalies. Based on monthly GWS fluxes, the GSF method requires no seasonal templates or specific recharge-event identification. Global mean annual recharge for 2004-2024 is estimated at 16,081.5 km $$^{3}$$ /year, consistent with existing global hydrological models and multi-study averages (14,806 ± 1,721 km $$^{3}$$ /year). Recharge ranges from <100 mm/year in arid zones to >300 mm/year in humid tropical areas, with a non-significant global trend of 0.34 mm/year. Arid basins show the highest interannual variability, with coefficients of variation of 48% for the Murray-Darling Basin (Australia), 40% for São Francisco (Brazil), and 36% for Colorado (USA). Validation against an Australian chloride mass balance (CMB) dataset shows strong spatial agreement ( $$\varvec{\rho }$$ = 0.82). In the Murray-Darling Basin, CMB validation confirms this performance ( $$\varvec{\rho }$$ = 0.83 and a standard deviation, STD, of 32.1 mm/year). The underlying GWS, validated against 259 boreholes in the basin, correlates at 0.47 with an STD of 33.9 mm, within the bootstrap uncertainty limit of 38.2 mm. Results should be interpreted at GRACE’s effective resolution ( $$\sim $$ 300 km), and grid-cell estimates in data-sparse or low signal-to-noise ratio areas should be used with caution.

title: A Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD)-enhanced Bayesian physics-informed neural network for uncertainty propagation in groundwater transport modeling
How does rewetting propagate through restored peatlands? An integrated surface–subsurface modelling analysis of water–table dynamics
abstract: Abstract Peatland restoration, through drainage suppression, is widely implemented to recover hydrological and ecological functions; however, the groundwater system responses governing rewetting efficiency remain insufficiently quantified across spatiotemporal scales. Here, a boreal fen is used as a process-representative system to resolve how restoration interventions, including ditch infilling and damming, reorganise catchment-scale water-table dynamics, drawing on calibrated, fully integrated three-dimensional physics-based modelling (HydroGeoSphere). Simulated restoration elevated domain-scale median water table by ~ 23 cm, with comparable gains (~ 22 cm) in nominally undisturbed areas, revealing that drainage legacy extends well beyond visibly ditched zones. Variogram analysis confirmed a shift from fragmented, drainage-controlled conditions to hydraulically connected systems with increased spatial correlation lengths. Water-table recovery propagated according to distinct hydrogeologic response regimes depending on restoration structure and subsurface properties. Low-permeability peat infillings generated strong localised responses with rapid exponential attenuation of water-table recovery (~ 70% decline within ~ 40 m), whereas dams produced broader, plateau-like responses extending up to ~ 100 m. Geomorphic setting further modulated recovery, with peat thickness and proximity to peat–mineral margins acting as primary controls through a threshold-like response regime. Seasonal hydroclimatic forcing modulated recovery, with wet-season response nearly doubling water-table rise relative to dry subarctic winters. These results demonstrate that drainage suppression reorganises peatland groundwater systems by enhancing lateral connectivity and controlling how hydraulic responses propagate across space. While the absolute magnitudes are site-specific, the identified controls and response patterns provide a mechanistic, transferable basis for guiding restoration in comparable boreal fens.

title: Groundwater storage in Quaternary deposits and bedrock buffers the discharge response of a small alpine catchment to climate change
abstract: Abstract Alpine areas play a major role in the water supply of downstream valleys by releasing water during dry periods. Groundwater storage could significantly influence how changing climatic conditions affect the discharge regime. However, these processes are still not well understood in alpine areas. Studies on how climate change impacts water resources in alpine areas rarely consider the influence of geology explicitly. An integrated surface–subsurface hydrologic model (HydroGeoSphere) was used to highlight the effect of groundwater in buffering future summer low flows and to give new insights into the role of geology in controlling discharge. The spatially explicit model allows the quantification of groundwater storage and its variation in different geological formations of an alpine catchment, under current and future conditions. The results suggest that, under future extreme climate change conditions, the average catchment groundwater storage in Quaternary deposits increases in winter and decreases in summer; the annual mean groundwater storage for the entire catchment decreases due to the decrease in mean annual groundwater recharge; and the total catchment discharge decreases and low-flow period shifts from winter to late summer by the end of this century. Future summer low flows will remain higher than the current winter low flows but will approach them closely after very dry summers. Proportionally, the decrease in groundwater storage will be less severe than the decrease in discharge. Finally, a sensitivity analysis illustrates that both Quaternary deposits (especially moraine and talus units) and bedrock play an important role in supporting discharge during low-flow periods.

title: Hydrogeochemical dynamics of a potential talik aquifer beneath the Kuuguluk River, Salluit, Nunavik (Québec, Canada)
abstract: Abstract Guaranteeing year-round access to safe, sustainable drinking water is a major challenge for many northern communities in Canada. This study offers the first hydrochemical and isotopic analysis of the Kuuguluk River and its river talik, in Salluit, Nunavik (Québec, Canada), based on water samples collected during a field campaign in October 2024. Major ion analyses showed a predominantly Ca–HCO 3 composition, with generally low mineral saturation indices in surface and shallow groundwater, suggesting, in conjunction with high tritium levels, recent meteoric recharge with minimal geochemical evolution. Deeper groundwater showed higher solute concentrations, enhanced sediment–water interactions, and slightly lower tritium levels, consistent with recent recharge, but longer residence time. Although tritium concentrations support the dominance of modern recharge, radiocarbon-depleted signatures of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon, particularly in deeper groundwater, suggest interaction with aged organic matter, potentially from degrading permafrost. Dissolved radon measurements qualitatively suggest increased downstream groundwater contributions, supporting numerical model predictions regarding hydraulic connectivity between the river talik and the river in this continuous permafrost environment. The findings emphasize the significance of groundwater in river talik as a potentially perennial drinking water resource in this area, an important finding that may be applicable to other continuous permafrost environments. Ongoing multidisciplinary monitoring (hydraulic head and temperature) and future modelling will be essential for ensuring the long-term viability of the Kuuguluk River talik aquifer as a potential municipal drinking water source for the community of Salluit.

title: Hydrogeological conceptual model for the Guarani Aquifer System outcrop area in Brazil: Insights from stable isotopes and rare earth elements
abstract: Abstract This study refines the hydrogeological conceptual model of the Guarani Aquifer System (GAS) outcrop area in São Paulo state in Brazil and highlights its complexity, particularly the coexistence of semi-confined and unconfined aquifers. Diabase sills act as aquitards, separating a Na⁺-HCO₃⁻ type deep groundwater from shallower Na⁺-Cl⁻-NO₃⁻ and mixed-HCO₃⁻/Cl⁻-NO₃⁻ type groundwater. Stable isotopes suggest that deep GAS groundwater was recharged under climatic conditions distinct from present-day conditions, whereas springs and surface waters reflect modern meteoric recharge. The study integrated major ion geochemistry, stable isotopes (δ 2 H and δ 18 O), and rare earth elements and yttrium (REY) concentrations of water samples collected from springs, surface waters, and shallow and deep aquifers. REY data revealed hydrogeochemical facies not previously detected with conventional hydrogeochemical tools, underscoring the potential of REY as tracers for aquifer connectivity. The results emphasize the need for a discussion about groundwater management, as the semi-confined aquifer is currently being tapped by water-supply wells in the GAS outcrop area, which is not accounted for in previous conceptual models.

title: Contrasting responses of unconfined and confined aquifers to an extreme flood event in the southeastern Caspian Sea Plain, Iran
Preventing a groundwater divide: Ensuring quality hydrogeology education for all in the age of online coursework following the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract The COVID-19 pandemic forced an almost overnight rethink of traditional hydrogeology education, elevating online delivery as the primary means of teaching hydrogeology during 2020–2021. This change has had far-reaching effects, some of which persist in the form of greater reliance on online teaching formats in many universities. This paper describes the experience of delivering hydrogeology coursework in a city affected by the longest COVID lockdown in the world. Key lessons for hydrogeology education are examined.
